lessons.title: Characteristics of Living Things
lessons.objective: Separate living from non-living things using the seven life processes, and name the process a question describes.

content.heading: Characteristics of living things
paragraphs: A car moves, a crystal grows and a flame uses oxygen, yet none of them is alive. Biology separates living from non-living things by a set of processes that must all be present, not by any single sign.

content.heading: Seven processes that define life
paragraphs: A parked car can move, a crystal can grow and a flame can use up fuel. Each mimics one sign of life, which is why one sign cannot decide the question. Living things carry out seven processes, and movement includes the whole body and the movement of substances inside it, and respiration releases energy from food.
Nutrition obtains and uses food. Excretion removes metabolic waste. Growth is a permanent increase in size or cell number.

Reproduction produces new individuals. Sensitivity, also called irritability, is the response to stimuli such as light, heat or touch. Only a living thing performs all seven, and a virus is a borderline case: it reproduces only inside a host cell and has no metabolism of its own.
bullets: All seven processes must be present; one alone proves nothing.
Movement includes internal transport, not only locomotion.
Growth in living things comes from cell division, not external addition.
content.takeaway: Life is the whole set of processes, never a single sign.

check.question: A crystal increases in size. Which characteristic does it imitate?
check.why: It looks like growth, but a crystal adds material on its outside; living growth is internal.

visual.caption: The same outward sign can have a different cause.

rows.right: Moved only by an outside force

content.heading: Nutrition and respiration
paragraphs: A green plant in sunlight and a boy eating rice both need energy, but they obtain it in opposite ways. Nutrition is how an organism obtains and uses food. Autotrophs, such as green plants, make their own food by photosynthesis, and heterotrophs, such as humans, fungi and most bacteria, depend on ready-made food, and holozoic feeders ingest solid food, saprophytes absorb dissolved food from dead matter, and parasites feed on a living host.

Respiration is the breakdown of food to release energy. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic respiration works without oxygen and releases less energy; in yeast it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Breathing is only the exchange of gases, not respiration itself.
bullets: An autotroph makes food; a heterotroph takes it ready-made.
Respiration releases energy; breathing only moves gases.
Anaerobic respiration yields less energy than aerobic respiration.
content.takeaway: Nutrition supplies the fuel; respiration releases its energy.

check.question: Which process releases energy from food inside a cell?
check.why: Respiration is the controlled breakdown of food that releases energy; breathing only exchanges gases.

content.heading: Excretion, reproduction and response
paragraphs: A student confuses sweating with passing faeces, and movement with responding to light. The exam tests exactly these boundaries.

Excretion removes waste made by metabolism, such as carbon dioxide, urea and excess salts. Egestion removes undigested food from the gut; it is not excretion because the material never entered the body's cells. Sweating is excretion of water and salts, while defecation is egestion.

Reproduction is the production of offspring. It is not needed for the survival of the individual, only for the species. Sensitivity, or irritability, is the response to a stimulus: a shoot bends towards light, a cockroach runs from a torch, and the pupil narrows in bright light.
bullets: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes undigested food.
Reproduction ensures the species, not the individual.
Sensitivity is a response to a stimulus.
content.takeaway: Name the process by its product, not by the organ that releases it.

check.question: Removal of undigested food from the alimentary canal is called
check.why: The food never entered the cells, so its removal is egestion, not excretion.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names an action, match it to the process that defines it: bending to light is sensitivity, shedding metabolic waste is excretion, and passing undigested food is egestion.

content.problem: A student argues that a burning candle is alive because it gives out heat and uses oxygen. Test the claim using the characteristics of living things.

steps.reason: Heat and oxygen use look like respiration, but respiration must release energy from food inside cells.
steps.result: The candle has no nutrition and no cells, so it cannot respire.
steps.predictPrompt: Which characteristic should you test first?

steps.reason: A candle does not grow from within and produces no metabolic waste.
steps.result: Growth and excretion are absent.

steps.reason: It cannot reproduce and does not respond to stimuli.
steps.result: Only one apparent sign remains.

steps.reason: Life requires the full set of processes, not one imitation.
steps.result: The candle is non-living.

content.heading: Go deeper: Growth from within, not adding on
paragraphs: A crystal grows by adding identical units onto its outside. Living growth works the opposite way: existing cells divide and make more cells inside the body. A seedling therefore becomes heavier because it makes new tissue, not because soil particles glue onto it.

Growth is a permanent increase in dry mass or cell number. A balloon swells when it is blown up and shrinks when it is emptied, so the change is temporary and no new material is made. A germinating bean, by contrast, builds new roots and leaves that remain after it is dried.

Nitrogen, phosphorus and other minerals make the building of new cells possible. Without them, a plant may grow tall for a short while and then stop, which is why nitrogen shortage produces yellow, stunted plants. This link between growth and cell division is why nutrition and growth must be considered together.
Growth can be checked by dry mass: weigh a plant, dry it and weigh again to remove water. A flame or a crystal fails that test because it does not add new cells.
bullets: Living growth is internal: cells divide to make more cells
Crystal growth is external addition; balloon swelling is temporary
Growth is measured as a permanent increase in dry mass

content.heading: Go deeper: Movement, locomotion and transport
paragraphs: Movement means any change of position of the whole body or its parts. A chameleon extending its tongue, a seedling turning toward light and a Paramecium beating its cilia all show movement. Locomotion is narrower: it is movement of the whole organism from one place to another.

Internal transport is also movement, although no part of the body changes place visibly. Blood moving through vessels, cytoplasm streaming in a leaf cell and sap rising through xylem are all movements of substances inside the organism. A plant can therefore exhibit movement without ever walking.

Tropisms expand the idea further. A shoot bending toward light is a growth movement, not a voluntary response. It shows sensitivity turning into movement, so the two characteristics often occur together in plants.
Seed dispersal is movement without locomotion by the parent. A pod bursting and throwing seeds, or wind carrying a winged fruit, moves the offspring while the parent plant stays rooted.
A dandelion clock shows the same principle in a plant: the fruit is built to be carried away while the parent stays fixed. Movement can therefore be shown by the offspring rather than by the adult.
bullets: Movement includes body parts and internal transport
Locomotion moves the whole organism from place to place
Tropisms are growth movements that show sensitivity

content.heading: Go deeper: Nutrition, respiration and why a virus is not alive
paragraphs: Autotrophs make their own organic food by photosynthesis, using light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Heterotrophs take ready-made food from other organisms and must digest it into usable substances.

Respiration is the controlled breakdown of that food inside cells. In aerobic respiration, oxygen accepts electrons and most energy is released as ATP. In anaerobic respiration, the breakdown is incomplete and little energy is released.

A virus fails the test because it has no cell, no membrane and no metabolism of its own. It can only multiply by taking over a host cell. Because it cannot feed, respire, grow or respond by itself, it is placed outside the living world rather than inside it.
Energy from respiration is used for active transport, muscle contraction and protein synthesis. That is why a starved organism cannot maintain its body temperature or repair wounds.

The oxygen used in aerobic respiration comes from the air or water around the cell. When oxygen is scarce, the cell falls back on anaerobic respiration and releases far less energy for the same amount of food.
bullets: Autotrophs build food; heterotrophs digest ready-made food
Aerobic respiration breaks glucose fully; anaerobic respiration does not
A virus has no cell or metabolism, so it is not living

content.question: A potted plant near a window bends its stem towards the light. Name the characteristic shown and explain why this is not locomotion.
hints: The plant is responding to a directional stimulus.
Locomotion is the movement of the whole organism from place to place.
The response is sensitivity, shown as positive phototropism.

lessons.title: Cell Structure and Function
lessons.objective: Identify the shared and distinguishing structures of plant and animal cells, and state the function of each organelle.

content.heading: Cell structure and function
paragraphs: Every living thing is built from cells, but plant and animal cells are not identical. Recognising the shared structures and the few differences is enough to answer most cell questions.

content.heading: What every cell shares
paragraphs: A cheek scraping and an onion epidermis look different under the microscope, yet both show the same basic machinery. The cell membrane is a thin, selectively permeable layer that controls what enters and leaves. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like medium where reactions occur and organelles sit, and the nucleus contains chromosomes made of DNA and controls the cell's activities.
Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration, releasing energy as ATP. Ribosomes build proteins from amino acids.
These five structures are enough to identify a cell as a cell. The membrane surrounds the cell, while the organelles work inside it.
bullets: The membrane controls exchange; the cytoplasm hosts reactions.
The nucleus holds DNA and controls activity.
Mitochondria release energy; ribosomes make protein.
content.takeaway: Membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are the shared kit.

check.question: Which organelle controls the cell's activities?
check.why: The nucleus contains the chromosomes that direct the cell.

content.heading: Plant and animal differences
paragraphs: A leaf cell and a liver cell both need energy, but only one of them can make its own food.

Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, giving shape and support. They also contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and a large permanent sap vacuole that stores water and salts and keeps the cell turgid.

Animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts. They usually have small, temporary vacuoles, and centrioles that help in cell division. Both cell types have a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
bullets: Plant-only: cellulose wall, chloroplasts, large sap vacuole.
Animal-only: centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.
Both share the membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
content.takeaway: The wall and chloroplasts are the plant give-aways.

check.question: Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
check.why: A cellulose cell wall surrounds plant cells; the membrane and organelles are shared.

visual.caption: Two shared kits, four separating features.

content.heading: Organelles that transport and package
paragraphs: A pancreas cell releases digestive enzymes. The protein must be built, moved, packaged and sent out without leaking into the cytoplasm.

Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum make proteins. The rough ER transports them; the smooth ER makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and secretes proteins, and lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and foreign material.

Vacuoles store water, salts, pigments and waste. The path of a secreted protein is ribosome, rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, membrane. A cell that secretes a lot, such as a pancreas cell, has many ribosomes and a large Golgi.
bullets: Rough ER makes and moves protein; smooth ER makes lipid.
The Golgi packages and secretes; lysosomes digest.
Secretory cells have many ribosomes and a large Golgi.
content.takeaway: Follow the protein: ribosome, ER, Golgi, vesicle, membrane.

check.question: Which organelle packages proteins for secretion?
check.why: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins into vesicles for release.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Never say the cell wall controls what enters. The wall is fully permeable and gives support; the cell membrane is the selectively permeable barrier that decides what enters and leaves.

content.problem: A microscope slide shows a cell with a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Name the cell type and state two structures it lacks that a liver cell would have.

steps.reason: A cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole are plant features.
steps.result: The cell is a plant cell.
steps.predictPrompt: Which features are shared by both cell types?

steps.reason: Animal cells have centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.
steps.result: These are the two structures to name.

steps.reason: Both cell types still have a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes.
steps.result: Do not list shared structures as differences.

steps.reason: Name only the structures the plant cell lacks.
steps.result: Centrioles and small temporary vacuoles.

content.heading: Go deeper: The membrane as a customs post
paragraphs: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. The lipid parts form a barrier that water and oxygen can cross but most ions cannot. Transport proteins act as gates, letting specific substances through without breaking the barrier down.

A plant cell wall is different from the membrane. It is made of cellulose and is fully permeable, so it gives support but controls nothing. A true customs post is the membrane, because it decides what enters and leaves on the basis of size and electrical charge.

Selective permeability is why osmosis and diffusion behave differently across a membrane. Water moves to equalise its own concentration, while ions are actively transported even against a gradient. The same membrane can therefore be passive for water and active for ions.
The cell wall still matters because it holds the cell shape and gives plant tissue its rigidity. Without it, a turgid cell would burst when water enters in a hypotonic solution.
bullets: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with transport proteins
The cellulose wall is fully permeable; the membrane is selective
Water crosses passively; ions may need active transport

content.heading: Go deeper: Vacuole, Golgi body and lysosomes
paragraphs: In a plant cell, the central vacuole takes up most of the cell volume. It stores water, salts, pigments and waste, and it keeps the cell turgid. When water leaves the vacuole, the cell becomes flaccid.

The Golgi body receives proteins in vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum. It modifies them, sorts them into new vesicles and sends them to the membrane or to storage vacuoles. A gland cell therefore has many Golgi bodies because it secretes a large volume of protein.

Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that can break down worn-out organelles, engulfed microbes and damaged cell parts. They are membrane-bound, so the enzymes stay inside and do not digest the rest of the cell.
The vacuole also stores mineral salts that the cell can release when they are needed. That storage makes a plant cell a small mineral bank, which is why turgid leaves stay crisp.

Chloroplasts are another membrane-bound organelle that some cells carry. They contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis, and their number changes with the light a leaf receives over time.
bullets: The plant vacuole stores contents and maintains turgidity
The Golgi body modifies, sorts and packages proteins
Lysosomes digest worn-out parts and incoming microbes

content.heading: Go deeper: How a cell makes and sends out proteins
paragraphs: A protein begins on a ribosome attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Short chains are folded there, while the membrane of the reticulum keeps them separate from the cytoplasm. The rough ER then passes them on in vesicles while they still have their folding structure.

The Golgi body adds final modifications, attaches labels that mark destination and splits the products for shipment. The vesicles that leave it move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and release their contents outside the cell.

This secretory path explains cell specialisation. Pancreas cells have many ribosomes and Golgi bodies because they secrete enzymes. Plant cells that make oil have different organelles in greater number, matched to the product they export.
Errors in this path can cause disease, because a misfolded protein may jam the channel or be sent to the wrong place. Cells therefore check and destroy badly folded proteins inside lysosomes.
The endoplasmic reticulum also makes lipids in its smooth regions. A cell that exports fats therefore has more smooth reticulum than a cell that mainly exports proteins.
bullets: Ribosomes build proteins on the rough endoplasmic reticulum
The Golgi body modifies and labels them for shipment
Vesicles fuse with the membrane to release the product

content.question: A cell contains many mitochondria and a large Golgi apparatus. Suggest one job the cell might do and explain why it needs both features.
hints: Many mitochondria mean the cell uses a lot of energy.
A large Golgi means the cell secretes a lot of protein.
A muscle cell or a gland cell fits both clues.

lessons.title: Levels of Organisation
lessons.objective: Trace the sequence from cell to tissue, organ, system and organism, and place a named structure at the correct level.

content.heading: Levels of organisation
paragraphs: Life is built in steps: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and systems form the organism. Each step adds a new function, not just more cells.

content.heading: Cell and tissue
paragraphs: A single cell can live alone, but a human body needs groups of cells that do the same job.

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit. A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin, performing the same function. Epithelial tissue covers and protects surfaces; muscle tissue contracts; nervous tissue conducts impulses; connective tissue supports and binds.

Plants have tissues too: the epidermis covers the leaf, palisade mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, xylem transports water and phloem transports food. Hydra is often used to show the tissue level because its body wall is built mainly from two layers of tissue.
bullets: Cell: the basic unit of structure and function.
Tissue: similar cells with a shared job.
Examples: epithelium, muscle, nerve, xylem and phloem.
content.takeaway: A tissue is a team of similar cells with one job.

check.question: A group of similar cells performing the same function is a
check.why: Similar cells with a common function form a tissue.

content.heading: Organs and systems
paragraphs: A stomach is not just a bag of cells: it has muscle, glands and nerves, and it works with the mouth and intestines.

An organ is made of two or more tissues working together for a specific function. The leaf, root, heart, stomach, eye and kidney are organs. The onion bulb is a modified shoot and is used as the syllabus example of an organ.

A system is a group of organs working together on a major life process. The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food; the excretory system removes waste; the reproductive system produces offspring. A mammal also has circulatory, respiratory, nervous and skeletal systems.
bullets: Organ: two or more tissues with a specific job.
System: organs cooperating on a major process.
The leaf and the onion bulb are organs, not tissues.
content.takeaway: An organ combines tissues; a system combines organs.

check.question: Which of these is an organ?
check.why: A leaf contains epidermis, mesophyll and vascular tissues, so it is an organ.

content.heading: The full sequence
paragraphs: A euglena is one cell that swims, feeds and responds; a human is trillions of cells arranged into systems. Both are organisms.

The sequence is cell, tissue, organ, system, organism. In a unicellular organism such as Euglena, Paramecium or Chlamydomonas, one cell performs all life processes, so the cell and the organism are the same level. In multicellular organisms the levels are distinct.

Not every organism has every level. A hydra has tissues but no true organs or systems; a flowering plant has organs but no organ systems in the animal sense. The sequence is a ladder of increasing complexity, not a rule that every rung must appear.
bullets: Cell, tissue, organ, system, organism.
Unicellular organisms live at the cell level.
Hydra stops at tissues; plants have organs but no animal-style systems.
content.takeaway: Each level adds a function the level below cannot perform alone.

check.question: Which organism is unicellular?
check.why: Chlamydomonas is a single-celled green alga; the others are multicellular.

visual.caption: Each level is built from the one before it.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: To place a named structure, ask what it is made of. A leaf is made of tissues, so it is an organ; a stomach works with other organs, so it belongs to a system.

content.problem: Arrange these from simplest to most complex: stomach, epithelial cell, digestive system, epithelial tissue, human. Name each level.

steps.reason: The epithelial cell is the basic unit.
steps.result: 1. Cell.
steps.predictPrompt: Which structure is made of similar cells?

steps.reason: Epithelial cells form epithelial tissue.
steps.result: 2. Tissue.

steps.reason: The stomach contains epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue.
steps.result: 3. Organ.

steps.reason: The stomach works with the mouth, liver and intestines.
steps.result: 4. System.

steps.reason: The human is the complete living thing.
steps.result: 5. Organism.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cells, tissues and organs
paragraphs: A cell is the smallest unit of life. Cells that look alike and do the same job group together as a tissue. Muscle tissue contracts, nerve tissue carries impulses and xylem tissue conducts water in plants.

An organ is a structure made of two or more tissues working together. A leaf contains epidermis, mesophyll and vascular tissues, so it is an organ. A heart contains muscle, nerve and connective tissues, so it is also an organ.

The tissue level explains why a microscope slide can show muscle fibres but not a whole heart. The structures are real at different scales, and each scale has its own vocabulary in examination questions.
A tissue can be studied in isolation because its cells share a structure. A single muscle cell can contract, but a whole muscle needs connective tissue to transmit the pull to a tendon.
Leaves show the same lesson in plants. A leaf contains epidermis, palisade and spongy tissues, and its veins carry xylem and phloem, so it is an organ made from several tissues.
bullets: Cells of similar structure and function form a tissue
An organ contains two or more tissues
Muscle, nerve and xylem are common tissues

content.heading: Go deeper: Systems and organisms
paragraphs: A system is a group of organs that work together to carry out a major function. The heart, blood vessels and blood together form the circulatory system. The stomach, intestines, liver and pancreas form the digestive system.

Flowering plants do not have organ systems in the animal sense. Their roots, stems and leaves are organs, but they are not grouped into a named system such as a circulatory system. Transport in plants is organised through vascular tissue instead.

The organism level is the whole living individual. In a unicellular organism such as Chlamydomonas, the cell and the organism are the same level. In a multicellular animal they are separated by tissues, organs and systems.

A circulatory system needs organs that make blood as well as vessels to carry it, which is why bone marrow is linked to the heart and vessels in one system. The liver and pancreas belong to digestion because they supply enzymes and bile.
Excretion shows how systems cooperate. The heart pumps blood to the kidneys, the kidneys filter it and the bladder stores the product, so three systems meet in one process, and the organism survives.
bullets: A system is organs working together for a major function
Plants have organs but no named organ systems
In a unicellular organism the cell is the organism

content.heading: Go deeper: The ladder traps examiners set
paragraphs: Examiners often place an unfamiliar structure in the ladder and ask its level. A hydra has tissues but no true organs, so it stops at the tissue level. A flowering plant has organs but is still not a system in the animal sense.

The sequence must therefore be read from the bottom up. A cell becomes a tissue, a tissue becomes an organ in combination, organs become a system and systems form an organism. Any missing rung changes the answer.

When two options look similar, look for the level that is definitely present. A leaf is an organ because it contains tissues; it is not a system because it does not join with other organs under one name.
The word "tissue" is the most misused rung. Blood is a tissue even though its cells are separated by fluid, and it is not an organ. A heart is never called a tissue.

Cell theory states that all living things are made of cells and that all cells come from pre-existing cells. The ladder therefore starts with the cell, because a tissue cannot exist without its cells.
bullets: Hydra has tissues but no true organs
A leaf is an organ, not a system
Read the ladder from cell to organism in order

content.question: A leaf is called an organ. Name two tissues it contains and explain why it is not a system.
hints: The leaf has an epidermis and palisade mesophyll.
It also has xylem and phloem in its veins.
A system is a group of organs, not a group of tissues.

lessons.title: The Five Kingdoms
lessons.objective: Place an organism in one of the five kingdoms, and explain the trend from a prokaryotic cell to specialised tissues and organs.

content.heading: The five kingdoms
paragraphs: A bacterium, a mushroom and a mango tree are all alive, but they are built on different plans. Biology sorts that variety into five kingdoms, then asks what each kingdom added to the basic unit of life: the cell.

content.heading: The first divide: nucleus or no nucleus
paragraphs: Every organism is made of cells, but not every cell is built the same way. A prokaryotic cell has no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, usually as a single circular chromosome.
Bacteria and blue-green algae are prokaryotes, and they form the kingdom Monera.

All the other kingdoms are eukaryotic. Their cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and compartments such as mitochondria, chloroplasts and a Golgi body. The nucleus is the first feature to check because it separates Monera from everything else.
bullets: Prokaryote: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryote: a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Monera is the only prokaryotic kingdom.
content.takeaway: The first question in classification is whether the cell has a nucleus.

check.question: A cell has free circular DNA but no nuclear membrane. Which kingdom does it belong to?
check.why: Free circular DNA and no nucleus are prokaryotic features, which define Monera.

visual.caption: The nucleus is the first feature that separates the kingdoms.

content.heading: The five kingdoms at a glance
paragraphs: Monera contains bacteria and blue-green algae. Protista contains mainly single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. Fungi contains mushroom, Rhizopus and yeast, and Plantae contains Spirogyra, mosses, ferns, cycads, maize and water leaf, and Animalia contains Hydra, earthworms, insects, fish, frogs, birds and mammals.
Two further features separate them. Plants make their own food by photosynthesis and have cellulose cell walls. Fungi absorb ready-made food and have chitin cell walls.
Animals ingest food and have no cell wall. Protists may be plant-like or animal-like, but they are not divided into tissues.
bullets: Monera: prokaryotic and mostly single-celled.
Protista: eukaryotic and mostly single-celled.
Fungi, Plantae and Animalia: eukaryotic and mostly multicellular.
content.takeaway: Name the kingdom from the cell plan and the way it feeds.

check.question: Which kingdom contains organisms with chitin cell walls and no chlorophyll?
check.why: Chitin walls and absorption of ready-made food are fungal features.

content.heading: What increasing complexity means
paragraphs: Complexity is not a single ladder, but the kingdoms do show a trend. A moneran is a prokaryotic cell with no nucleus. Protista is a single cell with a nucleus and organelles, and most fungi and plants build bodies from many cells, and plants add tissues and organs, and animals add specialised tissues, organs and organ systems.
The trend is about division of labour. A Paramecium carries out all life processes in one cell. A maize plant has roots for absorption, leaves for photosynthesis and vascular tissue for transport.

A mammal adds a heart, lungs, kidneys and a nervous system, each doing one job well. This five-kingdom scheme is the traditional school classification; modern biology often uses six kingdoms or three domains, but JAMB still examines the five-kingdom system.
bullets: More complexity means more cell types and more division of labour.
A single cell must carry out every life process itself.
Complexity is not the same thing as evolutionary superiority.
content.takeaway: Complexity is the number of specialised parts working together.

check.question: Which change most clearly shows increasing structural complexity?
options: Cells specialise into tissues and organs
check.why: Specialised tissues and organs are the structural step beyond a single cell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not classify by colour or habitat. Euglena is green and swims, but it is a protist. Blue-green algae are photosynthetic, but they are bacteria. A mushroom is neither a plant nor an animal.

content.problem: A specimen is single-celled, green, has a nucleus and swims with a flagellum. A student calls it a plant. Correct the classification.

steps.reason: A true nucleus rules out Monera, whose cells have free DNA.
steps.result: The specimen is eukaryotic.
steps.predictPrompt: Which kingdom can you already rule out?

steps.reason: It is one cell, with no tissues or organs.
steps.result: It cannot be Plantae, which is multicellular with tissues.

steps.reason: Chloroplasts allow photosynthesis, but the flagellum and eyespot are protist features.
steps.result: It fits Euglena in Protista.

steps.reason: Kingdom is decided by cell plan and body plan, not colour.
steps.result: The specimen is a protist, not a plant.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why Monera had to be split
paragraphs: The old kingdom Monera contained every organism without a true nucleus. Modern research shows that bacteria themselves are divided into two distinct groups, Archaea and Bacteria. They differ in the chemistry of their membranes and in how they transcribe genes.

The classification of life into three domains — Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya — follows that split. The domain level sits above the kingdom, so the older five-kingdom list does not show the full modern picture.

For examinations, Monera still appears because it is the term the syllabus uses. A locality answer about a prokaryote should therefore name Monera while remembering that modern biology divides prokaryotes more finely.
Archaea include some of the most extreme organisms on Earth, living in hot springs and salty lakes. They look like bacteria under a microscope but differ from them in cell chemistry.

Archaean membranes use different lipids from bacterial membranes, which is one reason they survive in boiling springs. The difference is invisible under a light microscope but decisive in modern classification.
bullets: Monera contained all prokaryotes, including Archaea and Bacteria
Modern life is divided into three domains
JAMB still examines the legacy five-kingdom names

content.heading: Go deeper: Protista as a convenience, and Fungi versus Plantae
paragraphs: Protista is a kingdom of convenience rather than a single evolutionary line. It holds eukaryotic organisms that are mostly single-celled and do not fit comfortably into the other four kingdoms. Algae, Amoeba and Paramecium therefore share a page without sharing a close ancestor.

Fungi and Plantae are separated by nutrition and cell walls. Fungi absorb ready-made food and have chitin walls, while plants make food by photosynthesis and have cellulose walls. A mushroom and a mango are both multicellular, but they belong to different branches of life.

The city-of-life lesson is that similar size or habitat does not guarantee the same kingdom. Classification starts with the cell, and for the multicellular kingdoms it then uses walls and feeding mode.

Some protists were once placed with plants because they photosynthesise. They are now placed with protists because they lack true tissues and often have flagella or eyespots. Colour alone therefore misleads.
Yeast shows that fungi can be unicellular as well as multicellular. It is still a fungus because it has a chitin wall and absorbs food, even though it lives as a single cell.
bullets: Protista is a grouping of convenience, not one lineage
Fungi: chitin walls and absorptive feeding
Plantae: cellulose walls and photosynthesis

content.heading: Go deeper: Reading a kingdom key
paragraphs: A kingdom key should be read in a fixed order. First decide whether the cell has a true nucleus, which separates Monera from everything else. Then look at the number of cells and whether tissues are present.

For a multicellular organism, the cell wall and the feeding mode are the next fork. A cellulose wall and photosynthesis mean Plantae, a chitin wall and absorption mean Fungi, and no wall with ingestion means Animalia.
Keeping that order prevents the usual traps. A green colour alone does not make a plant, and a stationary habit alone does not make a fungus. The cell plan and the feeding mode decide.
A wall drawn on a diagram is a strong clue only when the feeding mode matches. A chitin wall with absorption means fungi, while a cellulose wall with photosynthesis means plants.
Absence of a wall is also a clue when it is combined with ingestion. An animal cell has no wall and takes in solid food, which is why it cannot be placed with plants or fungi.
bullets: First split Monera by the absence of a nucleus
Then split the multicellular kingdoms by wall and feeding
Colour and habitat alone never decide the kingdom

content.question: A unicellular organism has no nucleus, a cell wall and a whip-like flagellum. Name its kingdom and explain why it cannot be a protist.
hints: Look for a nuclear membrane.
Protista is eukaryotic, so its cells have a true nucleus.
Monera is prokaryotic: free DNA and no membrane-bound organelles.

lessons.title: Monera and Protista
lessons.objective: Distinguish bacteria and blue-green algae from Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena using the nucleus, nutrition and movement.

content.heading: Two kingdoms of small organisms
paragraphs: A drop of pond water can hold bacteria, blue-green algae, Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. They are all microscopic, but they belong to two different kingdoms. The difference is the nucleus, and it decides how each cell feeds, moves and reproduces.

content.heading: Monera: cells without a nucleus
paragraphs: Bacteria are the best-known monerans. Each is a single prokaryotic cell with a cell wall, a cell membrane and free circular DNA. Many have a capsule, and some have flagella for movement.
They reproduce by binary fission, so one cell splits into two identical cells. Under harsh conditions, some form resistant endospores.

Blue-green algae, now called cyanobacteria, are also Monera. They contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise, but the pigment is not enclosed in a chloroplast. Some, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, fix nitrogen in rice fields, and bacteria decompose dead matter, cause disease, ferment food and supply antibiotics; cyanobacteria add nitrogen to the soil.
bullets: Binary fission, not mitosis, is the usual reproduction.
Cyanobacteria photosynthesise without chloroplasts.
Some bacteria fix nitrogen or form endospores.
content.takeaway: Monera is prokaryotic: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.

check.question: Why are blue-green algae placed in Monera and not in Plantae?
options: They are prokaryotic and have no chloroplasts
check.why: They photosynthesise, but their cells lack a nucleus and chloroplasts, so they are prokaryotes.

visual.caption: Both are microscopic, but only one has a nucleus.

content.heading: Protista: one cell with a nucleus
paragraphs: Protista are eukaryotes that are mostly single-celled. Amoeba moves and feeds with pseudopodia, flowing around food and engulfing it by phagocytosis. Paramecium is covered with cilia that beat in waves, and an oral groove sweeps food into a food vacuole, and contractile vacuoles pump out excess water.

Euglena has a flagellum, a light-sensitive eyespot and chloroplasts. It photosynthesises in light but can absorb food in the dark, so it is mixotrophic. Protists reproduce mainly by binary fission, and Paramecium can exchange genetic material by conjugation.
Contractile vacuoles also keep the cell from bursting in fresh water.
bullets: Amoeba: pseudopodia and phagocytosis.
Paramecium: cilia, oral groove and contractile vacuoles.
Euglena: flagellum, eyespot and chloroplasts.
content.takeaway: Protists are eukaryotic cells that live as a whole organism.

check.question: Which structure helps Paramecium move?
check.why: Paramecium is covered with cilia that beat in coordinated waves.

content.heading: Telling the two kingdoms apart
paragraphs: Start with the nucleus. If there is no nuclear membrane, the organism is Monera. If there is a true nucleus, it is eukaryotic, and then look at the organelles and the body, and a protist has membrane-bound organelles and is usually a single cell.

Nutrition and movement are secondary clues. Euglena is green, but it is a protist, not a plant, because it is unicellular and has no tissues. Blue-green algae are green and photosynthetic, but they are bacteria because they have no nucleus or chloroplasts.

Amoeba has no fixed shape, so a drawing of a round cell is not Amoeba. Monera and Protista are legacy groupings: modern taxonomy splits bacteria into domains and protists into several groups, but exams still use these kingdom names.
bullets: Nucleus first; colour and habitat second.
Green does not mean plant.
A single cell with a nucleus is a protist, not Monera.
content.takeaway: Classify by the nucleus, then by organelles and body plan.

check.question: An organism is single-celled, has a nucleus and chloroplasts, and swims with a flagellum. What is it?
check.why: It is eukaryotic and unicellular, so it is a protist; plants are multicellular with tissues.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A question may describe a green, motile cell and expect Euglena. Check the nucleus before you choose the kingdom, and check the organelles before you call it a plant.

content.problem: A pond sample contains two organisms. One has no nuclear membrane, a cell wall and a flagellum. The other has a nucleus, cilia and a contractile vacuole. Name the kingdom of each.

steps.operation: Test the first for a nucleus
steps.reason: No nuclear membrane means the DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
steps.result: The first organism is prokaryotic, so it belongs to Monera.
steps.predictPrompt: Which feature decides the kingdom before any other?

steps.operation: Test the second for a nucleus
steps.reason: A true nucleus makes it eukaryotic.
steps.result: The second organism is not Monera.

steps.reason: It is one cell with cilia and a contractile vacuole, which are protist features.
steps.result: The second organism is a protist, likely Paramecium.

steps.reason: A flagellum alone does not make an organism a protist; bacteria can have flagella too.
steps.result: The nucleus, not movement, separates the kingdoms.

content.heading: Go deeper: Bacteria in disease, food and drugs
paragraphs: Bacteria are useful and harmful in roughly equal measure. Legume bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, converting it into ammonia that plants can absorb. In the soil, decomposer bacteria break down dead matter and release mineral salts.

The same life style also makes bacteria dangerous. Pathogenic bacteria multiply in a host and release toxins, causing diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Fermentation by Lactobacillus turns milk into yoghurt and dough into bread by producing lactic acid and carbon dioxide.

Antibiotics are medicines made by slowing or killing competing bacteria. Penicillin was discovered because a mould suppressed the growth of nearby staphylococci. Bacteria and fungi therefore sit at the centre of both food production and medicine.

Bacteria survive in the stomach of a ruminant and in the gut of a termite, where they digest fibre that the host cannot break down. Without them, many animals would gain little energy from grasses and wood.
Pathogenic bacteria often attach to the gut wall with fimbriae before they multiply. The same attachment is used by harmless bacteria in the gut, so similar structures serve different owners.
bullets: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria enrich the soil around legumes
Fermentation by Lactobacillus makes yoghurt and bread rise
Antibiotics were inspired by microbial competition

content.heading: Go deeper: Movement and feeding in protists
paragraphs: Amoeba spreads pseudopodia, temporary foot-like extensions, and flows around food it cannot reach by cilia. Paramecium covers its surface with cilia and beats them in waves, sweeping water and food toward an oral groove. Euglena swims by a single flagellum and uses a light-sensitive eyespot.

Feeding follows the movement pattern. Amoeba engulfs, Paramecium traps and Euglena both photosynthesises and absorbs dissolved food. It is the combination of organelles, not the habitat, that identifies each protist.

Freshwater protists face an osmotic problem: water flows in because their cells are more concentrated than pond water. The contractile vacuole collects and expels that water. A marine protist, by contrast, has the opposite problem and needs to conserve water.
Euglena changes shape to squeeze through narrow spaces, which is why its body outline varies between drawings. Amoeba does the same when it spreads pseudopodia across a surface.
Paramecium beats its cilia in a wave that pushes the cell forward. The same beating also drives a current of water that brings food to the oral groove.
bullets: Amoeba: pseudopodia and engulfing; Paramecium: cilia and oral groove
Euglena: flagellum and eyespot, and it is mixotrophic
Contractile vacuoles remove excess water in fresh water

content.heading: Go deeper: Binary fission and why these names are legacy
paragraphs: Most bacteria and many protists reproduce by binary fission. The parent cell splits into two identical daughter cells. Under favourable conditions this is rapid, which is how a bacterial colony can appear overnight.

Binary fission is not mitosis. It lacks a spindle and the duplicated chromosomes are not pulled apart by fibres in the same way. Conjugation, in which Paramecium exchanges genetic material, is a separate process that increases variation without increasing cell number.

Monera and Protista persist as school names because they are convenient. Modern taxonomy splits Monera into domains and divides Protista into several lineages. An examiner may use the older names even though the modern picture is more detailed.
Because division is simple, bacteria can adapt quickly to antibiotics. A resistant mutant can become the whole population in a few generations, which is why misuse of antibiotics is so dangerous.

Protists that divide by binary fission can also form cysts under harsh conditions. The cyst wall protects the cell until water or food returns, just as a bacterial endospore protects an endospore-forming cell.
bullets: Binary fission splits one cell into two identical cells
Conjugation exchanges genetic material without cell division
Monera and Protista are legacy names kept for exams

content.question: A pond sample contains a green unicellular organism with a nucleus and a red eyespot. Name the organism and its kingdom, and explain why it is not a plant.
hints: The eyespot and flagellum point to a familiar protist.
A plant is multicellular and has tissues.
The organism is Euglena, in Protista.

lessons.title: Fungi
lessons.objective: Explain how fungi are built, how they feed and reproduce, and why they are neither plants nor animals.

content.heading: Fungi
paragraphs: A mushroom pushes through leaf litter after rain, and bread turns mouldy in a damp cupboard. Both are fungi, a kingdom that feeds by absorbing food rather than making it or swallowing it.

content.heading: The body of a fungus
paragraphs: A fungus is made of thread-like hyphae. A mass of hyphae is a mycelium, which spreads through soil, bread or dead wood. The cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose, and the cells store carbohydrate as glycogen, not starch, and Fungi have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise.
Some fungi are unicellular, such as yeast. Most are multicellular, such as Rhizopus and mushrooms. The visible mushroom is only the fruiting body.
Most of the organism is the mycelium hidden in the substrate. The fruiting body releases spores.
bullets: Hyphae make up the mycelium.
The cell wall is chitin and the storage carbohydrate is glycogen.
No chlorophyll means no photosynthesis.
content.takeaway: A fungus is a chitin-walled heterotroph built from hyphae.

check.question: A fungal cell wall is made mainly of
check.why: Fungi have chitin walls; plants have cellulose and bacteria have peptidoglycan.

visual.caption: A fungus looks plant-like but feeds like an animal.

content.heading: How fungi feed
paragraphs: Fungi are heterotrophs. Saprophytes, such as Rhizopus on bread and mushrooms on dead leaves, release enzymes onto the food and absorb the digested nutrients. Parasites feed on a living host and cause diseases such as ringworm and athlete's foot.
Mutualists live with another organism and both benefit. Lichens are fungi with algae, and mycorrhizae are fungi with plant roots.

This extracellular digestion is why mould softens bread and why a mushroom appears on rotting wood. The fungus digests the substrate outside its body, then absorbs the soluble products. No food is taken in as solid particles.
bullets: Saprophyte: dead matter digested outside the body.
Parasite: feeds on a living host.
Mutualist: both partners benefit.
content.takeaway: Fungi digest food outside the body, then absorb it.

check.question: Rhizopus growing on bread is best described as
check.why: It releases enzymes onto dead bread and absorbs the products.

content.heading: Reproduction and importance
paragraphs: Fungi reproduce by spores. Rhizopus forms sporangia on upright stalks. When they burst, spores scatter, germinate and grow into new mycelia, and a mushroom produces basidiospores on its gills, and yeast reproduces asexually by budding, and many fungi also have a sexual stage, which introduces variation.
Fungi are useful and harmful. Yeast ferments sugar in bread and brewing. Mushrooms are food.

Penicillium yields penicillin. Fungi decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients. They also spoil food, cause crop diseases such as rust and smut, and cause human infections, and some mushrooms are poisonous.
bullets: Spores are the main dispersal unit.
Yeast buds; Rhizopus uses sporangia.
Fungi decompose, ferment, produce antibiotics and cause disease.
content.takeaway: Fungi recycle matter, but they also spoil food and cause disease.

check.question: Which fungus is used to produce an antibiotic?
check.why: Penicillium produces penicillin.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Mould on bread is Rhizopus, a saprophyte, so do not call it a plant because it is stationary. Look for chitin cell walls, glycogen storage and the absence of chlorophyll before you classify any fungus.

content.problem: A student says a mushroom is a plant because it does not move. Give three features that place it in Fungi.

steps.reason: Plant walls are cellulose; fungal walls are chitin.
steps.result: The wall points to Fungi.
steps.predictPrompt: Which chemical test would help?

steps.reason: A mushroom has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.
steps.result: It absorbs ready-made food, like a heterotroph.

steps.reason: The body is a mycelium of hyphae, not roots, stems and leaves.
steps.result: It has no plant organs.

steps.reason: Stationary does not mean plant.
steps.result: The mushroom belongs to Fungi.

content.heading: Go deeper: The Rhizopus life cycle, step by step
paragraphs: A Rhizopus spore is a single cell with a thick wall. When it lands on damp bread it absorbs water, germinates and sends out a hypha. The hypha branches into a mycelium, and special hyphae called stolons run across the surface while rhizoids anchor the mould and absorb food.

When food runs short, upright sporangiophores rise from the mycelium. Each swells at the tip into a sporangium, where hundreds of haploid spores form by mitosis. The sporangium dries, splits and releases the spores, which scatter in air and start the cycle again.

Rhizopus can also reproduce sexually. When two compatible mating types meet, their hyphal tips fuse and form a thick-walled zygospore. The zygospore survives heat and drought, then undergoes meiosis and produces a germ sporangium that releases haploid spores, which is why mould returns after bread is dried or frozen: the spores and zygospores wait, and the sporangium is the black pinhead on mouldy bread; the pale threads underneath are the mycelium, and air currents carry the spores long distances, and one mouldy slice can contaminate a whole kitchen.
bullets: A spore germinates into hyphae, which branch into a mycelium.
Stolons spread the mould; rhizoids anchor it and absorb food.
Sporangia release spores; a zygospore carries the mould through harsh conditions.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a fungus digests food outside its body
paragraphs: A fungus cannot engulf food the way Amoeba does. It secretes enzymes such as amylase, protease and lipase into the material it grows on, breaking starch, protein and fat into small soluble molecules. The hyphae then absorb those molecules across the cell wall and membrane, and this absorptive feeding explains where moulds grow: they need a moist surface, a food source and oxygen, and jam, leather, timber and stored grain all support mould if moisture is present, and the same process is useful in food production: yeast ferments sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide, and Penicillium secretes penicillin.

Not every fungus is a saprophyte. Parasitic fungi feed on living hosts and cause diseases such as ringworm and athlete's foot. Mutualistic fungi live with roots as mycorrhizae, trading water and minerals for sugars, and lichens pair a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium.
The fungus grows fastest in warm, damp conditions, which is why food spoils quickly in a humid kitchen. In a lichen, the fungus provides shelter while the algal partner photosynthesises.
bullets: Extracellular enzymes break food down before absorption.
Moisture, food and oxygen decide where moulds grow.
Saprophytes, parasites and mutualists differ in where they get food.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fungi are not plants
paragraphs: A fungus looks plant-like, but its cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose, and it stores glycogen rather than starch. It has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, so it must obtain ready-made food. Its body is a network of hyphae rather than leaves, stems and roots, and a mushroom is only the fruiting body; most of the organism is the mycelium hidden in the substrate, and Fungi reproduce mainly by spores, and yeasts are unicellular fungi that reproduce by budding.

These differences matter in exams: bacteria are prokaryotic, while fungi are eukaryotic with a nucleus. Fungi are not plants, and mould is not a bacterium. The safe discrimination rule is: chitin wall, no chlorophyll, absorptive feeding and spores point to fungi.
The chitin wall is a useful drug target because human cells do not make chitin. Yeasts are used in bread and palm wine, while moulds spoil stored food and damage damp buildings.
bullets: Chitin wall and glycogen storage separate fungi from plants.
The mushroom is the fruiting body; the mycelium is the main body.
Fungi are eukaryotic; bacteria are prokaryotic.

content.question: Explain why a fungus cannot make its own food even when it grows in bright sunlight.
hints: Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll.
Fungi digest their food outside the body.
Saprophytes absorb the soluble products.

lessons.title: Plant Divisions
lessons.objective: Order Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta by vascular tissue, seeds and their dependence on water.

content.heading: Plant divisions
paragraphs: A moss, a fern and a mango tree all photosynthesise, but they solve the same problems differently. Plant divisions are grouped by how far each has moved from water, from thallus to seed.

content.heading: Thallophyta and Bryophyta
paragraphs: Thallophyta have a thallus, a body that is not divided into true roots, stems and leaves. Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga that lives in fresh water. Its cells contain spiral chloroplasts and pyrenoids that store starch, and it reproduces by fragmentation and conjugation.

Bryophyta include mosses and liverworts, such as Marchantia. They have rhizoids instead of true roots, no vascular tissue, and a dominant gametophyte generation. The leafy moss plant is the gametophyte; it produces gametes, and the fertilised egg grows into a stalked sporophyte that releases spores.
Their sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg, so they live in damp, shaded places and stay small.
bullets: Thallophyta: a thallus, with no true roots, stems or leaves.
Bryophyta: rhizoids, no vascular tissue, water needed for fertilisation.
Both are tied to damp habitats.
content.takeaway: Without vascular tissue, a plant cannot grow tall or far from water.

check.question: Which feature keeps mosses close to the ground?
check.why: Without xylem and phloem, mosses cannot transport water and food over long distances.

content.heading: Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta
paragraphs: Pteridophyta are ferns such as Dryopteris. They have true roots, stems and leaves, and vascular tissue of xylem and phloem, so they can grow taller than mosses. They still reproduce by spores and their sperm need water, so ferns are common in damp places, and the fern plant is the sporophyte; its spores grow into a small gametophyte that produces gametes, and the fertilised egg grows into a new fern.
Spermatophyta reproduce by seeds. Gymnosperms, such as cycads and conifers, bear naked seeds in cones. Angiosperms bear seeds enclosed in fruits.

They flower and are divided into monocots, such as maize, and dicots, such as water leaf. Pollen carries the male gamete, so fertilisation no longer needs water. The ovule becomes a seed, and the seed germinates into a new plant.
bullets: Ferns: vascular tissue, spores, water for fertilisation.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds, usually in cones.
Angiosperms: flowers, fruits, monocots and dicots.
content.takeaway: Seeds and pollen freed plants from standing water.

check.question: Which group produces seeds enclosed in fruits?
check.why: Angiosperms are flowering plants; their seeds develop inside fruits.

content.heading: The trend from water to land
paragraphs: The divisions show a series of innovations. Vascular tissue made tall growth possible. The seed protected the embryo and stored food.
Pollen removed the need for swimming sperm. Flowers and fruits improved pollination and seed dispersal. Each step reduced dependence on water.

The trend is not a straight line from one living plant to another, and lower plants are not failures. Mosses and ferns still thrive in damp habitats. But the sequence explains why a mango tree can grow on dry land while a moss cannot, and each innovation widened the range of habitats a plant could occupy, and thallophyta is a legacy grouping; modern botany places green algae among protists or plants, but the exam uses the traditional division.
bullets: Vascular tissue solved transport.
Seeds and pollen solved reproduction on land.
Flowers and fruits improved dispersal.
content.takeaway: Each plant division removes one more dependence on water.

check.question: Which innovation removed the need for water for fertilisation?
check.why: Pollen carries the male gamete to the ovule, so fertilisation does not need a film of water.

visual.caption: One innovation at a time, from water to land.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match each example to its division: Spirogyra is Thallophyta, Marchantia is Bryophyta, Dryopteris is Pteridophyta, and maize is an angiosperm. Name the key feature, such as vascular tissue or seeds, before choosing.

content.problem: A plant has vascular tissue, true leaves and spores, but no seeds. It grows in damp shade. Name its division and explain why it still needs water.

steps.reason: Xylem and phloem rule out Thallophyta and Bryophyta.
steps.result: The plant is either Pteridophyta or Spermatophyta.
steps.predictPrompt: Which groups lack vascular tissue?

steps.reason: Spores instead of seeds point to Pteridophyta.
steps.result: The plant is a fern, such as Dryopteris.

steps.reason: Fern sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg.
steps.result: Fertilisation ties the fern to damp shade.

steps.reason: Vascular tissue allows height, but reproduction still needs water.
steps.result: The plant is a pteridophyte.

content.heading: Go deeper: Alternation of generations in mosses and ferns
paragraphs: Plants switch between two bodies. The gametophyte is haploid and makes gametes by mitosis. The sporophyte is diploid and makes spores by meiosis, and in mosses the leafy plant is the gametophyte, while the stalked capsule that grows from it is the sporophyte, which depends on the gametophyte for food.

A moss spore germinates into a protonema, a green thread that grows into the leafy gametophyte. Antheridia release sperm that swim through a water film to archegonia. The fertilised egg grows into the sporophyte, and its capsule releases spores.

In ferns the sporophyte is the large plant with fronds. Sori on the underside of a frond produce spores. A spore grows into a small, heart-shaped prothallus, the gametophyte, which bears antheridia and archegonia, and water is still needed for the sperm to swim, so ferns are tied to damp habitats even though the sporophyte is independent, and the gametophyte and sporophyte stages look so different that early botanists described them as separate plants, and that is why the moss capsule and the leafy moss were once given different names.
bullets: Gametophyte: haploid, makes gametes; sporophyte: diploid, makes spores.
Moss: gametophyte dominant, sporophyte dependent.
Fern: sporophyte dominant, prothallus free-living.

content.heading: Go deeper: From pollen to seed
paragraphs: In seed plants the gametophytes are tiny and dependent: a pollen grain is the male gametophyte, and the ovule contains the female gametophyte and an egg. Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma or ovule, while fertilisation is the fusion of gametes and happens later. When pollen lands, it grows a pollen tube through the style to the ovule, and two male gametes travel down the tube, and in angiosperms one fuses with the egg to form the zygote, and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form the endosperm, the food store of the seed; this is double fertilisation.

The ovule becomes the seed, with the zygote as embryo and the integuments as the seed coat. The ovary becomes the fruit. Gymnosperms have no ovary, so their seeds sit naked on cone scales, while a monocot seed has one cotyledon, such as maize, and a dicot has two, such as cowpea.
The endosperm is why cereal grains such as maize and rice are starchy foods. The seed coat protects the embryo until conditions are right for germination.
bullets: Pollination moves pollen; fertilisation fuses gametes.
Double fertilisation makes the zygote and the endosperm.
Ovule to seed; ovary to fruit; gymnosperm seeds are naked.

content.heading: Go deeper: Reading the plant kingdom for exams
paragraphs: The divisions form a discrimination chain: thallophytes such as Spirogyra have no true roots, stems or leaves; bryophytes have rhizoids, no vascular tissue and a dominant gametophyte; pteridophytes have vascular tissue and true roots, stems and leaves but no seeds; spermatophytes have seeds. Within Spermatophyta, gymnosperms bear naked seeds, usually in cones, while angiosperms bear seeds enclosed in fruits. Angiosperms split into monocots and dicots, and the presence of a seed is the fastest way to separate a fern from a flowering plant; the absence of vascular tissue separates a moss from a fern.

A common trap is to call Spirogyra a bryophyte because it is green and grows in water. Spirogyra is a thallophyte, a green alga. Another trap is to say mosses have no roots at all: they have rhizoids, which anchor them but do not absorb like true roots.
A fern frond with sori is a sporophyte making spores, not a flower making seeds. Moss capsules also make spores, but the leafy moss plant makes gametes.
bullets: No vascular tissue: bryophyte. Vascular but no seed: pteridophyte. Seed: spermatophyte.
Naked seed: gymnosperm. Seed in fruit: angiosperm.
Spirogyra is a thallophyte, not a bryophyte.

content.question: A farmer wants a tall crop on dry land. Explain why an angiosperm is better suited than a moss or a fern.
hints: Compare vascular tissue first.
Then compare how each plant fertilises and disperses its young.
Seeds and pollen remove the need for a film of water.

lessons.title: Plant Life Spans
lessons.objective: Classify a plant as an annual, biennial or perennial from its life cycle, and give Nigerian examples of each.

content.heading: Plant life spans
paragraphs: A maize field is harvested and cleared within one season, while a mango tree fruits for decades. Both are flowering plants; their difference is the span of their life cycle, which decides how a farmer plants and harvests.

content.heading: Annuals: one season, one generation
paragraphs: An annual completes its life cycle within one growing season or year. It germinates, grows, flowers, forms fruit and seed, and then dies. Maize, rice, cowpea and sunflower are annuals; tomato is usually grown as an annual.
The whole plant dies after seeds are formed, so the species survives only as seed.

Farmers like annuals because the cycle is short and predictable. They can plant two or three crops a year where water and soil allow, and they can rotate cereals with legumes. The cost is that the field must be replanted every season, and the soil is bare between crops.
bullets: An annual completes its life cycle in one season, then dies.
Nigerian examples include maize, rice, cowpea and tomato.
Survival depends on seed, so seed storage matters.
content.takeaway: An annual spends everything on one generation of seed.

check.question: Which of these is an annual crop?
check.why: Maize germinates, flowers, sets seed and dies within one season.

content.heading: Biennials: two years, one seed crop
paragraphs: A biennial grows vegetatively in its first year, storing food in roots, stems or leaves. In the second year it uses that store to flower, fruit, set seed and die. Carrot, onion, cabbage, beet and turnip are common biennials.
The edible part is usually the first-year vegetative growth.

Cold treatment, or vernalisation, often triggers flowering in the second year. A young plant exposed to cold early may flower in its first year and lose its market value. A gardener who wants seed must leave the plant through the second season.
bullets: Year one: vegetative growth and food storage.
Year two: flowering, seed production and death.
Vernalisation often triggers the second-year flower.
content.takeaway: A biennial stores food first, then spends it on one seed crop.

check.question: A carrot plant flowers and sets seed in its second year. It is
check.why: It grows vegetatively in year one and reproduces in year two before dying.

content.heading: Perennials: many years, repeated fruiting
paragraphs: A perennial lives for more than two years and usually flowers and fruits many times. Mango, orange, cashew, oil palm, cocoa and most grasses are perennials. Some lose their leaves in the dry season and regrow; others stay evergreen.
A few, such as bamboo, flower once and die after many years, so perennial describes the lifespan, not a guarantee of repeated flowering.

Perennials invest in permanent structures: woody stems, deep roots and food reserves. They protect the soil, provide shade and give repeated harvests, but they take years to mature and cannot be shuffled with the seasons like annuals.
bullets: A perennial lives more than two years and usually fruits repeatedly.
Nigerian examples include mango, cashew, oil palm and cocoa.
Woody stems and deep roots are long-term investments.
content.takeaway: A perennial spreads its reproduction over many seasons.

check.question: Which set contains only perennials?
check.why: Mango, cashew and oil palm live and fruit for many years.

visual.caption: An annual completes this cycle in one season, then dies.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A biennial does not live two years and then fruit for years. It dies after its second-year seed crop. Carrot and onion are biennials; mango and oil palm are perennials.

content.problem: A farmer plants carrot in year one and sees only leaves. In year two the plant flowers, sets seed and dies. Classify the plant and explain what changed.

steps.reason: The plant grows in year one and reproduces in year two.
steps.result: It has a two-year life cycle.
steps.predictPrompt: Which class completes its cycle in one season?

steps.reason: The carrot root is a food store, not a seed crop.
steps.result: Year one is vegetative growth.

steps.reason: Cold treatment, or vernalisation, prepares the plant to flower.
steps.result: The stored food supports the second-year flower.

steps.reason: The plant dies after one seed crop in its second year.
steps.result: Carrot is a biennial.

content.heading: Go deeper: How annual, biennial and perennial clocks work
paragraphs: An annual completes its whole life cycle in one season. Maize germinates, grows, flowers in the rains, sets seed and dies before the dry season. A biennial takes two seasons: it grows vegetatively in the first year and flowers in the second before dying.

A perennial lives for many years and flowers repeatedly. A mango tree may fruit for decades because new shoots are produced each year from established stems. The trunk and roots survive the dry season while the annual shoots do not.

The difference is therefore in the meristems. Annuals invest everything in one flowering, biennials store food for a second flowering, and perennials keep a reserve of living stem and root tissue that can flower again.
Some perennials such as banana produce a new stem each year while the corm survives underground. A banana "tree" is therefore a giant herb that lives as a perennial through its corm.

Temperate biennials such as cabbage rely on vernalisation, but Nigerian biennials such as some onions need a cool dry season to trigger flowering. Farmers therefore time sowing so that the cool season meets the plant at the right age.
bullets: Annuals complete one season; biennials take two; perennials live for years
Maize is annual; mango is perennial
Meristems decide whether flowering happens once or repeatedly

content.heading: Go deeper: Why lifespan matters for farming
paragraphs: Farmers match crop lifespan to rainfall and to soil. A short-cycle annual such as maize suits the short rains of the north because it finishes before the dry season. A long-cycle perennial such as oil palm needs steady water and years to mature, so it is planted only where the climate can sustain it.

Biennials such as cabbage store resources in the first year and invest them in reproduction in the second. Farmers therefore manage the two years differently, protecting the stored reserves in year one and harvesting the reproduction in year two.
Planting depth, spacing and harvest time all follow from the life span. An annual is replanted every season, while a perennial is pruned and guarded for the long term.
A perennial plantation such as oil palm must be protected for years before it yields well. That long wait explains why it is planted only where rainfall and soil can support it throughout the year.
Annuals such as maize leave the soil bare for part of the year, so cover crops are planted to protect it. Perennial roots remain in the soil throughout the dry season and hold it together.
bullets: Rainfall decides whether an annual, biennial or perennial suits a place
Biennials store reserves in year one for flowering in year two
Perennials need protection of established stems and roots

content.heading: Go deeper: Vernalisation, dormancy and senescence
paragraphs: Some biennials need a period of cold before they will flower. This requirement is called vernalisation. Without the cold, a plant such as cabbage may grow without flowering, which is why cultivated biennials are often given artificial cold before planting.

Seed dormancy is a different delay. A viable seed may wait through the dry season because its coat is impermeable or because an inhibitor is present. Moisture and temperature break the dormancy and allow germination when conditions are suitable.

Senescence is the ageing that follows flowering in annuals and biennials. Nutrients are withdrawn from the leaves and sent to the seeds, and the parent plant dies. Perennials postpone senescence because they keep their meristems alive year after year.
Dormancy also protects seeds in fire-prone savannas, because heat can kill the embryo but break the coat. The seed survives the fire and germinates with the first rains after the burning.

Senescence is not simply death; it is an organised withdrawal of nutrients to the growing seeds. A maize plant yellows because its leaves are being emptied into the grain, not because it is merely drying out.
bullets: Vernalisation is a cold requirement for flowering
Dormancy delays germination until moisture and temperature allow it
Senescence moves nutrients from leaves to seeds before death

content.question: A student calls maize a perennial because it is planted every year. Correct the statement and give two differences between maize and mango.
hints: Being replanted every year is not the same as living for many years.
Maize completes its life cycle in one season and dies.
Mango has a woody stem and fruits repeatedly over many years.

lessons.title: Invertebrate Phyla
lessons.objective: Order the six named invertebrate phyla by symmetry, body cavity and segmentation, and identify their examples.

content.heading: Invertebrate phyla
paragraphs: More than nine in ten animals have no backbone. The syllabus names six invertebrate phyla, and each adds a body-plan feature that the next group builds on: symmetry, a body cavity, segmentation and jointed limbs.

content.heading: Coelenterata and Platyhelminthes
paragraphs: Coelenterata, also called Cnidaria, include Hydra and jellyfish. They have radial symmetry, two cell layers, a single opening to a gastrovascular cavity, and tentacles with stinging cells called nematocysts. Hydra lives in fresh water and can regenerate from a fragment.

Platyhelminthes are flatworms such as Taenia, the tapeworm. They have bilateral symmetry, a flattened body, no body cavity and no true segments. Taenia lives in the intestine of a vertebrate host, attaches with hooks and suckers, and absorbs digested food through its body surface.

Its life cycle needs two hosts. Eggs pass out in faeces and are eaten by a pig, where they form cysts in the muscle; a human is infected by eating undercooked pork, and the adult attaches to the intestine.
bullets: Coelenterata: radial symmetry, two layers, one opening.
Platyhelminthes: bilateral, flattened and with no body cavity.
Taenia is a parasite with hooks and suckers.
content.takeaway: The first invertebrate steps are symmetry and a fixed body plan.

check.question: Which feature is characteristic of Hydra?
check.why: Hydra is a coelenterate with radial symmetry and stinging tentacles.

content.heading: Nematoda and Annelida
paragraphs: Nematoda are roundworms such as Ascaris. They have bilateral symmetry, a cylindrical unsegmented body, a tough cuticle and a pseudocoelom, a body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm. Ascaris lives in the small intestine and produces large numbers of eggs that pass out in faeces.

Annelida are segmented worms such as the earthworm. They have a true coelom, a closed circulatory system, setae for grip and a body divided into repeating segments. Segmentation allows different regions to specialise.
The earthworm burrows through soil, aerating it and mixing organic matter into it.
bullets: Nematoda: round, unsegmented, cuticle and pseudocoelom.
Annelida: segmented, true coelom and setae.
Earthworms improve soil structure and fertility.
content.takeaway: Segmentation and a true coelom are the annelid advance.

check.question: Which feature separates Annelida from Nematoda?
options: A segmented body with a true coelom
check.why: Annelids are segmented and have a true coelom; nematodes are unsegmented with a pseudocoelom.

content.heading: Arthropoda and Mollusca
paragraphs: Arthropoda have a hard exoskeleton of chitin, jointed appendages and a segmented body. They include insects, crustaceans, arachnids and millipedes. The exoskeleton protects the body but must be shed by moulting for growth, and arthropoda is the largest phylum, and it contains more species than all the other animal phyla combined.

Mollusca have a soft unsegmented body, a muscular foot, a mantle and usually a shell. Snails, slugs, clams and octopuses are molluscs. The mantle secretes the shell, and the radula is a rasping tongue used for feeding.
Snails live in damp places on land and in water. Coelenterata is now called Cnidaria in modern taxonomy; the body plan is the same, so expect either name in questions.
bullets: Arthropoda: exoskeleton, jointed legs and moulting.
Mollusca: soft body, mantle, muscular foot and shell.
Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum.
content.takeaway: Jointed limbs and a mantle mark the two largest invertebrate groups.

check.question: A snail belongs to
check.why: Snails have a soft body, a mantle and a shell, which are mollusc features.

visual.caption: Two successful body plans: jointed outside, soft inside a shell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not call every worm an annelid. Taenia is a flatworm with no body cavity, Ascaris is a roundworm with a false cavity, and the earthworm is the segmented annelid with a true coelom.

content.problem: A specimen has a soft body, a shell and a muscular foot. Another has jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton. Name the phylum of each.

steps.reason: A soft body with a mantle and shell points to Mollusca.
steps.result: The first specimen is a mollusc, such as a snail.
steps.predictPrompt: Which phylum has a chitin exoskeleton?

steps.reason: Jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton are arthropod features.
steps.result: The second specimen is an arthropod.

steps.reason: A shell is secreted by the mantle; an exoskeleton is shed by moulting.
steps.result: The two phyla solve support differently.

steps.reason: Body covering and appendages decide the phylum.
steps.result: The specimens are Mollusca and Arthropoda.

content.heading: Go deeper: The Taenia life cycle
paragraphs: An adult Taenia lives in the human small intestine. It attaches by a scolex bearing hooks and suckers, and grows a chain of proglottids. Mature proglottids produce eggs, and gravid proglottids break off and pass out in faeces.

A pig eats contaminated food or water and swallows the eggs. In the pig's intestine an egg hatches into an oncosphere, a six-hooked larva that bores through the gut wall into the blood. It settles in muscle and develops into a cysticercus, a fluid-filled bladder with an invaginated scolex.

A human is infected by eating undercooked pork containing cysticerci. The scolex turns out and attaches to the intestine, and the worm matures. Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm, can also infect humans who swallow its eggs, causing cysticercosis when larvae encyst in tissues such as the brain, while Taenia saginata, the beef tapeworm, has cattle as its intermediate host, and the tapeworm has no mouth or gut, so it does not eat the host's food directly; it absorbs already digested nutrients through its skin, and gravid proglottids look like small white grains in the stool.
bullets: Gravid proglottids release eggs in faeces.
Pig: oncosphere to cysticercus in muscle.
Human: eats undercooked pork; scolex attaches in the intestine.

content.heading: Go deeper: Symmetry, body cavities and segmentation
paragraphs: Body plans are compared on three axes: symmetry, germ layers and body cavity. Hydra is radially symmetrical with two germ layers, while flatworms, roundworms, annelids, arthropods and molluscs are bilaterally symmetrical with three. Flatworms are acoelomate, roundworms are pseudocoelomate, and annelids, arthropods and molluscs are coelomate.

A true coelom is a cavity lined by mesoderm on both sides. A pseudocoelom is not fully lined by mesoderm. The coelom gives space for organs, allows the gut to move independently and can act as a hydrostatic skeleton.

Segmentation is another advance. Annelids have repeated body segments with a fluid-filled coelom in each, so muscles can squeeze one region while another anchors.
