Arthropods show fused segments and jointed appendages, and molluscs are unsegmented with a muscular foot and mantle, so these features, not size, are what exams compare, and cephalisation is the concentration of sense organs and nerve tissue at the front end, and it is most obvious in active, bilaterally symmetrical animals, and radial animals such as Hydra can meet the environment from any direction, so they have no front end.
bullets: Hydra: radial, two layers, no coelom.
Flatworm: bilateral, three layers, acoelomate. Roundworm: pseudocoelomate.
Annelid, arthropod, mollusc: coelomate; annelid and arthropod are segmented.

content.heading: Go deeper: How each phylum moves and feeds
paragraphs: Hydra moves by somersaulting or gliding on its basal disc, and feeds by discharging nematocysts from tentacles to paralyse small prey, then pushing food into the single opening. Taenia has no gut, so it absorbs digested food through its body surface and relies on the host's digestion. Ascaris has a complete gut and a tough cuticle; it moves by whipping the body against the pseudocoelomic fluid, and the earthworm crawls by alternating circular and longitudinal muscles against the coelom, gripping with setae.

Arthropods move with jointed limbs and moult the exoskeleton to grow. Molluscs glide on a muscular foot, and many scrape food with a radula. Each method fits the body plan: a hydrostatic skeleton, a jointed exoskeleton or a muscular foot.

A hydrostatic skeleton works because fluid cannot be compressed: when circular muscles contract the body lengthens, and when longitudinal muscles contract it shortens. Setae are bristles that grip the soil and stop the worm slipping backwards, and arthropods must moult because the exoskeleton cannot stretch.
bullets: Hydra: tentacles and nematocysts; one opening.
Taenia: no gut, absorbs through the body surface.
Earthworm: hydrostatic skeleton and setae; arthropod: jointed limbs and moulting.

content.question: Explain why segmentation is an advance over a solid, unsegmented body. Use the earthworm and a flatworm in your answer.
hints: Segments can carry different organs and appendages.
A true coelom gives space for organs and a hydrostatic skeleton.
A flatworm has a flattened body with no body cavity.

lessons.title: Insects and Their Importance
lessons.objective: Describe the insect body plan, distinguish complete from incomplete metamorphosis, and assess insects' economic and environmental importance.

content.heading: Insects and their importance
paragraphs: Insects are arthropods with three body regions, six legs and usually two pairs of wings. They are the most numerous animals on land, and JAMB tests both their body plan and their mixed value to people.

content.heading: The insect body plan
paragraphs: An insect has three body regions: head, thorax and abdomen. The head carries a pair of antennae, compound eyes and mouthparts. The thorax has three pairs of jointed legs and usually two pairs of wings.
The abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive organs. Breathing is through spiracles and tracheae, not lungs.

The exoskeleton is made of chitin. It protects the insect and reduces water loss, but it cannot stretch, so the insect must moult to grow. Insects have an open circulatory system, with haemolymph pumped by a dorsal heart, and their small size and tracheal system limit them to relatively short diffusion paths.
bullets: Head, thorax and abdomen; three pairs of legs.
Spiracles and tracheae carry air directly to the tissues.
The chitin exoskeleton must be moulted for growth.
content.takeaway: An insect is a three-part arthropod with six legs and tracheal breathing.

check.question: Which structure is found on the thorax of an insect?
check.why: The thorax bears the legs and wings; the head bears antennae and mouthparts.

content.heading: Complete and incomplete metamorphosis
paragraphs: Metamorphosis is the change in body form between the young and the adult. In complete metamorphosis the insect passes through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. Butterflies, mosquitoes, houseflies, bees and beetles do this.
The larva is often a feeding machine, while the adult specialises in reproduction and dispersal. The larva moults several times before it pupates.

In incomplete metamorphosis there are only three stages: egg, nymph and adult. The nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and has no wings or only wing buds. Cockroaches, grasshoppers, termites and dragonflies do this, and there is no pupal stage, and the nymph moults repeatedly.
bullets: Complete: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
Incomplete: egg, nymph and adult.
The pupa is the stage that separates the two patterns.
content.takeaway: Count the stages: four means complete, three means incomplete.

check.question: A cockroach hatches as a small wingless form that resembles its parent. This is
check.why: Egg, nymph and adult are the three stages of incomplete metamorphosis.

visual.caption: The pupa is the extra stage in complete metamorphosis.

content.heading: Economic and environmental importance
paragraphs: Insects are useful. Bees, wasps and butterflies pollinate crops and wild plants. Bees give honey and wax; silkworms give silk; lac insects give shellac.
Insects are food for birds, fish and reptiles, and some feed on pests as biological control agents. They decompose dung and dead matter, recycling nutrients.

Insects are also harmful. Locusts and armyworms destroy crops; weevils and beetles damage stored grain; aphids suck sap and transmit plant viruses. Mosquitoes transmit malaria, yellow fever and dengue; tsetse flies transmit sleeping sickness; houseflies carry typhoid and cholera organisms, and the same insect can be useful at one stage and harmful at another.
bullets: Pollination, honey, silk, wax and biological control.
Crop pests and stored-product pests.
Vectors of malaria, sleeping sickness and typhoid.
content.takeaway: Judge an insect by its stage, its numbers and its role in the food web.

check.question: Which insect is a vector of malaria?
check.why: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium parasite when it bites.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A butterfly is harmful as a larva and useful as an adult pollinator. Read the stage named in the question before deciding harmful or useful, and remember that the same insect can be both.

content.problem: A farmer finds caterpillars stripping leaves and adult butterflies visiting flowers. Are the insects harmful or useful? Explain.

steps.reason: The caterpillar is the larval stage; the butterfly is the adult.
steps.result: The same species is present at two stages.
steps.predictPrompt: Which stage feeds on leaves?

steps.reason: Caterpillars have chewing mouthparts and eat leaves.
steps.result: The larval stage damages the crop.

steps.reason: The adult visits flowers for nectar and transfers pollen.
steps.result: The adult stage pollinates crops.

steps.reason: The answer depends on the stage named in the question.
steps.result: The insect is both harmful and useful.

content.heading: Go deeper: Metamorphosis, stage by stage
paragraphs: Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult; the larva feeds and grows, moulting several times, and each stage between moults is an instar. The final larval instar becomes a pupa, inside which larval tissues are broken down and adult structures form. Hormones control the change: the brain releases a hormone that stimulates the prothoracic glands to make ecdysone, which triggers moulting, and juvenile hormone keeps the next moult larval, and when juvenile hormone falls, the next moult produces a pupa, and its absence produces an adult.

Incomplete metamorphosis has three stages: egg, nymph and adult. The nymph resembles a small adult, lives in the same habitat and gradually develops wings and reproductive organs. There is no pupa, and grasshoppers, cockroaches and termites develop this way, while butterflies, mosquitoes, houseflies, bees and beetles are complete.

The pupa is not a resting stage: inside it, larval organs are dismantled and adult wings, legs and reproductive organs are built. A butterfly pupa is called a chrysalis, and a fly pupa is enclosed in a hardened case.
bullets: Complete: egg, larva, pupa, adult. Incomplete: egg, nymph, adult.
Ecdysone triggers moulting; juvenile hormone keeps the larva larval.
A nymph resembles the adult; a larva usually does not.

content.heading: Go deeper: How an insect breathes without lungs
paragraphs: Air enters through spiracles, small openings along the sides of the thorax and abdomen. Each spiracle leads into a trachea, and the tracheae branch into fine tracheoles that reach individual cells. Oxygen diffuses directly through the tracheole walls into the tissues, and carbon dioxide diffuses out, and the system works without blood as an oxygen carrier, and in large, active insects, abdominal pumping and wing movements ventilate the tracheae, and spiracles can close to reduce water loss, which is why insects survive in dry places.

Diffusion is efficient only over short distances. That is one reason insects stay small; a very large insect could not move enough oxygen to its deepest tissues through tracheoles alone. Aquatic insect larvae often use gills or take air at the surface.

Tracheae are reinforced with spiral ridges of chitin, so they stay open even when the body bends. Some aquatic larvae, such as mosquito larvae, hang from the surface and draw air through a siphon, while others have gills that absorb oxygen dissolved in water. The same tracheal system supplies the flight muscles, which need more oxygen than any other tissue.
bullets: Spiracles to tracheae to tracheoles; gas exchange is direct.
Abdominal pumping ventilates the system; closing spiracles saves water.
Diffusion limits body size.

content.heading: Go deeper: Mouthparts and the damage they do
paragraphs: Mouthpart type predicts both the food and the damage. Biting-chewing mouthparts, as in grasshoppers and beetles, cut plant tissue and leave ragged edges. Piercing-sucking mouthparts, as in mosquitoes, aphids and tsetse flies, penetrate tissue and suck fluids; they can transmit pathogens.

Siphoning mouthparts, as in butterflies and moths, form a coiled tube for nectar. Sponging mouthparts, as in houseflies, mop up liquids and can pick up microbes from filth. Chewing-lapping mouthparts, as in bees, chew wax and lap nectar.

Control follows the damage. Chewing pests are attacked with stomach poisons or mechanical barriers; sucking pests need systemic or contact insecticides, and disease vectors need habitat control and personal protection. Mouthparts also explain why a butterfly is a pollinator while its caterpillar is a leaf eater, and aphids are piercing-sucking pests that weaken plants and can inject viruses, and locusts are biting-chewing pests that strip leaves and can destroy a whole field, while houseflies do not bite but their sponging mouthparts pick up bacteria from refuse and deposit them on food.
bullets: Biting-chewing: cuts tissue. Piercing-sucking: drains fluid and can carry disease.
Siphoning: nectar. Sponging: liquids and microbes. Chewing-lapping: bees.
Identify the mouthpart to predict damage and choose control.

content.question: Name one insect that is useful in one stage and harmful in another, and explain the difference.
hints: Think of a butterfly or a moth.
The larva usually feeds on leaves.
The adult may pollinate flowers.

lessons.title: Vertebrate Classes
lessons.objective: Compare Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia by skin, respiration, reproduction and heart, and trace the move from water to land.

content.heading: Vertebrate classes
paragraphs: A fish, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a goat all have a backbone, but each solves the problems of support, breathing and reproduction differently. The five vertebrate classes show a step-by-step move from water to land.

content.heading: Pisces and Amphibia
paragraphs: Pisces are fish. They have a streamlined body, scales, fins and gills. Cartilaginous fish, such as sharks and rays, have a skeleton of cartilage; bony fish, such as tilapia and catfish, have a bony skeleton, and most fish reproduce by external fertilisation, releasing eggs and sperm into water, and their heart has two chambers, and the eggs hatch into fry.
Amphibia include frogs and toads. Their moist, scale-less skin allows gas exchange, and they also have lungs. They lay jelly-covered eggs in water, and the young tadpole has gills and a tail.

Metamorphosis changes the tadpole into an air-breathing adult. The tadpole grows legs and loses its tail as it becomes a frog. Amphibians have a three-chambered heart and still depend on water for reproduction.
bullets: Pisces: gills, fins, scales, external fertilisation and a two-chambered heart.
Amphibia: moist skin, lungs, eggs in water and a three-chambered heart.
Amphibians are the bridge between water and land.
content.takeaway: Amphibians breathe air but still return to water to breed.

check.question: Which feature ties a frog to water for reproduction?
check.why: Frog eggs dry out on land, and the tadpole stage is aquatic.

content.heading: Reptilia and Aves
paragraphs: Reptilia include lizards, snakes, turtles and crocodiles. They have dry skin covered with scales, and they breathe with lungs. Their eggs have leathery or hard shells that resist drying, and fertilisation is internal, so reptiles can breed on land, and they are ectothermic, using the environment to regulate body temperature, and most have a three-chambered heart, but crocodiles have four, and the eggs hatch into juveniles.
Aves are birds. They have feathers, a beak, wings and hollow bones. Their heart has four chambers, and they are endothermic, generating their own heat.

Birds lay hard-shelled eggs and incubate them. Their lungs connect to air sacs, which make gas exchange efficient for flight. Birds have no teeth; the beak is shaped for the diet, and the eggs hatch into chicks.
bullets: Reptilia: dry scales, shelled eggs, internal fertilisation and ectothermy.
Aves: feathers, beak, four-chambered heart and endothermy.
Shelled eggs freed both groups from breeding in water.
content.takeaway: The shelled egg is the reptile and bird answer to life on dry land.

check.question: Which feature is shared by reptiles and birds?
check.why: Both groups fertilise internally and lay eggs with shells that resist drying.

visual.caption: The pivotal step: an egg that can survive out of water.

content.heading: Mammalia and the move to land
paragraphs: Mammalia include humans, cows, goats, bats and whales. They have hair or fur, mammary glands that produce milk, a diaphragm and a four-chambered heart. Most give birth to live young and care for them.

Mammals are endothermic and have differentiated teeth for different diets. Economically, fish, poultry and livestock provide food, while cattle, sheep and goats add hides, wool and manure; some vertebrates are pests or disease carriers.

The vertebrate classes show a trend. Gills give way to lungs, external fertilisation to internal fertilisation, jelly eggs to shelled eggs, and cold-bloodedness to warm-bloodedness. Each change reduces dependence on water, and the trend is not a straight line, and each class still has adaptations to its own habitat.
bullets: Mammalia: hair, mammary glands, milk and a four-chambered heart.
Trend: gills to lungs, external to internal fertilisation, jelly to shelled eggs.
Each class remains adapted to its own habitat.
content.takeaway: Vertebrates moved onto land by changing how they breathe, breed and control heat.

check.question: Which set of features is unique to mammals?
check.why: Hair and mammary glands are defining mammalian features.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Cold-blooded means ectothermic, not always cold. A lizard on a hot rock has a high body temperature because it gains heat from the environment; a mammal makes its own heat.

content.problem: A vertebrate has dry scales, lays shelled eggs on land and breathes with lungs. Name its class and one reason it is not an amphibian.

steps.reason: Dry scales and shelled eggs are reptile features.
steps.result: The animal belongs to Reptilia.
steps.predictPrompt: Which class has moist, scale-less skin?

steps.reason: Internal fertilisation and a shelled egg allow breeding on land.
steps.result: The animal does not need water to reproduce.

steps.reason: Amphibians lay jelly-covered eggs in water and have a larval stage.
steps.result: The animal has no aquatic larval stage.

steps.reason: Skin, egg and life cycle all point one way.
steps.result: The vertebrate is a reptile, not an amphibian.

content.heading: Go deeper: Metamorphosis in a frog
paragraphs: A frog egg is laid in water and covered by jelly. It hatches into a tadpole with external gills, a long tail and a horny beak. The tadpole feeds on plant material and grows, and its external gills are replaced by internal gills, and as metamorphosis begins, the hind limbs appear first, then the forelimbs; the tail is resorbed, the mouth widens and the gut shortens as the animal changes from a herbivore to a carnivore, and the gills disappear, the lungs expand and the skin becomes thicker.

Thyroxine from the thyroid gland drives the change. The adult returns to water to breed but breathes air and can live on land. The two lives are not separate animals: the tadpole and the frog are the same individual at different stages.

The tadpole has a two-chambered heart like a fish, and the adult develops a three-chambered heart. The adult also develops eyelids and a nictitating membrane, which protect the eyes out of water. The adult frog has no tail, and its hind legs are long and muscular for jumping.
bullets: Egg, tadpole with gills and tail, limbs appear, tail resorbed, adult.
Hind limbs appear before forelimbs; the gut shortens.
Thyroxine controls metamorphosis.

content.heading: Go deeper: How the heart and circulation changed
paragraphs: A fish has a two-chambered heart: one atrium receives deoxygenated blood and one ventricle pumps it to the gills. The blood loses oxygen in the gills and then flows to the body, so the circuit is single and the pressure falls before the tissues. An amphibian has two atria and one ventricle, and oxygenated blood from the skin and lungs enters the left atrium, deoxygenated blood enters the right, and both mix in the ventricle, and a reptile also has three chambers, but a partial septum reduces mixing; crocodilians have four.

Birds and mammals have four chambers and double circulation. The right side sends blood to the lungs and the left side sends oxygenated blood to the body at high pressure. Complete separation supports the high oxygen demand of endothermy and flight.

Blood pressure is highest in the aorta of birds and mammals because the left ventricle pumps against the resistance of the whole body. In a fish, the gills receive the full force of the ventricle, but the body receives blood after the pressure has dropped.
bullets: Fish: two chambers, single circulation.
Amphibian and most reptiles: three chambers, some mixing.
Bird and mammal: four chambers, double circulation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Eggs, fertilisation and the move to land
paragraphs: Fish usually release eggs and sperm into water, where fertilisation happens outside the body. A fish may lay thousands of eggs because most are eaten or fail. Amphibians also lay jelly-covered eggs in water, and the larvae remain aquatic, and reptiles fertilise internally and lay eggs with a leathery or hard shell, and the amniotic egg contains four membranes: the amnion surrounds the embryo in fluid, the yolk sac supplies food, the allantois stores waste and helps gas exchange, and the chorion surrounds the whole embryo, and the shell slows water loss, so reptiles can breed away from water.

Birds lay hard-shelled eggs and incubate them. Mammals usually retain the embryo inside the uterus, nourish it through a placenta and feed the young with milk. Each step reduces the young's dependence on standing water.

The amniotic egg is often called the key invention that freed reptiles from water. The shell is porous, so oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves, but water loss is limited. A mammal embryo is attached to the uterus by the placenta, and the umbilical cord carries nutrients and oxygen.
bullets: Fish and amphibians: eggs in water, external or jelly-covered.
Reptiles and birds: internal fertilisation and shelled eggs.
Mammals: internal development, placenta and milk.

content.question: Explain why a frog must return to water to breed while a lizard does not.
hints: Compare the egg coverings.
Compare where fertilisation happens.
A frog has an aquatic tadpole; a lizard hatches as a miniature adult.

lessons.title: Adaptive Colouration
lessons.objective: Distinguish cryptic colouration, countershading, warning colouration and mimicry, and explain what each does for the organism.

content.heading: Adaptive colouration
paragraphs: A stick insect disappears against a twig, a fish is dark above and pale below, and a bright frog warns that it is poisonous. All three use colour, but for different jobs. The exam asks you to name the job.

content.heading: Cryptic colouration: disappear into the background
paragraphs: Cryptic colouration, or camouflage, makes an organism hard to see against its background. The colour, pattern and shape all match the habitat. A stick insect looks like a twig, a praying mantis looks like a leaf, and a flounder changes its pattern to match the seabed.
The function works both ways. A prey animal avoids detection, while a predator waits unseen for a victim. The disguise fails when the animal moves, casts a shadow or sits on the wrong background.
Colour alone is not enough; behaviour must keep the animal still and in the right place.
bullets: Camouflage matches colour, pattern and shape to the background.
It hides prey from predators and predators from prey.
Movement and the wrong background break the disguise.
content.takeaway: Camouflage works by matching the background, not by being invisible.

check.question: A stick insect that looks like a twig is using
check.why: Its colour and shape match the background, so it is cryptic colouration.

content.heading: Countershading: dark above, pale below
paragraphs: Countershading is a pattern with a dark upper surface and a pale lower surface. It is common in fish, toads, snakes and many birds and mammals. From above, the dark back blends with the dark water or ground.
From below, the pale belly blends with the bright sky or water surface.

The pattern cancels the shadow that a rounded body casts. Without countershading, a fish seen from below would look like a dark silhouette. Countershading is a form of cryptic colouration, but the syllabus asks you to separate it from simple background matching.
bullets: Dark back, pale belly.
It hides the animal from above and from below.
It cancels the shadow that reveals a three-dimensional body.
content.takeaway: Countershading hides a body by cancelling its shadow.

check.question: A fish with a dark back and a silver belly is using
check.why: The dark top and pale underside cancel the body's shadow, which is countershading.

content.heading: Warning colouration and mimicry
paragraphs: Warning colouration, also called aposematic colouration, is a bright, conspicuous pattern that advertises a defence: red, yellow, orange and black bands are common, and the colours warn predators of poison, stings or a bad taste. Poison-dart frogs and wasps are standard examples. The syllabus also treats a conspicuous fungal cap as warning colouration, and the fly agaric has a bright red cap with pale spots and is toxic, so its colour can signal danger.

Mimicry is a resemblance to another organism or object: in Batesian mimicry a harmless species copies a harmful one, such as a hoverfly that looks like a wasp, while in Mullerian mimicry two harmful species share the same warning pattern. Mimicry borrows the signal; warning colouration owns it.
bullets: Warning colouration advertises a real defence.
The fly agaric is the syllabus example; a bright cap alone does not prove toxicity.
Mimicry copies a warning signal or another object.
content.takeaway: Warning colouration signals danger; mimicry borrows the signal.

check.question: A harmless hoverfly with yellow and black bands resembles a wasp. This is
check.why: The hoverfly is harmless but copies the wasp's warning pattern, which is mimicry.

visual.caption: One signal is earned; the other is borrowed.

rows.right: Not always; the mimic may be harmless
Gain protection from the model's signal

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Countershading is cryptic, not warning. Dark above and pale below hides the animal; bright bands advertise it. A bright mushroom cap can be warning colouration, so read the pattern before naming its function.

content.problem: A frog is bright red with black spots and is poisonous. A second frog is harmless but has the same pattern. Identify the two phenomena.

steps.reason: Bright colours plus a real poison advertise a defence.
steps.result: The first frog shows warning colouration.
steps.predictPrompt: Which pattern hides an animal instead of advertising it?

steps.reason: It is harmless but copies the warning pattern.
steps.result: The second frog is a Batesian mimic.

steps.reason: Warning colouration is honest; mimicry borrows the signal.
steps.result: The two looks have different causes.

steps.reason: The first pattern earns its signal; the second copies it.
steps.result: The pair shows warning colouration and mimicry.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cryptic colouration and the eye of the predator
paragraphs: Cryptic colouration works because the predator's visual system is set to find movement and contrast. A moth resting on bark breaks its outline, so the predator does not register a body at all. The camouflage succeeds even if the moth is large, provided the pattern matches the background in light and shadow.

Countershading extends the same idea to a three-dimensional body. A fish is dark above and pale below, so from above it matches the dark water and from below it matches the bright surface. The shadow that would reveal its shape disappears.

Crypsis is therefore a property of the background, not of the animal alone. The same insect can be cryptic on bark and obvious on a leaf, which is why habitat matching matters more than absolute brightness.

A predator also hunts by movement, so stillness is part of the camouflage. A grasshopper that freezes on a matching stem is safer than one that hops away and betrays its position. Movement therefore matters as much as colour in crypsis.
Zebras show that the pattern need not match a single background. Their stripes confuse the vision of biting flies and break the outline of the body when animals stand together in a group.
bullets: Cryptic colouration breaks the outline against a background
Countershading removes the shadow that reveals the body
Camouflage depends on the habitat, not only on the animal

content.heading: Go deeper: Warning colouration and aposematism
paragraphs: Warning colouration is the opposite strategy: it makes the animal easy to see. Bright bands, spots and contrasting colours advertise that the prey is unpleasant, poisonous or painful. The advertisement only works if the predator learns from one encounter.

Aposematism therefore relies on memory. A bird that eats a bright caterpillar and becomes ill will avoid similar patterns in future. The colour does not wound the predator; the chemistry inside the prey does.

Some bright colours are not warnings. A brightly coloured flower attracts pollinators, and a male Agama displays red to attract mates. Brightness must be read with behaviour and chemistry before it is called warning.

A warning must be honest to be useful in the long term. If a bright pattern appears without a defence, predators learn that it is safe and the advertisement collapses for the defended species as well.
The poison is often made or stored from food. A caterpillar that feeds on a toxic plant keeps the toxin in its body, so the predator learns that the colour means an unpleasant meal.
bullets: Warning colouration advertises a defence to predators
Aposematism needs learning from one bad encounter
Brightness alone does not prove warning colouration

content.heading: Go deeper: Mimicry, from Batesian to Müllerian
paragraphs: Mimicry is resemblance between species. In Batesian mimicry, an undefended species copies a defended model, and predators avoid both. A harmless hoverfly copies a wasp because the pattern is enough to deter the bird.

In Müllerian mimicry, two defended species converge on the same pattern. Predators need only learn one warning, and the lesson is shared between the species. The pattern spreads because both benefit from the same advertisement.

Mimicry is most convincing where the mimic and the model live together. A hoverfly mimicking a wasp absent from its habitat gains nothing, which is why resemblance must be judged in the place where the predator hunts.

Mimicry can also involve smell and sound, not only colour. A moth that smells like a hornet or a butterfly that imitates a warning call is mimicking in a different sense, and the principle is the same.
A mimic that is rarer than its model gains most. If the harmless copy becomes common, predators meet it often enough to learn that the pattern is safe, and the advantage fades.
bullets: Batesian mimicry: undefended mimic copies a defended model
Müllerian mimicry: two defended species share a pattern
Mimicry needs the model to be present in the habitat

content.question: A moth is brown and rests on bark, but flies when disturbed. Explain why its camouflage fails once it moves.
hints: Camouflage depends on matching the background.
Movement breaks the outline and attracts the eye.
A moving moth also casts changing shadows.

lessons.title: Social Insects: Termites and Bees
lessons.objective: Differentiate the castes of termites and bees and explain how division of labour helps the colony.

content.heading: Social insects
paragraphs: A termite mound and a beehive look like crowded chaos, but both are organised societies. A few individuals reproduce, while thousands of sterile workers keep the colony fed, defended and clean.

content.heading: Termite castes
paragraphs: Termites are social insects with a queen, king, workers, soldiers and alates. The queen has a swollen abdomen and lays eggs. The king stays beside her, unlike the male bee.
Workers are blind, pale and soft-bodied. They build galleries, forage, feed the queen and young, and some tend fungus gardens.

Soldiers have large heads and strong mandibles, and some squirt defensive fluid from a frontal gland. Alates are winged reproductives that swarm after rain, shed their wings and start new colonies. Sterile workers, overlapping generations and cooperative brood care make the colony eusocial.
bullets: The queen lays eggs and the king stays with her.
Workers build, forage and feed the colony.
Soldiers defend, while alates disperse and reproduce.
content.takeaway: Termite castes divide reproduction, work and defence.

check.question: Which termite caste has large mandibles and defends the colony?
check.why: Soldiers have enlarged heads and mandibles, and some also squirt defensive fluid.

content.heading: Bee castes
paragraphs: A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of sterile female workers and a few hundred male drones. The queen lays eggs and produces pheromones that suppress worker reproduction and keep the colony together. Workers are female.
Their jobs change with age: cleaning, nursing, comb building, guarding and foraging. They have pollen baskets, wax glands and a sting.

Drones are male. They fertilise a new queen on a mating flight and die after mating. They have no sting and are expelled before a period of food shortage, and only females have stings, because the sting is a modified ovipositor.
bullets: One queen, many sterile female workers and a few male drones.
Worker jobs change with age.
Drones mate once and die; workers defend the hive.
content.takeaway: Bee castes divide reproduction, housework and mating.

check.question: Which bee is male and fertilises the queen?
check.why: Drones are the male bees; they mate with a new queen and die afterwards.

content.heading: Division of labour and communication
paragraphs: Social life works because workers share genes with the queen's offspring, so helping the colony can pass on those shared genes. Division of labour also raises efficiency: each caste specialises in one job instead of every individual doing everything.

Pheromones coordinate the colony. The queen pheromone suppresses worker reproduction, alarm pheromones mobilise defenders, and trail pheromones guide termites to food. The bee waggle dance tells other workers the direction and distance of a food source.

Termites develop gradually through nymphs, while bees pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult. Termites recycle wood and return nutrients to the soil, but they also damage timber and buildings. Bees pollinate crops and produce honey and wax.
bullets: Division of labour raises colony efficiency.
Pheromones coordinate work, alarm and food trails.
Termites recycle wood; bees pollinate and make honey.
content.takeaway: A social insect colony is a division of labour held together by chemical signals.

check.question: The bee waggle dance communicates
options: The direction and distance of food
check.why: The dance encodes the direction and distance of a food source.

visual.caption: Two societies, two ways to divide the work.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Termites have a king; bees do not. Soldiers are termites; guard workers are bees. Termites are not ants, even though both live in colonies, so check the wings, waist and caste before answering.

content.problem: A mound contains a large egg-laying female, a male beside her, pale blind workers and large-headed soldiers. Identify the organisms and the castes.

steps.reason: A queen and a king living together point to termites.
steps.result: The colony is a termite colony.
steps.predictPrompt: Which social insect has no king?

steps.reason: The large egg-laying female is the queen.
steps.result: She is the colony's reproductive female.

steps.reason: Pale, blind, soft-bodied individuals do the building and feeding.
steps.result: They are workers.

steps.reason: Large heads and mandibles are soldier features.
steps.result: They are soldiers.

content.heading: Go deeper: Termite castes and the queen's pheromone
paragraphs: A termite colony contains a king and a queen, neuter workers and soldiers, and winged reproductives that leave to start new colonies. The king remains with the queen for life, unlike the ant king that dies after mating.

The queen produces a pheromone that suppresses reproduction in workers and soldiers. That signal holds the caste system together: when it fades, workers can become replacement reproductives. The colony therefore regulates its own development chemically.
Soldiers defend the nest with enlarged heads and mandibles, and some spray defensive fluid. Their size and strength are the reason a termite soldier is recognisable at a glance in an examination.
Winged reproductives swarm after the rains, mate in the air and land to found new colonies. Most are eaten by birds and frogs, so the swarm works only because so many individuals leave at once.
Workers feed the king and queen by trophallaxis, passing food mouth to mouth. That feeding also spreads the queen's pheromone through the colony, so the signal and the food travel together.
bullets: Termites have a king and queen that stay together for life
The queen's pheromone suppresses worker reproduction
Soldiers defend with large heads, mandibles or spray

content.heading: Go deeper: Bee castes and the waggle dance
paragraphs: A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of sterile female workers and a few hundred male drones. Workers are female, and their sting is a modified ovipositor, which is why only females sting.
Worker tasks change with age, from cleaning and nursing in the hive to foraging outside it. That age polyethism lets a young bee learn the hive before it is trusted with defence and food gathering.

The waggle dance encodes direction and distance to a food source. The angle of the dance relative to gravity gives direction, and the duration of the waggle gives distance. Followers read both and fly to the named place.
The dance is read on a vertical comb, where gravity marks the direction. A follower turns the same angle from vertical to recover the angle from the sun outside the hive.
A scout that finds food returns and dances, while followers decide whether to follow. The decision depends on the balance between the source named in the dance and the needs of the hive.
bullets: Bee workers are female; only females sting
Worker jobs change with age inside the hive
The waggle dance encodes direction and distance

content.heading: Go deeper: Pheromones and how colonies coordinate
paragraphs: Pheromones are chemicals released outside the body that affect other members of the same species. Alarm pheromones mobilise defenders, trail pheromones guide termites to food and the queen's pheromone suppresses reproduction. Each signal has its own effect.

A colony therefore coordinates without a brain directing every individual. Workers respond to chemical messages in the air and on surfaces. The result looks planned, but it is the sum of responses to a few signals.

Division of labour follows from the signals. Castes specialise because pheromones and nutrition channel each individual into one role, and that specialisation raises the efficiency of the whole colony.
A queen that is failing produces less pheromone, and workers then rear replacement reproductives. The colony therefore changes its own leadership by chemistry, not by election.
Alarm pheromone from a stung bee recruits defenders to the intruder. Workers that sting die because the barbed sting tears away, so the signal and the sacrifice happen together.
A colony that loses its queen can still survive if workers rear a new queen from a young larva. The pheromone that once suppressed them falls, and the colony replaces the loss.
bullets: Alarm, trail and queen pheromones coordinate the colony
Coordination is the sum of responses to chemical signals
Caste specialisation raises colony efficiency

content.question: Explain why a colony with sterile workers can still be successful.
hints: The queen reproduces, so the workers do not need to.
Workers share genes with the queen's offspring.
Division of labour lets each caste specialise.

lessons.title: Feeding Adaptations
lessons.objective: Relate bird beaks and feet, and insect mouthparts, to the food each organism eats.

content.heading: Feeding adaptations
paragraphs: A hawk's beak tears meat, a sunbird's beak probes a flower, and a mosquito's mouthparts pierce skin. Feeding structures are shaped by diet, and the exam asks you to match the structure to the food.

content.heading: Bird beaks
paragraphs: A bird's beak is its main feeding tool, and its shape follows the diet. Insectivorous birds have slender, pointed beaks for picking insects; the woodpecker uses a chisel beak and a long tongue to extract grubs. Granivorous birds have short, stout, conical beaks for cracking seeds, and nectar-feeding birds have long, slender, curved beaks for probing flowers.
Carnivorous birds have strong, hooked beaks for tearing flesh. Ducks have broad, flat beaks with lamellae for filtering food from water. Vultures have hooked beaks for tearing carrion.
Beaks are also used for preening, nest building and defence, so a single shape can serve more than one job.
bullets: Beak shape follows diet.
Hooked beaks tear, conical beaks crack and long beaks probe.
A woodpecker uses a chisel beak and a long tongue.
content.takeaway: Read the diet from the shape of the beak.

check.question: A short, stout, conical beak is best suited for
check.why: A short, stout, conical beak can crack hard seed coats.

content.heading: Bird legs and feet
paragraphs: Bird feet are adapted to habitat and hunting method. Perching birds have three toes forward and one back, which grip a branch. Raptors have strong talons for seizing prey.
Wading birds have long legs and spread toes for walking in shallow water. Swimming birds have webbed feet that push against water.

Running birds have long, strong legs and reduced toes. Climbing birds, such as woodpeckers and parrots, have two toes forward and two back, a grip that holds bark or branches. The same foot can be used for walking, scratching, defence and carrying food, so the structure reflects the bird's whole way of life.
bullets: Webbed feet swim; long legs wade.
Talons seize prey; perching feet grip branches.
Leg structure matches habitat and hunting method.
content.takeaway: Feet show where a bird lives and how it catches food.

check.question: A duck's webbed feet are an adaptation for
check.why: Webbed feet paddle efficiently through water.

content.heading: Insect mouthparts
paragraphs: Insect mouthparts are matched to food and feeding method. Biting-chewing insects, such as grasshoppers, cockroaches and beetles, have hard mandibles for cutting solid food. Piercing-sucking insects, such as the female mosquito, aphid and tsetse fly, have needle-like stylets that pierce and suck.

Siphoning insects, such as butterflies and moths, have a long coiled proboscis for nectar. Houseflies have sponging mouthparts that absorb liquids. Bees have chewing-lapping mouthparts for nectar and pollen.
The male mosquito feeds on nectar; only the female bites, because she needs blood for her eggs. Mouthpart type is one of the most reliable clues to an insect's diet.
bullets: Mosquito: piercing-sucking; butterfly: siphoning.
Housefly: sponging; bee: chewing-lapping.
Only the female mosquito takes blood.
content.takeaway: Insect mouthparts are tools matched to the food and feeding method.

check.question: A butterfly feeds on nectar with a coiled proboscis. Its mouthparts are
check.why: A long coiled proboscis that siphons nectar is the siphoning type.

visual.caption: Solid food is cut; liquid food is pierced and sucked.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The female mosquito bites; the male feeds on nectar. A butterfly's proboscis is coiled at rest and extended to feed. Read the sex and the food before choosing a mouthpart.

content.problem: A bird has a long, slender, curved beak. Another has a short, stout, conical beak. Match each to its diet.

steps.reason: A long, slender, curved beak can probe deep into a flower.
steps.result: The first bird feeds on nectar.
steps.predictPrompt: Which beak shape cracks seeds?

steps.reason: A short, stout, conical beak can apply force to a hard seed coat.
steps.result: The second bird feeds on seeds.

steps.reason: The beak is a tool, and the food is the job it must do.
steps.result: Shape and diet match.

steps.reason: The two beaks solve different feeding problems.
steps.result: One is nectarivorous and the other granivorous.

content.heading: Go deeper: Beaks, teeth and the diet behind the shape
paragraphs: A beak is a feeding tool whose shape follows the food it must handle. A short, stout, conical beak cracks hard seeds, while a slender, pointed beak picks insects and a hooked beak tears flesh. The shape can be read from the diet before any observation of feeding.

The same logic applies to mammalian teeth. Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind, and a dental formula counts each type. A sheep and a lion therefore carry different toolkits because their diets differ.

Beaks and teeth are also used for preening, defence and nest building, so a shape can serve more than one job. Examiners expect the diet to be the primary reading, with the other uses as supporting evidence.
A grazing antelope has a broad muzzle and high-crowned molars for grinding grasses. A carnivore such as a lion has shearing teeth and canines for cutting flesh, and a reduced grinding surface.
Horses are an exception that proves the rule. Their teeth are high-crowned because grass contains grit, so the molars wear down slowly enough to last a lifetime.
bullets: Beak shape follows diet: crack, pick, tear or probe
Teeth are toolkits: cut, tear and grind matched to diet
Other uses exist, but diet is the primary reading

content.heading: Go deeper: Feet, tongues and the handling of food
paragraphs: Feet gather and handle food after the beak or mouth has taken it. A woodpecker uses its bill and tongue to extract grubs from wood, while a duck uses its broad bill and lamellae to filter small organisms from water. The foot then supports the body in the feeding place.

Webbed feet paddle efficiently through water, and long toes spread weight on soft mud. A raptor's talons hold and tear prey. Each foot is therefore shaped for the surface where the animal feeds, not only for walking.

A long tongue is as much a feeding adaptation as a beak. A nectar-feeding bird probes a flower with a coiled tongue, while an antelope uses its tongue to wrap around grass. The tongue extends the reach of the mouth.
A flamingo filters water with lamellae while standing on one leg, so its feeding posture is part of the adaptation. The long neck reaches into water while the body stays clear of the surface.
A woodpecker also uses its stiff tail as a prop while it hammers. The tail, bill and tongue therefore form one feeding apparatus, not three separate adaptations.
bullets: The bill takes food; the foot holds the animal at the feeding place
Webbed feet, talons and long toes match surface and prey
Long tongues extend the reach of the mouth

content.heading: Go deeper: Insect mouthparts and the insects that compete with us
paragraphs: Insect mouthparts decide both diet and damage. Biting-chewing mouthparts cut plant tissue and leave ragged edges, while piercing-sucking mouthparts penetrate tissue and drain fluids. Siphoning mouthparts form a tube for nectar, and sponging mouthparts mop up liquids.

A locust is a biting-chewing pest that strips leaves and can destroy a whole field. An aphid is piercing-sucking, weakens the plant and can introduce viruses. A mosquito is also piercing-sucking, but its damage is the disease it transmits rather than the blood it drinks.

Control follows the damage. Chewing pests are attacked with stomach poisons, sucking pests with systemic insecticides, and vectors by habitat control. Identifying the mouthpart therefore predicts the control method.
Houseflies do not bite, yet their sponging mouthparts pick up bacteria from refuse and deposit them on food. Sponging therefore spreads disease without piercing the skin at all.
Aphids also walk a virus from plant to plant when they move. The mouthpart is therefore a route as well as a feeding tool, and control must break both routes.
bullets: Biting-chewing cuts tissue; piercing-sucking drains fluid
Damage and control follow the mouthpart type
Vectors harm through transmitted pathogens, not only by feeding

content.question: Why does a mosquito need piercing-sucking mouthparts while a butterfly does not?
hints: The mosquito feeds on blood or plant sap; the butterfly feeds on nectar.
Blood is inside a tissue; nectar is in a flower.
A proboscis can reach nectar without piercing skin.

lessons.title: Defence and Mating Adaptations
lessons.objective: Explain how structures and behaviour protect organisms from predators and help them secure mates.

content.heading: Defence and mating adaptations
paragraphs: A stick insect freezes like a twig, a praying mantis raises spiny forelegs, a toad inflates its body, and a male Agama flashes its red head. Defence and mating are both contests, and adaptations are the weapons.

content.heading: Defence: hide, startle, fight
paragraphs: Camouflage is the first defence. A stick insect resembles a twig and a praying mantis resembles a leaf, so a predator may pass without noticing them. If detected, a startle display can frighten an attacker: the praying mantis raises its spiny forelegs and wings, and the eyed hawk-moth exposes eyespots.

Physical barriers raise the cost of attack. Hedgehogs and porcupines have spines, snails have shells, and some caterpillars have irritating hairs. Chemical defence is common: toads secrete toxins from parotoid glands, millipedes release irritating fluids, and stink bugs spray a foul smell.
A toad can also inflate its body to look larger, and a lizard can drop its tail to escape.
bullets: Camouflage avoids detection; startle displays frighten.
Spines, shells and toxins raise the cost of attack.
Autotomy and fleeing remove the animal from danger.
content.takeaway: Defence works by hiding, startling, blocking or poisoning the attacker.

check.question: A toad's parotoid glands are an adaptation for
check.why: The glands secrete toxins that deter predators, which is chemical defence.

content.heading: Mating: signal, compete, display
paragraphs: Sexual dimorphism means males and females differ in size, colour or structure. In Agama lizards, the dominant male has a bright red or orange head and a blue body, while the female is duller. The male displays and defends a territory, and the colour advertises his condition to females and rivals, and a territory secures food, shelter and mates, and reduces fighting.

Birds use displays: a peacock fans his tail, a male weaver builds and displays a nest, and some males feed their partners during courtship. Males also compete directly. Kob antelopes lock horns, goats butt heads, and baboons fight for dominance, though most contests are ritualised rather than fatal.
Bright colours and large weapons carry costs: they attract predators and use energy.
bullets: Sexual dimorphism separates male and female appearance.
Display and territory advertise quality.
Bright colours and weapons carry survival costs.
content.takeaway: Mating adaptations advertise or defend access to a mate.

check.question: The bright red head of a male Agama lizard is mainly for
check.why: The red head is a sexual signal used in display and territory defence.

content.heading: Balancing defence and display
paragraphs: The same structure can serve defence and display. Antlers and horns are used in combat and also advertise strength. Bright colours attract mates but make a male easier for a predator to see.
A chameleon changes colour for camouflage, temperature control and communication, so one skin serves several jobs.

Parental care extends defence to offspring. Cichlid fish guard their eggs, birds mob predators near the nest, and mammals defend their young. The balance is never perfect: survival and reproduction pull in different directions, and each adaptation is a compromise that raises fitness in its own habitat.
bullets: One structure can serve defence and display.
Sexual signals trade safety for mating success.
Parental care is defence extended to offspring.
content.takeaway: Survival and reproduction pull in opposite directions, and adaptations balance them.

check.question: A peacock's large tail is best explained as
options: A sexual display that attracts mates
check.why: The tail is a courtship display; its cost is carried because it improves mating success.

visual.caption: Survival and reproduction pull in different directions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Agama males are the red-headed sex; females are duller. Bright male colour is sexual selection, not warning colouration. Not every horn is a defence structure, since some are used mainly in mating contests.

content.problem: A male bird has long tail feathers and bright plumage, and predators catch it more often than dull males. Explain why the trait persists.

steps.reason: Bright plumage and a long tail make the male easier to see and harder to escape.
steps.result: Survival is reduced.
steps.predictPrompt: Which sex usually chooses the mate?

steps.reason: Females prefer the display, so the male gets more mates.
steps.result: Reproduction is increased.

steps.reason: A trait spreads when its reproductive benefit outweighs its survival cost.
steps.result: The display raises the male's fitness.

steps.reason: This is sexual selection, not natural selection for survival alone.
steps.result: The trait persists because it wins mates.

content.heading: Go deeper: Camouflage, startle and chemical defence
paragraphs: Camouflage hides an animal before it is seen. Cryptic colour, countershading and spot patterns break the outline, so the predator does not register a body. A resting moth on bark is the standard example because its pattern matches the substrate in light and shadow.
Startle displays hide in the opposite way. A butterfly flashes bright eyespots to suggest a larger animal and frightens the bird away. The display works for a moment, which is long enough for escape.

Chemical defence is the last resort. Acids, toxins and irritants make the prey costly to eat, and many species advertise that cost with bright colours. The advertisement, the startle and the camouflage therefore form one defensive system.
The eyespots of a butterfly work because a bird mistakes them for the eyes of a larger animal. The bluff buys a moment, and the butterfly uses it to escape rather than to fight.
Some mantises show a sudden flash of eyespots on the underside of the wings. The flash is hidden at rest and revealed only when the predator is close enough to be startled.
bullets: Camouflage prevents detection by breaking the outline
Startle displays suggest a larger or dangerous animal
Chemical defence makes the prey costly to eat

content.heading: Go deeper: Sexual dimorphism and the territory
paragraphs: Sexual dimorphism is a difference in size, colour or structure between males and females. In Agama lizards the dominant male is bright red and blue, while the female is duller. The colour advertises condition to females and rivals.

A territory secures food, shelter and mates, and reduces fighting. A male that holds a territory defends it by display first and by force only when display fails. Territory therefore links mating to survival.

Kob antelopes, goats and baboons show the same pattern in different forms. Horns, butting and dominance contests advertise quality, and most contests are ritualised rather than fatal because a serious wound wastes the winner.
A territory holder spends energy on display and defence instead of feeding. That cost is why territory holders are often in better condition, and why females use it as a signal of quality.
A male that holds the best territory may mate more often even if he is not the largest male. Territory quality can therefore matter as much as body size in mating success.
bullets: Sexual dimorphism separates male and female appearance
Territories secure food, shelter and mates
Most mating contests are ritualised, not fatal

content.heading: Go deeper: Displays and the cost of being noticed
paragraphs: A peacock fans its train, a male weaver builds and displays a nest, and some males feed their partners during courtship. Each display is a signal that can be judged by the female before mating occurs.
Bright colours and large weapons carry costs. They attract predators, use energy and make the owner more visible to enemies. A trait persists only when its mating benefit outweighs that cost.
Mating adaptations therefore balance two pressures: sexual selection favours the signal, while natural selection favours survival. The final form of a display is the compromise between them.
A female that chooses a bright male may gain good genes but also marks her offspring as visible. The balance between those two pressures decides how bright the display can become in that habitat.
A weaver's nest is both a display and a shelter. A female chooses the nest she accepts, so the male builds under her judgment before the eggs are laid.
A dull male that holds a good territory may be chosen over a bright male with no territory. Female choice therefore weighs the display together with the home it guards.
bullets: Displays advertise quality to females before mating
Bright traits attract predators and use energy
A trait persists when mating benefit outweighs survival cost

content.question: A stick insect is camouflaged, while a male peacock is conspicuous. Explain why both strategies can succeed.
hints: The two species face different selection pressures.
Camouflage improves survival; display improves mating success.
Fitness depends on surviving and reproducing.

lessons.title: Temperature and Water Regulation
lessons.objective: Explain how organisms regulate body temperature and conserve water, using basking, hibernation, aestivation, skin coverings, spines and scales.

content.heading: Temperature and water regulation
paragraphs: A lizard basks on a rock, a frog buries itself in mud, an acacia has thorns, and a camel has thick fur. Each solves the same two problems: keeping the body at a workable temperature and holding on to water.

content.heading: Temperature regulation
paragraphs: Endotherms, such as birds and mammals, generate heat internally and keep a fairly constant body temperature. Hair, fur, feathers and blubber insulate. Sweating and vasodilation lose heat through the skin, panting loses heat through the mouth and lungs, and shivering and vasoconstriction conserve it, and ectotherms, such as lizards, amphibians and fish, gain heat from the environment, so their body temperature varies.

A lizard basks by flattening its body and turning broadside to the sun, then retreats to shade when it is too hot. Hibernation is winter dormancy, with low metabolism and stored fat. Aestivation is summer drought dormancy, used by lungfish and some snails.
The two look similar, but the season and the trigger are different.
bullets: Endotherms generate heat; ectotherms gain it from the environment.
Basking, shade and burrowing control temperature behaviourally.
Hibernation is winter; aestivation is summer drought.
content.takeaway: Temperature control is either internal heat production or behaviour in the habitat.

check.question: A lizard lying on a rock in the morning is
check.why: The lizard gains heat from the sun and the warm rock, which is basking.

content.heading: Water conservation in animals
paragraphs: Desert animals reduce water loss in several ways. Thick fur or scales limit evaporation, the kidneys produce concentrated urine, the faeces are dry, and sweat glands are few. Many are nocturnal or burrow during the day, and the camel stores fat in its hump as an energy reserve, while its kidneys and nose reduce water loss.

Reptile scales are waterproof keratin, and pangolin scales, the only mammalian scales, are keratin too; both reduce water loss and add protection. Insects have a waxy cuticle, spiracles that can close, and Malpighian tubules that concentrate waste. Freshwater fish excrete dilute urine, while marine fish drink water and excrete excess salts.
Each strategy keeps the body's water and salt balance within limits.
bullets: Waterproof coverings reduce evaporation.
Concentrated urine and dry faeces conserve water.
Nocturnal and burrowing behaviour avoids heat.
content.takeaway: Water conservation means reducing loss and concentrating waste.

check.question: Which feature helps a desert mammal conserve water?
check.why: Concentrated urine removes waste with less water loss.

content.heading: Water conservation in plants
paragraphs: Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry habitats. They have a thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled or hairy leaves, and reduced leaf area. Some have deep roots, others have shallow widespread roots, and succulents store water in thick stems or leaves, and CAM photosynthesis lets them open stomata at night, when water loss is lower.

In cactus, a desert plant, spines are modified leaves that reduce surface area and transpiration and deter herbivores. Nigerian xerophytes such as acacia and baobab rely more on deep roots and small leaves. Hydrophytes, such as water lilies, have large air spaces, a thin cuticle, stomata on the upper surface and poorly developed roots.
Mesophytes, including most Nigerian crops, sit between the two extremes.
bullets: Xerophytes reduce water loss with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata.
Spines are modified leaves that cut transpiration.
Hydrophytes have air spaces and little waterproofing.
content.takeaway: A plant's water strategy shows in its leaves, stomata and roots.

check.question: Cactus spines are modified leaves that mainly
check.why: Spines reduce leaf surface area and transpiration, and they deter herbivores.

visual.caption: The same plant body, tuned to opposite water conditions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Hibernation is winter dormancy; aestivation is summer drought dormancy. Spines are modified leaves, not stems. A camel's hump stores fat, not water, so do not repeat the common water-storage mistake.

content.problem: A cactus has spines, a thick stem and shallow roots. A water lily has broad leaves and air spaces. Match each plant to its habitat and explain.

steps.reason: Spines reduce water loss and a thick stem stores water.
steps.result: The cactus is a xerophyte, adapted to dry land.
steps.predictPrompt: Which plant has little waterproofing?

steps.reason: Air spaces keep the leaves afloat and supply oxygen to submerged parts.
steps.result: The water lily is a hydrophyte, adapted to water.

steps.reason: The cactus reduces leaf area; the water lily maximises it.
steps.result: The two leaves solve opposite problems.

steps.reason: Water availability shapes the plant body.
steps.result: Cactus is a xerophyte; water lily is a hydrophyte.

content.heading: Go deeper: Endothermy, ectothermy and behaviour
paragraphs: Endotherms generate heat internally and keep a fairly constant body temperature. Birds and mammals insulate themselves with feathers, hair and blubber, and they lose heat by sweating, panting and dilating blood vessels. They also conserve heat by vasoconstriction and shivering.

Ectotherms gain heat from the environment, so their body temperature varies with the day. A lizard basks by flattening its body broadside to the sun and retreats to shade when it is too hot. Behaviour therefore does for the ectotherm what physiology does for the endotherm.

Temperature regulation is thus either internal production or behavioural choice. An animal that can move between sun and shade is regulating temperature even though it generates little heat of its own.
A bird's high metabolism lets it stay active in cold weather when an ectotherm must bask. That advantage costs far more food, which is why endotherms feed more often than lizards of the same size.
A fish is an ectotherm that must find warm water to stay active. In the depths of a cold lake it becomes sluggish, which is why fish gather near the sunlit surface in the morning.
bullets: Endotherms generate heat; ectotherms gain it from the environment
Basking and shade are behavioural temperature control
Insulation, sweating, panting and shivering are physiological control

content.heading: Go deeper: Hibernation and aestivation as dormancy
paragraphs: Hibernation is winter dormancy. Metabolism falls, the body lives on stored fat and the animal wakes when food returns. It is used where winter makes feeding impossible for months.

Aestivation is summer drought dormancy. Lungfish and some snails bury themselves in mud and wait for the rains. The trigger is drought rather than cold, and the store is again fat, but the season is opposite.
The two are easily confused because both look like sleep. The season, the trigger and the stores decide the name: winter and cold mean hibernation, summer and drought mean aestivation.
Aestivation also occurs in snails that seal themselves in shells with a membrane. The animal can remain in that state for months until humidity returns, and it avoids the dry heat above ground.
A hibernator must fatten before winter, because the store decides how long it can sleep. A frog that is still feeding in December may not survive the cold that follows.
bullets: Hibernation is winter dormancy on stored fat
Aestivation is summer drought dormancy in mud
Season and trigger separate the two dormancies

content.heading: Go deeper: Water loss and how animals reduce it
paragraphs: Desert animals reduce water loss by waterproofing the body, concentrating urine and producing dry faeces. Many are nocturnal or burrow during the day, when evaporation is highest. The camel stores fat in its hump as an energy reserve and reduces water loss through its kidneys and nose.

Reptile scales are waterproof keratin, and pangolin scales are keratin too; both limit evaporation while adding protection. Insects have a waxy cuticle, spiracles that can close and Malpighian tubules that concentrate waste. Freshwater fish excrete dilute urine, while marine fish drink water and excrete excess salts.
Each strategy keeps water and salt within limits. An animal facing heat therefore conserves water by covering, concentrating and timing its activity, rather than by drinking more.
A camel's nose recovers moisture from exhaled air, so the breath it loses is drier at sunset than at dawn. That small saving, repeated all day, is part of its water economy.
A kangaroo rat never drinks in the wild but gains water from dry seeds. The water comes from respiration in metabolism, so the animal lives on the water made inside its own body.
bullets: Waterproof coverings reduce evaporation
Concentrated urine and dry faeces conserve water
Nocturnal and burrowing behaviour avoids daytime heat

content.question: Why can a camel go without drinking for days while a human cannot?
hints: The hump stores fat, which releases water when broken down.
Camels produce concentrated urine and dry faeces.
They can also tolerate a rise in body temperature and reduce sweating.

lessons.title: Root and Stem Anatomy
lessons.objective: Identify transverse sections of a root and a stem and relate their structure to their functions.

content.heading: Root and stem
paragraphs: A transverse section through a root or stem is a map you can read. From the outside in, each ring has a job, and the jobs follow the plant's two supply routes.

content.heading: The root slice
paragraphs: In a transverse section of a dicot root, the layers run outside to inside: epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, ending at the vascular cylinder.

The epidermis covers the root and bears root hairs, which take up water and dissolved mineral salts. The cortex stores starch and moves water inwards. The endodermis's Casparian strip is a waxy band that blocks the spaces between cells, so water and salts must cross its cell membranes before reaching the xylem.

The pericycle, just inside the endodermis, gives rise to branch roots. The vascular cylinder carries the xylem as a solid star in a dicot root, with phloem patches between the arms. In a monocot root, the centre is a large pith instead, and the xylem has many arms.
bullets: Epidermis with root hairs: absorbs water and salts.
Endodermis with Casparian strip: the checkpoint into the xylem.
Xylem star in dicots; pith centre in monocots.
content.takeaway: The root slice works from outside in: hair, membrane, xylem.

check.question: The Casparian strip is found in the cells of the
check.why: The Casparian strip blocks spaces between cells in the endodermis.

content.heading: The stem slice
paragraphs: In a transverse section of a dicot stem, the layers run outside to inside: cuticle and epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles arranged in a ring and a large pith at the centre.

Each vascular bundle has xylem on the inside, towards the pith, and phloem on the outside, with cambium between them. The cambium is meristematic and produces the thickening layer of wood in woody plants. In a monocot stem, the bundles are scattered through the ground tissue, there is no cambium, and secondary growth is absent.
The pith in a dicot stem stores starch and some nutrients; in monocots a distinct pith is usually not obvious because of the scattered bundles.
bullets: Epidermis and cuticle reduce water loss.
Xylem inside, phloem outside, cambium between.
Scattered bundles and no cambium: monocot stem.
content.takeaway: Ring plus cambium means wood; scattered bundles mean not.

check.question: In a dicot stem T.S., the xylem of a vascular bundle lies
check.why: Each dicot vascular bundle points its xylem inwards, towards the pith.

content.heading: Structure matched to function
paragraphs: Root hairs multiply the absorption surface; the waxy cuticle reduces evaporation; air spaces in the cortex supply the deeper cells. Xylem runs from root to leaf, moving water up; phloem runs from leaf to root, moving food down.

Lignified xylem and the sclerenchyma fibres supporting the vascular bundles give stems their rigidity. Where a stem is still young and tender, collenchyma under the epidermis bends instead of breaking. Roots anchor the plant, and their branch roots emerge from the pericycle.

When you see a section, match the arrangement to its organ: star-shaped xylem with no pith is a dicot root; a large pith centre is a monocot root; bundles in a ring with cambium is a dicot stem; scattered bundles is a monocot stem.
bullets: Root hairs increase the absorbing surface.
Xylem goes up; phloem goes down.
Ring plus cambium is dicot; scattered is monocot.
content.takeaway: A section is a map: read the arrangement and you name the organ.

check.question: Which pattern describes a monocot stem T.S.?
options: Bundles in a ring with cambium
A xylem centre with no phloem
check.why: Monocot stems carry scattered vascular bundles without cambium.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Xylem star with no pith is a dicot root; a star with a large pith centre is a monocot root; bundles in a ring is dicot stem; scattered bundles is monocot stem.

content.problem: A transverse section shows vascular bundles scattered through the ground tissue, with xylem on the inside of each bundle and no cambium. Name the organ and explain the xylem position.

steps.reason: Scattered bundles are a monocot stem signature.
steps.result: A monocotyledonous stem.
steps.predictPrompt: What pattern would a dicot stem show instead?

steps.reason: In every vascular bundle the phloem faces outwards and the xylem faces inwards.
steps.result: The xylem points toward the centre.
steps.predictPrompt: Why is the xylem inwards in a stem?

steps.reason: No cambium means no secondary growth, consistent with a monocot.
steps.result: The plant will not form wood.

content.heading: Go deeper: Dicot and monocot roots in section
paragraphs: A dicot root shows xylem in a solid star with phloem patches between the arms. The centre is xylem, not pith, and the number of arms is small. A monocot root has many arms and a large central pith.

The endodermis and its Casparian strip form the checkpoint into the vascular cylinder. Water that enters through root hairs must cross the endodermal membranes before it reaches the xylem. That control is why the root is more than a pipe.

The pericycle just inside the endodermis gives rise to branch roots. A branch root pushes through the cortex and epidermis, so its origin inside the main root distinguishes it from an adventitious root that forms elsewhere.

Adventitious roots grow from stems or leaves rather than from the main root. A maize prop root and a sweet-potato tuber root are adventitious, so their origin is outside the primary root system entirely.
A tap root is the main root of a dicot that grows straight down. A fibrous root system is a mass of similar roots that spreads through the soil, as in maize and grasses.
bullets: Dicot root: xylem star, small arms, no pith centre
Monocot root: many xylem arms and a large pith
Branch roots arise from the pericycle

content.heading: Go deeper: Dicot and monocot stems in section
paragraphs: A dicot stem shows vascular bundles in a ring, with cambium between xylem and phloem. That cambium adds new xylem inside and new phloem outside each year, so the stem thickens. A monocot stem has scattered bundles without cambium and does not thicken in the same way.

The epidermis protects the stem, the cortex stores food and the vascular bundles conduct. In a young stem, collenchyma just under the epidermis gives flexible support, while xylem adds strength and conduction together.

Reading a section therefore starts with the arrangement: ring means dicot and scattered means monocot. The presence of cambium is the second check, because it predicts whether the stem can grow thick with age.

Herbaceous stems remain soft because they lack much lignified xylem. A yam vine and a tomato stem can be supported by collenchyma and turgor alone, while a tree trunk needs the woody core to carry its own weight.
A ring of bundles with cambium predicts a woody stem that can live for decades. Scattered bundles without cambium predict a herbaceous stem that lives only one season.
bullets: Dicot stem: bundles in a ring with cambium
Monocot stem: scattered bundles without cambium
Cambium predicts thickening with age

content.heading: Go deeper: Vascular bundles and how water and food travel together
paragraphs: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upward, and phloem carries dissolved food both up and down. In a bundle they sit side by side, with xylem facing the centre and phloem facing outward. That pairing is why a vascular bundle is the unit of plant transport.
Root hairs increase the absorbing surface of the root without adding much volume. They are extensions of epidermal cells, not separate cells, so they extend the surface that meets the soil water.
A transverse section is an experiment in reading. Each tissue must be named in order from outside to inside, because examiners score the sequence rather than isolated labels.
A graft joins the vascular tissue of two plants so that water and food can pass between them. That is why the cambium of the scion and the stock must meet when a mango is grafted.
The Casparian strip is waxy and impermeable, so it blocks the cell wall route completely. Water must cross a living membrane to enter the xylem, and that crossing is where absorption is controlled.
bullets: Xylem conducts water up; phloem translocates food both ways
Root hairs extend the absorbing surface of the root
Read a section from outside to inside in order

content.question: Explain why a young maize stem does not get woody.
hints: Maize is a monocotyledon.
Its vascular bundles are scattered and lack cambium.
Without cambium there is no secondary thickening.

lessons.title: Leaf Anatomy
lessons.objective: Identify a transverse section of a leaf and relate leaf structure to photosynthesis and gas exchange.

content.heading: Leaf anatomy
paragraphs: A leaf is a solar panel and a gas-exchange surface in one. A transverse section shows how light reaches the chloroplasts and how air enters and leaves through the stomata.

content.heading: The upper surface
paragraphs: From outside in, the upper surface is a waxy cuticle, then the upper epidermis. The cuticle is a waterproof layer that limits uncontrolled evaporation, and the upper epidermis is usually transparent and contains no chloroplasts, so it passes light to the cells beneath.
Below the upper epidermis lie the palisade mesophyll cells, elongated, arranged in one or more rows and filled with chloroplasts. This is where most photosynthesis takes place.
Many leaves also have few or no stomata on the upper surface, and when they do, it is usually on a leaf that floats and receives light from above.
bullets: Cuticle: reduces uncontrolled water loss.
Upper epidermis: transparent, no chloroplasts.
Palisade mesophyll: chloroplast-packed, main photosynthesis tissue.
content.takeaway: Light arrives through the top; water is lost through the bottom.

check.question: Which layer blocks most uncontrolled water loss?
check.why: The cuticle is a waterproof layer over the epidermis.

content.heading: The middle: light and gas exchange
paragraphs: Between the palisade and the lower epidermis is the spongy mesophyll: loosely arranged parenchyma cells with large intercellular air spaces. Those spaces connect with the stomata below, so carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour diffuse quickly to and from the cells.

Veins run through the mesophyll, packed into vascular bundles. In most dicot leaves, xylem lies towards the upper side of the midrib and phloem towards the lower side. Xylem brings the water that photosynthesis needs; phloem carries the sugars away.
The veins also serve as the leaf's skeleton. The central midrib branches into smaller veins, giving the leaf its shape and plumbing the mesophyll.
bullets: Spongy mesophyll: loose with large air spaces.
Vein bundles: xylem above, phloem below.
Veins support the leaf and carry water in, food out.
content.takeaway: The middle of the leaf breathes and ships its cargo.

check.question: The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll mainly speed up
check.why: Large air spaces shorten the path for gas diffusion.

content.heading: The lower surface and veins
paragraphs: The lower epidermis carries the stomata. Each stoma is a pore bordered by two guard cells. When the guard cells take up water they swell and bend outwards, opening the pore; when they lose water they shrink and close it.

This controls water loss and gas exchange together. Most dicot leaves keep most stomata on the lower surface because the upper surface is exposed to light and heat; placing the stomata there would waste water. Shade leaves and the leaves of floating plants often have stomata on both surfaces.
In a T.S., stomata and guard cells are the signature of the lower epidermis. The midrib carries the main vein and gives the leaf its central ridge.
bullets: Most stomata sit on the lower side of the leaf.
Guard cells open and close the pore by changing turgor.
Midrib: carries the main vein and supports the leaf.
content.takeaway: Stomata are the leaf's adjustable windows.

check.question: Guard cells open a stoma when they
check.why: Guard cells swell as they take up water, bending apart to open the pore.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Read a leaf T.S. from the top: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis with stomata. If stomata appear on the upper side, the leaf is usually floating.

content.problem: Identify the tissues from the top of a T.S. to the bottom and state the job of each.

steps.reason: Start at the upper surface.
steps.result: Cuticle, transparent layer that reduces evaporation.
steps.predictPrompt: Why does the cuticle sit on top and not the bottom?

steps.reason: Identify the next layer.
steps.result: Upper epidermis, transparent and chloroplast-free.

steps.reason: Find the photosynthetic tissue.
steps.result: Palisade mesophyll, elongated cells packed with chloroplasts.

steps.reason: Identify the air space tissue.
steps.result: Spongy mesophyll, loose with air spaces for gas exchange.

steps.reason: Find the pores.
steps.result: Lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cuticle, epidermis and the light that reaches the cell
paragraphs: The upper epidermis is covered by a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss. In most leaves it is transparent, so light passes to the palisade cells beneath. A thick cuticle is therefore a water adaptation, not a barrier to light.
