Palisade mesophyll holds the most chloroplasts because it receives the strongest light. A deep green, flat leaf is built for photosynthesis in full sun, while a shade leaf is thinner and spreads the same tissue over a larger area.
The spongy mesophyll beneath the palisade has large air spaces. Those spaces shorten the path for carbon dioxide and oxygen between the stomata and the photosynthetic cells.
A desert leaf is often pale or grey because it reflects light. That reflection reduces heating and water loss, so the colour is a water adaptation as well as a light one.
A leaf in full sun is usually thicker than a shade leaf because it contains more palisade tissue. The extra tissue intercepts the stronger light without overheating the cells beneath.
bullets: The cuticle cuts water loss but lets light through
Palisade cells hold the most chloroplasts
Air spaces in spongy tissue shorten the gas path

content.heading: Go deeper: Stomata, guard cells and the water cost of breathing
paragraphs: A stoma is a pore bordered by two guard cells. When they take up water they become turgid, bend outward and open the pore. When they lose water they shrink, become straight and close it.

Opening the pore admits carbon dioxide for photosynthesis but at the cost of water loss. A leaf therefore trades one for the other, and it closes the pore when water is scarce even though carbon dioxide then becomes limiting.
Most dicot leaves keep most stomata on the lower surface, away from direct sun and heat. Floating leaves reverse the pattern because the lower surface faces the water.
Opening and closing is controlled by potassium and malate inside the guard cells. When potassium enters, water follows and the cells swell; when it leaves, the pore closes within minutes.
A wilting plant closes its stomata long before it dies. That closure saves water but starves the leaf of carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis falls as soon as the pores shut.
bullets: Guard cells open and close the pore by changing turgor
Gas exchange costs water, so pores close in drought
Most stomata sit on the lower, cooler surface

content.heading: Go deeper: Veins, midrib and how a leaf is plumbed
paragraphs: The midrib carries the main vein and gives the leaf its central ridge. The vein contains xylem bringing water and phloem carrying food away, so it is both a pipe and a beam. Without it the leaf would collapse under its own weight.
Smaller veins branch from the midrib and deliver water to every part of the lamina. The network divides the leaf into smaller units, so a damage to one vein does not dry the whole leaf.

A transverse section of a leaf therefore shows the same tissues as a stem but arranged for light and gas exchange. Epidermis, mesophyll and vascular tissue appear in a different order because the function is different.
A broken vein can be seen when a leaf is torn, because the xylem still conducts to the torn edge. That is why a leaf often wilts first at the margin after a vein is cut.
The midrib also protects the lamina from tearing. A leaf that is folded along the midrib resists cracking, which is why most leaves fold neatly rather than crumpling across the surface.
bullets: The midrib carries the main vein and supports the leaf
Vein networks shorten the path of water to each cell
Leaf tissue order follows light and gas exchange

content.question: Explain how the arrangement of palisade and spongy mesophyll suits the functions of the leaf.
hints: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts and face the light.
Spongy air spaces open into the stomatal chambers.
Xylem feeds water into both layers.

lessons.title: Supporting Tissues in Plants
lessons.objective: Identify collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem fibres and describe their distribution in roots, stems and leaves.

content.heading: Support without bones
paragraphs: A plant holds itself up with living, corner-thickened cells and dead, lignified ones. Where each kind sits tells you what the plant is doing with its support.

content.heading: The four supporting tissues
paragraphs: Collenchyma is living at maturity. Its cell walls are unevenly thickened, often at the corners, with cellulose and pectin. It hugs young stems, petioles and leaf stalks, giving flexible support that can bend.

Sclerenchyma is dead at maturity. Its walls are thickened with lignin. Fibres are long and spindle-shaped and give tensile strength to stems and leaves; sclereids are short and brittle and make hard shells, stone fruit and the gritty texture of a guava.

Xylem vessels and tracheids are dead at maturity and lignified, so they carry water and hold the stem rigid. Phloem fibres, lying within the phloem patches, are also lignified and are used where toughness is needed; they are also called bast fibres.
bullets: Collenchyma: living, corner-thickened, cellulose and pectin.
Sclerenchyma: dead, walls thickened with lignin.
Xylem and phloem fibres: lignified and rigid.
content.takeaway: Living cells bend; lignified cells hold.

check.question: Which supporting tissue is living at maturity?
check.why: Collenchyma is the living supporting tissue with cellulose/pectin corner thickening.

content.heading: Where the support sits
paragraphs: In a young stem, collenchyma lies directly under the epidermis. Sclerenchyma fibres cap the vascular bundles, especially in jute, kenaf and similar crop plants, and xylem lies inside. In leaves, the midrib and the main veins carry bundles of both tissues.
In roots, xylem occupies the centre because a root pushes through soil more than it lifts a canopy. There is usually little sclerenchyma because roots are rarely in tension.
Examples for exams: fibre caps in the stem are sclerenchyma; collenchyma in a young stem or leaf stalk bends without snapping; xylem supports the woody stem by way of its vessels and fibres.
bullets: Stem: collenchyma under epidermis, sclerenchyma caps the bundles.
Root: xylem at the centre.
Leaf: support runs in the midrib and main veins.
content.takeaway: Where the load is, the fibres are.

check.question: In a young stem, collenchyma is found
check.why: Collenchyma hugs the stem directly beneath the epidermis.

content.heading: How to read the section
paragraphs: Exam questions turn support into descriptions: uneven thickening and living cells give collenchyma; dead, lignified cells give sclerenchyma or xylem; dead cells in the phloem patches are the phloem fibres.

Then locate each tissue. Collenchyma beneath the epidermis in young stems is a young-plant clue; sclerenchyma in bast fibres is a jute or kenaf clue; xylem at the centre is a root clue; xylem inside and phloem outside in scattered patches is a monocot stem.
So the full answer chains together: the identity of the tissue, its wall chemistry, and its location in the organ.
bullets: Wall chemistry names the tissue: cellulose vs lignin.
Location: under epidermis, bundle caps, centre or veins.
Chain identity plus wall chemistry plus location.
content.takeaway: Name the tissue, state its wall, then say where it sits.

check.question: Cells described as dead at maturity with walls thickened by lignin are
check.why: Both sclerenchyma and xylem are lignified and dead at maturity.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the cell is living with corner thickening, it is collenchyma; if it is dead and lignified it is sclerenchyma or xylem; if the fibres lie among phloem patches, they are phloem fibres.

content.problem: Identify the tissue: 'Unevenly thickened at the corners and found under the epidermis of a sunflower stem.'

steps.reason: Uneven corner thickening with cellulose points to collenchyma.
steps.result: Collenchyma.
steps.predictPrompt: What if the same cells were dead and lignified instead?

steps.reason: Collenchyma is alive at maturity.
steps.result: Flexible support under tension.

steps.reason: It sits directly under the epidermis in a young stem.
steps.result: Matches the clue.

content.heading: Go deeper: Collenchyma, the living support
paragraphs: Collenchyma is a living supporting tissue with thickened cellulose and pectin walls, strongest at the corners. The thickening gives strength while the cell stays alive and can grow with the plant. It is found just under the epidermis of young stems and leaf stalks.
Because it is alive, collenchyma can support a growing organ that is still elongating. A seedling stem bends in wind and recovers, which a dead, lignified tissue could not do without breaking.
The tissue breaks easily under damage because the walls are not lignified. A bent celery stalk snaps the collenchyma first, which is why the same tissue is both flexible and vulnerable.
Collenchyma also occurs in the leaf stalk, where it must resist bending without breaking. A young petiole can flex in wind and recover because its support is alive and elastic.
Collenchyma thickens most at the corners, which is why a section shows bright patches just under the epidermis. Those corners give the stem its stringy texture when it is pulled apart.
bullets: Collenchyma is living, with cellulose and pectin corner thickening
It supports young, growing stems and leaf stalks
It bends without lignin but snaps under sharp damage

content.heading: Go deeper: Sclerenchyma, lignin and the hard tissues
paragraphs: Sclerenchyma is a dead supporting tissue whose walls are heavily lignified. Stone cells in a guava give the gritty texture, and fibres in jute and kenaf give bast fibre its strength for ropes and sacks.

Because the cells are dead at maturity, they cannot grow with the organ. They therefore appear in tissues that have finished elongating, such as husks, seed coats and the caps of vascular bundles in mature stems.
Lignin makes the wall waterproof and resistant to decay. That is why sclerenchymatous fibres survive rotting, while collenchyma does not.
Bast fibres are harvested by retting, in which microbes dissolve the middle lamella that holds the fibres together. The fibres are then spun into yarn for sacks and ropes.
Sclerenchyma is so hard that it is used to test for lignin in the laboratory. A stain that colours lignified walls red reveals the fibres and stone cells in a crushed sample.
Sclerenchyma is also found in the husk of a coconut, where the hard shell protects the seed. That shell survives rotting because lignin resists both water and microbes.
bullets: Sclerenchyma is dead with lignified walls
Stone cells give grit; bast fibres give rope strength
Lignin makes the tissue waterproof and hard to rot

content.heading: Go deeper: Xylem and phloem as supporting as well as conducting tissues
paragraphs: Xylem supports as well as conducts. Its vessels and fibres are lignified and form much of the wood of a tree. The trunk is strong because its conducting tissue is also its skeleton.

Phloem supports less, because its sieve tubes and companion cells are living and thin-walled. A stem that is mostly phloem, such as a young shoot, needs collenchyma for support while the xylem is still developing.
Distribution therefore predicts function. Sclerenchyma caps the bundles, collenchyma hugs the stem and xylem forms the woody core, so a section can be read from the outside in.
When a tree is ring-barked, the phloem is removed and food cannot reach the roots. The tree dies from the roots upward even though water still rises through the xylem.
The wood of a tree is secondary xylem made by the vascular cambium. Each year the cambium adds a ring of xylem inside and phloem outside, so the trunk grows from the inside out.
bullets: Xylem vessels and fibres form the wood and support the tree
Phloem is living and thin-walled, so it supports little alone
Read support from outside in: collenchyma, fibre caps, xylem

content.question: Explain why sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity and why this works well for support.
hints: Their walls are thickened with lignin.
No living contents are needed once the wall is rigid.
The empty cells save space and add strength.

lessons.title: Mammalian Internal Organs
lessons.objective: Examine the arrangement of the mammalian internal organs and describe the appearance and position of the digestive, reproductive and excretory organs.

content.heading: Inside the mammal
paragraphs: The diaphragm splits the trunk into thorax above and abdomen below. Once you know which systems live in which cavity, the organ map stops being a guessing game.

content.heading: The two body cavities
paragraphs: The thoracic cavity holds the lungs on either side, the heart between them, slightly to the left, and the thymus above. They are protected by the ribcage.

Below the diaphragm, the abdominal cavity holds the stomach high on the left, J-shaped; the liver and its gall bladder under the diaphragm on the right; the spleen behind the stomach; the pancreas behind the stomach; the kidneys on the posterior abdominal wall; and the intestines filling the lower cavity. The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm to reach the stomach.
The organs themselves are covered by membrane: pleura around the lungs and pericardium around the heart. In the abdomen, the visceral and parietal peritoneum wrap and suspend the gut organs.
bullets: Thorax: lungs and heart.
Abdomen: liver, stomach, pancreas, spleen.
Kidneys: posterior abdominal wall (retroperitoneal).
content.takeaway: Thorax is lung and heart territory; abdomen is the workshop.

check.question: Which organ sits mostly on the right side under the diaphragm?
check.why: The liver is the largest organ (after skin) and tucks under the diaphragm on the right.

content.heading: The digestive layout
paragraphs: Follow the food: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, ascending, transverse and descending colon, finally the rectum and anus.

Accessory organs feed the tract. The salivary glands open into the mouth; the liver produces bile which is stored in and released from the gall bladder; the pancreas makes digestive enzymes and insulin. Bile and pancreatic juice enter at the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine.

The small intestine is long and folded to maximise surface area for digestion and absorption. The large intestine reabsorbs water and houses bacteria; its appendix (vermiform) dangles from the caecum.
bullets: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon.
Liver makes bile; gall bladder stores it.
Pancreas: enzymes and hormones.
content.takeaway: The duodenum is where liver and pancreas meet the meal.

check.question: Bile is produced in the liver and stored in the
check.why: Bile flows to the gall bladder to be concentrated and stored.

content.heading: Excretory and reproductive position
paragraphs: The urinary system lives mostly in the abdomen. The kidneys are bean-shaped, about eleven centimetres long, on the posterior abdominal wall; the right kidney sits slightly lower because of the liver. Each kidney sends urine into a ureter that descends to the bladder; the urethra expels urine from the bladder.

In the male, the testes sit in the scrotum below the abdomen, keeping them a few degrees cooler than the abdominal cavity, which is essential for sperm production. Sperm travels through the epididymis and vas deferens past the prostate gland and out through the penis.

In the female, the ovaries lie on either side of the uterus in the pelvic cavity. Each ovary releases ova into a Fallopian tube, which carries them to the uterus, pear-shaped and midline, lying between the bladder and the rectum, and opening below into the vagina.
bullets: Kidneys: posterior wall, right lower than left.
Male: testes in the scrotum.
Female: ovaries, Fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina.
content.takeaway: Where an organ sits is the clue to what it does.

check.question: The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the position of the
check.why: The liver occupies the right upper abdomen and pushes the kidney down.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Halve the trunk at the diaphragm. Lungs and heart are above it; the liver lies on the right, the spleen on the left, and the kidneys posterior. The uterus sits midline between the bladder and rectum.

content.problem: Trace bile from production to the small intestine and name the organs it passes.

steps.reason: Hepatocytes make bile continuously.
steps.result: Bile drains through hepatic ducts.

steps.operation: Store it in the gall bladder
steps.reason: The common hepatic duct empties into the cystic duct to the gall bladder.
steps.result: Bile is stored between meals.

steps.reason: Fatty meals trigger cholecystokinin and sphincter relaxation.
steps.result: Bile flows via common bile duct to emulsify fats.

content.heading: Go deeper: The diaphragm and the body cavities
paragraphs: The diaphragm is a dome of muscle and tissue that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. Lungs and heart sit above it, while the liver, stomach, intestines, kidneys and bladder sit below it. Halving the trunk at the diaphragm therefore separates the systems at once.
The thoracic cavity is lined by pleura around the lungs and pericardium around the heart. The abdominal cavity is lined by peritoneum, which also anchors the organs and reduces friction as they move.
The diaphragm is not only a divider. When it contracts it flattens and enlarges the chest, drawing air into the lungs. Breathing and separation are therefore two roles of one muscle.
A pleural effusion fills the pleural space with fluid, so the lung cannot expand fully. That is one reason a chest infection makes breathing painful and shallow.
The peritoneum also holds the organs in place with folds called mesenteries. Those folds carry blood vessels to the intestines so the gut can absorb food while it moves.
bullets: The diaphragm separates chest from abdomen
Pleura and peritoneum line the two cavities
Diaphragm contraction drives breathing

content.heading: Go deeper: The digestive layout and the portal vein
paragraphs: The alimentary canal runs from mouth to anus, with accessory organs adding secretions. The liver makes bile, the gall bladder stores and concentrates it, and the pancreas supplies enzymes and bicarbonate. Each organ hands its product to the canal at a named point.

The hepatic portal vein links the intestinal capillaries to the liver capillaries. Food-rich blood therefore passes through the liver first, where glucose is stored and toxins are removed, before it joins the general circulation.
The liver also sits on the right side of the upper abdomen, pushing the right kidney lower than the left. That asymmetry is why the kidneys are not at the same height in a diagram.
The gall bladder concentrates bile by absorbing water, so the bile that reaches the duodenum is stronger than the bile made in the liver. The liver still makes the bile itself.
Bile emulsifies fat into droplets without digesting it. Pancreatic lipase then acts on the droplets, so the break-up by bile and the digestion by lipase are two separate steps.
bullets: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder
The hepatic portal vein carries food-rich blood to the liver
The liver pushes the right kidney lower than the left

content.heading: Go deeper: Excretory and reproductive position
paragraphs: The kidneys are bean-shaped organs about eleven centimetres long, on the posterior abdominal wall. Each sends urine through a ureter to the bladder, and the urethra expels it. The ureters descend behind the peritoneum, which is why kidney pain can be felt in the back.

In the female, the ovaries lie in the pelvis, the oviducts connect them to the uterus and the uterus sits midline between the bladder and the rectum. In the male, the testes lie in the scrotum and the vas deferens carries sperm to the urethra.
The midline position of the uterus and the posterior position of the kidneys are the two landmarks most often tested. A diagram that places them elsewhere is therefore wrong at once.
A testis that fails to descend remains at body temperature and cannot make sperm normally. That is why the scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the abdomen where they first form.
The bladder expands to store urine, so its wall stretches as it fills. The urethra is under voluntary control in humans, which is what makes continence possible.
bullets: Kidneys sit on the posterior abdominal wall
Ureters carry urine to the bladder; the urethra expels it
The uterus is midline between bladder and rectum

content.question: Explain why the testes are outside the abdominal cavity.
hints: Spermatogenesis runs best a few degrees below body temperature.
The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the core.
Cooling also protects sperm quality.

lessons.title: Modes of Nutrition
lessons.objective: Compare autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition and differentiate the holozoic, parasitic, saprophytic and carnivorous-plant types.

content.heading: Modes of nutrition
paragraphs: Two green plants can sit in the same soil and get fed very differently. That difference decides what a plant can and cannot survive on.

content.heading: Autotrophs make their own food; heterotrophs take it
paragraphs: A maize plant growing in a cassava farm in Ogun State feeds without eating anything. The same species planted in the same field, but in a dim, shaded spot, grows slowly and pale. The sunlight is mature feed for the first and missing feed for the second.

Autotrophs make their own organic food from simple inorganic ingredients, mainly carbon (IV) oxide and water, using energy from sunlight. Plants and algae are the examples JAMB wants, and the food they make is called organic. Flowering plants such as maize and non-flowering plants such as ferns are both autotrophs.

Heterotrophs cannot make their own food and must absorb or ingest ready-made organic food from a living or dead source. Man, sheep, Rhizopus, mushroom and tapeworm are heterotrophs; they need a food source that is already organic.
bullets: Autotrophs make their own organic food from simple inorganic ingredients.
Heterotrophs take in ready-made organic food.
Plants and algae are autotrophs; animals and fungi are heterotrophs.
content.takeaway: Autotrophs make food; heterotrophs take it.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches an autotroph to its plant group?
check.why: Ferns are non-flowering plants that photosynthesise; maize is flowering, while mushrooms and sheep are heterotrophs.

content.heading: Four heterotrophic patterns
paragraphs: A child eats eba, then the food is taken into the body and digested. A tapeworm inside the same child has no such step. Both feed heterotrophically, but the way each one gets its food is different.

Holozoic feeders ingest solid food into the body and digest it internally, for example man and sheep. Parasites absorb or ingest food from a living host while harming it, for example tapeworm, roundworm and Loranthus.
Saprophytes absorb food dissolved from dead matter, for example Rhizopus and mushroom. Carnivorous plants trap and digest insects, for example sundew and bladderwort.
bullets: Holozoic: ingest solid food and digest it, for example man and sheep.
Parasitic: feed on a living host without killing it, for example tapeworm, roundworm and Loranthus.
Saprophytic: absorb food from dead matter (Rhizopus, mushroom); carnivorous plants trap insects (sundew, bladderwort).
content.takeaway: Holozoic ingests, parasitic uses a host, saprophytes use dead matter.

check.question: Rhizopus that feeds on bread is an example of
check.why: Rhizopus secretes enzymes outside the body and absorbs food from dead bread.

content.heading: Nutrition is about sources, not the eater alone
paragraphs: A sundew in a marsh catches a fly and digests it. A tree beside it makes food all day. Both are plants; the diet differs in source, not in organ.

So judge by where the nutrition comes from: a holozoic eater ingests, a parasite uses a living host, a saprophyte uses dead matter, a carnivorous plant supplements minerals. Plants are usually autotrophs, but they may also be saprophytes or parasites, while no animal is an autotroph.
Exam hint: if the question asks about a plant that traps insects, it is not a carnivorous plant by anatomy; it is supplementing short minerals from insects while keeping its photosynthesis.
bullets: Saprophytes are mainly fungi; carnivorous plants are green plants that supplement minerals.
Parasites derive food from a living host and usually harm it.
Autotrophs manufacture food; heterotrophs absorb or ingest it.
content.takeaway: Name where the food comes from, not merely who eats.

check.question: A plant that makes its own food and also traps insects is both
check.why: Sundew and bladderwort photosynthesise and supplement minerals from insects.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Look for the source word: ingest means holozoic, host means parasitic, dead means saprophytic, and trap means carnivorous. Always name the food source, not just the organism, when you classify a mode of nutrition.

content.problem: Classify each feeding pattern: tapeworm in humans, mushroom on decaying wood, sundew leaves, and a yam plant.

steps.reason: Tapeworm lives and feeds inside a human intestine.
steps.result: Parasitic.
steps.predictPrompt: Which pattern is shown by mushroom on decaying wood?

steps.reason: Mushroom secretes enzymes onto rotten wood and absorbs the products.
steps.result: Saprophytic.

steps.reason: Sundew traps insects on sticky leaves.
steps.result: Carnivorous plant (also an autotroph).

steps.reason: Yam stores starch made in leaves from carbon (IV) oxide and water.
steps.result: Autotrophic.

content.heading: Go deeper: Photosynthesis and the chemistry of food
paragraphs: Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. The light reactions split water, release oxygen and store energy in ATP and NADPH. Those carriers then power the carbon cycle that fixes carbon dioxide into sugar.

The value of a food can therefore be traced to this process. A yam stores starch made by a leaf, a fish stores protein from its prey, and rice stores the product of an earlier harvest. Nutrition classifies food by the job it does in the body, not by where it came from.
The same chemistry explains why a plant in darkness cannot make food. Without light there is no energy to split water, so the leaf cannot fix carbon however much carbon dioxide surrounds it.
The carbon in a yam began as carbon dioxide in the air. The leaf fixed it, the plant stored it as starch and the tuber carried it underground, so a food store is a record of earlier photosynthesis.
A plant that is shaded makes less glucose and grows more slowly. That is why a seedling in a dark corner becomes pale and stretched, because its food supply is limited by light.
bullets: Light reactions split water and release oxygen
Food classes follow the job done in the body
Darkness stops photosynthesis by removing its energy source

content.heading: Go deeper: Holozoic, saprophytic and parasitic feeding
paragraphs: Holozoic feeding has four stages: ingestion, digestion, absorption and assimilation. An organism takes in solid food, breaks it down in a gut, absorbs the products into blood and uses them in cells. A human eating rice follows all four.
Saprophytes skip ingestion. Fungi secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the dissolved products. That extracellular digestion is why a mould can digest bread without a mouth.

Parasites feed on a living host and harm it. Loranthus on a mango tree and Taenia in the intestine both draw water or food from a living plant or animal, which is how they escape the competition that free-living saprophytes face.
A vulture is a saprophyte in this sense because it feeds on dead matter. It does not hunt live prey, so the vulture belongs with the decomposers rather than with the predators.
Assimilation is the step most often forgotten. It is the use of absorbed food in cells for energy and growth, which is why a meal that is absorbed but not used does not nourish.
bullets: Holozoic feeding: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation
Saprophytes digest outside the body and absorb the products
Parasites draw from a living host and harm it

content.heading: Go deeper: Carnivorous plants and the minerals they lack
paragraphs: Sundew and bladderwort photosynthesise but live on poor soils. They supplement nitrogen and phosphorus by trapping insects, so they are both autotrophs and carnivores. That double nutrition is why they are not classified as heterotrophs alone.
A trap is a modified leaf that catches and digests prey. The glue of a sundew, the suction of a bladderwort and the pitfall of a pitcher plant each solve the same mineral shortage in a different way.
Carnivory therefore answers a soil problem, not an energy problem. The plant still needs light for its sugar, and the insects supply the minerals that the soil does not.
A bladderwort bladder works by suction. It pumps water out until the pressure falls, then a trigger hair opens the door and the prey is drawn in with the incoming water.
A pitcher plant is a pitfall trap. Insects slip into a fluid-filled pitcher and cannot climb out, where enzymes digest them and release their minerals to the plant.
bullets: Sundew and bladderwort are autotrophs that also catch insects
Traps are modified leaves for minerals, not for energy
Carnivory solves a soil deficiency, not a light shortage

content.question: Explain why sundew is both an autotroph and a carnivorous plant.
hints: Its leaves contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise.
Insects supply the mineral salts the soil lacks.
Nutrition type describes the source of food, not one label per organism.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Mineral Requirements
lessons.objective: Differentiate the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis, show the necessity of light, carbon (IV) oxide and chlorophyll, and identify macro- and micronutrients with their deficiency symptoms.

content.heading: Photosynthesis and mineral requirements
paragraphs: A leaf in a covered jar can still be green but stop making starch. The leaf is alive; the missing ingredient is what the question is really testing.

content.heading: Light reactions and dark reactions
paragraphs: Place a leaf in light that has been filtered through a screen, and the part that forms starch is the part the light hit. Leaves kept in the dark do not form starch at all.

In the light reaction, chlorophyll absorbs light energy. The energy splits water (photolysis) into hydrogen and oxygen, and oxygen is released. The energy is trapped in carriers for the dark reactions.

In the dark reaction, glucose is manufactured from carbon (IV) oxide using the energy supplied by the light reaction. It does not need light, hence the name; the two reactions are linked by the energy carriers made in the light reaction.
bullets: Light reactions: need light, split water, release oxygen, make energy carriers.
Dark reactions: no light needed, fix carbon (IV) oxide into glucose.
Starch in a leaf is evidence that photosynthesis has occurred.
content.takeaway: Light splits water; the dark reactions fix carbon.

check.question: Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from the splitting of
check.why: Photolysis splits water and oxygen is released in the light reaction.

content.heading: Why no light, no carbon (IV) oxide, no chlorophyll means no starch
paragraphs: A variegated leaf with white patches and a green part produces starch only in the green part. A leaf covered so that light cannot reach it produces no starch at all. A destarched leaf enclosed in carbon (IV) oxide-free air produces no starch either.
Light delivers the energy, carbon (IV) oxide supplies the carbon skeleton of glucose, and chlorophyll captures the energy. All three are necessary; remove any one and starch formation stops.

The iodine test confirms starch: the leaf is boiled, treated with alcohol and iodine; a blue-black colour shows starch. A leaf that was kept in the dark next to a leaf in light is the control; the part that stays brown has no starch.
bullets: Light, carbon (IV) oxide and chlorophyll are all needed for photosynthesis.
Variegated leaf test: only the green part makes starch.
Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch.
content.takeaway: No light, no carbon (IV) oxide or no chlorophyll means no photosynthesis.

check.question: A destarched leaf is kept in light but in carbon (IV) oxide-free air. It produces no starch because
options: carbon (IV) oxide supplies the carbon skeleton
check.why: Photosynthesis needs carbon (IV) oxide as the carbon source; without it, glucose and starch cannot be made.

content.heading: Chemosynthesis and mineral requirements
paragraphs: Some bacteria in the soil do not need sunlight at all. They get their energy from oxidised chemicals, especially sulphur and iron compounds. That is chemosynthesis, distinct from photosynthesis because the energy source is chemical rather than light.

Plants need mineral salts for growth. The main macronutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK); calcium, magnesium and sulphur are also needed in larger amounts. Nitrogen builds proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus supports roots and seeds, and potassium controls stomata and enzymes.

Deficiency symptoms follow: nitrogen gives yellow older leaves, phosphorus stunted growth and purplish leaves, and potassium mottled leaves and weak stems. Micronutrients needed in small amounts include iron, manganese, zinc, boron and copper. Magnesium is needed in larger amounts and forms the centre of chlorophyll, so its shortage also causes chlorosis.
bullets: Chemosynthesis: energy from chemical oxidation, used by bacteria.
Macronutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur.
Micronutrients: iron, manganese, zinc, boron, copper; shortages cause chlorosis.
content.takeaway: Photosynthesis uses light; chemosynthesis uses chemicals, and balanced minerals keep plants healthy.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches a mineral deficiency to its symptom?
check.why: Nitrogen deficiency yellows older leaves first; phosphorus gives purple leaves and potassium mottling.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Photosynthesis needs light; chemosynthesis does not. Macronutrients include NPK; micronutrients are needed in traces. Chlorosis signals nitrogen, iron or magnesium deficiency, and iodine tests a leaf for starch.

content.problem: Suggest a remedy: a young orange tree shows pale green veins but dark green between them, and the older leaves are also pale.

steps.reason: Chlorosis shows depletion of a green-making nutrient.
steps.result: Chlorosis, characteristic of magnesium deficiency.
steps.predictPrompt: What nutrient is needed for chlorophyll?

steps.reason: Magnesium is the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.
steps.result: Established as magnesium deficiency.

steps.reason: Mineral salts must be replaced in soil fertiliser.
steps.result: Apply a magnesium-containing fertiliser (e.g. Epsom salts).

content.heading: Go deeper: Light reactions and the splitting of water
paragraphs: The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Light energy excites chlorophyll, splits water by photolysis and releases oxygen. The energy is stored in ATP and NADPH, which are carried to the stroma.

Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium drive growth, while magnesium sits at the centre of chlorophyll and calcium stabilises cell walls. A shortage of any one limits photosynthesis in a different way, which is how deficiency symptoms differ.

Chemosynthesis uses chemical energy instead of light. Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate, releasing energy that fixes carbon. The process therefore sustains the nitrogen cycle without light.

The ATP and NADPH made in the light reactions are used in the stroma without light. That separation is why the second stage is called light-independent even though it depends on the products of the first.
Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. Isotope labelling showed that the oxygen in the gas follows the water that was split in the leaf.
The stoichiometry of the light reactions links water splitting to oxygen release. Two molecules of water yield one molecule of oxygen and four protons, and those protons help make ATP.
bullets: Photolysis splits water and releases oxygen
Magnesium is at the centre of chlorophyll
Chemosynthesis fixes carbon without light

content.heading: Go deeper: The three necessities and how each is tested
paragraphs: Light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll are the three necessities of photosynthesis. A destarched leaf in carbon dioxide-free air makes no starch, and a variegated leaf makes starch only in its green portions. Each test removes one requirement.

The iodine test confirms the result. A leaf that was destarched and then illuminated turns blue-black where starch was made and stays brown where it was not. The colour is the evidence that the requirement was met.

The limiting factor is whichever requirement is scarcest. In bright light carbon dioxide may limit, while in shade light limits. Raising the limiting factor raises the rate until another begins to limit.
A variegated leaf is the classic test because its green and white parts receive the same light. Only the green part makes starch, which shows that chlorophyll and not light alone was differences.
The destarching step is essential before the test. Without it, a leaf that already contained starch would turn blue-black whether or not it had made new starch in the light.
bullets: Light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll are the three necessities
Iodine gives blue-black with starch
The limiting factor decides the rate of photosynthesis

content.heading: Go deeper: Mineral deficiencies and how to read them
paragraphs: Nitrogen deficiency yellows the older leaves first because nitrogen is withdrawn from them to supply new growth. Phosphorus deficiency gives purple leaves and stunted roots, while potassium deficiency produces mottled leaves and weak stems.

Micronutrients are needed in small amounts, including iron, manganese, zinc, boron and copper. Magnesium is needed in larger amounts than those, and its shortage also causes chlorosis because chlorophyll cannot be formed without it.

Farmer's practice follows the symptoms. A nitrogen shortage is corrected with urea or manure, a potassium shortage with potash, and a magnesium shortage with a magnesium salt. The symptom therefore points to the fertiliser.
Chlorosis is the yellowing that follows a shortage of nitrogen, magnesium or iron. The pattern of yellowing, whether in older or younger leaves, points to which element is missing.
A farmer corrects the symptom only after naming the missing element. Adding a general fertiliser to a potassium shortage wastes money, so the diagnosis must precede the treatment.
bullets: Nitrogen: yellow older leaves; phosphorus: purple leaves
Micronutrients are needed in traces, magnesium in larger amounts
Symptoms point to the fertiliser that will correct them

content.question: Explain why a variegated-leaf experiment proves chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.
hints: The white parts lack chlorophyll.
They receive light and carbon (IV) oxide but cannot trap energy.
Starch is found only in the green parts after iodine testing.

lessons.title: Classes of Food and Balanced Diet
lessons.objective: Identify the six classes of food, indicate their sources and importance, perform food tests, and relate each class to its deficiency disease.

content.heading: Classes of food and balanced diet
paragraphs: Two children eat lunch at the same Lagos school: one eats rice, beans and fish; the other eats only puff-puff. By term's end, the second is often tired and pale. The difference is the mix of food classes.

content.heading: The six classes and where they come from
paragraphs: Carbohydrates supply energy and are found in yam, rice, eba, maize, bread and plantain. Proteins build and repair tissues; fish, meat, eggs, beans and milk are the main sources. Fats and oils store energy, insulate the body and protect organs; palm oil, groundnut oil, margarine and butter are the sources.

Mineral salts build bones and teeth, regulate body fluids and help enzymes work; iron comes from leafy vegetables, fish and blood-rich meats, while calcium comes from milk, fish bones and leafy greens. Water regulates body temperature, dissolves wastes and transports nutrients.
Vitamins regulate body processes; vitamin A prevents night blindness, vitamins B and C prevent beriberi and scurvy, vitamin D prevents rickets.
bullets: Carbohydrates: energy (yam, rice, maize, bread).
Proteins: growth and repair (fish, meat, eggs, beans).
Fats and oils: energy store and insulation (palm oil, groundnut oil).
Mineral salts and water: structure, transport and regulation; vitamins A, B, C and D regulate body processes.
content.takeaway: Six classes: energy, building blocks, protection and regulation.

check.question: Proteins are needed in the body for
check.why: Proteins build and repair cells and tissues.

content.heading: Food tests identify each class
paragraphs: To know what a food sample contains, use chemical tests. Iodine solution gives a blue-black colour with starch. Benedict's solution, when heated with a reducing sugar, changes from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red.
For protein, the biuret test gives a purple colour. For fats, the emulsion test gives a white emulsion when alcohol is mixed with the sample. These tests identify food types from experiment results.
Use the tests as a checklist: blue-black is starch; a colour change in Benedict's is reducing sugar; purple in biuret is protein; emulsion is fat.
bullets: Starch: blue-black with iodine.
Reducing sugar: blue to brick-red with Benedict's solution.
Protein: purple with biuret solution.
Fat: white emulsion with alcohol.
content.takeaway: Iodine for starch, Benedict's for sugar, biuret for protein, emulsion for fat.

check.question: A food sample that turns iodine solution blue-black contains
check.why: Iodine gives a blue-black colour in the presence of starch.

content.heading: Balanced diet and deficiency diseases
paragraphs: A balanced diet supplies each class in proportions the body needs. A school lunch of rice (carbohydrates), beans (protein), palm oil (fats), vegetable (vitamins and minerals) and water is balanced; puff-puff and fanta alone is not.

When one class falls short, a deficiency disease appears. Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C and shows bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Rickets is caused by lack of vitamin D and calcium and shows bow legs and soft bones in children, and kwashiorkor is caused by lack of protein and shows a swollen belly, oedema and listlessness.

Marasmus is a more severe protein-energy malnutrition showing a 'skin and bones' appearance. Night blindness shows lack of vitamin A; beriberi shows lack of vitamin B. Recognising each pattern links the food class to the disease.
bullets: Balanced diet: all six classes in recommended proportions.
Scurvy: vitamin C deficiency; night blindness: vitamin A deficiency.
Rickets: vitamin D and calcium deficiency.
Kwashiorkor and marasmus: protein deficiency.
content.takeaway: A balanced diet has all six classes; each deficiency has a name.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches a deficiency to its disease?
check.why: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy; vitamin D and calcium deficiency cause rickets; protein deficiency causes kwashiorkor.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match each deficiency to the missing class: vitamin C is scurvy, vitamin D and calcium are rickets, and protein is kwashiorkor or marasmus. Night blindness points to vitamin A, so learn the pairings.

content.problem: An experiment: a food extract turns iodine blue-black, a second turns Benedict's solution brick-red, and a third gives a purple colour with biuret. Identify each food type.

steps.reason: Blue-black indicates starch.
steps.result: Starch.
steps.predictPrompt: What test confirms protein?

steps.reason: Blue to brick-red indicates a reducing sugar.
steps.result: Reducing sugar (glucose, fructose).

steps.reason: Purple indicates protein.
steps.result: Protein.

content.heading: Go deeper: The six classes and how each is used
paragraphs: Carbohydrates supply energy, proteins build and repair, and fats store energy and insulate. Water dissolves and carries, mineral salts build structure and regulate fluids, and vitamins regulate process chemistry. Each class has a job that the others cannot do.

A yam-based meal is therefore incomplete without a protein source and vegetables. Rice, beans and fish together cover energy, growth and micronutrients, while puff-puff and a soft drink cover only energy and added sugar.
The six classes are a checklist, not a menu. A diet that lacks one class will show a deficiency even if the total calories are enough, because the missing job is not done by the other classes.
A yam-and-egusi meal covers energy, protein and oil in one dish. Fish or beans then add the minerals and vitamins that the staple alone cannot supply in enough quantity.
Proteins are not used for energy first. The body burns carbohydrates and fats for energy and reserves protein for building and repair, which is why a protein-rich meal is not an energy meal.
A balanced diet also needs water in quantity, not only in trace amounts. Water is lost daily in sweat, urine and breathing, so a diet that is balanced in classes can still fail if water is scarce.
bullets: Carbohydrates for energy; proteins for growth; fats for storage
Water, mineral salts and vitamins regulate and carry
Calories alone do not make a balanced diet

content.heading: Go deeper: Food tests and what each colour means
paragraphs: Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch, a brown colour without it. Benedict's solution gives a brick-red precipitate with a reducing sugar when heated, and a purple colour with a protein when biuret solution is added.
Fat gives a white emulsion with alcohol because it is insoluble in water. That test is therefore physical rather than chemical: the emulsion is the evidence, not a colour change in the reagent.
A test can be specific without being general. Iodine detects starch but not protein, so a battery of tests is needed to name the classes present in an unknown sample.
A reducing sugar is one with a free aldehyde or ketone group. Glucose and fructose are reducing, while sucrose is not until it is hydrolysed, which is why Benedict's is used to test honey and fruit.
A biuret test that stays blue has no protein, while a purple colour confirms it. The test is therefore a negative check as well as a positive one when the colour does not appear.
bullets: Iodine: blue-black with starch
Benedict's: brick-red with reducing sugar; biuret: purple with protein
Fat: white emulsion with alcohol

content.heading: Go deeper: Deficiency diseases and how to recognise them
paragraphs: Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C and shows bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Rickets is caused by lack of vitamin D and calcium and shows bow legs and soft bones in children. Night blindness shows lack of vitamin A.

Kwashiorkor is caused by lack of protein and shows a swollen belly, oedema and listlessness. Marasmus is a more severe protein-energy malnutrition showing a skin-and-bones appearance. Beriberi shows lack of vitamin B.
The pattern must be learned as a pair: disease to missing class. Kwashiorkor is protein, rickets is vitamin D and calcium, scurvy is vitamin C, night blindness is vitamin A and beriberi is vitamin B.
A swollen belly with oedema is the sign of kwashiorkor, while a skin-and-bones body is marasmus. Both are protein-related, but the swollen belly distinguishes the first from the second.
A diet of only starchy staples can cause several deficiencies at once. The signs therefore overlap, and the missing class must be identified from the most distinctive sign.
bullets: Scurvy: vitamin C; rickets: vitamin D and calcium
Kwashiorkor and marasmus: protein deficiency
Night blindness: vitamin A; beriberi: vitamin B

content.question: Why is a meal of yam, pepper soup and water not balanced? Name what is missing.
hints: Yam supplies carbohydrates only.
Pepper soup has vitamins but very little protein.
Protein for growth and repair is missing.

lessons.title: Mammalian Teeth and Alimentary Canal
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of a typical mammalian tooth, differentiate the types and relate them to their functions, compare dental formulae, and relate the alimentary canal and its accessory organs to their functions.

content.heading: Mammalian teeth and alimentary canal
paragraphs: A goat grazing tough grass and a dog tearing meat both have molars, but the rest of the mouth differs sharply. The mouth shows what the animal eats.

content.heading: Structure of a tooth
paragraphs: A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root below. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body, which resists acids and wear. The root is held in a socket by cement and anchored by gum and ligaments.

Beneath the enamel is dentine, a hard but sensitive layer. The pulp cavity at the centre holds nerves and blood vessels. Mammalian teeth are heterodont, meaning they differ in shape within the same mouth.
Each tooth is adapted by shape to a job: incisors are chisel-shaped for cutting, canines are pointed for tearing, premolars and molars are flat-topped for grinding.
bullets: Crown (enamel) resists wear; root anchors the tooth.
Dentine is sensitive; pulp carries nerves and vessels.
Heterodont: different shapes, different jobs.
content.takeaway: Enamel resists, dentine senses, and shape decides the job.

check.question: The hardest substance in the body, covering the tooth crown, is
check.why: Enamel is the hardest tissue and protects the crown.

content.heading: Tooth types and dental formulae
paragraphs: Man has incisors for biting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding. Dogs have large canines and shearing carnassial teeth for meat. In herbivores like sheep, the upper incisors are replaced by a horny dental pad, and the cheek teeth are high-crowned for grinding grass.

A dental formula lists, in order, incisors, canines, premolars and molars in the upper and lower jaw. Man: 2/2, 1/1, 2/2, 3/3 = 32 teeth; dog: 3/3, 1/1, 4/4, 2/3 = 42 teeth; sheep: 0/3, 0/1, 3/3, 3/3 = 32 teeth.
The number and pattern show diet: many grinders mean herbivory, strong canines mean carnivory, and an even mix means omnivory.
bullets: Incisors bite, canines tear, cheek teeth grind.
Man has 32 teeth; dog 42; sheep 32 with a dental pad.
Dental formula: incisors/canines/premolars/molars, upper over lower.
content.takeaway: Count the teeth and you know the diet.

check.question: Which dental feature is typical of a grass-eating herbivore?
options: A horny dental pad instead of upper incisors
check.why: Sheep and goats have a dental pad in place of upper incisors.

content.heading: The alimentary canal and its accessory organs
paragraphs: Food moves through the canal in steps, each part doing a job. The salivary glands moisten food and contain amylase. The oesophagus pushes food by peristalsis, rhythmic muscular contraction, and the stomach churns food while secreting hydrochloric acid and protease.

Digestive enzymes are reusable proteins that work best at a particular pH. In the small intestine, bile from the liver emulsifies fats, pancreatic juice supplies amylase, trypsin and lipase, and succus entericus finishes the work. The end products are glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol; bile and pancreatic juice enter at the duodenum.

Absorption happens mainly in the ileum, whose villi multiply the surface area. Nutrition runs ingestion, digestion, absorption and assimilation, with assimilation building food into tissues. The large intestine reabsorbs water, and the rectum stores faeces until egestion.
bullets: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon.
Enzymes are reusable proteins; each works best at a particular pH.
End products: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
content.takeaway: The gut moves, churns, digests, absorbs and then expels.

check.question: Peristalsis is the movement of food through the oesophagus by
check.why: Waves of muscular contraction push food along the oesophagus.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Dental formula always lists I/C/P/M, counting upper and lower jaws separately. Bile emulsifies fats but does not digest them; enzymes yield glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.

content.problem: An animal has a dental formula 0/3, 0/1, 3/3, 3/3. What does it eat and why?

steps.reason: No upper incisors and no upper canines, but many cheek teeth.
steps.result: The animal grinds rather than bites or tears.
steps.predictPrompt: Which mammal has a dental pad like this?

steps.reason: Cheek teeth for grinding suit fibrous plant food.
steps.result: It is a herbivore, like sheep.

steps.reason: Canines would indicate meat-tearing; their absence excludes a carnivore.
steps.result: Concluded as herbivore.

content.heading: Go deeper: Tooth structure and the dental formula
paragraphs: A tooth has enamel covering the crown, dentine beneath it and pulp containing nerves and blood vessels. Enamel is the hardest tissue in the body and protects the crown, but it cannot repair itself once it is worn away.

Mammals have differentiated teeth: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. A dental formula counts each type in one jaw, so a sheep and a lion carry different toolkits that match their diets.
The root anchors the tooth in the jaw, and the neck is the narrow part between crown and root. A tooth without a root cannot withstand the forces of biting and grinding.
Enamel is harder than dentine but brittle, so a tooth that bites on stone can chip. The dentine beneath is living and sensitive, which is why a chipped tooth aches when it is exposed.
Ruminants such as cattle have a dental pad instead of upper incisors. The pad meets the lower teeth and crops grass, so the formula records the pad instead of incisors.
bullets: Enamel covers the crown; dentine lies beneath; pulp holds nerves
Incisors cut, canines tear, molars grind
A dental formula counts each tooth type in one jaw

content.heading: Go deeper: The alimentary canal from mouth to anus
paragraphs: Food is ingested at the mouth, chewed by teeth and mixed with saliva. The oesophagus then moves it by peristalsis, waves of muscular contraction that push food downward without gravity. The stomach churns it with acid and enzymes.
The small intestine absorbs the products, and the large intestine absorbs water. The caecum in herbivores houses microbes that digest fibre, while in humans it is reduced and carries the appendix.
The canal is therefore a sequence of jobs: ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion. Each organ hands the food to the next at a named junction.
The stomach churns food into chyme by muscular action as well as by acid. That churning breaks food into small particles before it enters the duodenum in a controlled release.
The large intestine does not absorb food, only water and salts. That is why the products of digestion must have been absorbed in the small intestine or they are lost as faeces.
Saliva begins the breakdown of starch in the mouth, but most starch digestion happens in the small intestine. That is why a meal that is chewed poorly can still be digested, only more slowly.
bullets: Peristalsis pushes food along the oesophagus
The small intestine absorbs; the large intestine absorbs water
The caecum and appendix are reduced in humans

content.heading: Go deeper: Bile, enzymes and the chemistry of digestion
paragraphs: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum. It emulsifies fat into droplets and does not itself digest anything. That distinction is the most tested point about bile.

Enzymes break large food molecules into small ones that can be absorbed. Amylase acts on starch, protease on protein and lipase on fat, and each acts best at its own pH. The stomach is acid for protease, the duodenum alkaline for amylase and lipase.
Absorption across the ileum wall moves glucose and amino acids into blood and fatty acids into lymph. The products therefore enter different transport routes after digestion.
A gall bladder that is removed does not stop fat digestion. Bile is still made in the liver and flows without storage, so fatty meals are less well emulsified but are still digested.
Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralises the acid from the stomach in the duodenum. Without it, the enzymes of the small intestine would be destroyed by the low pH of the chyme.
bullets: Bile emulsifies fat; it contains no digestive enzymes
Amylase, protease and lipase act on starch, protein and fat
Glucose and amino acids enter blood; fatty acids enter lymph

content.question: Why does bile help digestion without itself digesting?
hints: Bile contains no digestive enzymes.
Bile salts emulsify large fat droplets into smaller ones.
Emulsification increases the surface area for pancreatic lipase to act on.

lessons.title: Why Transport?
lessons.objective: Relate increasing size and complexity to the need for transport, identify the materials transported and their sources, and name the media and channels used.

content.heading: Why transport?
paragraphs: A pond Amoeba and an elephant both need oxygen, but only the Amoeba can rely on diffusion through its surface. Increasing size and complexity create a transport problem.

content.heading: Why size changes the problem
paragraphs: An Amoeba in pond water is one cell, so oxygen and food reach the cytoplasm by diffusion over a very short distance. Its surface area is large compared with its volume, and no part of the cell is far from the water outside.

A maize plant or a goat is different. Most cells sit deep inside the body, far from the air and food, so diffusion alone would be too slow to supply them. The distance is too long and the demand too high.

Larger, more active organisms therefore need a transport system: a set of channels and a moving medium that carries materials quickly between organs. The system links the surfaces where materials enter or leave with the tissues that use or make them.
bullets: Small organisms: short diffusion distances and a large surface-to-volume ratio.
Large organisms: long distances and high demand.
A transport system carries materials between surfaces and tissues.
content.takeaway: Size creates distance; transport closes it.

check.question: Why does a large, active animal need a transport system?
options: Its cells are too small to absorb oxygen
Its surface has no exchange organs
Diffusion alone is too slow over long distances
It cannot make its own food
check.why: Large bodies have long diffusion distances and high demand, so bulk transport is needed.

content.heading: What the transport system carries
paragraphs: Blood does not carry one substance. It carries gases, digested food, manufactured food, excretory products, mineral salts, water and hormones, and each has a source and a destination.

Oxygen enters at the lungs and travels to every tissue, while carbon (IV) oxide travels the other way. Glucose and amino acids enter at the small intestine and reach the liver and cells; urea is made in the liver and carried to the kidneys.

Plants move sucrose and amino acids from leaves to growing parts, and water with dissolved mineral salts from roots to leaves. Hormones such as insulin travel in blood from endocrine glands to target organs, so the system also carries chemical messages.
bullets: Gases: oxygen to tissues; carbon (IV) oxide to the lungs.
Food and wastes: glucose and amino acids to cells; urea to the kidneys.
Water, mineral salts and hormones also travel in the transport medium.
content.takeaway: Transport carries raw materials, wastes and messages.

check.question: Urea is transported from the liver to the
check.why: Urea is a nitrogenous waste carried in blood to the kidneys for excretion.

content.heading: Media and channels
paragraphs: The medium is what actually carries the material. In Amoeba it is the cytoplasm; in a plant cell it is the cell sap; in an insect it is the body fluid called haemolymph; in a mammal it is blood and lymph.

The channel is the route. Mammals have blood vessels, plants have xylem and phloem, and very small organisms may have no special channel at all. A medium without a channel can still move by diffusion, but a large organism needs both.
Open systems such as those of insects pour haemolymph into body spaces, while closed systems keep blood inside vessels. The next lessons follow the mammalian and plant systems in turn.
bullets: Media: cytoplasm, cell sap, haemolymph, blood and lymph.
Channels: blood vessels in mammals; xylem and phloem in plants.
Large organisms need both a medium and a channel.
content.takeaway: A medium carries; a channel directs.

check.question: Which of these is a channel for transport in a flowering plant?
check.why: Xylem and phloem are the plant's transport channels; the other options are media.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often asks for the source and destination of a material. Say where it is made or absorbed, what carries it, and where it is used or removed.

content.problem: A goat eats grass. Trace four materials from their source to their destination.

steps.reason: Starch in grass is digested to glucose in the small intestine.
steps.result: Absorbed into blood and carried to the liver and muscles.
steps.predictPrompt: Where is urea made?

steps.reason: The liver breaks down excess amino acids and forms urea.
steps.result: Carried by blood to the kidneys and excreted in urine.

steps.reason: Oxygen is absorbed at the lungs and bound by haemoglobin.
steps.result: Carried by blood to respiring cells.

steps.reason: The pancreas makes insulin and releases it into blood.
steps.result: Carried to the liver and muscles, where it lowers blood glucose.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why size forces transport
paragraphs: Diffusion works over micrometres, not centimetres. A small Amoeba can exchange through its surface, but a whale must move oxygen and glucose from one end of the body to the other. The larger the body, the longer the diffusion distance becomes.

Surface area sets a second limit. Volume grows with the cube of length while surface area grows with the square, so a large cell has too little surface for its volume. Every multicellular animal therefore needs bulk transport.
Transport does not change what is carried. It moves oxygen, glucose, hormones, nitrogenous waste and heat from where they are made to where they are used or removed.
A leaf is thin enough for diffusion to supply its cells from the air. A tree trunk is not, so it must rely on xylem and phloem to move materials between distant parts.
A unicellular organism can exchange directly because every cell is near the surface. A specialised cell deep inside a whale cannot, so the whale needs blood to reach each of its trilions of cells.
A leaf is thin enough for diffusion to supply its cells from the air. A tree trunk is not, so it must rely on xylem and phloem to move materials between distant parts.
bullets: Diffusion is too slow beyond micrometres
Volume grows faster than surface area in large bodies
Transport moves materials; it does not change them

content.heading: Go deeper: The materials and the media
paragraphs: Animal transport carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin, glucose, amino acids, urea and hormones. Plant transport carries water and mineral salts upward in xylem and dissolved food both ways in phloem. The media are therefore different even though the need is the same.
Blood is a medium that carries its load dissolved or bound in plasma. Haemoglobin is a protein that reversibly binds oxygen, so blood can carry far more oxygen than water alone could hold.
The choice of medium decides the load. A gas that is poorly soluble in water needs a carrier, while a sugar that is soluble can travel dissolved in plasma or sap.
Hormones are carried in blood but act only on target organs. The carrier is general, while the response is specific, which is how one medium serves many different messages.
Sap in xylem is mostly water with dissolved salts, while sap in phloem is mostly sucrose. The two saps therefore move in opposite directions at different speeds through the same bundle.
bullets: Blood carries oxygen, glucose, amino acids, urea and hormones
Xylem carries water upward; phloem carries food both ways
Haemoglobin lets blood carry oxygen beyond solubility

content.heading: Go deeper: Channels and the pressure that drives them
paragraphs: A channel must sustain flow without leaking. Artery walls are muscular and elastic, so they stretch under pressure and recoil. Veins are thinner, with valves that stop backflow when pressure is low.

In plants, xylem vessels are dead tubes with lignified walls, so they conduct without cells to maintain them. Phloem sieve tubes are living but lack a nucleus, and they depend on companion cells for their proteins.
Flow is therefore driven by gradients in both kingdoms: pressure in animals and evaporation in plants. Without a gradient, a channel is only a pipe.
A lymphatic vessel has no pump of its own. Skeletal muscle compresses it as the body moves, so movement drives lymph flow in the same way that it helps venous return.
A valve in a vein fails when the vein overfills around it. The blood then pools in the legs, which is why varicose veins appear in the lower limbs of people who stand for long hours.
bullets: Artery walls stretch and recoil; vein valves stop backflow
Xylem vessels are dead tubes; phloem tubes need companion cells
Pressure and evaporation are the gradients that drive flow

content.question: Explain why an Amoeba does not need a circulatory system but a goat does.
hints: Compare surface area with volume in each organism.
Diffusion is fast only over very short distances.
A goat has a high demand for oxygen and food in cells deep inside its body.

lessons.title: The Mammalian Circulatory System
lessons.objective: Describe the mammalian heart and double circulation, compare arteries, veins and capillaries, and relate the named vessels to their functions.

content.heading: The mammalian circulatory system
paragraphs: A cyclist climbing a Lagos bridge feels her heart pound. The pump is moving oxygen faster because her muscles now demand more of it. That is the circulatory system at work.

content.heading: The heart and double circulation
paragraphs: The mammalian heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria above and two thick-walled ventricles below. The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body.

Valves between the chambers and at the exits keep blood moving one way. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must push blood around the whole body, while the right ventricle only reaches the lungs.

This is a double circulation: pulmonary through the lungs and systemic through the body. Insects have an open system instead, with haemolymph bathing the organs, while mammals keep blood in closed vessels.
bullets: Right side: body to lungs. Left side: lungs to body.
Valves prevent backflow; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.
Mammals have closed circulation; insects have an open system.
content.takeaway: Two circuits, one pump, and valves that keep blood moving forward.

check.question: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body?
check.why: The left ventricle sends blood into the aorta and around the systemic circuit.

content.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
paragraphs: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, elastic muscular walls and a narrow lumen, which withstand the high pressure produced by each heartbeat. The pulmonary artery is an exception to the oxygen rule: it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

Veins carry blood back to the heart. Their walls are thinner, their lumen wider, and valves stop backflow in the low-pressure system. Capillaries are one cell thick, so gases, glucose and wastes can pass between blood and tissue fluid.
Arteries branch into arterioles, then capillaries, then venules and veins. The capillary network is where exchange happens; the great vessels are only the delivery roads.
bullets: Arteries: thick walls, narrow lumen, blood away from the heart.
Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves, blood back to the heart.
Capillaries: one-cell walls for exchange with tissue fluid.
content.takeaway: Arteries deliver, veins return, capillaries exchange.

check.question: Which blood vessel has valves along its length to prevent backflow?
check.why: Veins carry blood at low pressure and use valves to keep it moving toward the heart.

content.heading: Named vessels and what they carry
paragraphs: Some vessels are named for the organ they serve. The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body. The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle with deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

The hepatic portal vein is unusual. It carries blood from the small intestine and other digestive organs to the liver, so digested food is processed before entering the general circulation. It is not the hepatic vein, which drains the liver into the vena cava.

The renal artery takes oxygenated blood to the kidney, and the renal vein carries filtered, deoxygenated blood away. The hepatic portal vein therefore has two capillary beds in series, while the renal vessels serve one organ.
bullets: Aorta: left ventricle to body; pulmonary artery: right ventricle to lungs.
Pulmonary vein: lungs to left atrium; renal artery and vein: kidney.
Hepatic portal vein: intestine to liver, carrying digested food.
content.takeaway: Read the name: pulmonary means lungs, hepatic means liver, renal means kidney.

check.question: Which vessel carries digested food from the intestine to the liver?
check.why: The hepatic portal vein links the intestinal capillaries to the liver capillaries.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not judge a vessel by its oxygen content alone. The pulmonary artery is deoxygenated and the pulmonary vein oxygenated; the hepatic portal vein carries food-rich blood from the gut to the liver.

content.problem: Trace a red blood cell from the right atrium to the aorta. Name the chambers, valves and vessels in order.

steps.reason: Blood flows from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.
steps.result: Right ventricle.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the right ventricle send blood?

steps.reason: The right ventricle contracts and pushes blood into the pulmonary artery.
steps.result: Lungs, where the blood becomes oxygenated.

steps.reason: Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein.
steps.result: Left atrium.

steps.reason: Blood passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta.
steps.result: Aorta and the systemic circulation.

content.heading: Go deeper: The four chambers and the valves
paragraphs: The heart has two atria and two ventricles. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body at high pressure. The left ventricle wall is therefore much thicker than the right.

Valves keep blood moving in one direction. The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening and the bicuspid guards the left, while semilunar valves guard the exits to the aorta and pulmonary artery. The heart sounds are the valves closing.
The cardiac cycle repeats about seventy times in a resting minute. Atria contract together, then ventricles contract together, so filling and emptying alternate without mixing the two sides.
The heart muscle is supplied by coronary arteries that branch from the aorta. Those arteries fill during diastole, when the heart itself is relaxed, rather than during contraction.
A heart murmur is the sound of a valve that does not close neatly. The timing of the murmur in the cardiac cycle tells the doctor which valve is at fault.
bullets: Right side to lungs; left side to the body
Left ventricle wall is thicker than the right
Atrioventricular and semilunar valves enforce one-way flow

content.heading: Go deeper: Artery, vein and capillary
paragraphs: An artery has a thick muscular wall and a narrow lumen. It stretches as the ventricle contracts and recoils as the ventricle relaxes, smoothing the pulse. A vein has a thin wall and a wide lumen, with valves and skeletal muscle to help return blood.
A capillary has a single layer of endothelial cells. That thin wall is the exchange surface, because diffusion across it is fast and every tissue cell is close to a capillary.
The pressure falls from aorta to capillaries to venae cavae. A vessel can therefore be judged by its wall and its pressure, not only by whether it carries oxygenated blood.
Capillary walls are so thin that white cells must deform to pass through them. That narrowness also makes them the most likely site for a blockage by a clot or an embolus.
An arteriogram can show narrowing by atheroma, which raises the resistance of that artery. The heart must then work harder to maintain the same flow through the narrowed vessel.
A venous pulse can be felt in the neck because the jugular vein is close to the surface. That pulse is the volume change of the right atrium with each heartbeat.
bullets: Arteries: thick muscular wall, narrow lumen
Veins: thin wall, wide lumen, valves
Capillaries: one cell thick, the exchange surface

content.heading: Go deeper: Double circulation and the named vessels
paragraphs: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice for each circuit of the body. It goes heart to body to heart, then heart to lungs to heart. A fish has only one circuit, so its tissues receive blood after pressure has fallen.

The hepatic portal vein links intestinal capillaries to liver capillaries. Food-rich blood therefore passes through the liver before it joins the general circulation. The renal vein returns filtered blood from the kidney to the vena cava.
The pulmonary artery is deoxygenated and the pulmonary vein is oxygenated, which reverses the usual rule. A vessel must be judged by its destination, not only by its oxygen content.
The aorta branches into arteries that narrow to arterioles before the capillaries. That narrowing raises resistance, so the pressure that leaves the heart falls steadily toward the veins.
The renal portal system in birds and reptiles returns blood from the tail to the kidney before it reaches the heart. Mammals have no equivalent, so their kidney blood comes directly from the aorta.
bullets: Double circulation: body circuit then lung circuit
Hepatic portal vein: gut capillaries to liver capillaries
Pulmonary artery is deoxygenated; pulmonary vein is oxygenated

content.question: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
hints: Compare the distance blood travels in the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
The systemic circuit has greater resistance to flow.
A thicker wall can produce a higher pressure.

lessons.title: Blood and Lymph
lessons.objective: State the composition and functions of blood and lymph, and explain how tissue fluid, plasma, blood cells and platelets carry out transport and defence.

content.heading: Blood and lymph
paragraphs: A blood donation session in Abuja separates whole blood into plasma, cells and platelets. Each part has a different job in transport and defence, and lymph is the second fluid.

content.heading: Plasma: the liquid cargo
paragraphs: Plasma is about 55% of blood volume and is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, mineral salts, glucose, amino acids, hormones, urea and carbon (IV) oxide. It is the medium that carries blood cells and dissolved materials around the body.
The plasma proteins have separate jobs. Fibrinogen is needed for clotting; albumin helps hold water in the blood and keeps osmotic pressure steady; globulins include antibodies that fight infection.
Plasma also distributes heat from active organs and buffers small changes in pH. Serum is plasma after clotting proteins have been removed, which is why serum is used in some tests.
bullets: Plasma is mostly water and carries dissolved food, wastes and hormones.
Fibrinogen clots, albumin holds water, globulins include antibodies.
Plasma distributes heat and buffers pH; serum is plasma without clotting proteins.
content.takeaway: Plasma is the liquid road; its proteins clot, balance water and fight infection.

check.question: Which plasma protein is needed for blood clotting?
check.why: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin threads during clotting.

content.heading: Red cells, white cells and platelets
paragraphs: Red blood cells are biconcave discs without a nucleus in mammals. They are packed with haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues; their shape gives a large surface area and their flexibility lets them squeeze through capillaries.

White blood cells defend the body. Phagocytes engulf bacteria and debris, while lymphocytes make antibodies and coordinate immune responses. They are fewer than red cells but can leave the blood to reach an infection.
Platelets are cell fragments that start clotting when a vessel is damaged. They clump at the break and help convert fibrinogen into fibrin threads, which trap blood cells and form a plug.
bullets: Red cells: haemoglobin, biconcave shape, about 120 days in circulation.
White cells: phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies.
Platelets: cell fragments that start clot formation.
content.takeaway: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells defend, platelets seal leaks.

check.question: Which blood component produces antibodies?
check.why: Lymphocytes are white blood cells that produce antibodies against specific antigens.

content.heading: Lymph and tissue fluid
paragraphs: Blood pressure at the arterial end of a capillary pushes water and small solutes into the spaces between cells. This fluid is tissue fluid; it supplies cells and collects their wastes, but it has no red cells or platelets.

Most tissue fluid returns to the venous end of the capillary. The rest enters blind-ended lymph capillaries and becomes lymph, which passes through lymph nodes and is returned to the blood through veins near the neck.

Lymph carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats from the villi, and its valves and body movements keep it moving. If lymph vessels are blocked, tissue fluid accumulates and causes oedema, as in filariasis.
bullets: Tissue fluid bathes cells and exchanges materials with them.
Lymph returns excess tissue fluid via lymph nodes and veins.
Lymph carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats; blockage causes oedema.
content.takeaway: Tissue fluid bathes cells; lymph returns the excess.

check.question: Lymph differs from blood because lymph lacks
check.why: Red cells and platelets stay in capillaries, so lymph is clear and carries lymphocytes.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Blood has red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma; lymph has lymphocytes but no red cells. Tissue fluid is the fluid between cells, and lymph is tissue fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel.

content.problem: A patient has swollen legs and a blocked lymph vessel. Explain the swelling and trace the normal return of tissue fluid.

steps.reason: The swelling is tissue fluid that has not returned to the blood.
