steps.result: Tissue fluid accumulation, called oedema.
steps.predictPrompt: What vessel normally drains tissue fluid?

steps.reason: A blocked lymph vessel raises the pressure in the lymph capillaries.
steps.result: Less tissue fluid can drain away, so it collects in the tissues.

steps.reason: Lymph capillaries join larger lymph vessels and pass through lymph nodes.
steps.result: Lymph returns to the blood through veins near the neck.

content.heading: Go deeper: Plasma, red cells and clotting
paragraphs: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, carrying dissolved food, hormones and waste. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen, while white blood cells fight disease and platelets seal wounds. Each cell type has a different job.

Clotting replaces lost blood by forming a mesh of fibrin. Platelets release thrombokinase, which converts prothrombin to thrombin, and thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin threads. The threads trap cells and form the clot.
A blood group matters because the wrong group brings antigens that agglutinate red cells. That is why transfusion must be matched, and why the Rhesus factor is tested in pregnancy.
Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly, so it releases oxygen where the partial pressure is low. In the lungs it loads, in the tissues it unloads, and the same protein serves both directions.
Plasma also carries carbon dioxide as hydrogencarbonate ions. That dissolved form is the main way carbon dioxide travels, not bound to haemoglobin as oxygen does.
Red cells have no nucleus, so they cannot divide. They are made in the bone marrow and live for about 120 days before the spleen removes them when they wear out.
bullets: Plasma carries dissolved food, hormones and waste
Fibrinogen to fibrin threads form the clot
Blood groups prevent agglutination in transfusion

content.heading: Go deeper: White cells, antibodies and phagocytosis
paragraphs: White blood cells are of two kinds: phagocytes that engulf microbes and lymphocytes that make antibodies. Phagocytes such as neutrophils and monocytes move by amoeboid motion and close around their prey.

Lymphocytes produce antibodies that are specific to one antigen. The antibody binds the antigen and marks it for destruction, so a second infection by the same pathogen is met more quickly. That is the basis of immunity.
Platelets are not cells but cell fragments from megakaryocytes. They have no nucleus, yet they release the clotting factors that start the fibrin mesh at a wound.
The Rhesus factor is a protein on red cells that most people carry. A Rhesus-negative mother can become sensitised by a Rhesus-positive fetus, which is why the first pregnancy is usually safe.
A lymphocyte that meets its matching antigen multiplies into a clone. That clonal expansion is why the second response is faster and stronger than the first.
A white cell count rises during infection because more phagocytes are released from the marrow. That rise is therefore a sign that the body is fighting, not that the blood is infected.
bullets: Phagocytes engulf microbes; lymphocytes make antibodies
Antibodies are specific to one antigen
Platelets are fragments that release clotting factors

content.heading: Go deeper: Tissue fluid and lymph
paragraphs: Tissue fluid is the liquid between cells, formed when hydrostatic pressure forces plasma through capillary walls. It carries oxygen, glucose and hormones to the cells and collects carbon dioxide and waste from them.

Lymph is tissue fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel. It contains lymphocytes but no red cells, because red cells are too large to leave the capillaries, and it returns to the blood at the subclavian veins.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and make lymphocytes. That is why infection in a limb can swell the nodes in the armpit or groin: the nodes are working on the fluid from that limb.
Tissue fluid that is not returned becomes oedema. That swelling occurs when venous pressure rises or when protein is lost from the blood, because less fluid is reabsorbed at the venule end.
The liver makes most plasma proteins, so liver failure reduces the protein in blood. Less protein means less reabsorption of tissue fluid, and oedema follows.
bullets: Tissue fluid is forced from capillaries into the tissues
Lymph has lymphocytes but no red cells
Lymph nodes filter lymph and make lymphocytes

content.question: Explain why lymph normally contains lymphocytes but no red blood cells.
hints: Lymph begins as tissue fluid forced out of blood capillaries.
Red cells are too large to pass through the capillary wall.
Lymphocytes can leave capillaries and enter the lymph.

lessons.title: Plant Transport
lessons.objective: Relate xylem and phloem structure to function, explain translocation, and compare transpiration pull, root pressure and active transport.

content.heading: Plant transport
paragraphs: A cassava plant wilts at midday and recovers at night. Water is moving through its xylem all the time, even when the leaves look still, and transpiration drives the flow.

content.heading: Xylem: water and mineral salts upward
paragraphs: Root hairs increase the surface for absorbing water. Water enters by osmosis, moves across the root and up the xylem, which is made of dead, hollow cells with lignified walls. The walls stop the tubes collapsing under tension, and xylem and phloem run through roots, stems and leaves as vascular bundles.

Water travels as a continuous column from root to leaf. It is pulled upward mainly by transpiration, the loss of water vapour through stomata, and helped by cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to the xylem walls.

Mineral salts are not simply dragged along. They are absorbed by active transport and then carried in the xylem stream to the leaves, where they are used to make proteins, chlorophyll and other compounds.
bullets: Xylem: dead, hollow, lignified cells that carry water upward.
Root hairs absorb water by osmosis; minerals enter by active transport.
Cohesion and adhesion keep the water column unbroken.
content.takeaway: Xylem is a one-way water pipeline from root to leaf.

check.question: Which tissue carries water and mineral salts from roots to leaves?
check.why: Xylem vessels and tracheids form the water-conducting pipeline of the plant.

content.heading: Phloem: food in both directions
paragraphs: Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis. Sieve tubes are living cells with perforated end walls, and each has a companion cell that supplies energy and controls loading.

Sucrose and amino acids move from a source, such as a mature leaf, to a sink, such as a growing shoot, root, fruit or storage organ. This movement is called translocation, and it can go upward or downward because the source and sink change with the season.

Loading sucrose into the phloem draws water in by osmosis, raising pressure that pushes sap toward the sink. The process uses energy from respiration, so phloem transport is active, unlike the passive pull in xylem.
bullets: Phloem: living sieve tubes with companion cells.
Translocation moves sugars and amino acids from source to sink.
Loading uses energy and pressure, so phloem transport is active.
content.takeaway: Phloem moves food from source to sink, in either direction.

check.question: The movement of sugars through phloem is called
check.why: Translocation is the transport of dissolved food through phloem from source to sink.

content.heading: Transpiration pull, root pressure and active transport
paragraphs: Transpiration pull is the main upward force in tall plants. Evaporation from the leaf lowers pressure in the xylem, and the continuous water column is pulled upward; cohesion and adhesion keep the column unbroken.

Root pressure pushes water up from below. It develops when minerals accumulate in the root and water follows by osmosis, and it is strongest at night when transpiration is low; it can cause guttation, droplets at leaf tips.

Active transport moves mineral ions against their concentration gradient using energy from respiration. Diffusion and osmosis also move materials over short distances, while bulk flow in xylem and phloem moves them over long distances.
bullets: Transpiration pull: passive upward pull driven by evaporation.
Root pressure: osmotic push, strongest at night; can cause guttation.
Active transport: uses energy to move mineral ions against a gradient.
content.takeaway: Transpiration pulls, root pressure pushes, active transport pumps.

check.question: Which mechanism mainly explains water rising in a tall tree on a hot day?
check.why: Rapid evaporation from the leaves creates the tension that pulls the water column upward.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Xylem is dead and carries water upward; phloem is living and carries food both ways. Transpiration pull is passive, while active transport needs energy, so match the process to its tissue.

content.problem: A gardener removes a ring of bark from a young tree. Predict what happens above and below the ring.

steps.reason: The bark contains the phloem, which lies outside the xylem.
steps.result: Phloem transport is interrupted.
steps.predictPrompt: Which tissue remains able to carry water?

steps.reason: Sugars made in the leaves cannot pass down through the removed phloem.
steps.result: Sugars accumulate above the ring and the bark may swell.

steps.reason: The roots receive no sugars from the leaves.
steps.result: Root growth and respiration decline.

steps.reason: The root system starves while the shoot keeps photosynthesising.
steps.result: The tree may eventually die.

content.heading: Go deeper: Xylem vessels and why they are dead
paragraphs: Xylem vessels are dead at maturity. Their end walls disappear so the cells form continuous tubes, and lignin in the walls prevents collapse under tension. A dead tube can conduct because conduction needs no living machinery.

A vessel element is therefore a pipe, not a pump. The force that moves water is evaporation from the leaves, transmitted as tension through the continuous water column. The xylem only has to hold the column together.
A ring-barked stem still conducts water upward through its xylem. The phloem, not the xylem, is removed by the ring, so food cannot reach the roots even though water still rises.
A vessel element is wider than a tracheid and has a larger lumen. That width makes vessels efficient, which is why they are found in flowering plants rather than in most ferns.
Tracheids are narrower cells with tapered ends that overlap. They conduct less efficiently than vessels but occur in conifers, which have survived without vessels for millions of years.
bullets: Xylem vessels are dead at maturity with no end walls
Lignin stops the tubes collapsing under tension
Ring barking removes phloem, not xylem

content.heading: Go deeper: Phloem, sieve tubes and translocation
paragraphs: Phloem sieve tubes are living but have no nucleus. Their sieve plates allow food to pass, and companion cells supply the proteins and energy that the sieve tube cannot make for itself. The two cells are therefore partners.

Translocation moves dissolved food from source to sink. A source is a leaf or storage organ that loads sucrose, and a sink is a growing fruit, root or seed that unloads it. Direction is therefore set by demand, not by gravity.
Translocation needs energy because it is active. Sucrose is loaded into the sieve tube by active transport, and water follows by osmosis, raising pressure. The pressure then pushes food to the sink.
A sink can become a source as seasons change. A storage root that unloads food in the rains loads it again from leaves in the next year, so direction follows the season.
Aphids tap sieve tubes with their stylets and feed for hours. The honeydew they excrete is the excess sucrose that the plant was translocating, so the insect is stealing translocated food.
bullets: Sieve tubes lack nuclei and depend on companion cells
Source loads food; sink unloads it
Loading is active; pressure drives translocation

content.heading: Go deeper: Transpiration, root pressure and active transport
paragraphs: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves. Evaporation creates tension at the top of the water column, and that tension pulls water up through the xylem. Stomatal opening therefore controls the whole pull.
Root pressure is a smaller push from below. Water entering root hairs raises pressure in the xylem, which can cause guttation on leaf margins at night. It is not enough to lift water to a tall tree.

Active transport moves ions against a gradient using energy from respiration. It is how mineral salts are taken up by roots and how sucrose is loaded into phloem, so it links water relations to nutrition.
Guttation is the loss of liquid water from leaf margins at night. It is the only visible sign of root pressure under normal conditions in the field.
A potometer measures transpiration by the movement of a bubble in a capillary. The rate rises with light, temperature and wind, which is why a drying wind wilts a plant that is well watered.
bullets: Transpiration pull comes from evaporation at the leaves
Root pressure causes guttation but cannot lift water high
Active transport uses energy to move ions against a gradient

content.question: Why does a plant wilt on a hot, windy afternoon even when the soil is wet?
hints: Transpiration can remove water faster than roots absorb it.
Water loss lowers the turgor pressure that keeps leaves firm.
Wilting reduces water loss and can reverse when transpiration slows.

lessons.title: Diffusion, Osmosis and Water Relations
lessons.objective: Describe diffusion and osmosis, and explain plasmolysis and turgidity as the responses of plant cells to water movement.

content.heading: Diffusion, osmosis and water relations
paragraphs: A slice of fresh okra left in salt water goes limp within minutes. Water has crossed a membrane, and the direction of movement is the whole story.

content.heading: Diffusion: movement down a gradient
paragraphs: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is passive, so it uses the random motion of particles rather than energy from respiration.

Oxygen diffuses from the air in the lungs into blood, and from blood into respiring cells. Carbon (IV) oxide diffuses the other way. In a leaf, carbon (IV) oxide enters through stomata and oxygen leaves.

The rate depends on the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance. Small, thin surfaces with a steep gradient speed diffusion up; that is why alveoli and root hairs are finely branched and thin.
bullets: Diffusion: particles move from high to low concentration.
It is passive and depends on random particle motion.
Steep gradients, large surfaces and short distances speed it up.
content.takeaway: Diffusion is passive movement from high to low concentration.

check.question: Diffusion is described as passive because it
options: Depends on the random movement of particles
check.why: Diffusion needs no metabolic energy; particles spread by their own random motion.

content.heading: Osmosis: water across a membrane
paragraphs: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. The dilute solution has more water molecules, so water moves toward the side with less water and more solute.
An animal cell placed in distilled water gains water and may burst; in strong salt solution it loses water and shrinks. A plant cell behaves differently because its cell wall resists expansion.
Root hairs use osmosis to absorb soil water, and water moves from cell to cell across the root. Osmosis is passive, but it depends on a water potential gradient and a membrane the water can cross.
bullets: Osmosis: water moves through a partially permeable membrane.
Water moves from dilute (high water) to concentrated (low water).
Animal cells may burst or shrink; plant cell walls resist expansion.
content.takeaway: Osmosis is water movement toward the more concentrated solution.

check.question: Water moves by osmosis from
options: A concentrated solution to a dilute solution
A dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
A region of low water potential to high water potential
Any cell to any other cell
check.why: Water moves down its own gradient, from the dilute side to the more concentrated side.

content.heading: Plasmolysis and turgidity
paragraphs: When a plant cell is in pure water, water enters its vacuole by osmosis. The vacuole swells, pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall and the cell becomes turgid; turgor pressure keeps herbaceous plants upright.

In a concentrated salt or sugar solution, water leaves the vacuole. The protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall, and the cell is plasmolysed. The plant tissue becomes limp, which is why salted vegetables lose their crispness.

Plasmolysis is reversible if the cell is returned to water before the protoplast is badly damaged. Turgidity and plasmolysis explain wilting, food preservation with salt or sugar, and why fresh vegetables crisp up in cold water.
bullets: Turgid: water enters, vacuole swells, cell is firm.
Plasmolysed: water leaves, protoplast pulls away from the wall.
Turgidity supports plants; plasmolysis makes tissue limp.
content.takeaway: Turgid cells are firm; plasmolysed cells are limp.

check.question: A plant cell placed in concentrated salt solution will
options: Burst because it has no cell wall
Take in salt and become flaccid
check.why: The external solution is more concentrated, so water leaves the vacuole and the protoplast shrinks.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Diffusion moves any particles; osmosis moves only water through a selectively permeable membrane. Plasmolysis is the plant-cell result of water loss, while turgidity is the result of water gain.

content.problem: Three potato strips are placed in distilled water, a dilute salt solution and a concentrated salt solution. Predict their firmness.

steps.reason: The cell sap is more concentrated than the surrounding water.
steps.result: Water enters by osmosis; the strip becomes turgid and firm.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens in the concentrated salt solution?

steps.reason: The gradient is small, so there is little net water movement.
steps.result: The strip stays firm, with little change in mass.

steps.reason: The external solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.
steps.result: Water leaves the cells; the strip becomes limp and plasmolysed.

content.heading: Go deeper: Diffusion and the gradient it follows
paragraphs: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is passive, so it uses the random motion of particles rather than energy from respiration. A gradient is therefore the force, and it disappears as the particles spread.

The rate depends on distance, temperature and surface area. A short distance, a large surface and a warm medium all speed diffusion, which is why thin exchange surfaces are so common in gills, lungs and leaves.
A gas such as oxygen can diffuse through air far faster than through water. That is why a fish must move water over its gills rather than wait for oxygen to diffuse through the pond.
Diffusion also explains the spread of a scent across a room. The molecules move from high concentration near the source to low concentration everywhere else until the air is evenly mixed.
Diffusion in still air is slow over metres, which is why a smell takes time to reach the back of a classroom. Mixing by currents does most of the spreading over large distances.
bullets: Diffusion follows a concentration gradient and needs no energy
Rate rises with shorter distance and larger surface
Oxygen diffuses faster in air than in water

content.heading: Go deeper: Osmosis and the selectively permeable membrane
paragraphs: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the more concentrated solution. Only water moves, and it moves down its own gradient. The membrane decides what is allowed through, so osmosis is diffusion of water with a barrier.

A plant cell in pure water becomes turgid because water enters the vacuole and pushes the protoplast against the wall. The wall prevents bursting, so the cell stops taking up water when the pressure balances the gradient.
Plasmolysis is the reverse. A cell in a concentrated solution loses water, the protoplast shrinks from the wall and the cell becomes flaccid. That shrinkage is the visible sign that water has left.
A red cell in distilled water swells and can burst, which is why pure water is poisonous to a cell that lacks a wall. A plant cell survives the same solution because its wall resists the pressure.
Raisins swell in water because the concentrated sap draws it in. Placed in concentrated sugar they shrivel, which is the same experiment as plasmolysis with household materials.
bullets: Osmosis moves only water across a selectively permeable membrane
Turgidity is water gain; plasmolysis is water loss
The cell wall prevents a turgid cell from bursting

content.heading: Go deeper: Water potential and the direction of flow
paragraphs: Water potential is a measure of the free energy of water. It is highest in pure water and lowest in a concentrated solution under pressure. Water moves from higher to lower potential, which unites diffusion, osmosis and root uptake in one rule.
Solute lowers potential, while pressure raises it. A turgid cell therefore has higher potential than pure water under the same conditions, which is why it stops taking up water at equilibrium.

A root hair in soil takes up water because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water. If the soil becomes saltier than the cell, the gradient reverses and the plant wilts even though water is present.
Cut flowers wilt because the stem is severed and water cannot be replaced. Recutting the stem under water restores the continuous column and the flower recovers without any new metabolism.
Water potential unites the uptake of water by roots, the rise in stems and the loss from leaves. Each step moves water toward lower potential, from soil to root to leaf to air.
bullets: Water moves from higher to lower water potential
Solute lowers potential; pressure raises it
Salty soil can reverse the gradient and cause wilt

content.question: Explain why a wilted lettuce leaf becomes crisp again when placed in cold water.
hints: The leaf cells have lost water and become flaccid.
The water outside is more dilute than the cell sap.
Water enters the vacuoles by osmosis and restores turgor pressure.

lessons.title: Respiration and Energy
lessons.objective: Explain the significance of respiration, describe ATP as the energy currency, and distinguish aerobic from anaerobic respiration.

content.heading: Respiration and energy
paragraphs: A sprinter leaves the blocks and is breathing hard ten seconds later. The muscles are spending energy that was stored in food and released inside cells.

content.heading: Respiration is not breathing
paragraphs: Respiration is the controlled release of energy from organic food inside cells. Breathing is only the movement of air that supplies oxygen and removes carbon (IV) oxide; respiration happens in every living cell, including cells with no lungs.

Glucose is broken down in a series of enzyme-controlled reactions. The energy released is used to make ATP, run active transport, build large molecules, contract muscles and keep the body warm. Some energy is always lost as heat.

Respiration is catabolic: it breaks larger molecules into simpler ones. Respiring seeds in a vacuum flask release carbon (IV) oxide, which turns limewater milky, and warm the flask, showing that respiration produces gas and heat. Photosynthesis does the opposite, storing energy in glucose, and both processes depend on enzymes.
bullets: Respiration releases energy from food inside cells.
Breathing supplies oxygen and removes carbon (IV) oxide.
The released energy powers cell work, and respiring seeds release carbon (IV) oxide and heat.
content.takeaway: Respiration is a chemical process in cells, not breathing.

check.question: Respiring seeds in a vacuum flask turn limewater milky and warm the flask. This shows that respiration produces
check.why: The limewater test detects carbon (IV) oxide, and the warmth shows that respiration releases heat energy.

content.heading: ATP: the energy currency
paragraphs: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a small molecule that carries usable energy from respiration to the reactions that need it. When its terminal phosphate is removed, ATP becomes ADP and energy is released.
Cells can make ATP when needed and break it down at the same place, so energy is delivered in small packets rather than one large burst. This is why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.

ATP powers muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses and the synthesis of proteins and other molecules. It is not a long-term store; the energy store is the food molecule, while ATP is the spendable form.
bullets: ATP carries energy from respiration to cell reactions.
Removing the terminal phosphate releases energy and leaves ADP.
ATP is spendable energy; food is the long-term store.
content.takeaway: Food stores energy; ATP spends it.

check.question: ATP releases useful energy when it is converted to
check.why: Breaking the terminal phosphate bond of ATP yields ADP, phosphate and usable energy.

content.heading: Aerobic and anaerobic at a glance
paragraphs: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and breaks glucose down completely to carbon (IV) oxide and water. It releases a large amount of ATP and happens mainly in the mitochondria.
Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen. Glucose is only partly broken down, so less ATP is released; the products are lactic acid in muscles or ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast.
Both pathways begin with glycolysis in the cytoplasm. Oxygen decides which route follows, so the same glucose can yield very different amounts of energy depending on whether oxygen is present.
bullets: Aerobic: oxygen, complete breakdown, large ATP yield.
Anaerobic: no oxygen, partial breakdown, small ATP yield.
Products: lactic acid in muscles; ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast.
content.takeaway: Oxygen is the switch between high-yield aerobic and low-yield anaerobic respiration.

check.question: Which product is formed in anaerobic respiration in yeast but not in human muscle?
check.why: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide, while human muscle forms lactic acid.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Respiration is a chemical process in cells, not breathing. Respiring seeds release carbon (IV) oxide and heat; limewater turns milky. Aerobic uses oxygen and makes much more ATP than anaerobic.

content.problem: A student says a resting plant cannot respire because it is not breathing. Correct the statement and trace the energy.

steps.reason: Breathing is ventilation; respiration is a chemical reaction in cells.
steps.result: The plant respires even though it has no lungs.
steps.predictPrompt: How does a leaf exchange gases?

steps.reason: Leaves use stomata and woody stems use lenticels.
steps.result: Oxygen enters and carbon (IV) oxide leaves by diffusion.

steps.reason: Glucose is broken down and the energy is transferred to ATP.
steps.result: ATP powers the plant's active transport and growth.

steps.reason: Not all the energy is captured in ATP.
steps.result: Some is released as heat, even in a resting plant.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ATP is the currency of the cell
paragraphs: ATP stores energy in a phosphate bond that cells can break when work is needed. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy for movement, synthesis and active transport. The cell then remakes ATP in respiration.

That cycle is why ATP is called the energy currency. Food is the income, respiration is the mint that issues the coins, and every task spends the coins. A cell cannot store much ATP, so it respires continuously.
The value of the currency depends on the breakdown. Aerobic respiration releases far more energy from glucose than anaerobic respiration, so it is the normal mint for most cells.
ATP is constantly recycled. A human turns over roughly an amount of ATP equal to the body mass each day, which is why respiration must be continuous rather than occasional.
Phosphocreatine is a short-term store that remakes ATP in muscle when work is sudden. It covers only seconds of effort, after which respiration must take over to rebuild the store.
ATP is hydrolysed at the site of work, not in a distant tissue. That local spent is why muscle uses its own phosphocreatine for a sudden sprint rather than waiting for blood to deliver more ATP.
bullets: ATP hydrolysis supplies energy for cellular work
Respiration remakes ATP from food
Aerobic breakdown yields far more ATP than anaerobic

content.heading: Go deeper: Breathing is not respiration
paragraphs: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs. It does not break down food or release energy. A person can breathe without respiring for a short while, and a plant can respire without breathing at all.

Respiration occurs in mitochondria and in the cytoplasm. It needs oxygen for the aerobic pathway and produces carbon dioxide and water. The products are therefore found in the cells, not in the air that was breathed.

The limewater test detects carbon dioxide from respiration, not from breathing. A respiring seedling that turns limewater milky is producing carbon dioxide in its cells, and the warmth it gives off is the energy released.
A drowned person can have breathed recently without respiring in the tissues. The two events are therefore separated by a circulation that must carry oxygen from the air to the cells.

Once oxygen is dissolved in blood, it must diffuse from capillaries into cells. That final diffusion is respiration, while the ventilation of the lungs is only breathing, according to the definitions.
bullets: Breathing moves air; respiration breaks down food
Respiration occurs in cells, not in the lungs
Limewater detects carbon dioxide from respiration

content.heading: Go deeper: Where respiration happens and what limits it
paragraphs: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen. The later stages need mitochondria, so a cell without mitochondria must rely on the anaerobic pathway. Yeast and muscle are the standard examples.
Temperature and oxygen supply limit the rate. A seedling respires faster when warm and when oxygen is plentiful, which is why germinating seeds are kept in warm, aerated soil.
The rate can also be measured by oxygen uptake or carbon dioxide output. A respirometer therefore measures respiration without touching the food that is being broken down.
A thermometer in a flask of germinating seeds rises because respiration releases heat. That rise is the simplest confirmation that the seeds are respiring and not merely growing.

A germinating seed with no oxygen in compacted soil makes ethanol, which can poison and kill the embryo. That is why a seed sown in compacted soil rots rather than germinates, even if water is present.
bullets: Glycolysis is cytoplasmic; later stages are mitochondrial
Temperature and oxygen limit the rate
Respiration can be measured by gas exchange

content.question: Why does a cell use ATP rather than spending glucose directly?
hints: Glucose is a stable storage molecule, not a ready payment.
ATP releases a small, controlled amount of energy.
Coupling ATP breakdown to cell reactions avoids a wasteful burst of heat.

lessons.title: Respiratory Organs and Surfaces
lessons.objective: Describe body surfaces, gills, tracheae, lungs, stomata and lenticels, and relate the features of a respiratory surface to efficient gas exchange.

content.heading: Respiratory organs and surfaces
paragraphs: A fish in a Lagos lagoon and a grasshopper on the bank both need oxygen, but neither has a lung. Their surfaces show how anatomy follows habitat.

content.heading: What makes a good respiratory surface
paragraphs: Gas exchange happens by diffusion, so a respiratory surface must be thin, moist and permeable. It also needs a large surface area and a steep concentration gradient, usually maintained by ventilation or blood flow.

These features are summarized in Fick's law: the rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area and concentration difference, and inversely proportional to thickness. A thick, dry surface slows exchange.
Terrestrial surfaces lose water easily, so land animals keep their exchange surfaces inside the body. Aquatic animals can use exposed gills because water supports them and prevents drying.
bullets: Thin, moist and permeable for fast diffusion.
Large area and a steep concentration gradient for more exchange.
Ventilation and blood flow maintain the gradient.
content.takeaway: Thin, moist, large and well supplied: the four tests of a respiratory surface.

check.question: Which feature would decrease the rate of gas exchange across a surface?
check.why: Thickness and dryness increase diffusion distance and slow gas exchange.

content.heading: Body surface, gills and tracheae
paragraphs: An Amoeba exchanges gases over its whole body surface. An earthworm uses moist skin, kept thin and vascular by mucus and a good blood supply. These surfaces work only where the distance is short and the body is not too thick.

Fish use gills with many thin lamellae. Water flows over the gills in the opposite direction to blood, a countercurrent arrangement that keeps a concentration gradient along the whole gill and extracts more oxygen.

Insects use tracheae: air enters through spiracles, travels along tubes and reaches cells through fine tracheoles. This system delivers oxygen directly, so insect blood does not need haemoglobin for most gas transport.
bullets: Body surface: Amoeba and earthworm, thin and moist.
Gills: fish, many lamellae with countercurrent water and blood flow.
Tracheae: insects, air delivered directly to cells through tracheoles.
content.takeaway: Body surface suits small animals; gills suit water; tracheae pipe air directly.

check.question: The countercurrent flow in fish gills
options: Makes water and blood flow in the same direction
Maintains a concentration gradient along the gill
Cools the fish in warm water
check.why: Opposite flows keep oxygen diffusing into the blood along the whole length of the gill.

content.heading: Lungs, stomata and lenticels
paragraphs: Mammals use lungs, where millions of alveoli give a huge, thin, moist surface. Each alveolus is surrounded by capillaries, and ventilation plus blood flow keeps oxygen coming in and carbon (IV) oxide leaving.
Plants have no lungs. Leaves exchange gases through stomata, each guarded by two guard cells; woody stems use lenticels, and roots absorb oxygen through root hairs and air spaces in the soil.
The exchange surface matches the habitat: moist skin in damp soil, gills in water, tracheae in air, alveoli in a sealed lung. The same diffusion rules apply to all of them.
bullets: Lungs: alveoli give a large, thin, moist surface with capillaries.
Leaves use stomata; woody stems use lenticels; roots use air spaces.
Every surface follows the same diffusion rules.
content.takeaway: The surface follows the habitat, but diffusion follows the same rules.

check.question: Which structure is the respiratory surface of a woody stem?
check.why: Lenticels are loose patches of cells in the bark that allow gas exchange.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match the surface to the organism: moist skin for the earthworm, gills for fish, tracheae for insects, alveoli for mammals, and stomata or lenticels for plants. Name the surface before explaining the mechanism.

content.problem: An unknown animal has moist skin, no lungs and lives in damp soil. Identify its respiratory surface and explain why it cannot live in dry sand.

steps.reason: The whole body surface is thin, moist and supplied with blood.
steps.result: Body surface, as in an earthworm.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to that surface in dry air?

steps.reason: The surface must stay moist for oxygen to dissolve and diffuse.
steps.result: Dry sand would dry the skin and stop gas exchange.

steps.reason: The animal has no internal lung to protect its surface from drying.
steps.result: It is restricted to damp soil or water.

content.heading: Go deeper: The four features of a good exchange surface
paragraphs: A good exchange surface is thin, moist, permeable, large and well supplied with blood or air. Thinness shortens the diffusion path, moisture dissolves gases, a large area increases the rate, and a blood supply keeps the gradient steep.

An earthworm has all four in its skin. It must stay damp because gases cannot diffuse through a dry surface, which is why it hides in soil after rain. A fish gill has the same features in a different form.
Any surface that lacks one feature is a poor exchanger. A thick, dry, waxy surface therefore protects against water loss but cannot exchange gases quickly.
The moist surface is essential because gases must dissolve before they can diffuse. That is why a fish gill must be kept wet and why a dry skin cannot exchange gases.
The frog uses its skin as well as its lungs, so it must stay near water. A toad with thicker, drier skin is less tied to water because it relies more on lungs.
bullets: Thin, moist, permeable, large and well supplied
Earthworm skin and fish gills share the same features
A thick dry surface is protective but a poor exchanger

content.heading: Go deeper: Gills, tracheae and lungs compared
paragraphs: A fish gill is a set of lamellae over which water flows. Blood flows in the opposite direction to the water, so oxygen is taken up along the whole length. That counter-current current keeps the gradient steep.
An insect tracheal system carries air directly to the tissues through spiracles and tracheae. Diffusion does the last step through tracheoles, so no blood is needed as an oxygen carrier.
A lung is an internal air sac that is ventilated by muscles. The alveoli are thin-walled and surrounded by capillaries, so the same four features appear inside the body rather than on the surface.
A bird lung uses air sacs to keep air flowing in one direction. That one-way flow keeps the gradient steep, which is how a bird extracts more oxygen than a mammal lung of the same size.
An insect larva in water may use gills, while the adult uses tracheae. The same animal therefore changes its exchange surface when it changes its habitat and its stage.
The double circulation of a mammal keeps alveolar oxygen high because the lung circuit is separate from the body circuit. That separation is part of why a mammal can sustain a high metabolism.
bullets: Fish: counter-current flow keeps the gradient steep
Insects: air carried directly to the tissues
Lungs: internal alveoli ventilated by muscles

content.heading: Go deeper: Stomata and lenticels in plants
paragraphs: Stomata are pores in the leaves bordered by guard cells. When the cells are turgid the pore opens, when flaccid it closes. That opening lets carbon dioxide in and water vapour out, so the leaf trades one for the other.
Lenticels are loose patches of cells in the bark that allow gas exchange in stems and roots. A stem cannot open stomata through its bark, so lenticels are its route to the air.
Roots also need oxygen for respiration. Lenticels and the air spaces of the soil supply it, which is why waterlogged soil that excludes air kills roots even when water is plentiful.
A cactus opens its stomata at night and keeps them closed in the day. Its photosynthesis therefore occurs with the least water loss, which is the CAM strategy already named in the core.
A submerged leaf cannot use stomata because water blocks gas entry. Many aquatic plants therefore have stomata on the upper surface, where they meet the air above the water.
bullets: Stomata open and close by guard-cell turgor
Lenticels allow gas exchange through bark
Waterlogged soil kills roots by excluding air

content.question: Why does a fish die when it is taken out of water, even though air contains more oxygen than water?
hints: Gill lamellae are supported by water and collapse in air.
Collapsed lamellae greatly reduce the exposed surface area.
The gill surface also dries, so oxygen cannot dissolve.

lessons.title: Gas Exchange in Plants
lessons.objective: Describe the opening and closing of stomata, identify lenticels and root surfaces as gas-exchange routes, and compare leaf gas exchange in light and darkness.

content.heading: Gas exchange in plants
paragraphs: A maize leaf at noon is losing water through thousands of tiny pores while it takes in carbon (IV) oxide. The same pores must balance food-making against water loss.

content.heading: Stomata and the guard cells
paragraphs: Each stoma is a pore between two guard cells. Guard cells are kidney-shaped, have thicker inner walls and contain chloroplasts. When they take up water and become turgid, they bow outward and the pore opens; when they lose water, they become flaccid and the pore closes.
The movement is driven by osmosis. Potassium ions enter the guard cells, lowering their water potential so water follows; when potassium leaves, water leaves and the pore shuts.

Stomata usually open in light and close in darkness or drought. This lets carbon (IV) oxide enter for photosynthesis while limiting water loss, but the balance changes with humidity, temperature and wind.
bullets: Stoma: a pore between two guard cells.
Turgid guard cells open the pore; flaccid guard cells close it.
Potassium ions and osmosis drive the opening and closing.
content.takeaway: Guard cells open the pore when turgid and close it when flaccid.

check.question: A stoma opens when its guard cells
options: Take in water and become turgid
Are covered by a waxy cuticle
check.why: Water uptake makes the guard cells turgid and their curved walls pull the pore open.

content.heading: Lenticels, roots and other surfaces
paragraphs: Most gas exchange in a leaf happens through stomata, but the leaf surface is covered by a waxy cuticle that limits diffusion. The stomata are therefore the main controllable gates.

Woody stems have lenticels, loose patches of cells in the bark that let oxygen in and carbon (IV) oxide out. Roots take up oxygen from air spaces in the soil, and root hairs increase the surface for this exchange.
Submerged plants may have no stomata and exchange gases over thin leaves, while floating leaves keep stomata on the upper surface. The surface is positioned where the gas supply is.
bullets: Leaves: stomata through the cuticle.
Woody stems: lenticels in the bark.
Roots: root hairs and air spaces in the soil.
content.takeaway: Stomata serve leaves, lenticels serve stems, and root surfaces serve roots.

check.question: Which surface allows gas exchange in a woody stem?
check.why: Lenticels are loose patches in the bark that connect the stem's air spaces to the atmosphere.

content.heading: Day and night in the leaf
paragraphs: In daylight, photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration. The leaf takes in carbon (IV) oxide and releases oxygen, so the net exchange hides the respiration that is still going on.
At night, photosynthesis stops but respiration continues. The leaf takes in oxygen and releases carbon (IV) oxide, which is why a respiring plant can be shown with limewater in the dark.
Respiration in plants also produces heat and uses stored food. The gas exchange of the whole plant depends on stomata, lenticels and root surfaces working together, not on one organ.
bullets: Day: photosynthesis dominates; carbon (IV) oxide enters and oxygen leaves.
Night: respiration dominates; oxygen enters and carbon (IV) oxide leaves.
Limewater turns milky when carbon (IV) oxide is bubbled through it.
content.takeaway: In light the leaf gains carbon and loses oxygen; at night the direction reverses.

check.question: At night, a leaf releases more
check.why: Photosynthesis stops at night, so respiration releases carbon (IV) oxide and uses oxygen.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Stomata open when guard cells are turgid and close when flaccid. Light, water supply and carbon (IV) oxide control this opening. Lenticels serve woody stems, while roots take oxygen from soil air.

content.problem: A potted plant is sealed in a clear container with limewater and kept in the dark. Predict what happens to the limewater and why.

steps.reason: Photosynthesis cannot run without light.
steps.result: The plant stops taking in carbon (IV) oxide.
steps.predictPrompt: Does respiration stop too?

steps.reason: Respiration continues day and night in living cells.
steps.result: The plant releases carbon (IV) oxide into the container.

steps.reason: Carbon (IV) oxide reacts with limewater.
steps.result: The limewater turns milky.

content.heading: Go deeper: The guard cell mechanism
paragraphs: A guard cell swells when it takes up water, but its inner wall is thicker than its outer wall. The cell therefore bends outward and opens the pore. When it loses water it becomes straight and the pore closes.
Potassium and malate control the swelling. When potassium enters the guard cell, water follows by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid. When potassium leaves, water follows and the pore closes.
Opening is therefore an osmotic event, not a muscular one. A plant can open and close thousands of pores without any muscle at all.
The outer wall of a guard cell is thicker than the inner wall, so swelling bends it outward. That asymmetry is what turns a pressure change into an opening movement.
Abscisic acid closes stomata during drought. It is the signal that the plant is losing water faster than the roots can replace it, and closure is its immediate response.
A leaf that wilts at midday but recovers by night has closed its stomata against water loss. Its carbon dioxide supply falls at the same time, so photosynthesis dips even though light is strong.
bullets: Guard cells bend outward when turgid and open the pore
Potassium and malate drive the water movement
Opening is osmotic, not muscular

content.heading: Go deeper: Day and night in a leaf
paragraphs: In daylight a leaf photosynthesises and respires both. Carbon dioxide is taken in, oxygen is released and water is lost through the same pores. The net exchange depends on which process is faster.

At night photosynthesis stops but respiration continues. The leaf then takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, so the direction of exchange reverses. A leaf at night is a net emitter of carbon dioxide.
A desert plant reduces that daytime loss by opening its stomata at night. It fixes carbon dioxide in the cool hours and stores it for photosynthesis in the day.
A leaf that is kept in darkness for a night must draw on its starch reserves to respire. A destarched leaf therefore shows no starch after a night, which is the basis of the iodine test.
A leaf in bright light may lose more water through open stomata than it gains from roots. It can therefore wilt at midday even when the soil is wet, which is midday depression.
A plant that is kept in light for two days and then in darkness will exhaust its starch. That exhaustion is why a destarched leaf must be kept in darkness before any test for photosynthesis.
bullets: Day: photosynthesis and respiration both occur
Night: only respiration, so carbon dioxide is released
CAM plants open stomata at night to save water

content.heading: Go deeper: Lenticels, roots and the air in soil
paragraphs: A stem exchanges through lenticels, loose patches in the bark that connect internal air spaces to the atmosphere. When the stem is submerged, those patches are blocked and the internal tissues can suffocate.
Roots respire and need oxygen from the soil air. A waterlogged soil has no air spaces, so roots respire anaerobically and produce ethanol, which damages them.
Aerenchyma is a tissue with large air spaces that carries air to submerged roots. Rice and water lilies therefore survive in water that would kill a plant without those spaces.
Rice survives flooding because its aerenchyma carries air from the shoot to the root. A plant without that tissue, such as a bean, dies quickly in waterlogged soil.

The potato tuber is a stem that respires in soil air throughout long winter storage. It needs lenticels to exchange gases underground, which is why a stored tuber must be aired and not sealed in plastic.
bullets: Lenticels connect stem air spaces to the atmosphere
Waterlogged soil suffocates roots
Aerenchyma carries air to submerged roots

content.question: Why do stomata close on a hot, dry afternoon even though photosynthesis needs carbon (IV) oxide?
hints: Open stomata lose water vapour as well as exchange gases.
Water loss lowers guard-cell turgor and can wilt the leaf.
Closing the stomata protects the plant from drying out.

lessons.title: Aerobic Respiration
lessons.objective: Outline glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain, and explain how oxygen allows a large ATP yield.

content.heading: Aerobic respiration
paragraphs: A runner's muscles keep working long after the first few seconds because oxygen is available. Aerobic respiration unlocks most of the energy in glucose in three linked stages.

content.heading: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
paragraphs: Glycolysis is the first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. It happens in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. One glucose molecule (6 carbons) is split into two pyruvate molecules (3 carbons each).
The process uses two ATP to start and produces four ATP, so the net gain is two ATP. It also transfers energy to NADH, which will carry electrons to later stages.
Glycolysis is a chain of enzyme-controlled steps, not a single explosion. Because it can run without oxygen, it gives a cell a quick supply of ATP when oxygen is short.
bullets: Location: cytoplasm; oxygen not required.
Glucose (6C) splits into two pyruvate (3C) molecules.
Net gain: 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
content.takeaway: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and gives a small net ATP gain.

check.question: The net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule is
check.why: Four ATP are made but two are used to start glycolysis, leaving a net gain of two.

content.heading: The Krebs cycle in the mitochondrion
paragraphs: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl CoA, releasing carbon (IV) oxide and forming NADH. Acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle in the matrix.
In the Krebs cycle, acetyl CoA joins a four-carbon acceptor to make a six-carbon acid. The acid is broken down in steps, releasing carbon (IV) oxide and transferring energy to ATP, NADH and FADH2.
Each glucose produces two turns of the cycle. The cycle itself makes only a small amount of ATP directly; most of the energy is now carried by NADH and FADH2 to the inner membrane.
bullets: Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA, releasing carbon (IV) oxide.
The Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose and releases more carbon (IV) oxide.
It makes a little ATP and loads NADH and FADH2 with energy.
content.takeaway: Krebs strips carbon and loads electron carriers.

check.question: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
check.why: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle are in the mitochondrial matrix.

content.heading: Oxygen and the electron transport chain
paragraphs: NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons pass along the chain, energy pumps protons and the return flow drives ATP synthesis.

Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. It combines with electrons and protons to form water, and this step keeps the chain running; without oxygen, the carriers stay reduced and the whole aerobic pathway stalls.

The complete breakdown of one glucose yields carbon (IV) oxide, water and a large amount of ATP. Many textbooks quote 36-38 ATP, while modern estimates are nearer 30-32; both show the large aerobic yield. Some energy is released as heat, which helps maintain body temperature.
bullets: Electron transport chain: inner mitochondrial membrane.
Oxygen accepts the final electrons and forms water.
Most ATP is made here; some energy is lost as heat.
content.takeaway: Oxygen accepts the last electrons and lets the ATP pipeline run.

check.question: The role of oxygen in aerobic respiration is to
options: Accept the final electrons and form water
Make carbon (IV) oxide in the Krebs cycle
Carry electrons to the Krebs cycle
check.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Remember the order: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, Krebs in the matrix, and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane. The chain makes most ATP, and oxygen is needed only at the last stage.

content.problem: One glucose molecule yields 2 ATP in glycolysis and 2 ATP in the Krebs cycle. The electron transport chain brings the textbook total to 38 ATP. How many ATP come from the chain, and why does oxygen matter?

steps.reason: Glycolysis and Krebs make ATP directly.
steps.predictPrompt: Where is the rest of the energy released?

steps.reason: The total is 38 ATP, so subtract the direct yield.
steps.result: 38 - 4 = 34 ATP from the electron transport chain.

steps.reason: Oxygen accepts the final electrons and keeps the chain running.
steps.result: Without oxygen the chain stops and the large ATP yield is lost.

content.heading: Go deeper: Glycolysis step by step
paragraphs: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two molecules of pyruvate in the cytoplasm. Four ATP are made, but two are used to start the process, so the net yield is two ATP. That net gain is the same with or without oxygen.

Glycolysis is therefore the universal first stage. Aerobic and anaerobic respiration both begin there, and they diverge only after pyruvate is made. The earlier stages of the two pathways are identical.
The two pyruvate molecules then enter the mitochondrion in aerobic respiration. In yeast and muscle they do not, because those cells lack sufficient oxygen.
The two ATP used at the start are an investment. The four made later repay that investment with a profit of two, which is why the net yield of glycolysis is two.
Glycolysis can start without any prior enzyme synthesis. The enzymes are already present, so a cell can respond to sudden demand within seconds of the signal that it needs energy.
The NADH made in glycolysis must be reoxidised for glycolysis to continue. Aerobic respiration reoxidises it in mitochondria, while lactate and ethanol do so without oxygen.
bullets: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate
Net yield of glycolysis is two ATP
Aerobic and anaerobic pathways share glycolysis

content.heading: Go deeper: The Krebs cycle in the matrix
paragraphs: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate loses carbon dioxide to form acetyl-CoA. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group to carbon dioxide, releasing carriers that deliver energy to the electron transport chain.
The cycle turns once for each pyruvate, so one glucose drives it twice. Its products are therefore carbon dioxide, reduced carriers and a small direct yield of ATP.
The enzymes of the cycle sit in the matrix because that is where acetyl-CoA is made. A mitochondrion that lacks the matrix enzymes cannot complete aerobic respiration.
The cycle is amphibolic, meaning it both breaks down and builds up. Its intermediates are withdrawn to make amino acids and other products, so it links energy to growth.
The cycle needs ADP and phosphate to continue. When ATP is plentiful, the cycle slows, so the rate of respiration is set by demand rather than by supply.
The carbon dioxide from the cycle is released into the matrix and diffuses out. That is the carbon dioxide of respiration, not the carbon dioxide that was fixed in photosynthesis.
bullets: Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA to carbon dioxide
One glucose drives the cycle twice
Cycle enzymes sit in the mitochondrial matrix

content.heading: Go deeper: The electron transport chain and oxygen
paragraphs: Reduced carriers from glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the link reaction deliver electrons to the chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain.
As electrons pass along the chain, protons are pumped across the membrane. Their return through ATP synthase makes ATP, so the large yield of aerobic respiration comes from this stage.
Cyanide blocks the chain by binding to its proteins, and carbon monoxide competes with oxygen for haemoglobin. Both therefore stop aerobic respiration even though oxygen may still be present.
The ATP made per glucose depends on which shuttle carries electrons into the mitochondrion. That is why textbooks quote a range rather than a single number for the aerobic yield.
The heat felt in a germinating flask comes from the energy lost as heat at each step of the chain. That heat is a small price for the large yield of ATP that the chain provides.
That chain is therefore the site of most of the energy.
bullets: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor
Proton flow through ATP synthase makes most ATP
Cyanide and carbon monoxide block aerobic respiration

content.question: Why does a muscle cell switch to anaerobic respiration when oxygen runs out?
hints: The electron transport chain needs oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
Without oxygen, NADH cannot be reoxidised to NAD+.
Glycolysis can continue only if NAD+ is regenerated, so pyruvate is converted to lactic acid.

lessons.title: Anaerobic Respiration and Fermentation
lessons.objective: Explain lactic acid formation and oxygen debt in muscles, describe fermentation in yeast, and compare aerobic with anaerobic respiration.

content.heading: Anaerobic respiration and fermentation
paragraphs: A sprinter finishes a race gasping for air, while a bowl of dough rises quietly on a kitchen table. Both are using anaerobic respiration, but their products are different.

content.heading: Lactic acid in muscles
paragraphs: During hard exercise, muscles may use oxygen faster than blood can deliver it. Glycolysis continues, but pyruvate is converted to lactic acid instead of entering the Krebs cycle, so only two ATP are gained per glucose.

Lactic acid lowers the pH of muscle tissue and contributes to fatigue during intense exercise. Cramp is mainly a neuromuscular problem, not simply a lactic acid build-up. The muscle is not poisoned permanently; when oxygen returns, some lactic acid is oxidised to carbon (IV) oxide and water, and some is converted back to glucose in the liver.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to remove lactic acid is called the oxygen debt. Breathing stays fast because the body is repaying that debt, not because the muscles are still working hard.
bullets: Muscle anaerobic respiration: glucose to lactic acid, net 2 ATP.
Lactic acid contributes to fatigue and cramp.
Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed to remove lactic acid.
Lactic acid lowers pH and contributes to fatigue.
content.takeaway: No oxygen means lactate, two ATP and an oxygen debt.

check.question: The product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle is
check.why: Human muscle converts pyruvate to lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient.

content.heading: Ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast
paragraphs: Yeast is a single-celled fungus that respires aerobically when oxygen is present but ferments sugar when oxygen is low. Glycolysis yields two ATP, and the pyruvate is then converted to ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide.

Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast and some other microbes. The carbon (IV) oxide makes bread dough rise, while the ethanol evaporates during baking; in palm wine, beer and wine, ethanol is the product people want.
Yeast is also used to make bioethanol, yeast extract, vitamins and animal feed. Its ability to ferment sugar is therefore economically important in food, drink and fuel production.
bullets: Yeast fermentation: glucose to ethanol + carbon (IV) oxide, net 2 ATP.
Carbon (IV) oxide raises bread dough; ethanol is the aim in drinks and fuel.
Yeast is economically important in food, drink and bioethanol production.
content.takeaway: Yeast turns sugar into ethanol, carbon (IV) oxide and a little ATP.

check.question: Which gas makes bread dough rise during yeast fermentation?
check.why: Carbon (IV) oxide released by yeast forms bubbles that expand the dough.

content.heading: Aerobic versus anaerobic
paragraphs: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, breaks glucose completely and yields about 30-38 ATP depending on the textbook. Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen, breaks glucose only partly and yields two ATP, so it is much less efficient per glucose molecule.

Aerobic respiration happens mainly in mitochondria and releases carbon (IV) oxide and water. Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm and releases lactic acid in muscle, or ethanol and carbon (IV) oxide in yeast and waterlogged roots.
Anaerobic respiration is fast and useful in short bursts, but the waste products limit it. Aerobic respiration is slower to start but sustains long activity because it releases far more energy.
bullets: Aerobic: oxygen, mitochondria, complete breakdown, about 30-38 ATP.
Anaerobic: no oxygen, cytoplasm, partial breakdown, 2 ATP.
Anaerobic is fast but wasteful; aerobic sustains long activity.
content.takeaway: Aerobic is efficient but oxygen-dependent; anaerobic is fast but wasteful.

check.question: Which statement correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
options: Aerobic releases more ATP per glucose than anaerobic
Anaerobic releases more ATP per glucose than aerobic
Both release the same amount of ATP per glucose
Anaerobic requires oxygen but aerobic does not
check.why: Complete aerobic breakdown releases far more ATP than partial anaerobic breakdown.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Muscle anaerobic respiration gives lactic acid and no carbon (IV) oxide. Yeast fermentation gives ethanol plus carbon (IV) oxide. Both yield only 2 ATP per glucose, far less than aerobic respiration.

content.problem: A sealed flask of yeast and glucose solution is connected to limewater. Predict two observations and explain them.

steps.reason: Yeast ferments glucose and releases carbon (IV) oxide.
steps.result: Bubbles appear in the flask and gas travels to the limewater.
steps.predictPrompt: What will the limewater do?

steps.reason: Carbon (IV) oxide turns limewater milky.
steps.result: The limewater becomes milky.

steps.reason: The flask is sealed, so oxygen is soon used up and fermentation takes over.
steps.result: Ethanol is formed, giving a characteristic smell.

content.heading: Go deeper: Lactic acid in muscle and the oxygen debt
paragraphs: When oxygen is insufficient, muscle converts pyruvate to lactic acid. The conversion regenerates the carriers needed to keep glycolysis running, so two ATP continue to be made even without oxygen.

Lactic acid lowers the pH of the tissue and contributes to fatigue during intense exercise. Cramp is mainly a neuromuscular problem, not simply a lactic acid build-up, and it is not removed by massage alone.
When oxygen returns, some lactic acid is oxidised to carbon dioxide and water and some is converted back to glucose in the liver. The extra oxygen needed for that repayment is the oxygen debt.
The liver converts lactate back to glucose by the Cori cycle. That glucose returns to muscle, so the debt is repaid between organs rather than within the muscle alone.
After exercise, breathing stays fast because the body is repaying the debt. The extra oxygen oxidises lactate and restores ATP stores, so the breathing is a recovery process.
bullets: Lactate regenerates carriers so glycolysis continues
Lactic acid lowers pH and contributes to fatigue
Oxygen debt repays the lactic acid after exercise

content.heading: Go deeper: Yeast fermentation and its uses
paragraphs: In yeast, pyruvate is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carrier step is the same as in muscle, but the products differ. The net yield is still two ATP from glycolysis.
The carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise and determines the flavour of beer and palm wine. Yeast therefore converts a food store into a gas and a liquid that humans value.
Fermentation is therefore a controlled anaerobic process. It is the same chemistry that makes dough rise and the same chemistry that sours milk, directed to different products.

Fermentation also occurs in rumen microbes that digest fibre. The products are short-chain fatty acids that the host absorbs, so the microbes gain food and the host gains energy from the same process.
Fermentation also preserves food by excluding oxygen and lowering pH. Pickling and ensiling work because the microbes that ferment make conditions that other microbes cannot tolerate.
The same fermentation makes palm wine from sap. Wild yeast converts the sugar in the sap to ethanol and carbon dioxide, so the drink is fermented rather than distilled.
bullets: Yeast: pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide makes dough rise
Fermentation is controlled anaerobic respiration

content.heading: Go deeper: Aerobic versus anaerobic as a decision
paragraphs: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, occurs in mitochondria and breaks glucose completely. It yields about 30 to 38 ATP depending on the textbook and the shuttle used. Anaerobic respiration yields two ATP and leaves lactate or ethanol behind.
The decision depends on oxygen supply. A muscle cell that is well supplied with oxygen respires aerobically; the same cell under intense demand without oxygen switches to lactate.
The products therefore read the history of the cell. Lactate means oxygen was short, ethanol means yeast was fermenting, and carbon dioxide with water means aerobic respiration ran to completion.
A seed that is sown too deep may respire anaerobically before it reaches the surface. That is why depth of sowing is decided by the oxygen that diffusion can supply to the seed.
A diving duck can switch to lactate and repay the debt on surfacing. That switch lets it stay under water far longer than aerobic respiration alone could allow.
A yo-yo cyclist can burn muscle glucose aerobically at a steady pace. The same cyclist on a hill switches to lactate because demand outruns oxygen supply.
bullets: Aerobic: oxygen, mitochondria, complete breakdown
Anaerobic: no oxygen, two ATP, leftover products
Lactate or ethanol reads the oxygen history of the cell

content.question: Why does a sprinter breathe heavily after a race rather than only during the first few seconds?
hints: The muscles built up lactic acid while oxygen was short.
Extra oxygen is needed to oxidise the lactic acid.
The fast breathing after exercise is repaying the oxygen debt.

lessons.title: Excretion and Excretory Products
lessons.objective: Define excretion, distinguish it from egestion and secretion, explain its significance, and compare ammonia, urea and uric acid as nitrogenous wastes.

content.heading: Excretion and excretory products
paragraphs: A patient with kidney failure becomes drowsy when wastes build up in the blood. The body's cleaning system has stopped working, and the waste must be removed by dialysis.

content.heading: Excretion is not egestion
paragraphs: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products from the body. These wastes are made inside cells, such as carbon (IV) oxide from respiration and urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids.

Egestion is different: it is the removal of undigested food from the alimentary canal, and the material was never part of the body's metabolism. Secretion is also different, because it releases useful substances such as enzymes and hormones.
Excretion therefore includes lungs, kidneys, skin and plant stomata, but not the rectum. A useful substance released by a gland is a secretion, even though it leaves the cell.
bullets: Excretion: metabolic wastes such as carbon (IV) oxide and urea.
Egestion: undigested food removed as faeces.
Secretion: useful substances such as enzymes and hormones.
content.takeaway: Excretion removes metabolic waste; egestion removes unabsorbed food.

check.question: Which process removes undigested food from the body?
check.why: Egestion removes unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal; it was never part of metabolism.

content.heading: Why excretion matters
paragraphs: Metabolic wastes can be toxic. Carbon (IV) oxide lowers blood pH, urea raises the concentration of nitrogenous waste, and excess salts disturb the balance of water between cells and blood.
Excretion keeps the internal environment steady: water balance, salt balance, pH and temperature. This steady state is called homeostasis, and the kidneys are its main control organs in mammals.

If excretion fails, wastes accumulate and cells cannot work properly. Dialysis can temporarily remove urea and excess salts from the blood when the kidneys fail, but it does not replace every kidney function.
bullets: Wastes can be toxic and disturb pH and water balance.
Excretion helps maintain homeostasis.
Dialysis removes some wastes but is not a full substitute for kidneys.
content.takeaway: Excretion protects cells by keeping the internal environment steady.

check.question: The main control organs of water and salt balance in mammals are the
check.why: The kidneys filter blood and adjust water and salt reabsorption to control urine concentration.

content.heading: Nitrogenous wastes: ammonia, urea and uric acid
paragraphs: Ammonia is formed when amino acids are broken down. It is very soluble and highly toxic, so aquatic animals such as fish can release it directly into water, where it is quickly diluted.

Land animals convert ammonia to urea in the liver. Urea is less toxic and needs less water to excrete, which suits mammals; birds, reptiles and insects convert it to uric acid, a semi-solid paste that conserves even more water.
The choice reflects habitat: ammonia needs plenty of water, urea needs moderate water, and uric acid needs little. The trade-off is that making urea and uric acid costs energy.
bullets: Ammonia: very soluble, toxic, released by fish into water.
Urea: less toxic, made in the liver, excreted by mammals.
Uric acid: semi-solid, conserves water, used by birds, reptiles and insects.
content.takeaway: Ammonia is fast and watery; urea is balanced; uric acid saves water.

check.question: Which nitrogenous waste is least soluble and conserves the most water?
check.why: Uric acid is excreted as a semi-solid paste, which limits water loss.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Excretion is metabolic waste; egestion is undigested food. Ammonia suits fish, urea suits mammals, and uric acid suits birds, reptiles and insects, so match the nitrogenous waste to its advantage.

content.problem: A student says faeces are an excretory product. Correct the statement and classify three wastes.

steps.reason: Faeces contain unabsorbed food that never entered cell metabolism.
steps.result: Faeces are removed by egestion, not excretion.
steps.predictPrompt: How should carbon (IV) oxide be classified?

steps.reason: It is made during respiration inside cells.
steps.result: An excretory product removed by the lungs.

steps.reason: It is made in the liver from excess amino acids.
steps.result: An excretory product removed by the kidneys.

content.heading: Go deeper: Excretion versus egestion and secretion
paragraphs: Excretion removes metabolic waste, that is, the waste made by cells during metabolism. Carbon dioxide, urea and excess salts are therefore excretory products because they were made inside the body. The material must have entered the cells to count as excretion.

Egestion removes undigested food from the gut. That food never entered the cells, so its removal is not excretion however large the material may be. Sweating is excretion of water and salts, while defecation is egestion of never-absorbed food.

Secretion is different again. Sweat glands secrete sweat, but the sweat is also an excretory product because it carries waste. Endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood, and those hormones are not waste.

Salt is excreted by the kidney and the skin, but it is also needed in small amounts. Excretion therefore removes excess rather than all of a substance, and the kidney decides how much excess there is.
A kidney stone is a crystal of salts that failed to be excreted in solution. It shows that excretion must keep salts dissolved, which is why the volume of urine matters as much as its composition.
bullets: Excretion removes metabolic waste made in cells
Egestion removes undigested food that never entered cells
Secretion is release of a useful product, not of waste

content.heading: Go deeper: Ammonia, urea and uric acid
paragraphs: Ammonia is the nitrogenous waste of fish. It is very toxic, but it dissolves easily in water, so a fish can release it into the surrounding water and dilute it at once. That cheap disposal is possible only where water is plentiful.
Urea is less toxic and is excreted by mammals. It is made in the liver and carried in blood to the kidneys. Urea needs more energy to make than ammonia, but it needs far less water to carry away.
Uric acid is the least toxic and the least soluble. Birds, reptiles and insects excrete it as a semi-solid paste, which conserves water. A desert animal therefore pays in energy to save water.
A tadpole excretes ammonia because it lives in water that dilutes it. The adult frog, on land, needs a less water-demanding waste, so its nitrogenous waste changes with its habitat.
The nitrogen in waste comes from protein. A high-protein meal therefore produces more urea, which is why a meat-rich diet increases the work of the kidneys.
bullets: Ammonia suits fish: toxic but diluted by water
Urea suits mammals: less toxic, moderate water cost
Uric acid suits birds, reptiles, insects: water saved

content.heading: Go deeper: Homeostasis and why excretion matters
paragraphs: Cells need a steady internal medium, and waste poisons that medium. Excretion therefore maintains homeostasis by removing nitrogenous waste, excess salts and water, and by helping to control pH. A kidney failure shows how quickly the medium becomes unfit.

The lungs and skin assist. Lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour, while skin excretes water and salts in sweat. Those routes do not replace the kidney, but they share the work of keeping the blood steady.

Plants excrete too, but they store or shed much of their waste. Gases are released through stomata, tannins and resins accumulate in old tissue, and leaves that carry waste are shed. That is why a plant can survive without a kidney.

Blood pH is held by the lungs and the kidneys together. The lungs remove carbon dioxide and the kidneys remove acids, so a failure in either organ disturbs the balance that the other must compensate for.
Excretion also removes drugs and their breakdown products. That is why a patient with kidney failure must be given smaller doses, because the drug is not being cleared.
bullets: Excretion maintains the steady medium cells need
Lungs and skin assist the kidney in excretion
Plants store or shed waste in leaves and bark

content.question: Why do desert reptiles excrete uric acid rather than ammonia?
hints: Ammonia is highly toxic and very soluble.
Excreting ammonia would require a lot of water.
Uric acid is semi-solid and conserves water, though making it costs energy.

lessons.title: Excretory Structures
lessons.objective: Relate the structure of contractile vacuoles, flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, kidneys, stomata and lenticels to their excretory functions.

content.heading: Excretory structures
paragraphs: A pond Amoeba, a tapeworm, an earthworm and a grasshopper all get rid of wastes without owning a kidney. Each has a different excretory structure suited to its body plan and habitat.

content.heading: Contractile vacuole, flame cell and nephridium
paragraphs: An Amoeba lives in fresh water, where water constantly enters by osmosis. Its contractile vacuole collects the excess water and expels it, preventing the cell from bursting; the same organelle removes some dissolved wastes.

A flame cell is a hollow cell with a tuft of cilia that beats like a flame. It drives fluid through a network of tubules in flatworms such as Taenia, filtering wastes while useful materials are reabsorbed.
A nephridium is a coiled tubule in an earthworm. It opens into the body cavity, takes up coelomic fluid, reabsorbs useful salts and water, and releases urine through a pore in the body wall.
bullets: Contractile vacuole: collects and expels excess water.
Flame cell: ciliated cell that drives fluid through tubules in flatworms.
Nephridium: coiled tubule that filters coelomic fluid in earthworms.
content.takeaway: Contractile vacuole pumps water; flame cells and nephridia filter body fluid.

check.question: Which structure prevents a freshwater Amoeba from bursting?
check.why: The contractile vacuole expels excess water that enters the cell by osmosis.

content.heading: Malpighian tubules and kidneys
paragraphs: Insects use Malpighian tubules, fine tubes that open into the gut. They take up uric acid and salts from the body fluid and empty them into the hindgut, where water is reabsorbed and the waste leaves with faeces.
The vertebrate kidney is a compact organ packed with nephrons. Each nephron filters blood under pressure, reabsorbs useful glucose, salts and water, and leaves urea and excess ions in the urine.

The structures get more complex with body size: a contractile vacuole in a single cell, flame cells and nephridia in worms, Malpighian tubules in insects, and paired kidneys in vertebrates. The principle is the same: remove waste and reclaim what is useful.
bullets: Malpighian tubules: take up uric acid and empty it into the hindgut.
Kidney nephrons: filter blood, reabsorb useful materials, leave urine.
The structures become more complex as body size increases.
content.takeaway: Filter, reabsorb, then excrete: the same logic at every level.

check.question: Malpighian tubules empty waste into the
check.why: Malpighian tubules connect to the hindgut, where water is reabsorbed before waste is passed out.

content.heading: Stomata and lenticels
paragraphs: Plants do not have kidneys. Their main excretory surfaces are stomata in leaves and lenticels in woody stems, which release carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour and allow oxygen to leave.
Some plant wastes are stored rather than expelled. Tannins, resins, gums, mucilage and alkaloids are kept in vacuoles, ducts or specialized cells, and may be released when the plant is damaged.

Storage protects the plant from its own toxic products and can also deter herbivores. The excretory structure therefore matches the organism: a pump in a protist, a tubule in a worm, a kidney in a mammal, and a pore in a leaf.
bullets: Stomata and lenticels release gases and water vapour.
Tannins, resins, gums, mucilage and alkaloids may be stored.
Storage protects the plant and can deter herbivores.
content.takeaway: Animal excretory organs filter; plant surfaces release or store wastes.

check.question: Which pair are plant excretory surfaces?
check.why: Leaves use stomata and woody stems use lenticels for gas and water-vapour exchange.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Contractile vacuole = water; flame cell or nephridium = filtered body fluid; Malpighian tubule = uric acid; kidney = urea; stoma or lenticel = gases and water vapour.
