content.problem: Match each organism to its excretory structure: Amoeba, earthworm, grasshopper and mammal.

steps.reason: A single freshwater cell must expel water that enters by osmosis.
steps.result: Contractile vacuole.
steps.predictPrompt: Which structure serves the earthworm?

steps.reason: Coelomic fluid is filtered by coiled tubules that open to the outside.
steps.result: Nephridia.

steps.reason: Fine tubules take up uric acid and empty it into the hindgut.
steps.result: Malpighian tubules.

steps.reason: Blood is filtered under pressure and useful materials are reabsorbed.
steps.result: Kidneys with nephrons.

content.heading: Go deeper: Contractile vacuole and flame cells
paragraphs: A pond Amoeba faces continuous water entry because its cell sap is more concentrated than pond water. The contractile vacuole collects that water and expels it in pulses, so the cell does not burst. That pumping is the excretory work of a cell without organs.

A flatworm such as Planaria has flame cells, blind tubules with beating tufts that drive fluid along. The fluid flows to excretory pores, carrying nitrogenous waste with it. The animal has no kidney, yet it still controls water and salts.

Both structures are local solutions. The vacuole suits a single cell, the flame cell suits a small flat body, and neither solution is a kidney. That is why the same pond Amoeba and a flatworm solve excretion in different ways.
A marine Amoeba does not need a contractile vacuole because water does not flood in. The vacuole is therefore a freshwater adaptation, and its presence tells the habitat of the cell.
A flame cell tubule has no muscles, so it cannot pump by contraction. Its beating tufts create the current, which is why the cell is named for the flame-like motion of its cilia.
bullets: Contractile vacuole expels excess water in pulses
Flame cells drive fluid to excretory pores
Each body plan has its own local solution

content.heading: Go deeper: Nephridia and Malpighian tubules
paragraphs: An earthworm has nephridia, coiled tubules that open into the coelom and discharge through pores. Nitrogenous waste enters the tubule, useful substances are reabsorbed and the remainder leaves. The nephridium is therefore a filter and a reabsorber in one.

An insect has Malpighian tubules floating in the body cavity. They remove waste from the haemolymph and release it into the hindgut, where water is reabsorbed. The dry faeces that result conserve water.

The two structures differ in what they take waste from. A nephridium takes fluid from the coelom, while a Malpighian tubule takes it from the blood. That difference decides which animals can use which structure.
A nephridium can also carry gametes to the outside. In some worms the same tubule serves reproduction, so the excretory and reproductive systems share a structure.
A cockroach that is denied water excretes almost dry faeces. Its Malpighian tubules and hindgut together show how an insect can live in a dry habitat without a kidney.
bullets: Nephridia filter coelomic fluid and reabsorb useful substances
Malpighian tubules take waste from haemolymph to the hindgut
Water is reabsorbed in the hindgut, leaving dry faeces

content.heading: Go deeper: Kidneys, stomata and lenticels
paragraphs: A kidney is a paired organ that filters blood and reabsorbs what is still useful. It is far more effective than a nephridium or a tubule because it can concentrate urine and respond to hormones. That is why a mammal can live in a desert where a worm cannot.

A leaf uses stomata to release gases and water vapour. A stem uses lenticels to exchange gases through bark. Those openings are excretory in the sense that they let waste gases leave, but they are primarily exchange organs.
The list therefore spans scales: a vacuole in a cell, tubules in a worm, lungs and skin in a mammal, and pores in a leaf. Each structure is matched to the body that carries it.
A desmodium leaf can fold its leaflets at night to reduce water loss. That movement is not excretion, but it protects the stomata that must stay open for gas exchange by day.
A fish kidney makes dilute urine because water is plentiful and must be lost. A desert mammal kidney makes concentrated urine because water is scarce and must be saved.
bullets: Kidneys filter blood and reabsorb useful substances
Stomata release gases; lenticels exchange through bark
Excretory structures match the scale of the body

content.question: Why are Malpighian tubules well suited to insects living on land?
hints: Insects must conserve water.
The tubules excrete uric acid rather than ammonia.
Water is reabsorbed from the hindgut before the waste is passed out.

lessons.title: The Mammalian Kidney
lessons.objective: Relate the structure of the kidney and nephron to ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and osmoregulation.

content.heading: The mammalian kidney
paragraphs: A football match in Kano leaves a player thirsty and passing concentrated urine. The kidneys are adjusting water loss to keep the blood steady, a balance controlled partly by ADH.

content.heading: Kidney structure
paragraphs: The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs behind the abdominal cavity, supplied by the renal artery and drained by the renal vein. Each kidney has an outer cortex, an inner medulla and a central pelvis that leads to the ureter.

The functional unit is the nephron; a kidney contains about a million of them. The nephron begins with a glomerulus inside a Bowman's capsule and continues through the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.

Blood enters the glomerulus at high pressure and leaves through the efferent arteriole, while the filtrate passes along the tubule. The arrangement of cortex, medulla and pelvis is what lets the kidney filter, reabsorb and then drain urine.
bullets: Cortex outside, medulla inside, renal pelvis draining to the ureter.
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, tubules and collecting duct form the nephron.
content.takeaway: Cortex filters, medulla concentrates, pelvis drains.

check.question: The functional unit of the kidney is the
check.why: Each nephron filters blood and modifies the filtrate to form urine.

content.heading: Ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption
paragraphs: In ultrafiltration, blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea through the capillary wall and capsule into the nephron. Blood cells and large proteins remain in the blood because they are too large.

Selective reabsorption follows. The proximal tubule uses active transport and osmosis to reclaim glucose, amino acids, most salts and much of the water; its cells have microvilli and many mitochondria for this work.

The loop of Henle creates a salt gradient in the medulla, and the collecting duct uses that gradient to reabsorb more water. Anything not reabsorbed, mainly urea, excess salts and water, leaves as urine through the ureter, bladder and urethra.
bullets: Ultrafiltration: pressure forces small molecules into Bowman's capsule.
Selective reabsorption: glucose, amino acids, salts and water are reclaimed.
Urine contains urea, excess salts and water, not glucose or protein.
content.takeaway: Filter under pressure, then take back what the body still needs.

check.question: Which substance is normally absent from urine?
check.why: Glucose is normally reabsorbed completely in the proximal tubule.

content.heading: Osmoregulation
paragraphs: Osmoregulation is the control of water and salt balance. When a person is dehydrated, the hypothalamus detects rising blood solute concentration and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH.

ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and a small amount of concentrated urine is produced. When a person drinks plenty of water, ADH falls and dilute urine is produced.

The kidney therefore controls both excretion and water balance. Alcohol and some drugs increase urine output by reducing ADH, while kidney failure reduces filtration and allows urea to accumulate in blood.
bullets: Dehydration raises ADH; ADH increases water reabsorption.
Hydration lowers ADH; more dilute urine is produced.
Kidney failure reduces filtration and causes waste accumulation.
content.takeaway: ADH tells the collecting duct to save water.

check.question: ADH increases water reabsorption by acting on the
check.why: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water returns to the blood.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Ultrafiltration keeps cells and proteins; reabsorption keeps glucose and useful salts; ADH keeps water. Urine normally contains urea, salts and water, not glucose or protein, so check each substance.

content.problem: A patient's urine contains glucose and protein. Explain what each result suggests about the nephron.

steps.reason: Glucose should be reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, or filtered only when blood glucose is very high.
steps.result: The tubule may be damaged, or the blood glucose may exceed the reabsorption limit.
steps.predictPrompt: Where should protein be stopped?

steps.reason: Large proteins should not pass through the glomerular filter.
steps.result: Protein in urine suggests damage to the filtration barrier.

steps.reason: Two abnormal findings point to a kidney problem rather than a normal variation.
steps.result: The patient needs medical tests to locate the damage.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cortex, medulla and the nephron
paragraphs: The kidney is divided into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. Glomeruli lie in the cortex and loops of Henle descend into the medulla. That arrangement puts filtration where blood arrives and concentration where the gradient is steepest.

A nephron begins with a glomerulus inside a Bowman's capsule. Pressure forces fluid from the glomerulus into the capsule, and that glomerular filtrate then flows through the tubule. The tubule is where the useful substances are recovered.

The loop of Henle builds the gradient that lets the kidney concentrate urine. Without that gradient, urine could not be made more concentrated than blood, and a desert mammal could not conserve water.
A nephron is about three centimetres long, so a kidney contains more than a million of them. That number is why a kidney can be so much more efficient than a single tubule.
The medulla is striped because the loops of Henle run there in parallel. That striping is the visible sign of the gradient that concentrates urine.
bullets: Glomeruli in cortex; loops descend into medulla
Filtration at the glomerulus; recovery in the tubule
The loop builds the gradient for concentrated urine

content.heading: Go deeper: Ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption
paragraphs: Ultrafiltration forces small molecules through the glomerular filter. Water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea pass, while red cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood. The filtrate is therefore protein-free.

Selective reabsorption then removes the useful substances from the tubule. All glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, which is why urine normally contains none. Sodium and the required amount of water are reabsorbed under hormonal control.
What remains is urea, excess salts and the water that must be lost. That remainder is urine, and its volume is decided by how much water the body can afford to lose.
Protein that appears in urine signals a damaged glomerular filter. That is why a urine test for protein is a first check for kidney disease in the clinic.
The filtrate that leaves the glomerulus is almost identical to plasma except for the proteins. That comparison is the proof that filtration is a sieving process, not a secretion.
The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtrate. That is the largest share of recovery, so a defect there changes the whole composition of urine.
bullets: Ultrafiltration passes small molecules but not cells or proteins
Glucose and amino acids are fully reabsorbed
Urine holds urea, excess salts and excess water

content.heading: Go deeper: ADH, aldosterone and the volume of urine
paragraphs: ADH controls water reabsorption from the collecting duct. When the blood is concentrated, ADH makes the duct permeable, water returns to the blood and a small volume of concentrated urine is made. When the blood is dilute, ADH falls and a large volume of dilute urine is made.

Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption from the distal tubule. More aldosterone means more sodium returned to the blood and more potassium lost into the tubule. That trade keeps blood pressure and volume steady.

A football match in Kano therefore changes urine in two ways. Sweat loss concentrates the blood, ADH rises and sodium is conserved, so the player passes less urine and loses more water through the skin.
Caffeine increases urine output by reducing ADH release. A drink that makes more urine can therefore be dehydrating, which is why water remains the better drink after exercise.
Alcohol suppresses ADH, so a drinker passes more urine and becomes dehydrated. That is why alcohol is a poor drink after exercise even though it contains water.
bullets: ADH controls water reabsorption in the collecting duct
Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule
Dehydration raises ADH and conserves sodium

content.question: Why does a dehydrated person produce less urine?
hints: Blood solute concentration rises when water is lost.
The posterior pituitary releases more ADH.
The collecting ducts reabsorb more water, leaving concentrated urine.

lessons.title: Lungs and Skin as Excretory Organs
lessons.objective: Identify the excretory products and functions of the lungs and skin, and explain how sweating and skin blood flow control body temperature.

content.heading: Lungs and skin as excretory organs
paragraphs: After a long run in Lagos, a runner's breath is moist and his shirt is wet with sweat. The lungs and skin are both disposing of waste.

content.heading: Lungs: carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour
paragraphs: The lungs are the excretory route for carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour. Carbon (IV) oxide is made in every respiring cell, carried in blood to the lungs and diffused into the alveoli to be breathed out.
Water vapour is lost with every exhale because the alveolar surface is moist. The lungs also lose heat, which is why breathing hard in a cold room produces visible vapour.
Lungs are not a route for urea. Their excretory role is tied to respiration and the need to keep blood pH stable; too much carbon (IV) oxide lowers pH and triggers faster breathing.
bullets: Lungs excrete carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.
They also lose heat with each breath.
Lungs do not excrete urea; they help control blood pH.
content.takeaway: Lungs excrete carbon (IV) oxide, water vapour and heat.

check.question: The main excretory product removed by the lungs is
check.why: Carbon (IV) oxide produced by respiration is carried to the lungs and breathed out.

content.heading: Skin: sweat and temperature control
paragraphs: The skin has sweat glands in the dermis. Each gland coils below the surface and opens at a pore; its secretion, sweat, contains water, salts, urea and lactic acid.
Sweating removes small amounts of nitrogenous waste, but its main job is cooling. As sweat evaporates it takes latent heat from the skin, helping to keep body temperature near 37°C.
Blood vessels in the skin widen in heat and narrow in cold. Wider vessels bring more blood to the surface for heat loss, while narrower vessels keep heat in the core; shivering generates extra heat.
bullets: Sweat contains water, salts, urea and lactic acid.
Evaporation of sweat removes latent heat and cools the body.
Vasodilation loses heat; vasoconstriction and shivering conserve or make heat.
content.takeaway: Sweat cools the body and carries a little urea and salt.

check.question: The main function of sweating is to
options: Remove all urea from the blood
check.why: Evaporating sweat takes latent heat from the skin and lowers body temperature.

content.heading: Working with the kidneys
paragraphs: The kidneys are the main excretory organs for urea and salts, but the lungs, skin and gut also remove wastes. Lungs remove carbon (IV) oxide, skin removes some urea and salts, and the gut removes bile pigments in faeces.

When kidneys fail, urea accumulates and the skin may carry more urea in sweat, but sweating cannot replace filtration. Dialysis takes over part of the kidney's work by cleaning blood outside the body.
Excretion is therefore a team effort: each organ removes the waste it is suited to handle, and together they keep the internal environment stable.
bullets: Kidneys: main route for urea and excess salts.
Lungs: carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.
Skin and gut: small contributions; dialysis supports failing kidneys.
content.takeaway: Lungs handle volatile waste, skin handles water and some urea, kidneys do the main filtration.

check.question: Which organ is the main route for urea excretion?
check.why: The kidneys filter urea from blood and excrete it in urine.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Lungs = carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour; skin = water, salts, urea and heat; kidneys = urea and excess salts. Do not credit the lungs with urea.

content.problem: A patient with kidney failure sweats heavily and has urea on the skin. Explain why this does not solve the problem.

steps.reason: Sweat carries water, salts and a small amount of urea.
steps.result: Only a tiny fraction of the waste is removed.
steps.predictPrompt: Can the skin filter blood?

steps.reason: The kidney filters the whole blood volume and adjusts reabsorption.
steps.result: Sweating cannot control urea concentration or water balance.

steps.reason: The failing kidney needs filtration to be replaced.
steps.result: Dialysis or a kidney transplant is required.

content.heading: Go deeper: The lungs as excretory organs
paragraphs: The lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour. Carbon dioxide from respiration dissolves in blood, is carried to the alveoli and diffuses out along its gradient. Water vapour leaves with the same breath.

That excretory role is distinct from breathing. Breathing is the ventilation of the lungs, while gas exchange is the diffusion across the alveoli. The lungs therefore excrete without filtering anything.
A person who holds the breath raises carbon dioxide in the blood until the urge to breathe becomes irresistible. That urge is the signal that the excretory load must be cleared.
The oxygen that leaves in breath comes from the air, not from the blood as a waste. The lung therefore both takes in a useful gas and gives out a waste gas in the same ventilation.
The carbon dioxide that leaves in breath was made in mitochondria. The lung therefore carries a respiratory waste that the kidney cannot remove, which is why the two organs are complementary.
The alveoli are only one cell thick, so carbon dioxide diffuses out rapidly. That thinness is the same feature that makes them efficient for oxygen uptake.
bullets: Lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour
Gas exchange is diffusion across the alveoli
Retained carbon dioxide drives the urge to breathe

content.heading: Go deeper: The skin in sweat and temperature control
paragraphs: Sweat is water with dissolved salts, produced by sweat glands in the dermis. When the body is hot, sweating increases and evaporation cools the skin. That cooling is the reason sweat is excretory and thermoregulatory at once.
Vasodilation helps the same process. Blood vessels in the skin widen, more blood reaches the surface and heat is lost there. Vasoconstriction does the reverse and conserves heat in the cold.
The skin also excretes urea in small amounts, but the kidney remains the main route. Sweat therefore assists excretion without replacing it.
A fever raises the set point of temperature control, so the body shivers to generate heat. Sweating then follows when the fever breaks, which is why a patient sweats as the fever falls.
Sweat glands are most numerous on the palms and soles. The skin therefore concentrates its excretory and cooling work on the surfaces that are most exposed to heat.
bullets: Sweat carries water and salts and cools by evaporation
Vasodilation loses heat; vasoconstriction conserves it
Skin assists excretion but does not replace the kidney

content.heading: Go deeper: Why lungs and skin matter for the kidney
paragraphs: The kidney shares its work with lungs and skin because each route carries a different waste. Carbon dioxide must leave as a gas, water vapour as a vapour and salts in sweat. No single organ can carry all three forms.

That sharing also decides how much water the kidney must save. On a hot day the skin loses more water in sweat, so the kidney makes less urine. The organs are therefore coordinated through ADH and through temperature.
A patient with kidney failure shows the limit of that sharing. Lungs and skin can carry some load, but urea and salts accumulate in the blood, which is why dialysis must replace the kidney.
Dialysis replaces filtration but not the hormonal roles of the kidney. A patient on dialysis must therefore also be given erythropoietin to make red cells, because the kidney that made it has failed.
A patient who cannot breathe well retains carbon dioxide and becomes acidotic. The kidney then compensates by excreting more acid, so the two systems trade work when one fails.
bullets: Each waste has its own form and its own organ
Sweat loss reduces the water the kidney must excrete
Dialysis replaces the kidney when sharing is not enough

content.question: Why does the skin become red and sweaty during heavy exercise?
hints: Muscles produce extra heat during exercise.
Vasodilation brings more blood to the skin surface.
Sweat evaporation removes latent heat and cools the body.

lessons.title: Plant Excretion and Its Products
lessons.objective: Identify the excretory products of plants, including gases and stored chemicals, and explain their economic importance.

content.heading: Plant excretion and its products
paragraphs: A rubber tapper cuts a tree and collects a milky sap; a carpenter smells resin in pine wood. Plants make and store many chemicals that people use.

content.heading: Gases and water vapour
paragraphs: Plants exchange carbon (IV) oxide, oxygen and water vapour with the air through stomata and lenticels. Carbon (IV) oxide is a product of respiration, while oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis and leaves during the day.

These gases are not waste to every organism. Oxygen supports respiration in animals and is used in hospitals, while carbon (IV) oxide is used by plants for photosynthesis and in soft drinks and fire extinguishers.

Water vapour is also lost through transpiration, though the main stored excretory products discussed here are the organic chemicals. The plant cannot store these gases, so they diffuse out as soon as they are made.
bullets: Carbon (IV) oxide is released by respiration.
Oxygen is released by photosynthesis during the day.
Water vapour leaves through stomata and lenticels.
content.takeaway: Plants release gases and water vapour through stomata and lenticels.

check.question: Which gas is released by photosynthesis and passes out through stomata?
check.why: Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis and diffuses out through the stomata.

content.heading: Tannins, resins, gums and mucilage
paragraphs: Tannins are bitter phenolic compounds stored in vacuoles and bark. They deter herbivores and microbes, and people use them to tan leather, make dyes and produce astringent medicines.
Resins are sticky mixtures secreted into ducts, especially in conifers. They seal wounds and repel insects, and are used in varnishes, adhesives, incense and some medicines.

Gums and mucilage are polysaccharides that swell in water. Gums exuded from acacia and other trees are used as adhesives, thickeners and emulsifiers; mucilage from okra and cactus holds water and soothes irritated tissue.
bullets: Tannins: tan leather, make dyes and astringent medicines.
Resins: seal wounds; used in varnish, adhesives and incense.
Gums and mucilage: thicken, emulsify and hold water.
content.takeaway: Tannins tan, resins seal, gums glue and mucilage thickens.

check.question: Which plant product is used to tan leather?
check.why: Tannins bind to proteins in animal hides and preserve them as leather.

content.heading: Alkaloids and the economic ledger
paragraphs: Alkaloids are nitrogen-containing compounds that taste bitter and often affect the nervous system. Plants store them in leaves, bark, roots or seeds, where they deter herbivores and kill microbes.

Many alkaloids are medicines in the right dose: quinine from cinchona treats malaria, morphine from opium poppy relieves pain, and caffeine from coffee is a stimulant. Nicotine from tobacco is an insecticide but is harmful to people.
The economic importance of plant excretions is therefore double-edged. They provide medicines, tannins, resins, gums, dyes and food additives, but some are toxic and must be used carefully.
bullets: Alkaloids are bitter, nitrogen-containing defensive compounds.
Quinine, morphine and caffeine are useful alkaloids.
Some alkaloids are toxic, so dose and preparation matter.
content.takeaway: Plant wastes become medicines, materials and poisons depending on dose.

check.question: Quinine, used to treat malaria, is obtained from
check.why: Quinine is an alkaloid extracted from the bark of the cinchona tree.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Tannins tan leather, resins make varnish and incense, gums and mucilage thicken, and alkaloids include quinine and morphine. Plants also release oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide and water vapour.

content.problem: A factory wants to use local plant waste. Evaluate three options: tannin-rich bark, acacia gum and cinchona bark.

steps.reason: Tannins bind proteins and are astringent.
steps.result: Suitable for tanning leather and making dyes.
steps.predictPrompt: What can acacia gum be used for?

steps.reason: The gum swells in water and forms a sticky gel.
steps.result: Suitable as an adhesive, thickener or emulsifier.

steps.reason: It contains quinine, an alkaloid used against malaria.
steps.result: Valuable for medicine, but extraction and dose control are essential.

content.heading: Go deeper: Gases, tannins and the waste a plant keeps
paragraphs: A plant releases oxygen from photosynthesis and carbon dioxide from respiration. Those gases leave through stomata, so the leaf is an excretory surface for gases even though it is primarily a photosynthetic organ.
Tannins, resins and gums accumulate in old tissue and heartwood. They are not released to the environment but stored away from living cells. That storage is excretion by isolation.
Alkaloids such as nicotine and quinine are nitrogenous wastes that the plant keeps. They poison insects and mammals that eat the plant, so storage also serves as defence.
A gum tree exudes gum when its bark is wounded. The gum seals the wound and discourages insects, so a waste product becomes a repair material.
A plant that is wounded exudes resin to seal the wound. The resin is therefore both an excretory product and a repair material, which is why it is valuable in varnish.
A plant also excretes excess water through hydathodes in wet conditions. That guttation is the liquid form of the water loss that stomata lose as vapour in dry air.
bullets: Oxygen and carbon dioxide leave through stomata
Tannins, resins and gums are stored in old tissue
Alkaloids are stored nitrogenous waste that deters herbivores

content.heading: Go deeper: Shedding and the leaf as a waste store
paragraphs: A leaf that accumulates waste is shed at the end of the season. The tree therefore excretes by abscission, losing the waste with the fallen leaf. That is why leaf fall is more than protection against drought.
Bark is also shed. Tannins and resins that accumulate in outer bark leave with it when the bark peels. The plant therefore has two disposable stores: leaves and bark.
A perennial stores waste for years in heartwood, while an annual sheds it each season. The lifespan therefore changes the excretory strategy.
An evergreen sheds as it grows, not all at once. Its leaves therefore have a longer life in which to accumulate waste, but they are replaced gradually rather than seasonally.
A deciduous tree sheds all its leaves at once, so its waste leaves in one season. An evergreen spreads that loss over the year, so each leaf must last longer in service.
bullets: Leaves are shed with accumulated waste
Bark is shed with tannins and resins
Perennials store waste in heartwood for years

content.heading: Go deeper: Economic uses of excretory products
paragraphs: Waste products become useful when they protect or flavour. Tannins preserve leather, resins make varnish and gum arabic is used as an emulsifier. Quinine from cinchona bark treats malaria, and nicotine is used as an insecticide.

That usefulness does not make the products secretions. They are still wastes from the plant's point of view, stored because they cannot be released safely. Humans value them because they are potent chemicals.
A plant that excretes into storage therefore pays a cost in tissue and gains a benefit in defence. The balance of that trade decides which wastes a species keeps.
Tannin from the bark of a pod protects the tree by sealing wounds. The same chemical preserves leather because it hardens proteins, so the plant's defence becomes human industry.
Gum arabic is harvested from Acacia trees that exude it after wounding. That harvest is sustainable because the tree seals the wound and continues to produce gum in later seasons.
Nicotine was once used as a general insecticide because it is poisonous to insects. Its toxicity to humans is why that use has been restricted in many places.
bullets: Tannins tan leather; resins make varnish; gum emulsifies
Quinine treats malaria; nicotine kills insects
Usefulness to humans does not make a waste a secretion

content.question: Why can a plant store toxic alkaloids without poisoning itself?
hints: Alkaloids are kept inside vacuoles or specialized ducts.
They are separated from the cytoplasm where most metabolism occurs.
The same compartmentation makes them available for defence when the plant is damaged.

lessons.title: Why Support and Movement?
lessons.objective: Explain why organisms need support and movement, and compare how plants and animals achieve both.

content.heading: Why support and movement?
paragraphs: A maize plant stands upright in the wind while a grasshopper beside it jumps out of reach. Both need support and movement, but they solve the problem with very different materials.

content.heading: Why support and movement matter
paragraphs: Support gives an organism shape and posture. It holds organs in place, keeps leaves facing light, anchors roots in soil and lets a body grow tall without collapsing under its own weight.

Movement lets an organism change position or move part of its body. Animals use it to find food, escape predators, seek mates and build shelters; plants move more slowly, growing towards resources or folding leaves when touched.

Support and movement are linked. A moving body needs a frame to pull against, and a frame needs muscles or turgor to move it. The two demands compete for materials and energy, so each organism strikes a different balance.
bullets: Support holds shape, organs and posture.
Movement finds food, escapes danger and reproduces.
A moving body needs a frame and a force to act on it.
content.takeaway: Support resists gravity; movement changes position.

check.question: Which statement best explains why support and movement are linked?
options: Support alone is enough for movement
A moving body needs a frame to pull against
Movement prevents an organism from growing
Support and movement use no energy
check.why: Muscles or turgor must act on a supporting frame to produce controlled movement.

content.heading: Plants: turgor and lignified walls
paragraphs: A herbaceous plant such as a young maize shoot is held up mainly by turgor. Water fills the vacuoles of parenchyma and collenchyma cells, pressing the cell walls outwards and keeping the stem firm.

Woody plants add lignified xylem and sclerenchyma fibres. These dead, rigid cells resist bending and compression, so a tree can carry a heavy canopy; the same tissues run through roots, stems and leaves.
Plant movement is usually slow growth or a reversible change in turgor. A shoot bends towards light as cells on one side elongate, and a Mimosa leaf folds within seconds when its pulvini lose water.
bullets: Turgor pressure supports young, soft stems.
Lignified xylem and sclerenchyma support woody plants.
Plant movement uses growth or reversible turgor changes.
content.takeaway: Plants stand on water pressure and lignified walls.

check.question: Which tissue keeps a young herbaceous stem firm?
check.why: Turgor pressure in living parenchyma and collenchyma cells keeps soft stems upright.

content.heading: Animals: skeletons and muscles
paragraphs: Animals use three main support systems. An earthworm has a hydrostatic skeleton, in which fluid under pressure in body segments works against circular and longitudinal muscles; an insect has a hard exoskeleton; a mammal has an internal endoskeleton of bone and cartilage.

Movement happens when muscles pull on the support. Muscles can contract and shorten but cannot push, so they work in antagonistic pairs across joints: one pulls a limb one way while the other pulls it back.

The choice of support carries trade-offs. A hydrostatic skeleton suits soft bodies and burrowing, an exoskeleton protects but must be moulted, and an endoskeleton grows with the body and allows large size at the cost of more internal tissue.
bullets: Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pressure plus muscles.
Exoskeleton: external covering, must be moulted.
Endoskeleton: internal bone and cartilage, grows with the body.
content.takeaway: Every animal moves by pulling against a support.

check.question: Which support system must be shed for the animal to grow?
check.why: A rigid exoskeleton cannot expand, so arthropods moult and grow a new one.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Support holds shape and posture; movement changes position and uses energy. Plants use turgor and lignified walls, while animals use hydrostatic skeletons, exoskeletons or endoskeletons and pull with antagonistic muscles.

content.problem: An earthworm has no hard skeleton, yet it burrows; a grasshopper has a hard covering, yet it jumps. Compare how each combines support and movement.

steps.reason: Fluid in the coelom resists compression, and circular and longitudinal muscles change the body shape.
steps.result: A hydrostatic skeleton produces burrowing movement.
steps.predictPrompt: What supports the grasshopper instead?

steps.reason: Chitin forms a jointed exoskeleton outside the body.
steps.result: Muscles inside pull on the exoskeleton to move the legs.

steps.reason: The earthworm's soft body grows continuously, but chitin cannot stretch much.
steps.result: The grasshopper must moult to grow.

steps.reason: Both animals use muscles that pull against a support.
steps.result: Different materials, same principle of movement.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why large organisms need support
paragraphs: A plant must hold itself upright against gravity to reach light. Turgor pressure in growing cells provides that support for a seedling, while lignified xylem provides it for a tree. The same need is met by different materials at different sizes.

An animal must support its weight and move it. Bone gives rigid support, muscles provide movement and joints allow the support to change shape. Without a skeleton an animal would be a soft, shapeless mass.
Support therefore precedes movement. A hydrostatic skeleton in a worm is a support first and a movement device second, because the fluid must be incompressible before muscles can push against it.
A mushroom avoids the problem by staying small and growing quickly. It recruits support from turgor and a chitin wall only for the season in which it fruits.
A jellyfish avoids a skeleton by living in water that supports it. That buoyancy is a support by displacement, so the animal needs no tissue of its own.
A plant that is supported by turgor can recover from wilting within hours. A tree that loses its xylem cannot recover, because the dead tissue cannot be revived.
bullets: Plants use turgor and lignified xylem for support
Animals use bone, muscle and joints together
Support must be incompressible before it can be moved

content.heading: Go deeper: Turgor, lignin and the plant skeleton
paragraphs: Turgor is the pressure of the cell contents against the wall. In a turgid cell that pressure stiffens the wall, so a whole plant made of turgid cells stands upright. A wilted plant has lost that pressure.

Lignin is the material that makes xylem and sclerenchyma rigid. It is waterproof and resistant to decay, so a woody stem can support a heavy crown for decades. Collenchyma, by contrast, supports young stems that are still growing.
A plant without a skeleton would still be alive but would trail on the ground. Height therefore depends on support, not only on growth.
A cactus stores water in parenchyma and uses it to stiffen its stem. That water skeleton lets it stand upright in a desert where lignified wood would be too costly to build.
Leaves use turgor in their petioles to hold the lamina upright. When water is short, the petiole wilts first and the leaf droops before the stem does.
bullets: Turgor stiffens turgid cells into a support
Lignin makes xylem rigid and waterproof
Collenchyma supports young, growing stems

content.heading: Go deeper: Animal skeletons compared
paragraphs: An exoskeleton is an external shell of chitin that protects and supports. It must be moulted for growth, which limits how fast an arthropod can grow between moults. An endoskeleton grows with the animal and needs no moulting.
A hydrostatic skeleton is a fluid-filled cavity enclosed by muscles. An earthworm has no bone at all, yet it moves by pushing against its own fluid. That skeleton is the simplest of the three.
Each skeleton is matched to habitat and size. A heavy animal needs bone, a small animal can rely on fluid, and an arthropod trades growth for protection.
A snail uses a calcium carbonate shell that is an exoskeleton by position but not a moulted one. The shell grows by addition, so it is an exception to the moulting rule.
A hedgehog rolls into a ball by flexing its spines and muscles together. Its exoskeleton of spines protects it without a shell, so protection and support are one structure.
A shell that is shed cannot be worn while it is soft. A crab is therefore defenceless for a short time after moulting, which is when it is most vulnerable.
bullets: Exoskeleton: chitin shell that must be moulted
Endoskeleton: bone that grows with the animal
Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pushed by circular muscles

content.question: Why can a plant stand upright without a skeleton?
hints: Turgor pressure in living cells pushes the walls outward.
Lignified xylem and sclerenchyma resist bending in older parts.
When cells lose water, the plant wilts because that pressure falls.

lessons.title: Plant Movements and Tropisms
lessons.objective: Distinguish tropic, tactic and nastic movements, describe sleep movements, and explain the role of auxin in growth regions.

content.heading: Plant movements and tropisms
paragraphs: A sunflower turns towards the sun, a pond Euglena swims towards light, and a Mimosa leaf folds when touched. All three are plant-like movements, but they work in different ways.

content.heading: Tropisms: growth in a direction
paragraphs: A tropism is a growth response whose direction depends on the stimulus. Shoots usually show positive phototropism and negative geotropism, while roots show positive geotropism and negative phototropism; roots also grow towards water (hydrotropism) and tendrils curl around support (thigmotropism).

The response begins in the growing regions. At the shoot tip, the zone of cell division makes new cells, the zone of elongation lengthens them, and the zone of differentiation matures them; auxin, made at the tip, moves down and controls elongation.

In phototropism, auxin gathers on the shaded side of a shoot and makes those cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards light. In a root, auxin gathers on the lower side and inhibits elongation there, so the root bends downwards.
bullets: Tropism: directional growth towards or away from a stimulus.
Shoot tip and root tip are the growth regions; auxin controls elongation.
Auxin promotes shoot elongation but inhibits root elongation at high levels.
content.takeaway: A tropism is growth bending towards or away from a stimulus.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches a tropism to its stimulus?
check.why: Hydrotropism is growth towards water; phototropism responds to light, geotropism to gravity and thigmotropism to touch.

content.heading: Tactic movements: the whole organism moves
paragraphs: A tactic movement is a movement of the whole organism or cell in response to a stimulus. Phototaxis is movement towards or away from light, chemotaxis is movement along a chemical gradient, and geotaxis is movement in response to gravity.

Euglena and Chlamydomonas swim towards light using their flagella, so photosynthesis can continue. Some plant and invertebrate sperm swim towards chemicals released by the egg, and bacteria move towards nutrients or away from toxins.

Tactic movements are usually fast and reversible, and they are common in small aquatic organisms that cannot grow towards a resource. The direction of movement is set by the stimulus, not by the direction of growth.
bullets: Taxis: whole organism moves towards or away from a stimulus.
Examples: phototaxis in Euglena, chemotaxis in fern sperm and bacteria.
Fast, reversible and common in small aquatic organisms.
content.takeaway: A taxis moves the whole organism; a tropism bends a growing part.

check.question: A sperm cell swimming towards the egg is an example of
check.why: The sperm follows a chemical gradient released by the egg, which is chemotaxis.

content.heading: Nastic movements and sleep
paragraphs: A nastic movement is a response to the intensity of a stimulus rather than its direction. The whole organ may fold, droop or open, and the movement is reversible because it depends on turgor rather than growth.

Seismonasty is the folding of Mimosa pudica leaves after touch or shaking; the pulvini at the leaf bases lose water and the leaflets collapse. Photonasty and thermonasty open and close petals in response to light and temperature.

Sleep movements, or nyctinasty, are the nightly folding of leaves in many legumes, such as tamarind and some beans. The leaves return to their daytime position when light returns, so the movement follows a daily rhythm rather than a permanent change in shape.
bullets: Nastic movement: non-directional, reversible, driven by turgor.
Seismonasty: Mimosa folds when touched.
Nyctinasty or sleep movement: leaves fold at night.
content.takeaway: Nastic movements answer how strong a stimulus is, not where it comes from.

check.question: The folding of Mimosa leaves after touch is called
check.why: Seismonasty is a reversible turgor response to touch or shaking.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Tropism = directional growth; taxis = whole-organism movement; nasty = non-directional turgor movement. Link auxin to shoot and root bending, and remember Mimosa pudica as the standard example of seismonasty.

content.problem: A bean seedling on a windowsill bends towards the window, while its roots grow downwards. Explain both responses using auxin.

steps.reason: Light comes mainly from one side.
steps.result: The shoot shows positive phototropism.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does auxin collect?

steps.operation: Place the auxin in the shoot
steps.reason: Auxin moves away from light to the shaded side.
steps.result: Shaded cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the window.

steps.reason: Gravity pulls auxin to the lower side of the root.
steps.result: High auxin inhibits root cell elongation, so the upper side grows faster and the root bends down.

steps.reason: The shoot is positively phototropic and negatively geotropic; the root is positively geotropic.
steps.result: One hormone, two opposite growth effects depending on the organ.

content.heading: Go deeper: Tropisms and the auxin story
paragraphs: A tropism is a growth movement in response to a directional stimulus. Phototropism follows light, geotropism follows gravity, hydrotropism follows water and thigmotropism follows touch. Each is a permanent bending, not a temporary response.

Auxin promotes shoot elongation but inhibits root elongation at high levels. In a shoot lit from one side, auxin collects on the shaded side, that side elongates faster and the shoot bends toward the light. The bending is therefore growth, not movement of the whole plant.

Gravity is sensed by statoliths in root caps and shoot ends. When a plant is laid on its side, those granules settle on the lower side and redirect auxin. That is how a shoot grows up and a root grows down after disturbance.
A root that meets an impenetrable layer bends along it by geotropism and hydrotropism together. The bending is therefore a compromise between gravity and water, not a response to one alone.
A climbing tendril is thigmotropic because it coils on contact. The same auxin that bends a shoot toward light coils a tendril around a support.
A root that meets an impenetrable layer bends along it by geotropism and hydrotropism together. The bending is therefore a compromise between gravity and water, not a response to one alone.
bullets: Phototropism: light; geotropism: gravity; hydrotropism: water
Auxin collects on the shaded side of a shoot
Statoliths settle and redirect auxin after disturbance

content.heading: Go deeper: Tactic movements and the whole organism
paragraphs: A tactic movement is the movement of the whole organism toward or away from a stimulus. Euglena swims toward light by phototaxis, and bacteria move toward nutrients by chemotaxis. The organism itself changes place.
Tactic responses are rapid and reversible, unlike tropisms. A Euglena that is shaded swims back toward light within seconds. That speed is possible because no growth is involved.
The two kinds of movement therefore differ in what moves. A tropism bends a stationary plant, while a taxis moves a free-living organism.
Bacteria use flagella to swim toward nutrients by chemotaxis. That is the same organelle that a Euglena uses to swim toward light, so one structure serves two kinds of taxis.
Bacteria use chemotaxis to find nutrients and to escape toxins. That single tactic therefore serves both feeding and defence in the same organism moving through soil water.
Chemotaxis in bacteria is the model for how a tactic response works. The cell compares the concentration now with the concentration a moment ago and decides whether to continue.
bullets: Taxis moves the whole organism toward or away from a stimulus
Phototaxis: light; chemotaxis: nutrients or toxins
Taxis is rapid and reversible; tropism is growth

content.heading: Go deeper: Nastic movements and sleep
paragraphs: A nastic movement is a response in a fixed direction, such as the closing of a Mimosa leaf when touched. The direction does not depend on the direction of the stimulus. The movement is rapid and temporary.

Sleep movements are the folding of leaves at night in plants such as Desmodium. The pulvinus at the base of the leaflet loses turgor on one side and gains it on the other, so the leaflet folds without growth.
The difference from a tropism is the mechanism. A tropism grows, a nastic movement changes turgor, and a taxis swims. Those three mechanisms cover all the movements a plant can show.
A sleep movement is also called nyctinasty because it follows the day-night cycle. A plant that folds its leaves by night and opens them by day shows that rhythm.
A Mimosa leaf folds within seconds of touch and recovers in minutes. That recovery shows that no growth was involved, because growth cannot be reversed in that time.
bullets: Nastic: fixed direction, rapid and temporary
Sleep movements fold leaves by turgor change
Tropism grows; nastic changes turgor; taxis swims

content.question: Why does a Mimosa leaf fold quickly when touched, but a sunflower does not?
hints: Mimosa uses turgor changes in pulvini, not growth.
The response is reversible and can repeat.
A sunflower's phototropism depends on differential growth, which is slower.

lessons.title: Supporting Tissues in Animals
lessons.objective: Relate the location and structure of chitin, cartilage and bone to their supporting functions.

content.heading: Supporting tissues in animals
paragraphs: A grasshopper's armour, a cow's ear and a goat's thigh bone all support the body, yet one is flexible, one springs back, and one is rigid. Their materials explain the difference.

content.heading: Chitin: support outside the body
paragraphs: Chitin is a tough, lightweight polysaccharide containing nitrogen. It forms the exoskeleton of insects, crabs, prawns and other arthropods, and is also found in the cell walls of fungi.

The chitin covering protects the body, resists water loss and gives a surface for muscles to pull against. In insects it is divided into plates and jointed sections, so the animal can move while still being supported.

Chitin cannot stretch much, so an arthropod must moult to grow. The old exoskeleton splits and is shed, and a new, soft one expands before it hardens; this leaves the animal vulnerable until hardening is complete.
bullets: Chitin: nitrogen-containing polysaccharide, tough and waterproof.
Forms the jointed exoskeleton of arthropods.
Must be moulted for growth; the soft new shell is vulnerable.
content.takeaway: Chitin supports from outside but must be shed to grow.

check.question: Arthropods must moult because chitin
options: Cannot stretch enough to allow growth
check.why: The rigid exoskeleton cannot expand, so it is shed and replaced as the animal grows.

content.heading: Cartilage: flexible support
paragraphs: Cartilage is a firm but flexible tissue made of collagen fibres in a gel-like matrix. Its cells, chondrocytes, sit in small spaces called lacunae, and the tissue has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.
Cartilage is found in the pinna of the ear, the tip of the nose, the trachea, the intervertebral discs and the ends of long bones. In each place it supports without making the part rigid.

At joints, articular cartilage covers the bone ends, reduces friction and absorbs shock. In the trachea, C-shaped cartilage rings keep the airway open; in the ear, flexible cartilage bends without breaking.
bullets: Cartilage: flexible, avascular, chondrocytes in lacunae.
Locations: ear, nose, trachea, discs and bone ends.
Functions: support, shock absorption and low-friction surfaces.
content.takeaway: Cartilage supports where the body must bend or absorb shock.

check.question: Which property of cartilage makes it suitable for the tip of the nose?
options: It is flexible and springs back
It has a rich blood supply
check.why: Flexible cartilage bends under pressure and returns to shape without breaking.

content.heading: Bone: rigid living support
paragraphs: Bone is a living tissue with a matrix of collagen fibres and calcium phosphate. Osteocytes lie in lacunae, and blood vessels run through channels, so the tissue can grow and repair.
Compact bone forms the hard outer layer, while spongy bone inside is lighter and has a network of struts. The periosteum covers the outside, and red marrow in spongy bone makes blood cells.

Bones form the endoskeleton, protect organs, store calcium and phosphate, and give muscles a place to attach. Their rigidity supports the body, while their joints allow movement; bone is therefore both a frame and a mineral bank.
bullets: Bone: collagen and calcium phosphate matrix, living cells.
Compact bone is hard; spongy bone is light and holds marrow.
Functions: support, protection, attachment, mineral store and blood cell production.
content.takeaway: Bone is a living frame that also stores minerals.

check.question: The hardness of bone comes mainly from
check.why: Mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate, harden the collagen framework of bone.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Chitin is outside and must be moulted; cartilage is flexible and avascular; bone is rigid, vascular and living. Match each material to its location: arthropod covering, ear or joint, and skeleton.

content.problem: A student compares a crab's shell, a shark's skeleton and a cow's thigh bone. Identify the supporting material in each and one consequence.

steps.reason: It is a hard external covering made of chitin.
steps.result: An exoskeleton that protects but must be moulted.
steps.predictPrompt: What supports the shark?

steps.reason: The skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone.
steps.result: A flexible endoskeleton that grows with the body.

steps.reason: Bone contains calcium phosphate and collagen.
steps.result: A rigid endoskeleton that supports weight and stores minerals.

steps.reason: Each material sits in a different place and does a different job.
steps.result: Chitin covers, cartilage flexes, and bone bears load.

content.heading: Go deeper: Chitin on the outside
paragraphs: Chitin is a polysaccharide that hardens into exoskeletons and fungal walls. In arthropods it forms a shell that protects, supports and gives muscles a surface to pull against. That shell must be moulted for growth.

Moulting is therefore the price of protection. An insect grows by moulting several times, each time secreting a new shell under the old one before shedding it. Between moults the animal cannot grow at all.
Chitin is also the material of a fungal wall, which is how the same polysaccharide serves two kingdoms. The wall that supports a mushroom and the shell that supports a beetle are the same chemistry.
A chitin shell also reduces water loss from an insect. That protection is part of why insects could colonise dry land before vertebrates did.
A chitin shell must be thick enough to resist predators yet thin enough to moult. That trade decides the size to which an arthropod can grow between moults.
Chitin is also the material of a fungal wall. The wall that supports a mushroom and the shell that supports a beetle are the same chemistry in two kingdoms.
bullets: Chitin forms exoskeletons and fungal walls
Moulting is the price of a rigid shell
The same polysaccharide serves two kingdoms

content.heading: Go deeper: Cartilage where flexibility is needed
paragraphs: Cartilage is a living tissue with collagen fibres in a gel. It is flexible but strong, so it caps the ends of bones and separates them at joints. A shark skeleton is made entirely of cartilage.
Cartilage also forms the nose and ears because those structures must bend without breaking. Bone would be too brittle for a nose, and a nose made of tendon would be too soft to hold its shape.
The tissue therefore matches the mechanical need. Where a structure must bend and recover, cartilage is used; where it must bear load, bone is used.
Cartilage is also used in the windpipe, where rings of cartilage keep the airway open. The rings must bend with the neck yet resist collapse when air is drawn in.
Cartilage in the trachea is C-shaped, open at the back where it meets the oesophagus. That shape keeps the airway open while allowing the oesophagus to expand for food.
Cartilage in the trachea is C-shaped, open at the back. That shape keeps the airway open while allowing the oesophagus behind it to expand for food.
bullets: Cartilage caps bone ends and separates joints
Cartilage forms nose and ears that must bend
Flexibility needs cartilage; load needs bone

content.heading: Go deeper: Bone, marrow and the mineral bank
paragraphs: Bone is a living tissue. Osteocytes lie in lacunae, blood vessels run through channels and the matrix of collagen and calcium phosphate can grow and repair. A broken bone heals because the tissue is alive.
Bone stores calcium and phosphate that the blood can draw on. That storage is why a skeleton is also a mineral bank, not only a frame. Bone marrow inside long bones makes red and white blood cells.
The location of each tissue therefore predicts its role. Bone bears load, cartilage bends and marrow makes cells. A question that names a tissue has also named its job.
Bone is remodelled throughout life. Osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts lay down new bone, so the skeleton that an adult carries is not the one it was born with.
A marrow cavity is hollow, so a long bone is light for its strength. That lightness is what lets a bird fly with bones that are strong enough to bear its weight.
bullets: Bone is living and can grow and repair
Bone stores calcium and phosphate
Marrow makes red and white blood cells

content.question: Why is cartilage better than bone for the ends of long bones?
hints: It is smooth and reduces friction at the joint.
It absorbs shock during movement.
It has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly, but it suits a moving surface.

lessons.title: Skeletons and Their Functions
lessons.objective: Distinguish exoskeletons, endoskeletons and hydrostatic skeletons, and relate the mammalian skeleton's layout to support, protection, movement and breathing.

content.heading: Skeletons and their functions
paragraphs: A beetle's shell, an earthworm's fluid-filled body and a footballer's rib cage all support and protect, but only one is a true skeleton of bone. The differences shape how each animal moves and grows.

content.heading: Exoskeleton, endoskeleton and hydrostatic skeleton
paragraphs: An exoskeleton lies outside the body. Arthropods use chitin, and some molluscs use calcium carbonate shells; the covering protects the body and gives muscles a surface to pull against, but it must be moulted or added to as the animal grows.

An endoskeleton lies inside the body. Vertebrates use bone and cartilage, and the skeleton grows with the animal, supports a large body and protects internal organs; muscles attach to the outside of the bones.

A hydrostatic skeleton uses fluid under pressure, as in earthworms and jellyfish. Muscles change the shape of the fluid-filled body, producing movement without hard parts; this suits soft-bodied animals but cannot support great weight on land.
bullets: Exoskeleton: outside, protective, must be moulted.
Endoskeleton: inside, grows with the body, allows large size.
Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pressure and muscles, no hard parts.
content.takeaway: Where the skeleton sits decides how the animal grows and moves.

check.question: Which skeleton grows with the animal without moulting?
check.why: An internal endoskeleton enlarges as the animal grows and does not need to be shed.

content.heading: The mammalian skeleton layout
paragraphs: The mammalian skeleton is divided into the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton. The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; the appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle and limbs.

An adult human has about 206 bones, joined at joints and held by ligaments. The skull protects the brain, the vertebral column supports the trunk and protects the spinal cord, and the rib cage surrounds the heart and lungs.

The limbs are built as levers: the humerus, radius and ulna in the arm, and the femur, tibia and fibula in the leg. Girdles attach the limbs to the axial skeleton, so body weight is transferred to the legs during standing and walking.
bullets: Axial: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.
Appendicular: girdles and limbs.
About 206 bones in an adult human, linked by joints and ligaments.
content.takeaway: Axial protects the core; appendicular moves the body.

check.question: Which group belongs to the axial skeleton?
check.why: The axial skeleton forms the central axis and includes the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.

content.heading: Support, protection, movement and breathing
paragraphs: Support: the skeleton holds the body upright, gives it shape and anchors soft organs. Protection: the skull, rib cage and vertebral column shield the brain, heart, lungs and spinal cord.

Movement: muscles attach to bones by tendons, and bones act as levers at joints, so a small muscle contraction can move a limb. Respiration: the ribs and sternum move with the diaphragm, changing the volume of the thorax and drawing air in or out.

Bones also store calcium and phosphate and house marrow that makes blood cells. These functions explain why a broken rib can affect breathing and why a broken long bone can disturb the whole body, not just the limb.
bullets: Support and protection of organs.
Movement through muscles, tendons and joints.
Breathing through rib movement; mineral storage and blood cell production.
content.takeaway: The skeleton is a frame, shield, lever and pump handle.

check.question: The skeleton helps breathing mainly by
options: Moving the ribs and sternum to change thorax volume
check.why: Rib and sternum movements, with the diaphragm, change thoracic volume and move air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Exoskeleton outside, endoskeleton inside, hydrostatic skeleton from fluid pressure. For mammals, link axial bones to protection and the rib cage to breathing, not just movement; the same skeleton also stores minerals.

content.problem: A footballer breaks a rib and later a leg bone. Explain how each injury affects a different function of the skeleton.

steps.reason: Ribs protect the lungs and move during breathing.
steps.result: A broken rib can make breathing painful and reduce ventilation.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the leg bone do?

steps.reason: The femur supports weight and acts as a lever for walking.
steps.result: A broken femur affects support and movement.

steps.reason: Protection, support, movement and breathing are separate but connected functions.
steps.result: The same skeleton serves all four, so the effect depends on which bone is damaged.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exoskeleton, endoskeleton and hydrostatic skeleton
paragraphs: An exoskeleton lies outside the body and is made of chitin in arthropods. It protects and supports, but it must be moulted for growth. A crab therefore grows by shedding its shell and quickly hardening a new one.

An endoskeleton lies inside the body and is made of bone or cartilage. It grows with the animal, protects organs and gives muscles a place to attach. A mammal, a bird and a fish all have endoskeletons.

A hydrostatic skeleton is a fluid-filled cavity enclosed by muscles. An earthworm has no bone, yet it moves by pushing against its fluid. That skeleton needs no joint, only an incompressible fluid and circular muscles.
A hydrostat can also be used for burrowing. An earthworm anchors its front with setae, lengthens, anchors its back and pulls the front forward in turn.
A crab moults by splitting the old shell along the back. The soft animal then emerges, expands with water and hardens the new shell within hours.
bullets: Exoskeleton: chitin shell that must be moulted
Endoskeleton: bone or cartilage that grows with the animal
Hydrostatic skeleton: fluid pushed by muscles

content.heading: Go deeper: The axial and appendicular layout
paragraphs: The axial skeleton is the central axis: skull, vertebral column and ribs. It protects the brain and spinal cord and supports the trunk. A broken rib can therefore affect breathing as well as movement.

The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that attach them. It is the part that moves the animal through its habitat. An injury to a limb bone therefore affects locomotion more than protection.
The two names are a map. Axial means the axis, appendicular means the appendages, and a question that asks for one has already told the candidate where to look.
The pelvis is part of the appendicular skeleton because it carries the hind limbs. That is why a pelvis injury affects walking even though the pelvis also protects organs.
The clavicle is the only bone of the appendicular skeleton that articulates with the axial skeleton at the sternum. That single articulation is what makes the shoulder a true joint.
The sternum is part of the axial skeleton because it anchors the ribs. The clavicle and scapula belong to the appendicular skeleton because they carry the forelimbs.
bullets: Axial: skull, vertebral column and ribs
Appendicular: limbs and girdles
Axial protects; appendicular moves

content.heading: Go deeper: Support, protection, movement and breathing
paragraphs: A skeleton supports the body, protects organs, anchors muscles and in some cases assists breathing. The ribs protect the heart and lungs while allowing the chest to expand, so protection and breathing are shared.
Bones also store calcium and phosphate and house marrow. A skeleton therefore does mechanical, protective and chemical work at once. A fracture can disturb all three.
The keel of a bird is a special case. It is a ridge on the breastbone that anchors the flight muscles, so a bird skeleton is a support for flight as much as for walking.
The skull protects the brain but its sutures are fibrous, so it cannot move at all. Protection there demands rigidity, while the ribs must move to allow breathing.
A tortoise shell is an exoskeleton fused to the skeleton inside. That fusion is why a tortoise cannot leave its shell, unlike a crab that moults.
A bird keel is a ridge that anchors the flight muscles. That is why a bird with a weak keel cannot fly even if its wings are intact.
bullets: Skeleton supports, protects, anchors muscles and assists breathing
Bone stores minerals and houses marrow
The bird keel anchors flight muscles

content.question: Why can an insect not simply grow larger inside its exoskeleton?
hints: Chitin is rigid and cannot stretch much.
The old shell must be shed and a new one expanded.
Moulting leaves the insect soft and vulnerable, so it must hide.

lessons.title: Joints and Movement
lessons.objective: Differentiate fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints, describe synovial joint structure, and explain antagonistic muscle action.

content.heading: Joints and movement
paragraphs: A goalkeeper's shoulder rotates, a runner's knee bends and the bones of the skull stay locked together. The type of joint decides how much movement is possible.

content.heading: Three classes of joint
paragraphs: A joint is a place where two or more bones meet. Fibrous joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are held by tough fibres and allow no movement; cartilaginous joints, such as those between vertebrae, allow slight movement.
Synovial joints are freely movable. They have a cavity between the bone ends, filled with synovial fluid, and are the joints used in walking, throwing and writing.

The amount of movement depends on the tissue between the bones: dense fibres lock, cartilage allows a little, and a fluid-filled cavity allows a lot. Injury to any of these tissues can limit movement.
bullets: Fibrous: immovable, e.g. skull sutures.
Cartilaginous: slightly movable, e.g. between vertebrae.
Synovial: freely movable, e.g. knee, shoulder and elbow.
content.takeaway: The joint's tissue sets how far the bones can move.

check.question: Which joint type allows the greatest movement?
check.why: A synovial joint has a fluid-filled cavity that allows free movement.

content.heading: Inside a synovial joint
paragraphs: The ends of the bones are covered by articular cartilage, which reduces friction and absorbs shock. A synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage.

Ligaments hold bone to bone and keep the joint stable, while tendons attach muscle to bone and transmit the pull. A joint capsule encloses the cavity, and bursae are small fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction where tendons rub.

Synovial joints come in shapes that suit their work: hinge joints at the elbow and knee, ball-and-socket joints at the shoulder and hip, pivot joints between the atlas and axis, and gliding joints between the carpals and tarsals.
bullets: Cartilage reduces friction; synovial fluid lubricates.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
Hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot and gliding joints suit different movements.
content.takeaway: Cartilage, fluid, ligaments and tendons make a joint work.

check.question: Which structure attaches a muscle to a bone?
check.why: A tendon attaches skeletal muscle to bone and transmits the muscle's pull.

content.heading: Muscles pull in pairs
paragraphs: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons. When a muscle contracts, it shortens and pulls the bone; it cannot push, so movement in the opposite direction needs another muscle.

At the elbow, the biceps contracts to flex the joint and the triceps contracts to extend it. These antagonistic muscles work in pairs: while one contracts, the other relaxes, and the joint moves smoothly.

The bone acts as a lever, the joint as the fulcrum and the muscle as the effort. Nerve impulses trigger contraction, and ATP supplies the energy; without either, the joint may be stable but cannot move.
bullets: Muscles contract and pull; they never push.
Antagonistic pairs move a joint in opposite directions.
Bone = lever, joint = fulcrum, muscle = effort.
content.takeaway: Joints direct movement; antagonistic muscles provide the pull.

check.question: The biceps and triceps at the elbow are described as antagonistic because they
options: Pull the joint in opposite directions
check.why: The biceps flexes and the triceps extends the elbow, so their pulls oppose each other.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Fibrous joints do not move, cartilaginous joints move slightly, and synovial joints move freely. In a synovial joint, cartilage and fluid reduce friction; ligaments hold bones, tendons hold muscles, and bursae reduce rubbing.

content.problem: A patient cannot straighten the knee after an injury. Identify the joint type, the structures that may be damaged and the muscle that extends the knee.

steps.reason: The knee is a hinge synovial joint.
steps.result: It allows flexion and extension in one plane.
steps.predictPrompt: What structures stabilise it?

steps.reason: Ligaments hold bone to bone, and tendons attach muscles.
steps.result: Damage to the quadriceps tendon or patellar ligament can block extension.

steps.reason: The quadriceps on the front of the thigh straightens the knee.
steps.result: A weakened quadriceps or damaged tendon prevents extension.

steps.reason: The hamstrings flex the knee and are antagonistic to the quadriceps.
steps.result: Balanced pairs are needed for controlled movement.

content.heading: Go deeper: Fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints
paragraphs: A fibrous joint is fixed by dense connective tissue. The sutures of the skull are fibrous, so the skull bones do not move relative to one another. That fixed joint protects the brain by making the skull a rigid case.
A cartilaginous joint allows slight movement. The vertebrae are joined by cartilage discs that compress and allow bending. A spine therefore bends at many small joints rather than at one hinge.
A synovial joint is freely movable and has a fluid-filled cavity. The elbow, knee and shoulder are synovial, so they allow the large movements that locomotion needs.
The pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint that relaxes in pregnancy. Hormones soften it so the pelvis can widen for birth, which is why it is a special case.
The gap between vertebrae is filled by a disc that allows bending. When a disc slips, it presses on a nerve, which is why a slipped disc causes pain down a limb.
A skull suture is fibrous but not fused at birth. That gap allows the head to pass through the birth canal and to grow after birth.
bullets: Fibrous: fixed, as in skull sutures
Cartilaginous: slight movement, as in vertebrae
Synovial: freely movable, as in elbow and knee

content.heading: Go deeper: The synovial joint in detail
paragraphs: A synovial joint is enclosed by a synovial membrane that secretes fluid into the cavity. That fluid lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage, which has no blood supply of its own.

The ends of the bones are capped by articular cartilage, and ligaments hold the bones together. Muscles provide the force, tendons attach them to bones and the fluid reduces friction. All four parts are needed for a working joint.
A sprain tears a ligament, not a muscle. That is why a sprained ankle must be rested until the ligament heals, even though the muscles around it are intact.
Synovial fluid is also a shock absorber. Its viscosity cushions the cartilage when a joint is compressed, which is why a jump does not damage the knee at once.
A joint that is not used becomes stiff because the cartilage loses fluid. Movement therefore maintains a joint, which is why rest after injury must be followed by gentle use.
That fluid is therefore both a lubricant and a nutrient route.
bullets: Synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes cartilage
Cartilage caps the bones; ligaments hold them together
A sprain tears a ligament, not a muscle

content.heading: Go deeper: Antagonistic muscles and how they work
paragraphs: Muscles can only pull, never push. Movement therefore needs an antagonistic pair: one muscle contracts while the other relaxes. The biceps and triceps of the upper arm are the standard pair.

When the biceps contracts, the forearm bends at the elbow. When the triceps contracts, the forearm straightens. The same pair therefore allows both flexion and extension without any muscle having to push.
Tendons attach muscles to bones and do not stretch much. That stiffness is what makes the pull effective, because a stretchy tendon would waste the contraction.
The same antagonistic principle governs the iris and the ciliary muscle of the eye. One set contracts to narrow the pupil, the other relaxes to widen it.
The same antagonistic pair moves the eye. One set turns the eye inward and the other turns it outward, so the eye is positioned for binocular vision.
The same antagonistic principle moves the eye. One set turns the eye inward and the other turns it outward, so the eye is positioned for binocular vision.
bullets: Muscles can only pull, never push
Antagonistic pairs allow flexion and extension
Tendons transmit the pull without stretching

content.question: Why does a footballer need both strong ligaments and strong muscles around the knee?
hints: Ligaments hold the bones together and limit unwanted movement.
Muscles produce the movement and absorb forces.
Cartilage and synovial fluid reduce friction but do not replace strength.

lessons.title: Asexual and Sexual Reproduction
lessons.objective: Differentiate asexual from sexual reproduction, and describe binary fission and budding with examples.

content.heading: Asexual and sexual reproduction
paragraphs: A Paramecium in a pond splits into two within an hour, while a goat must find a mate before it can produce a kid. The two routes to offspring could hardly be more different.

content.heading: Two routes to offspring
paragraphs: Asexual reproduction uses one parent. There are no gametes and no fertilisation, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to one another; the process is usually fast and can produce many offspring.
Sexual reproduction uses two parents. Male and female gametes fuse at fertilisation, so each offspring receives a mixture of genes and differs from both parents and from its siblings.

Asexual reproduction suits stable environments where a successful parent can be copied, while sexual reproduction generates variation that may help a population survive disease or change. Many organisms can use both routes at different times.
bullets: Asexual: one parent, no gametes, identical offspring.
Sexual: two parents, gamete fusion, varied offspring.
Asexual is fast; sexual creates variation.
content.takeaway: Asexual copies; sexual mixes.

check.question: Which feature distinguishes sexual from asexual reproduction?
check.why: Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes, which asexual reproduction does not.

content.heading: Fission: one cell becomes two
paragraphs: Binary fission is the division of a single cell into two daughter cells. In Paramecium, the cell divides transversely; in Amoeba, the nucleus divides first and the cytoplasm then separates, producing two similar individuals.
The process is a form of mitosis, so each daughter receives a complete set of genes. Under good conditions, Paramecium can divide several times a day, and a small population can grow rapidly.
Bacteria also divide by binary fission, but they have no true nucleus. Fission is therefore a simple, efficient way for unicellular organisms to increase numbers without a mate.
bullets: Binary fission: one parent cell divides into two.
Paramecium divides transversely; Amoeba divides after nuclear division.
Mitosis gives each daughter a complete gene set.
content.takeaway: Fission copies one cell into two.

check.question: Binary fission in Paramecium is best described as
options: Transverse division of one cell into two
check.why: Paramecium divides across its body into two similar daughter cells.

content.heading: Budding: a new individual from a bud
paragraphs: In budding, a small outgrowth forms on the parent and develops into a new individual. The bud may detach or remain attached, so budding can produce a colony of identical individuals.
Yeast is a single-celled fungus that buds rapidly: the nucleus divides, one daughter nucleus moves into the bud, and the bud pinches off. Hydra, a freshwater cnidarian, also reproduces by budding.

Budding differs from fission because the parent keeps its original body and the new individual starts as a small outgrowth. Both processes are asexual, so both produce genetically identical offspring.
bullets: Budding: a small outgrowth becomes a new individual.
Yeast and Hydra are standard examples.
The bud may detach or stay attached as a colony.
content.takeaway: Budding grows a new individual from the parent's side.

check.question: Which organism is the standard example of budding?
check.why: Yeast reproduces asexually by forming buds that pinch off from the parent cell.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Asexual reproduction uses one parent and makes clones; sexual reproduction uses two parents and makes variation. Fission splits a cell into two; budding grows a new individual from an outgrowth.

content.problem: A student observes a Paramecium dividing across its middle and a yeast cell forming a small outgrowth. Identify each process and explain one consequence.

steps.reason: The cell divides transversely into two similar cells.
steps.result: Binary fission.
steps.predictPrompt: What is the yeast doing?

steps.reason: A small bud forms and receives a nucleus before pinching off.
steps.result: Budding.

steps.reason: Both processes are asexual and involve mitosis.
steps.result: The offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

steps.reason: Rapid asexual reproduction suits stable, favourable conditions.
steps.result: Populations can grow quickly without mates.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why two parents help a species
