paragraphs: After imbibition, gibberellin from the embryo triggers the aleurone layer to produce amylase. That enzyme digests stored starch into maltose, which is then converted to glucose for the embryo. The food store therefore feeds the growing seedling.
The radicle emerges first and grows downward by geotropism. It anchors the seed and absorbs water and mineral salts. The plumule then grows upward and pushes through the soil.
A seed that has exhausted its store before its leaves emerge will die. That is why a seed must be sown at a depth from which the plumule can reach the surface.
The radicle is positively geotropic and the plumule negatively geotropic. That opposition is why a seed sown on its side still sends its root down and its shoot up.
The endosperm of a maize grain is the food store that feeds the embryo. That is why a maize grain is a seed with a built-in lunch for its first days.
The plumule is the first shoot and the radicle is the first root. Those two tips are what the seedling must produce from its store before the store runs out.
bullets: Gibberellin triggers amylase in the aleurone
The radicle emerges first and grows downward
The store must last until the leaves emerge

content.heading: Go deeper: Dormancy and what breaks it
paragraphs: Dormancy is the failure of a viable seed to germinate even when conditions are suitable. It can be caused by a hard coat, by inhibitors or by a requirement for cold. Dormancy therefore spreads germination over time.

Scarification breaks a hard coat by abrasion, acid or fire. Stratification breaks a cold requirement by keeping the seed in moist cold. Light breaks dormancy in species that germinate only on the soil surface.
Dormancy is an adaptation to a variable climate. A seed that germinates after the first rain may die if the rain does not return, so a fraction of seeds waits for a more certain signal.
A hard coat can be broken by fire, which is how some savanna seeds germinate after a burn. The fire that clears the land therefore also prepares the seed bed.
A seed that needs light germinates only on the soil surface. That requirement prevents a seed that is buried too deep from wasting its store before it can emerge.
bullets: Dormancy stops germination even when conditions suit
Scarification, stratification and light break dormancy
Dormancy spreads germination over time

content.question: Why does a seed need oxygen before its first leaf appears?
hints: The embryo is already respiring.
Aerobic respiration releases ATP from stored food.
Without oxygen, germination stalls even if water is present.

lessons.title: Epigeal and Hypogeal Germination
lessons.objective: Differentiate epigeal from hypogeal germination, give examples of each, and relate the pattern to seedling survival.

content.heading: Epigeal and hypogeal germination
paragraphs: A bean seedling lifts its two thick seed leaves above the soil, while a maize seedling sends up a rolled shoot and keeps its seed leaves underground. The difference is called epigeal versus hypogeal germination.

content.heading: Epigeal germination
paragraphs: In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl, the region below the cotyledons, elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the soil. The cotyledons turn green and photosynthesise for a time before they shrivel and drop.
The hypocotyl often forms a hook as it emerges, protecting the delicate plumule from damage as it pushes through the soil. Bean, castor and sunflower are standard examples.

Because the cotyledons leave the seed and enter the light, the seedling can start photosynthesis early. The cost is that the exposed cotyledons and shoot are vulnerable to frost, grazing and drying. This early start can give the seedling an advantage in a sunny gap.
bullets: Hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground.
Cotyledons turn green and photosynthesise before shrinking.
Examples: bean, castor and sunflower.
content.takeaway: Epigeal germination lifts its seed leaves into the light.

check.question: In epigeal germination, the cotyledons are carried above the soil by the
check.why: The hypocotyl is the region below the cotyledons, and its elongation lifts them above the soil.

content.heading: Hypogeal germination
paragraphs: In hypogeal germination, the cotyledons remain below the soil and the epicotyl, the region above the cotyledons, elongates to push up the plumule. The cotyledons stay in the seed and supply food rather than turning green.

Maize, pea, rice and groundnut are standard examples. The shoot emerges as a tight spike or rolled leaf, which reduces friction and protects the growing tip. The protected shoot can push through a crusted soil surface.
Keeping the cotyledons underground protects the food store and the shoot base from frost, grazing and drying. The seedling depends on stored food for longer, so it may grow more slowly at first.
bullets: Epicotyl elongates and pushes the plumule above ground.
Cotyledons stay below ground and supply food.
Examples: maize, pea, rice and groundnut.
content.takeaway: Hypogeal germination keeps its food store underground.

check.question: Which plant shows hypogeal germination?
check.why: Maize cotyledons remain below ground while the epicotyl pushes the plumule upwards.

content.heading: Comparing the two patterns
paragraphs: The key difference is the position of the cotyledons and the region that elongates. Epigeal seedlings lift their cotyledons with the hypocotyl; hypogeal seedlings keep them below ground while the epicotyl elongates.

The pattern affects planting depth and early survival. Epigeal seeds should not be buried too deeply, because the hypocotyl must reach the surface; hypogeal seeds can be planted deeper, since the food store stays protected.

Neither pattern is universally better. Epigeal seedlings gain early photosynthesis but are exposed; hypogeal seedlings are protected but rely on stored food for longer, which matters in poor light or cold soil.
bullets: Epigeal: cotyledons above ground, hypocotyl elongates.
Hypogeal: cotyledons below ground, epicotyl elongates.
Planting depth and exposure differ between the two.
content.takeaway: Cotyledon position and the elongating region separate the two patterns.

check.question: The main difference between epigeal and hypogeal germination is the
options: Number of seeds in the fruit
check.why: Epigeal cotyledons rise above the soil, while hypogeal cotyledons remain below it.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Epigeal: hypocotyl lifts cotyledons above ground, as in bean and castor. Hypogeal: epicotyl lifts the plumule while cotyledons stay below ground, as in maize and pea. Plant epigeal seeds shallower than hypogeal seeds.

content.problem: A gardener plants bean and maize seeds at the same depth. The maize emerges well, but many bean seedlings fail. Explain the difference.

steps.reason: Bean is epigeal and maize is hypogeal.
steps.result: Bean lifts its cotyledons; maize keeps them below ground.
steps.predictPrompt: Why would depth affect the bean more?

steps.reason: The bean hypocotyl must push the cotyledons to the surface.
steps.result: Deep planting exhausts the seedling before it reaches light.

steps.reason: The maize food store stays underground and the epicotyl is adapted to push through.
steps.result: Maize emerges from the same depth more successfully.

content.heading: Go deeper: Hypocotyl and epicotyl in the two patterns
paragraphs: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and carries the cotyledons above the soil. A bean is epigeal because its cotyledons emerge and are the first leaves to appear. The hypocotyl is the part of the stem below the cotyledons.
In hypogeal germination the epicotyl elongates and carries the plumule above the soil. The cotyledons stay below. A maize grain is hypogeal because its single cotyledon remains in the soil.
The distinction is therefore which part elongates. Hypocotyl means below the cotyledons, epicotyl means above them, and the pattern follows from which one grows.
The hypocotyl is below the cotyledons and the epicotyl is above them. A longitudinal section of a germinating seed therefore shows which part has elongated.
Both patterns start the same way, with the radicle emerging first. The difference appears only after that, when the hypocotyl or the epicotyl elongates to lift the shoot.
The names are Greek: hypo means below and epi means above. That is why the hypocotyl is below the cotyledons and the epicotyl is above them.
bullets: Epigeal: hypocotyl carries cotyledons above the soil
Hypogeal: epicotyl carries the plumule above the soil
Bean is epigeal; maize is hypogeal

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the position of the cotyledon matters
paragraphs: An epigeal seedling carries its food store above the soil, where it is exposed to light and to grazing. That exposure is a risk, because the cotyledon is both the food and the first leaf. A hypogeal seedling keeps its store below, where it is safe.

The depth of sowing therefore differs. An epigeal seed must be shallow enough for the hypocotyl to lift the cotyledons through, while a hypogeal seed can be deeper because only the plumule must emerge.
That is why a bean is sown shallow and a maize grain deeper. The sowing depth follows the germination pattern.
An epigeal cotyledon turns green and photosynthesises once it emerges. That first leaf is therefore both the food store and the first photosynthetic organ.
A hypogeal cotyledon stays below and feeds the seedling from underground. That is why a maize seedling can grow for days without any leaf above the soil.
An epigeal cotyledon that emerges early can photosynthesise sooner. That advantage is why some epigeal species establish faster in open light than hypogeal ones.
bullets: Epigeal stores are exposed; hypogeal stores are safe
Epigeal seeds are sown shallow; hypogeal deeper
Sowing depth follows the germination pattern

content.heading: Go deeper: Examples and the planting decision
paragraphs: Bean, cowpea and groundnut are epigeal because their cotyledons emerge. Maize, sorghum and yam are hypogeal because their cotyledons stay below. A farmer can therefore predict sowing depth from the example.
The radicle still emerges first in both patterns and grows downward. The difference is only in which stem part elongates next. That order is why the radicle is common to both.
A garden that mixes both patterns must therefore sow at two depths. A single depth would be too deep for the epigeal seed and too shallow for the hypogeal one.
A groundnut that germinates epigeally pushes its cotyledons up. That is why it must be sown shallow, so the hypocotyl can lift them through the soil.
A yam sett is planted shallow because it is hypogeal. A deep planting would bury its cotyledon and waste its store before the plumule could emerge.
A cowpea that germinates epigeally pushes its cotyledons up and must be sown shallow. A sorghum grain that germinates hypogeally can be sown deeper.
bullets: Bean, cowpea, groundnut: epigeal; maize, sorghum, yam: hypogeal
The radicle emerges first in both
Mixed gardens need two sowing depths

content.question: Why might a farmer plant bean seeds more shallowly than maize seeds?
hints: Bean is epigeal and must lift its cotyledons to the surface.
Maize is hypogeal and its food store stays underground.
Deep planting uses up the bean's stored food before the shoot reaches light.

lessons.title: Nervous Coordination and Neurons
lessons.objective: Explain the need for coordination, compare nervous and hormonal control, and describe neuron structure, impulse transmission and synapses.

content.heading: Nervous coordination and neurons
paragraphs: A student touches a hot plate and pulls the hand away before thinking about it. Receptors, neurons and muscles have already coordinated the reflex response.

content.heading: Why coordination matters
paragraphs: Coordination links a stimulus to a response. A receptor detects the stimulus, a coordinator processes the information, and an effector such as a muscle or gland carries out the response; this sequence keeps the body working as a whole.

The nervous system provides fast, short-lived control through electrical impulses and chemical synapses. The endocrine system provides slower, longer-lasting control through hormones carried in the blood.

Both systems maintain homeostasis. Nervous control suits rapid actions such as blinking or balancing, while hormonal control suits gradual changes such as growth, puberty and blood glucose regulation.
bullets: Stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
Nervous control is fast and short-lived; hormonal control is slower and longer-lasting.
Both systems help maintain a steady internal environment.
content.takeaway: Nerves switch responses quickly; hormones tune the body slowly.

check.question: Which sequence correctly describes a coordinated response?
check.why: A stimulus is detected by a receptor, processed by a coordinator and answered by an effector.

content.heading: The neuron
paragraphs: A neuron is a nerve cell specialised for carrying impulses. It has a cell body containing the nucleus, dendrites that receive signals, and a long axon that carries the impulse away towards another cell.

Many axons are wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath, which insulates the fibre and speeds up transmission. The sheath is interrupted at nodes of Ranvier, where the impulse jumps from node to node in saltatory conduction.

Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, motor neurons carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors, and relay neurons connect the two inside the brain or spinal cord.
bullets: Dendrites receive; the axon transmits; the cell body contains the nucleus.
Myelin insulates and speeds up the impulse.
Sensory, motor and relay neurons have different jobs.
content.takeaway: A neuron is built to receive, carry and pass on an impulse.

check.question: Which part of a neuron carries impulses away from the cell body?
check.why: The axon is the long fibre that conducts the impulse away from the cell body.

content.heading: Impulse transmission and synapses
paragraphs: At rest, the neuron membrane is polarised, with a negative charge inside and a positive charge outside. A stimulus makes the membrane permeable to sodium ions, which rush in and reverse the charge; this is the action potential.

The impulse travels along the axon as a wave of depolarisation. Behind it, potassium ions move out and restore the resting charge, so the neuron can carry another impulse after a short recovery period.

At a synapse, the impulse cannot jump the gap. The presynaptic knob releases a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft; the chemical binds to receptors on the next neuron and starts a new impulse, so transmission is one-way.
bullets: Action potential: sodium ions enter and reverse the membrane charge.
Potassium ions restore the resting potential.
Neurotransmitters carry the signal across the synaptic cleft in one direction.
content.takeaway: Electric along the axon, chemical across the synapse.

check.question: The gap between two neurons is crossed by
check.why: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the next neuron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Nervous control is fast and short-lived; hormonal control is slower and longer-lasting. Neurons carry impulses, myelin speeds them up, and neurotransmitters cross synapses in one direction, so signals travel one way only.

content.problem: A toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors at a synapse. Predict the effect on a muscle and explain why.

steps.reason: Acetylcholine normally binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
steps.result: The signal cannot pass from the motor neuron to the muscle.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens to the muscle?

steps.reason: Without a new impulse, the muscle fibre is not stimulated.
steps.result: The muscle cannot contract and becomes weak or paralysed.

steps.reason: Synapses transmit in one direction only.
steps.result: The block stops communication at that synapse, not along the axon behind it.

content.heading: Go deeper: Nerves versus hormones
paragraphs: Nerves carry impulses as electrical changes along axons and across synapses. They are fast, reaching a muscle in milliseconds, but their effect is brief. Hormones are carried in blood and act more slowly, yet their effect lasts longer.

A reflex is the fastest nerve pathway. It travels from receptor to spinal cord to muscle without the brain, which is why a hand is withdrawn before the pain is felt. A voluntary action takes longer because it includes the brain.

The two systems also differ in reach. A nerve acts on a specific muscle, while a hormone can act on many target organs at once. That spread is why hormones control growth and reproduction while nerves control movement.
A synapse is the place where the two systems meet. The nerve ends there and a chemical is released, so the message that began as electrical ends as chemical.
A hormone acts only on its target because only that organ has receptors for it. That specificity is why adrenaline speeds the heart without directly speeding the gut.
bullets: Nerves: fast, brief, specific; hormones: slow, long, widespread
Reflexes bypass the brain and are fastest
Hormones control growth and reproduction

content.heading: Go deeper: Neurons and the synapse
paragraphs: A sensory neuron carries impulses from a receptor to the brain or cord. An interneuron links them, and a motor neuron carries the response to a muscle or gland. The three kinds together form a relay.

At a synapse the impulse is carried by a neurotransmitter across a gap. That chemical step means the signal is one-way, so a synapse cannot conduct backward. The gap also allows integration, where several inputs meet.
Myelin speeds conduction by insulating the axon. A demyelinating disease therefore slows impulses even though the axon itself is intact, because the insulation is missing.
A motor neuron is very long because it must reach a distant muscle. That length is why a foot muscle is controlled by a cell whose body sits in the spinal cord.
A resting potential is maintained by pumps that keep sodium out and potassium in. That potential is the charge that an impulse must depolarise before it can travel.
The resting potential is about -70 millivolts inside the axon. An impulse depolarises it to +40 millivolts before it repolarises, which is the electrical event that travels.
bullets: Sensory, interneuron and motor neurons form a relay
Synapses are one-way because of neurotransmitters
Myelin speeds conduction by insulation

content.heading: Go deeper: Stimulus, response and the sequence
paragraphs: Every response has the same sequence: stimulus, receptor, sensory neuron, brain or cord, motor neuron, effector. A heat stimulus on the hand therefore ends as a muscle contraction that withdraws the hand.
The effector is the muscle or gland that responds. A pupil is an effector for light, a sweat gland for heat and a muscle for touch. The same sequence therefore serves many different responses.
A reflex arc is the shortest form of that sequence. A voluntary arc adds the brain and is therefore slower but more modifiable, which is why learning changes voluntary responses and not reflexes.
A reflex is the same sequence with the brain left out. That omission is why a reflex is faster than a voluntary action that follows the same path.
The sequence can be short-circuited by learning. A driver who has practised braking does not think about it, because the voluntary act has become a reflex.
The brain can also inhibit a reflex that it knows is harmless. That inhibition is why a person can hold a hot object for a moment before withdrawing.
bullets: Stimulus to receptor to cord to effector
Effectors are muscles and glands
Reflex arcs are short; voluntary arcs include the brain

content.question: Why does a reflex withdrawal from a hot object happen before the person feels the pain?
hints: The reflex arc can complete in the spinal cord.
The brain receives the sensory information at the same time.
Feeling and conscious interpretation take longer than the spinal response.

lessons.title: Brain, Spinal Cord and Reflexes
lessons.objective: Describe the central nervous system, the main regions of the brain, the spinal cord, and how reflex arcs produce fast involuntary responses.

content.heading: Brain, spinal cord and reflexes
paragraphs: A footballer ducks a flying ball, and a student blinks as dust blows into the eye. Both responses depend on the central nervous system, which sorts the signal and triggers the action.

content.heading: The central nervous system
paragraphs: A footballer ducks a ball and a student blinks as dust blows into the eye. Both responses run through the central nervous system, which sorts signals and issues commands.

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The brain sits in the skull, the spinal cord runs inside the vertebral column, and both are wrapped in membranes called meninges and cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid.

Inside, grey matter holds cell bodies and synapses, while white matter holds myelinated axons. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is the network of cranial and spinal nerves linking the CNS to receptors and effectors.
bullets: CNS: brain and spinal cord; PNS: cranial and spinal nerves.
Meninges and cerebrospinal fluid protect the CNS.
Grey matter holds cell bodies; white matter is myelinated.
content.takeaway: The CNS is the control centre; the PNS is the wiring.

check.question: Which structure cushions the brain and spinal cord in fluid?
check.why: Cerebrospinal fluid surrounds and cushions the CNS, while the meninges are the membranes that enclose it.

content.heading: The brain and spinal cord
paragraphs: Different regions of the brain do different jobs. The cerebrum, with its folded outer layer, handles conscious thought, memory, language, vision, hearing and voluntary movement. The cerebellum, behind it, coordinates balance, posture and learned movement, making actions smooth.

The medulla oblongata at the base of the brain controls involuntary activities such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. The hypothalamus monitors temperature, hunger and thirst, and links the nervous system to the pituitary gland.
The spinal cord is more than a cable. It carries sensory impulses up and motor impulses down, and it contains reflex centres that produce fast responses without waiting for the brain.
bullets: Cerebrum: thought, memory, senses and voluntary movement.
Cerebellum: balance, posture and smooth movement.
Medulla and hypothalamus: involuntary control and internal balance.
content.takeaway: The brain decides; the spinal cord can also act alone.

check.question: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
check.why: The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and smooth movement.

content.heading: Reflex and voluntary actions
paragraphs: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus. It protects the body before the brain has time to think.

The pathway is called a reflex arc. It runs from receptor to sensory neuron, then to a relay neuron in the spinal cord, then to a motor neuron and an effector such as a muscle. Blinking, the knee jerk and pulling the hand from a hot object are simple reflexes.

A voluntary action begins in the brain and is under conscious control, so it is slower and can be learned or stopped. A conditioned reflex is a learned link between a stimulus and a response, such as salivating at the smell of food or riding a bicycle after practice.
bullets: Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay → motor neuron → effector.
Reflexes are rapid, involuntary and protective.
Voluntary actions are conscious; conditioned reflexes are learned.
content.takeaway: Reflexes take the short road; voluntary actions take the long one.

check.question: Which sequence correctly shows a reflex arc?
options: Receptor → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → effector
Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Effector → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → receptor
Receptor → relay neuron → sensory neuron → effector → motor neuron
check.why: A reflex arc runs from receptor to sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, protected by meninges and cerebrospinal fluid. The cerebrum handles conscious activity, the cerebellum balance, and the medulla involuntary functions. Reflex arcs pass through the spinal cord for speed.

content.problem: A doctor taps a patient's knee and the leg kicks out, but the patient feels nothing until afterwards. Explain the pathway and why the response is involuntary.

steps.reason: The tap stretches a tendon, and stretch receptors in the thigh muscle detect the change.
steps.result: A sensory impulse starts towards the spinal cord.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the impulse go next?

steps.reason: The sensory neuron synapses with a relay neuron in the spinal cord, which synapses with a motor neuron.
steps.result: The motor neuron stimulates the thigh muscle to contract.

steps.reason: The response leaves the spinal cord before the brain has processed the signal.
steps.result: The leg kicks automatically, and the brain is informed afterwards.

content.heading: Go deeper: The central nervous system and its protection
paragraphs: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The skull protects the brain and the vertebral column protects the cord. Cerebrospinal fluid cushions both against shock.

The spinal cord carries impulses between the brain and the body. A spinal reflex can be completed without the brain, which is why a reflex is faster than a voluntary action. The cord is therefore both a cable and a processor.

The brain is divided into cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla. The cerebrum is for conscious thought, the cerebellum for coordination and the medulla for heartbeat and breathing. Each region has its own job.
Cerebrospinal fluid is replaced several times a day. That circulation cushions the brain and removes waste, so it is both a shock absorber and a drain.
The vertebral column protects the cord from injury. A fracture that crushes the cord therefore disconnects the brain from the body below the injury.
The meninges cover the brain and cord and contain the cerebrospinal fluid. That fluid carries nutrients and removes waste as well as cushioning blows.
bullets: CNS: brain and spinal cord, protected by skull and vertebrae
The cord is both a cable and a processor
Cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla have distinct jobs

content.heading: Go deeper: Brain regions and what each controls
paragraphs: The cerebrum controls conscious thought, memory and voluntary movement. Its two hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, and each side controls the opposite side of the body. A stroke on one side therefore weakens the other.
The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and learned movement, making actions smooth. Damage to it produces clumsiness without paralysis, which is how its role is recognised in a patient.

The medulla controls the autonomic actions that cannot be willed: heartbeat, breathing and reflexes of the gut. That is why a medulla injury is so dangerous even when the limbs can still move by reflex.
The cerebrum is folded to increase its surface. That folding packs a large sheet of cortex into a small skull, which is why the brain has space for its size.
The cerebrum shows lateralisation, with language dominant in one hemisphere. That is why a stroke on one side affects speech in a way that a stroke on the other does not.
Damage to the pons disturbs the transfer between cerebrum and cerebellum. That is why a pontine lesion affects coordination as well as consciousness.
bullets: Cerebrum: conscious thought; each hemisphere controls the opposite side
Cerebellum: balance, posture and smooth movement
Medulla: heartbeat, breathing and gut reflexes

content.heading: Go deeper: Reflex and voluntary actions
paragraphs: A reflex action is involuntary and immediate. A knee jerk, a pupil response and a withdrawal from heat are reflexes. The spinal cord completes them without the brain.
A voluntary action is willed and slower. Walking, writing and speaking are voluntary because the cerebrum is involved. A voluntary action can be learned and modified, while a reflex cannot.
A conditioned reflex is the bridge between them. A dog that salivates at a bell has learned to respond to a new stimulus. That learning shows that even a reflex can be retrained.
A conditioned reflex needs repetition before it is learned. Pavlov's dog salivated at the bell only after the bell had been paired with food many times.
A reflex can be modified by the brain. A person who knows a pin is coming can suppress the withdrawal, which shows that the cerebrum can override the cord.
A knee jerk uses a monosynaptic arc with only two neurons. That short arc is why it is the fastest reflex that can be tested at the bedside.
bullets: Reflex: involuntary, immediate, spinal
Voluntary: willed, slower, cerebral, learned
Conditioned reflex: a learned response to a new stimulus

content.question: Why does a person blink when an object comes towards the eye, even when they try to keep the eye open?
hints: Blinking is a protective reflex.
The reflex arc can be completed quickly through the brain stem.
Conscious control is slower than the reflex pathway.

lessons.title: Skin, Nose and Tongue
lessons.objective: Relate the structure and function of the skin, nose and tongue to touch, smell and taste, and explain common defects of these sense organs.

content.heading: Skin, nose and tongue
paragraphs: A hand feels the roughness of bark, the nose catches smoke, and the tongue detects salt in soup. Each sense organ turns a different kind of stimulus into nerve impulses.

content.heading: The skin as a tactile organ
paragraphs: The skin is the largest sense organ. Its dermis contains several kinds of receptor: touch corpuscles near the surface, deeper pressure corpuscles, separate cold and heat receptors, and free nerve endings for pain.
The receptors are unevenly distributed. Fingertips, lips and the tongue carry many touch receptors, which is why they detect fine detail, while the back is much less sensitive.

Receptors also adapt. A ring left on the finger soon feels normal because the touch receptors stop responding to a constant stimulus, yet a new change is detected at once. This is why we notice a fly landing but not the feel of clothing.
bullets: Skin receptors detect touch, pressure, temperature and pain.
Fingertips and lips are most sensitive because they have more receptors.
Receptors adapt to a constant stimulus.
content.takeaway: Skin reports touch, pressure, temperature and pain.

check.question: A ring feels tight when first worn but soon becomes unnoticeable. This is due to
check.why: Receptors stop responding to an unchanging stimulus, so the ring is no longer noticed.

content.heading: The nose and smell
paragraphs: The nose detects chemicals in the air. At the roof of the nasal cavity, the olfactory epithelium contains receptor cells with fine cilia, and mucus dissolves arriving molecules so they can bind to the receptors.

The receptor cells send impulses along the olfactory nerve to the cerebrum, where the smell is identified. A blocked nose, a cold or damaged receptor cells can cause anosmia, the loss of the sense of smell.
Smell and taste work together. Much of what we call flavour comes from odours rising from the mouth into the nasal cavity, so food tastes bland when the nose is blocked.
bullets: Olfactory receptor cells sit in the roof of the nasal cavity.
Mucus dissolves odour molecules so receptors can detect them.
Blocked noses cause anosmia and dull the taste of food.
content.takeaway: The nose reads dissolved chemicals and sends smell signals to the brain.

check.question: Why does food taste bland when you have a cold?
options: Odour molecules cannot reach the olfactory receptors
check.why: A blocked nose prevents odour molecules from reaching the olfactory receptors, so the smell component of flavour is lost.

content.heading: The tongue and taste
paragraphs: The tongue detects dissolved chemicals through taste buds, which sit in small bumps called papillae. Each bud contains receptor cells that respond to one or more of five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

Impulses travel along cranial nerves to the medulla and then to the cerebrum. Taste is not fixed to a single zone: the old tongue map is wrong, because most of the tongue can detect every taste, though sensitivity varies.

Taste buds are damaged by very hot food, and their sensitivity falls when the mouth is dry because chemicals cannot dissolve. Smoking and some medicines also dull taste, while ageing reduces the number of working buds.
bullets: Taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
Taste impulses travel by cranial nerves to the brain.
Heat, dryness and ageing damage or dull taste buds.
content.takeaway: The tongue identifies dissolved chemicals as five basic tastes.

check.question: Which list gives the five basic tastes?
check.why: The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Skin receptors detect touch, pressure, temperature and pain and adapt to constant stimuli. The nose detects dissolved odours, and the tongue detects five basic tastes. Smell and taste combine to produce flavour.

content.problem: A cook loses the sense of smell after a head injury and complains that food has lost its flavour, although tests show normal taste buds. Explain the observation.

steps.reason: The tongue and taste buds still detect the five basic tastes.
steps.result: The cook can still tell sweet from sour or salty.
steps.predictPrompt: Why is flavour still missing?

steps.reason: The injury has damaged the olfactory pathway, so odours cannot reach the brain.
steps.result: The smell component of flavour is lost.

steps.reason: The brain builds flavour from both taste and smell.
steps.result: Food tastes bland even though the tongue is working.

content.heading: Go deeper: Receptors in the skin
paragraphs: The skin contains receptors for touch, pressure, temperature and pain. Each kind responds to a different stimulus, and each has its own threshold. A receptor therefore answers only a narrow range of events.

Adaptation reduces the response to a steady stimulus. A watch that is worn all day stops being felt, because the pressure receptors have adapted. That adaptation is why a constant touch is soon ignored.
Pain receptors do not adapt in the same way. A steady pain therefore continues to be felt, which is why it is a useful warning that tissue is being damaged.
A receptor that adapts is called phasic, and one that does not is tonic. Pain receptors are tonic, touch receptors are often phasic, which is why pain persists and touch fades.
Free nerve endings are pain receptors spread through the skin. They have no capsule, so they respond to damage rather than to gentle touch.
A burn activates pain receptors and also heat receptors. The pain that follows the burn is therefore a separate signal from the heat that caused it.
bullets: Touch, pressure, temperature and pain have separate receptors
Receptors adapt to steady stimuli
Pain receptors adapt slowly, which is why pain persists

content.heading: Go deeper: The olfactory epithelium and taste buds
paragraphs: Smell is detected by the olfactory epithelium in the upper nasal cavity. It has millions of receptor cells, each sensitive to a range of chemicals. Those cells are neurons that send impulses directly to the brain.
Taste is detected by taste buds on the tongue, most of which are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. The buds are chemical receptors, so taste and smell together identify food.
A cold that blocks the nose therefore removes flavour without removing taste. That is why food tastes flat when the nose is blocked.
Olfactory receptors are neurons that are replaced throughout life. That replacement is unusual, because most neurons are not replaced after birth.
Taste buds are replaced every ten days or so. That turnover is why the tongue can recover from a burn without losing its sense of taste for long.
An olfactory receptor that is damaged by a virus can be replaced. That is why smell returns after a cold even when it fails for weeks.
bullets: Olfactory receptors send impulses directly to the brain
Taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami
Flavour needs both taste and smell

content.heading: Go deeper: How the senses work together
paragraphs: The senses are not separate in daily life. A ripe mango is judged by sight, smell, touch and taste together. The brain combines the separate signals into one object.
That combination is why a meal can be appealing or repulsive before it is eaten. Colour and smell set an expectation that taste then confirms or rejects.
A loss of one sense therefore changes the others. A person who cannot smell loses flavour, and a person who cannot see must rely more on touch and hearing.
A sweet smell can make a bitter taste seem sweeter. The brain therefore does not add the senses as separate numbers; it judges the food as a whole.
A diner who sees a red pepper expects heat before tasting it. That expectation comes from sight and smell, so the senses prepare the mouth for the taste to come.
A person who loses sight compensates by listening more closely. That compensation shows that the brain reallocates attention among the senses that remain.
bullets: The brain combines separate senses into one object
Colour and smell set the expectation that taste confirms
Loss of one sense increases reliance on the others

content.question: Why can a person still recognise sweet and salty foods when the nose is blocked, but not the full flavour of a meal?
hints: Taste buds detect basic tastes without help from the nose.
Most flavour comes from odours reaching the olfactory epithelium.
The brain combines taste and smell into one experience.

lessons.title: The Eye
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of the eye, explain focusing and the pupil reflex, and identify common eye defects and their corrections.

content.heading: The eye
paragraphs: The eye turns light into nerve impulses. Its curved surfaces focus light on a light-sensitive retina, and the brain builds the image we see from those signals.

content.heading: Structure of the eye
paragraphs: Light enters the eye through the transparent cornea and passes through the pupil, the hole controlled by the coloured iris. The lens then focuses the light onto the retina at the back of the eye.

The retina contains rods, which work in dim light but see only black and white, and cones, which detect colour and sharp detail in bright light. The fovea has the highest concentration of cones and gives the clearest vision.

The optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain. Where it leaves the eye there are no receptor cells, creating a blind spot. The sclera is the tough white outer coat, and the choroid supplies blood.
bullets: Cornea and lens focus light; iris controls pupil size.
Rods work in dim light; cones detect colour and detail.
Optic nerve carries impulses; the blind spot has no receptors.
content.takeaway: The eye focuses light and the retina converts it to impulses.

check.question: Which cells in the retina are responsible for colour vision?
check.why: Cones detect colour and sharp detail in bright light.

content.heading: Focusing and the pupil reflex
paragraphs: The eye focuses by changing the shape of the lens, a process called accommodation. To look at something close, the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker; to look far away, the muscles relax and the lens becomes thinner.

The pupil reflex controls how much light enters. In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil narrows. In dim light the reverse happens and the pupil widens.

These responses are reflexes, not conscious decisions. The retina detects the light level and the brain stem sends the command, protecting the retina from bright light and letting in more light when it is dark.
bullets: Accommodation: ciliary muscles change lens thickness.
Bright light constricts the pupil; dim light dilates it.
Both are reflexes controlled by the nervous system.
content.takeaway: Near vision thickens the lens; bright light narrows the pupil.

check.question: To focus on a nearby object, the ciliary muscles
options: Relax and the lens becomes thinner
Contract and the lens becomes thicker
check.why: Near vision requires the ciliary muscles to contract, slackening the suspensory ligaments so the lens becomes thicker.

content.heading: Defects of the eye
paragraphs: Short sight, or myopia, happens when the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong, so distant images focus in front of the retina. It is corrected with a concave lens that spreads the rays before they enter the eye.

Long sight, or hypermetropia, happens when the eyeball is too short or the lens too weak, so near images focus behind the retina. A convex lens brings the rays together. Astigmatism is caused by an uneven cornea or lens and is corrected with a cylindrical lens.

Other defects include presbyopia, the loss of lens elasticity with age; cataract, a clouding of the lens; glaucoma, raised pressure inside the eye; and colour blindness, usually a defect in the red or green cones.
bullets: Myopia: distant blur, concave lens.
Hypermetropia: near blur, convex lens.
Cataract, glaucoma and colour blindness also affect sight.
content.takeaway: Match the defect to its lens: concave for short sight, convex for long sight.

check.question: A person cannot see distant objects clearly. Which defect and correction are correct?
check.why: Myopia is short sight, and a concave lens spreads the rays so the image falls on the retina.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The cornea and lens focus light on the retina, where rods and cones make impulses. Near vision thickens the lens; bright light constricts the pupil. Myopia needs a concave lens and hypermetropia a convex lens.

content.problem: A student complains that the board is blurry but reading a book is fine. Identify the likely defect, explain where the image falls, and state the correction.

steps.reason: Clear near vision with blurred distant vision is short sight.
steps.result: The student probably has myopia.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the image form?

steps.reason: In myopia the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong.
steps.result: Distant rays focus in front of the retina.

steps.reason: A concave lens spreads the rays before they enter the eye.
steps.result: The image moves back onto the retina.

content.heading: Go deeper: The eye as a camera
paragraphs: The eye focuses light on the retina by two lenses: the cornea, which does most of the focusing, and the lens, which adjusts for distance. The pupil controls how much light enters, and the retina converts the image into nervous impulses.
The retina has rods for dim light and cones for colour. Rods are more sensitive but do not distinguish colour, while cones do. That division is why a dim room appears grey and not in colour.
The image on the retina is inverted and reduced. The brain reads it as upright because it has learned to interpret that pattern, not because the eye corrects it.
The aqueous and vitreous humours hold the eye in shape. Vitreous is a gel that fills the main cavity, so the retina is pressed against the wall it must read.
The fovea at the centre of the retina has only cones, so reading is sharp. The periphery has more rods, so dim objects at the edge of vision are easier to see.
The fovea is therefore the region of sharpest vision.
bullets: Cornea does most focusing; lens adjusts for distance
Rods for dim light; cones for colour
The retinal image is inverted and reduced

content.heading: Go deeper: Accommodation and the pupil reflex
paragraphs: Accommodation changes the shape of the lens. Ciliary muscles contract to make it fatter for near objects and relax to make it thinner for far objects. The lens therefore has more power for near vision than for far.

The pupil reflex narrows the pupil in bright light and widens it in dim light. That response is a reflex arc through the midbrain, so it is fast and involuntary. A bright torch therefore makes the pupil contract at once.
Both responses protect the retina. The lens brings the image into focus and the pupil limits the light that reaches the receptors.
The ciliary muscles are smooth muscle, so they can act for a long time without tiring. That is why a person can read for hours without the muscles failing.
The pupil reflex is faster than accommodation because it has a shorter arc. That is why the eyes water in bright light before they have adjusted for distance.
bullets: Ciliary muscles make the lens fatter for near objects
The pupil narrows in bright light by reflex
Both responses protect the retina

content.heading: Go deeper: Myopia, hypermetropia and correction
paragraphs: Myopia is short sight. The eyeball is too long or the lens too powerful, so the image forms in front of the retina. A concave lens diverges the rays and pushes the focus back onto the retina.
Hypermetropia is long sight. The eyeball is too short or the lens too weak, so the image forms behind the retina. A convex lens converges the rays and brings the focus forward.
Astigmatism is an irregular cornea that focuses at two points. A cylindrical lens corrects it by focusing in one meridian more than the other. Each defect therefore has its own lens.
A concave lens is thinner in the middle and thicker at the edge. That shape diverges rays, while a convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges them.
A concave lens cannot be worn too strong or it will cause headache. That is why a short-sighted person needs the correct power and not a stronger one.
Contact lenses correct the same defects by sitting on the cornea. Their advantage is that they move with the eye rather than sitting in front of it.
bullets: Myopia: image in front of retina; concave lens corrects
Hypermetropia: image behind retina; convex lens corrects
Astigmatism: irregular cornea; cylindrical lens corrects

content.question: Why does the pupil become smaller in bright sunlight even when a person tries to keep it open?
hints: The pupil reflex is involuntary.
The retina detects the light level.
Circular muscles of the iris contract in bright light.

lessons.title: The Ear
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of the ear, explain how sound is converted into impulses, describe balance, and identify common ear defects.

content.heading: The ear
paragraphs: The ear turns sound waves into nerve impulses. It also contains organs of balance, which tell the brain how the head is moving and help us keep our balance.

content.heading: Structure and hearing
paragraphs: Sound waves are collected by the pinna and travel down the auditory canal to the tympanum, or eardrum. The eardrum vibrates and passes the vibration through three small bones, the malleus, incus and stapes, to the oval window.
From the oval window, the vibrations enter the fluid-filled cochlea. Hair cells inside the cochlea convert the vibrations into nerve impulses, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain.

The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat and keeps air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum. The ossicles also amplify the vibration, because the middle ear must transfer energy from air to fluid.
bullets: Pinna and canal collect sound; eardrum vibrates.
Ossicles pass vibrations to the cochlea.
Hair cells make impulses; the auditory nerve carries them.
content.takeaway: Sound travels as vibrations until hair cells make impulses.

check.question: Which structure converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses?
check.why: Hair cells in the cochlea convert vibrations into impulses carried by the auditory nerve.

content.heading: Balance and the inner ear
paragraphs: Balance is detected by the vestibular system in the inner ear. Three semicircular canals, set at right angles to each other, contain fluid that moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells and signalling the direction of movement.
The utricle and saccule detect straight-line acceleration and the pull of gravity. They contain small stones called otoliths that press on hair cells when the head tilts or moves.

Impulses from these organs travel to the cerebellum and other brain centres, which adjust posture and eye movements. Spinning quickly disturbs the fluid, so the brain still receives movement signals after stopping, which causes dizziness.
bullets: Semicircular canals detect rotation of the head.
Utricle and saccule detect gravity and straight-line movement.
Balance signals go to the cerebellum.
content.takeaway: Canals sense turning; otolith organs sense gravity and speed.

check.question: Which part of the ear detects rotational movement of the head?
check.why: Fluid in the semicircular canals moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells.

content.heading: Defects of the ear
paragraphs: Conductive deafness happens when sound cannot reach the inner ear. Causes include wax blocking the canal, a torn eardrum, fluid from otitis media, or damaged ossicles; hearing aids often help because they make the sound louder.

Sensorineural deafness happens when hair cells or the auditory nerve are damaged, for example by very loud noise, some medicines, infection or ageing. It is usually permanent, and a cochlear implant may restore some hearing by stimulating the nerve directly.

Tinnitus is a ringing in the ears without an external sound, while Ménière's disease causes episodes of dizziness, hearing loss and a blocked feeling. Ear infections are common in children because their Eustachian tubes are short and horizontal.
bullets: Conductive deafness: sound blocked; hearing aids help.
Sensorineural deafness: hair cells or nerve damaged; often permanent.
Otitis media and loud noise are common causes.
content.takeaway: Blocked sound is conductive; damaged nerve is sensorineural.

check.question: Damage to the hair cells of the cochlea causes which type of deafness?
check.why: Hair cell damage affects the conversion of vibrations into impulses, which is sensorineural deafness.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Sound passes from pinna to eardrum, ossicles, cochlea and auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation, while the utricle and saccule detect gravity. Conductive deafness blocks sound; sensorineural deafness damages hair cells or the nerve.

content.problem: A factory worker develops hearing loss after years of loud noise, while another person loses hearing because wax blocks the ear canal. Distinguish the two types and their likely outcomes.

steps.reason: Loud noise damages hair cells in the cochlea.
steps.result: The worker has sensorineural deafness.
steps.predictPrompt: Is it likely to recover?

steps.reason: Wax prevents sound from reaching the eardrum and inner ear.
steps.result: The second person has conductive deafness.

steps.reason: Wax can be removed, but damaged hair cells do not usually regenerate.
steps.result: Conductive loss is often reversible; sensorineural loss is usually permanent.

content.heading: Go deeper: The outer and middle ear
paragraphs: Sound waves are collected by the pinna and channelled through the auditory canal to the eardrum. The pinna helps locate the source of a sound, because its shape delays one ear more than the other for sounds from the side.

The eardrum vibrates and drives three ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes. Those bones amplify the vibration about twenty times before it reaches the oval window. That amplification compensates for the change from air to fluid.
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. It equalises pressure on the two sides of the eardrum, which is why swallowing relieves the fullness felt in an aeroplane.
Wax in the canal traps dust and insects. That trapping is protective, but an excess of wax can block the canal and cause conductive deafness.
The ossicles are the smallest bones in the body. That smallness lets them move quickly enough to transmit high pitches without lag.
The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates easily. That thinness lets it respond to very soft sounds as well as to loud ones.
bullets: Pinna collects and locates sound
Ossicles amplify vibration about twenty times
The Eustachian tube equalises pressure on the eardrum

content.heading: Go deeper: The cochlea and hearing
paragraphs: The cochlea is a coiled tube in the inner ear. When the stapes moves, it pushes the fluid inside, and that movement bends hair cells on the basilar membrane. Each pitch bends hair cells at a different place along the coil.

High pitches bend cells near the base and low pitches bend cells near the apex. The brain therefore receives a place code for pitch, not a timing code alone. Damage to one place loses one range of notes.
The auditory nerve carries the impulses to the brain. A sensorineural deafness is damage to the hair cells or nerve, while conductive deafness is damage to the canal, eardrum or ossicles.
The hair cells are delicate and can be damaged by loud noise. That is why prolonged exposure to loud music causes permanent loss of high pitches first.
The basilar membrane is wider at the apex than at the base. That width difference is what maps low pitches to the apex and high pitches to the base.
A hearing aid amplifies sound before it reaches the cochlea. That amplification helps a conductive loss but not a sensorineural one.
bullets: Hair cells bend at different places for different pitches
High pitches at the base; low pitches at the apex
Sensorineural: hair cells; conductive: canal, drum or ossicles

content.heading: Go deeper: Balance and the semicircular canals
paragraphs: Balance is not a function of the cochlea. It is a function of the semicircular canals and the utricle and saccule. Those organs detect rotation and gravity, and they send signals that the brain uses to steady the body.

Three canals at right angles detect rotation in every plane. When the head turns, fluid in the canals lags and bends hair cells. That bending tells the brain that the head has moved before the body has fallen.

The utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and gravity. They tell the brain whether the head is upright or tilted, which is the information that keeps a person from falling when standing still.
Motion sickness occurs when the canals and the eyes disagree. The brain receives conflicting signals from the vestibular system and the vision, which is why it produces nausea.
The utricle and saccule also carry otoliths that press on hair cells. Gravity therefore bends them, which is how the brain knows the head is tilted.
bullets: Balance uses semicircular canals, utricle and saccule
Three canals detect rotation in every plane
Utricle and saccule detect gravity and linear acceleration

content.question: Why does a cold often cause temporary hearing loss and a blocked feeling in the ear?
hints: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat.
A cold causes swelling and mucus in that tube.
Unequal pressure on the eardrum reduces its movement.

lessons.title: Animal Hormones
lessons.objective: State the location of the main endocrine glands, relate each hormone to its function, and explain disorders caused by hormone imbalance.

content.heading: Animal hormones
paragraphs: Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. They act on target organs more slowly than nerves, but their effects usually last longer and can be widespread.

content.heading: The endocrine system and the pituitary
paragraphs: An endocrine gland has no duct. It releases hormones straight into the blood, and the hormone acts only on cells that carry the matching receptor, called target cells.

The pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain, attached to the hypothalamus. It is called the master gland because it controls several other glands. Its anterior lobe releases growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone; the posterior lobe releases antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.
Growth hormone promotes growth of bones and muscles. Too little in childhood causes dwarfism, too much causes gigantism, and excess in adulthood causes acromegaly.
bullets: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into blood.
The pituitary is attached to the hypothalamus and controls other glands.
Growth hormone excess or deficiency changes body growth.
content.takeaway: The pituitary is the master gland because it commands other glands.

check.question: Which gland is called the master gland because it controls other endocrine glands?
check.why: The pituitary releases hormones that control the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads.

content.heading: Thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal glands
paragraphs: The thyroid gland lies in the neck, just below the larynx. It releases thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism and needs iodine to be made. A lack of iodine causes goitre, an enlarged thyroid, while too little thyroxine in a child causes cretinism and in an adult causes myxoedema.

The parathyroid glands sit on the posterior surface of the thyroid and release parathormone, which raises blood calcium. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The cortex releases cortisol, which helps the body cope with stress, and aldosterone, which controls salt balance.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline. In danger, adrenaline raises heart rate, widens the airways and releases glucose, preparing the body for fight or flight.
bullets: Thyroxine controls metabolism and needs iodine.
Parathormone raises blood calcium.
Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight.
content.takeaway: Thyroid sets the metabolic rate; adrenaline meets emergencies.

check.question: Which hormone raises blood calcium?
check.why: Parathormone from the parathyroid glands raises the level of calcium in the blood.

content.heading: Pancreas and gonads
paragraphs: The pancreas lies behind the stomach and contains small groups of cells called the islets of Langerhans. Beta cells release insulin, which lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen; alpha cells release glucagon, which raises blood glucose by converting glycogen back to glucose.

Too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus, with high blood glucose, thirst, frequent urination and glucose in the urine. The ovaries lie in the pelvis and release oestrogen and progesterone, which control the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and female secondary sexual characteristics.

The testes lie in the scrotum and release testosterone, which controls sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics. These hormones are carried in the blood but act only on target organs that have the matching receptors.
bullets: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
Ovaries release oestrogen and progesterone.
Testes release testosterone.
content.takeaway: Insulin and glucagon are opposites; the gonads set sexual development.

check.question: Which cells release insulin?
check.why: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin, which lowers blood glucose.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Pituitary: growth and control of other glands. Thyroid: thyroxine and metabolism. Parathyroid: calcium. Adrenal: cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline. Pancreas: insulin and glucagon. Gonads: sex hormones. Learn each gland with its hormone and one disorder.

content.problem: A patient is always thirsty, passes urine often and has glucose in the blood. Which gland and hormone are involved, and what is the probable condition?

steps.reason: Thirst, frequent urination and glucose in the urine point to high blood glucose.
steps.result: The patient may have diabetes mellitus.
steps.predictPrompt: Which hormone normally lowers glucose?

steps.reason: Insulin from the beta cells of the pancreas lowers blood glucose.
steps.result: Too little insulin explains the high glucose.

steps.reason: Glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine by osmosis.
steps.result: The patient passes large volumes of urine and becomes thirsty.

content.heading: Go deeper: The pituitary and the glands it controls
paragraphs: The pituitary has an anterior lobe that makes GH, TSH, ACTH and gonadotrophins, and a posterior lobe that stores ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe is controlled by releasing hormones, while the posterior lobe releases what it receives.

TSH controls the thyroid, ACTH controls the adrenal cortex and gonadotrophins control the gonads. That is why the pituitary is called the master gland, although it does not control the pancreas or the parathyroid.

Growth hormone promotes the growth of bones and muscles. Too little in childhood causes dwarfism, too much causes gigantism and excess in adulthood causes acromegaly. The same hormone therefore has different effects at different ages.
The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary by releasing hormones down a portal vein. That link is why the pituitary is an endocrine gland and not a nerve.
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drives labour and milk ejection. That release is triggered by stretch and suckling, not by a direct nerve to the gland.
That control is negative feedback. A low level of thyroid hormone raises TSH, and a high level suppresses it.
bullets: Anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, ACTH and gonadotrophins
TSH thyroid, ACTH adrenal cortex, gonadotrophins gonads
GH excess: dwarfism, gigantism or acromegaly by age

content.heading: Go deeper: Thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal glands
paragraphs: Thyroxine from the thyroid controls metabolic rate and is needed for normal growth. Its synthesis needs iodine, so iodine deficiency causes goitre. Cretinism is the effect of thyroxine shortage in infancy.

Parathormone from the parathyroid glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid raises blood calcium. Calcitonin from the thyroid does the opposite by lowering it. Those two hormones therefore oppose each other on calcium.

The adrenal cortex releases cortisol for stress and aldosterone for salt balance. The medulla releases adrenaline for flight. Cortisol helps the body cope with stress, aldosterone controls salt and adrenaline prepares for emergency.
Adrenaline prepares the body for flight by raising heart rate and blood glucose. That preparation is why a frightened person has a racing heart and dry mouth.
Adrenaline also dilates the bronchioles in the lungs. That widening helps a frightened or exercising person breathe faster, which is part of the flight response.
Cortisol also raises blood glucose during stress. That rise supplies extra fuel for muscles that may need it.
bullets: Thyroxine: metabolism; iodine shortage causes goitre
Parathormone raises calcium; calcitonin lowers it
Adrenal cortex: cortisol and aldosterone; medulla: adrenaline

content.heading: Go deeper: Pancreas and gonads
paragraphs: The pancreas lies behind the stomach and contains the islets of Langerhans. Beta cells release insulin, which lowers blood glucose, and alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it. Those two hormones therefore oppose each other on glucose.

The ovaries in the pelvis release oestrogen and progesterone, which control the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and female secondary sexual characteristics. The testes in the scrotum release testosterone, which controls sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics.
A disorder of a gland therefore has a specific sign. Diabetes mellitus is insulin shortage, cretinism is thyroxine shortage in infancy and dwarfism is growth hormone shortage in childhood.
Insulin also promotes the uptake of glucose by muscle and liver. That uptake is why a diabetic who lacks insulin cannot lower blood glucose even when food is eaten.
Testosterone also builds muscle and bone in puberty. That building is why a boy grows taller and stronger at the same time as his voice deepens.
Glucagon acts on the liver to convert glycogen to glucose. That conversion raises blood glucose between meals, which is why it is the fasting hormone.
bullets: Islets: beta insulin lowers glucose; alpha glucagon raises it
Ovaries: oestrogen and progesterone; testes: testosterone
Diabetes, cretinism and dwarfism are gland disorders

content.question: Why does adrenaline make the heart beat faster and the breathing rate rise during an emergency?
hints: Adrenaline is released from the adrenal medulla.
Muscles need more oxygen and glucose for action.
The response prepares the body for fight or flight.

lessons.title: Plant Hormones
lessons.objective: Describe the functions of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene, and relate phytohormones to plant responses and agricultural use.

content.heading: Plant hormones
paragraphs: Plants have no nerves, yet they still respond to light, gravity and touch. Chemical messengers called phytohormones coordinate their growth and development, and their effects depend on concentration and tissue.

content.heading: Auxins and tropisms
paragraphs: Auxins are made in the shoot tips, root tips and young leaves. They move from cell to cell and can spread sideways, so the side of a shoot that receives less light collects more auxin.

In a shoot, high auxin concentration makes cells elongate. The shaded side therefore grows faster than the lit side, and the shoot bends towards the light, which is positive phototropism. In a root, the same high concentration inhibits elongation, so the lower side grows more slowly and the root bends downwards, which is positive geotropism.
Auxin also causes apical dominance: the growing tip produces auxin that suppresses the growth of side buds. Removing the tip releases those buds and makes the plant bushier.
bullets: Auxin is made at shoot and root tips.
Uneven auxin makes shoots bend towards light and roots downwards.
Apical dominance suppresses side buds.
content.takeaway: Auxin redistributes growth; the darker side grows more.

check.question: A shoot bends towards light because auxin
options: Collects on the dark side and makes cells elongate
Collects on the light side and makes cells elongate
Is destroyed by light on both sides
check.why: Auxin gathers on the shaded side, where it makes cells elongate so that side grows faster and the shoot bends towards the light.

content.heading: Gibberellins and cytokinins
paragraphs: Gibberellins are growth promoters that stimulate stem elongation, seed germination and fruit development. During germination, gibberellin moves from the embryo to the aleurone layer of the seed and triggers the production of amylase, which digests stored starch into maltose for the growing seedling.

Cytokinins stimulate cell division and delay the ageing of leaves. They are produced mainly in root tips and move upwards in the xylem, and they also promote the growth of side shoots and the mobilisation of nutrients towards young tissues.

Flowering is also hormone-controlled: leaves in the right photoperiod produce a signal that travels to the shoot tip, where gibberellins and cytokinins promote flower buds. Growers use these hormones in agriculture. Gibberellin can make seedless grapes larger and break dormancy in some seeds, while cytokinins are used to keep cut leaves and flowers fresh for longer.
bullets: Gibberellins promote stem growth, germination and fruit development.
Cytokinins promote cell division and delay ageing.
Both are used in agriculture and horticulture.
content.takeaway: Gibberellins stretch and wake seeds; cytokinins divide and delay decay.

check.question: Which hormone breaks seed dormancy by triggering amylase production?
check.why: Gibberellin stimulates the aleurone layer to produce amylase, which digests stored starch for the embryo.

content.heading: Abscisic acid and ethylene
paragraphs: Abscisic acid is the main growth inhibitor. It builds up when a plant is short of water, closes the stomata to reduce water loss, and keeps seeds dormant until conditions improve. It also slows growth and helps leaves and fruits fall.

Ethylene is a gas that acts as a hormone. It speeds up the ripening of fruit, the ageing of flowers and the abscission of leaves and fruits. Because it is a gas, ethylene from one ripening fruit can trigger ripening in its neighbours.
Farmers and traders use these effects. Ethylene is used to ripen bananas and tomatoes uniformly, while chemicals that block ethylene slow ripening and reduce spoilage during storage and transport.
bullets: Abscisic acid closes stomata and maintains dormancy.
Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes abscission.
Both are used to control ripening and storage.
content.takeaway: ABA puts the brakes on; ethylene moves ripening along.

check.question: Which gas promotes the ripening of fruit?
check.why: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone that speeds up fruit ripening and the ageing of plant parts.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Auxin drives phototropism and apical dominance. Gibberellins promote stem growth and germination. Cytokinins promote cell division. Abscisic acid closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant, while ethylene ripens fruit and causes abscission.

content.problem: A farmer picks tomatoes while they are still green so they can survive transport. Explain how ethylene can be used, and why the storage room must be ventilated.

steps.reason: Ethylene speeds up the changes that soften and colour fruit.
steps.result: The green tomatoes ripen uniformly before sale.
steps.predictPrompt: Why ventilate the room?

steps.reason: Ethylene is a gas, so it spreads from fruit to fruit.
steps.result: One ripening fruit can trigger ripening in the whole batch.

steps.reason: Ventilation removes excess ethylene and slows over-ripening.
steps.result: Spoilage is reduced and the fruit lasts longer.

content.heading: Go deeper: Auxins and tropisms
paragraphs: Auxins promote shoot elongation but inhibit root elongation at high levels. They are made in shoot tips and move downward. That difference in sensitivity is why a shoot and a root respond oppositely to the same concentration.
In phototropism auxin collects on the shaded side of a shoot. That side elongates faster, so the shoot bends toward the light. The bending is therefore growth, not movement of the whole plant.
Auxin also promotes apical dominance. The apex suppresses the buds below it, so a plant grows upward rather than bushily. Removing the apex therefore releases the side buds.
A root that is laid on its side bends down by geotropism within hours. That bending is growth, so it cannot be reversed by turning the plant upright again.
A synthetic auxin is used as a weedkiller because it makes weeds grow too fast. That overdose of a natural hormone is lethal, which is why it can be selective.
Auxin also promotes root initiation in a cutting. That is why a hormone powder is applied to cuttings before they are planted.
bullets: Auxin promotes shoot growth but inhibits root growth at high levels
Auxin collects on the shaded side in phototropism
Apical dominance suppresses side buds

content.heading: Go deeper: Gibberellins and cytokinins
paragraphs: Gibberellins stimulate stem elongation, seed germination and fruit development. During germination, gibberellin moves from the embryo to the aleurone layer and triggers amylase, which digests stored starch into maltose for the seedling.
Cytokinins stimulate cell division and delay the ageing of leaves. That delay is called the stay-green effect, because a leaf treated with cytokinin remains green longer than an untreated leaf.

Flowering is hormone-controlled. Leaves in the right photoperiod produce a signal that travels to the shoot tip, where gibberellins and cytokinins promote flower buds. Growers use those hormones to make seedless grapes larger and to keep cut flowers fresh.
Cytokinins delay the ageing of a leaf because they maintain its protein. A leaf that is treated with them stays green while an untreated leaf yellows.
Gibberellin can make a stem grow without the cold that normally triggers it. That is why it is sprayed on grapes to make seedless berries larger.
Cytokinins also break apical dominance in some cases. That release lets a side bud grow into a shoot after the apex is removed.
bullets: Gibberellins: stem growth, germination, fruit development
Cytokinins: cell division and delayed ageing
Flowering needs a leaf signal to the shoot tip

content.heading: Go deeper: Abscisic acid and ethylene
paragraphs: Abscisic acid closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant. It is the hormone of stress, because it reduces water loss and suspends growth when conditions are unfavourable. A seed that contains it will not germinate in the mother plant.

Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes abscission. A ripening fruit makes ethylene, which ripens its neighbours, which is why one ripe fruit ripens a whole bowl. Abscission is the shedding of leaves, flowers and fruits.
Those two hormones oppose growth. Gibberellin and cytokinin promote it, while abscisic acid and ethylene bring it to a close. A plant therefore balances promotion and arrest throughout its life.
Abscisic acid also keeps buds dormant in winter. A bud that contains it will not open until the cold is past, which is why spring growth follows the winter.
Ethylene also promotes the ripening of a climacteric fruit. That is why a single ripe banana ripens its neighbours in a bowl.
Abscisic acid also keeps a bud dormant in winter. That dormancy prevents a warm spell in winter from forcing a bud to open.
bullets: ABA closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant
Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes abscission
Promotion and arrest are balanced throughout the life

content.question: Why does removing the shoot tip of a hedge make it grow bushier?
hints: The shoot tip is the main source of auxin.
Auxin suppresses the growth of side buds.
Removing the tip releases the side buds from apical dominance.

lessons.title: Homeostasis
lessons.objective: Explain homeostasis and negative feedback, describe temperature regulation, and explain how the kidneys control salt and water balance.

content.heading: Homeostasis
paragraphs: Your body keeps its temperature, water and salt within narrow limits even when the weather changes. This steady internal state is called homeostasis, and nerves and hormones do the adjusting.

content.heading: The principle of homeostasis
paragraphs: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a steady internal environment despite changes outside the body. It keeps temperature, blood glucose, water and salt within narrow limits so that enzymes and cells can work properly.

Control usually works by negative feedback. A receptor detects a change, a coordinator such as the hypothalamus compares it with the set point, and an effector produces a response that reverses the change. When temperature rises, for example, the body cools itself and the rise is corrected.

Negative feedback keeps conditions stable rather than perfectly constant. Values drift above and below the set point, and the response always pushes them back towards it. Positive feedback, which amplifies a change, is much rarer and is used in events such as childbirth.
bullets: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable.
Negative feedback reverses a change.
Receptor, coordinator and effector form the control loop.
content.takeaway: Negative feedback pushes conditions back to the set point.

check.question: Which sequence describes negative feedback?
options: Stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response that reverses the change
Stimulus → effector → coordinator → receptor → response that increases the change
Receptor → stimulus → effector → coordinator → no response
Coordinator → receptor → stimulus → effector → response that increases the change
check.why: A receptor detects the stimulus, a coordinator processes it, and an effector reverses the change.

content.heading: Temperature regulation
paragraphs: Humans are endotherms, so they generate heat by metabolism and keep a core temperature near 37 °C. The hypothalamus acts as the thermostat, comparing blood temperature with the set point and triggering responses.

When the body is too hot, blood vessels in the skin widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost by radiation. Sweat glands release sweat, and evaporation cools the skin. Behaviour also helps: we seek shade and wear lighter clothes.

When the body is too cold, skin blood vessels narrow (vasoconstriction) to keep heat in, shivering muscles generate heat, and hair erects to trap a layer of air. Thyroxine and adrenaline raise the metabolic rate. Fever, which is a raised set point, helps fight infection.
bullets: Hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat.
Heat loss: vasodilation and sweating.
Heat gain: vasoconstriction, shivering and hair erection.
content.takeaway: Too hot: radiate and sweat. Too cold: conserve and shiver.

check.question: Which response helps cool the body on a hot day?
check.why: Vasodilation brings more blood to the skin surface and sweating adds evaporative cooling.

content.heading: Salt and water regulation
paragraphs: The kidneys control water and salt balance by filtering the blood and reabsorbing what the body needs. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released from the posterior pituitary.

When the blood is too concentrated, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change and trigger ADH release. ADH makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood and the urine becomes small and concentrated.

When the blood is too dilute, ADH release falls and the kidneys excrete more dilute urine. Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex helps conserve sodium, and the sensation of thirst also drives water intake. This feedback keeps the tissue fluid at a suitable concentration.
bullets: Kidneys adjust water and salt reabsorption.
ADH increases water reabsorption and concentrates urine.
Aldosterone conserves sodium.
content.takeaway: ADH holds water back; aldosterone holds salt back.

check.question: A person sweats heavily and drinks little. What happens to ADH and urine?
options: ADH rises; urine becomes more concentrated
ADH rises; urine becomes more dilute
ADH falls; urine becomes more concentrated
ADH falls; urine becomes more dilute
check.why: Water loss concentrates the blood, so ADH rises and the kidneys reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Homeostasis uses negative feedback. The hypothalamus controls temperature, and the kidneys control water and salt with ADH and aldosterone. Vasodilation and sweating cool the body; vasoconstriction and shivering warm it.

content.problem: A worker spends a hot afternoon sweating heavily and drinks very little water. Explain how the body responds to conserve water.

steps.reason: Sweating removes water, so the blood becomes more concentrated.
steps.result: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are stimulated.
steps.predictPrompt: Which hormone is released?

steps.reason: The posterior pituitary releases more antidiuretic hormone.
