steps.result: The collecting ducts become more permeable to water.

steps.reason: More water is reabsorbed into the blood.
steps.result: Urine becomes small and concentrated, and thirst encourages drinking.

content.heading: Go deeper: Negative feedback and the set point
paragraphs: Homeostasis keeps the internal medium steady by negative feedback. A rise in a variable triggers a response that lowers it, and a fall triggers a response that raises it. The set point is the value around which the variable is held.
Temperature is the standard example. A fall in body temperature triggers shivering and vasoconstriction, which raise it, while a rise triggers sweating and vasodilation, which lower it.

Positive feedback does the opposite by amplifying the change. Oxytocin in labour is positive feedback, because each contraction releases more oxytocin until the baby is born. That is why labour accelerates rather than steadies.
A thermostat in a house is negative feedback. It turns the heater off when the set temperature is reached, just as the body turns sweating off when it cools.
Blood glucose is negative feedback. A rise releases insulin and a fall releases glucagon, so the variable is held around its set point.
A blood pressure that is too high stretches baroreceptors in the aorta. That stretch signals the medulla to dilate vessels and slow the heart.
bullets: Negative feedback opposes the change that started it
Set point: the value around which the variable is held
Positive feedback amplifies, as in labour

content.heading: Go deeper: Temperature regulation in detail
paragraphs: The hypothalamus detects body temperature and coordinates the responses. It is the thermostat of homeostasis, because it receives the signal from blood temperature and sends orders to muscle, skin and glands.

Shivering generates heat by rapid muscle contraction. Vasoconstriction conserves heat by narrowing skin vessels, while vasodilation loses heat by widening them. Sweating loses heat by evaporation, and panting loses it through the mouth and lungs.
A fever is a raised set point, not a failure of regulation. The body shivers to reach the higher point and sweats to leave it, which is why those signs appear in that order.
A hot-water bottle works by conduction to the skin. That external heat warms the blood without the body generating it, which is why it is used for a cold patient.
A baby has a large surface area for its mass. That is why it loses heat quickly and must be kept warm, even though it cannot shiver as effectively as an adult.
A hot-water bottle works by conduction to the skin. That external heat warms the blood without the body generating it.
bullets: The hypothalamus is the thermostat
Shivering makes heat; vasoconstriction conserves it
Fever is a raised set point

content.heading: Go deeper: Salt, water and ADH
paragraphs: ADH controls water reabsorption from the collecting duct. When the blood is concentrated, ADH makes the duct permeable, water returns to the blood and a small volume of concentrated urine is made. When the blood is dilute, ADH falls and dilute urine is made.
Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption from the distal tubule. More aldosterone means more sodium returned to the blood and more potassium lost. That trade keeps blood pressure and volume steady.
Osmoregulation therefore uses two hormones for two variables. ADH decides water, aldosterone decides sodium, and the kidney executes both decisions in the tubule.
A salt meal makes the blood more concentrated, so ADH rises and urine falls. That is why a salty meal makes a person thirsty.
Urine that is very dilute means ADH is low. That urine is made when the blood is dilute, which is why a person who drinks a lot passes a lot.
Aldosterone also controls potassium loss into the tubule. That trade means more sodium is kept at the cost of more potassium.
bullets: ADH controls water reabsorption in the collecting duct
Aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule
Two hormones, two variables, one kidney

content.question: Why does a person produce more urine after drinking a large volume of water?
hints: Drinking water dilutes the blood.
Osmoreceptors detect the dilution and reduce ADH release.
Less ADH makes the collecting ducts less permeable to water.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting the Distribution of Organisms
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain how abiotic, edaphic and biotic factors determine where organisms live in Nigeria.

content.heading: Factors Affecting the Distribution of Organisms
paragraphs: During the harmattan dry season in Kano, farmers notice that pond fish crowd into the deepest part of the dugout as the water shrinks and warms.

content.heading: Abiotic Factors: Temperature, Rainfall and Altitude
paragraphs: Temperature controls enzyme activity and survival. Organisms with thick fur, fat layers or behavioural changes such as basking favour a warmer microclimate when temperatures fall. In cold highland areas, only species that tolerate low temperatures can survive and reproduce.

Rainfall, humidity and wind also shape distribution. Plants in wet southern Nigeria differ from those in the dry north, while wind speed and direction spread seeds and drive evaporation. A rain gauge measures rainfall, a thermometer measures temperature, and a hygrometer measures humidity.

Altitude changes temperature and rainfall together. As height increases, air becomes colder and thinner, so mountain crops and animals differ from lowland species. Organisms adapt through small size, thick coats, or timing of breeding to match the short cool season.
bullets: Thermometer: measures temperature in degrees Celsius
Rain gauge: measures amount of rainfall collected
Hygrometer: measures relative humidity of air
content.takeaway: Temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and altitude limit survival and shape adaptation.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches an instrument to the factor it measures?
check.why: An anemometer measures wind speed; a rain gauge measures rainfall, a thermometer temperature and a hygrometer humidity.

content.heading: Water and Soil Factors: Salinity, Turbidity and pH
paragraphs: Salinity is the amount of dissolved salts in water. Freshwater fish die in salty sea water because osmosis removes water from their bodies. Estuaries where rivers meet the sea have changing salinity, so only tolerant species thrive there.

Turbidity measures how cloudy water is due to suspended particles. A Secchi disc lowered into water shows how far light penetrates, which affects photosynthesis by algae and eelgrass. Very turbid water in polluted rivers limits fish that need clear water.

Soil, or edaphic factors, include texture, water retention, air space, humus and pH. Sandy soil drains quickly and suits cassava, while clay soil holds water and suits rice. Soil pH affects nutrient availability, so acidic soil may favour pineapple while alkaline soil suits other crops.
bullets: Secchi disc: measures turbidity by depth of disappearance
pH meter: measures acidity or alkalinity of water and soil
Soil thermometer: measures temperature at root depth
content.takeaway: Salinity, turbidity, pH and soil texture control which species survive in water and on land.

check.question: A Secchi disc is used to measure what?
check.why: A Secchi disc measures turbidity by how deep it remains visible in water.

content.heading: Biotic Factors and Human Activities
paragraphs: Biotic factors are living influences such as food, predators, disease and competition. A species may be absent from an area if its food is scarce or its predators too many. Competition removes resources, so the weaker species may move away or decline in number.

Human activities now shift distributions faster than climate alone. Farming, dams, urbanisation, pollution and deforestation destroy habitats and block movement. Irrigated rice farms near dams in northern Nigeria attract fish and water birds to new wetlands, while Lake Chad shrinking forces species into smaller refuges.

During harmattan, dry winds and dust reduce water for plants and animals, so habitats contract. Pollution from factories and oil spills poisons water, while new roads and cities fragment forests. Conservation, reforestation and planned dams help species keep suitable habitat.
bullets: Food and disease: affect population size and spread
Predation and competition: remove or reduce a species locally
Dams and farms: create wetlands but flood old habitats
content.takeaway: Biotic pressures and human change move species, so conservation must protect food, habitat and movement routes.

check.question: Which pair lists a biotic factor and a human activity?
check.why: Predation is biotic and dam building is human; the other pairs are abiotic factors.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, first decide whether the factor is abiotic, edaphic or biotic. Remember: temperature and rainfall are abiotic, soil texture is edaphic, and predation or competition is biotic.

content.problem: A Kano farmer finds fewer fish near the dam where water is very turbid, though algae feed is plentiful. What is limiting, and what should he test?

steps.operation: Identify the limiting factor from the scenario
steps.reason: Turbid water reduces light for algae and gills
steps.result: Turbidity, not food, is the main limit
steps.predictPrompt: What would a Secchi disc show here?

steps.reason: Secchi disc measures water clarity directly
steps.result: Lower Secchi disc depth means higher turbidity
steps.predictPrompt: What would you do if the depth is very shallow?

steps.operation: Suggest control of the human cause
steps.reason: Runoff and erosion raise turbidity in dams
steps.result: Plant grass strips and reduce soil erosion
steps.predictPrompt: How would clearer water help fish return?

content.heading: Go deeper: Abiotic factors and the instruments that measure them
paragraphs: Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions that decide where an organism can live. Temperature, rainfall, wind, altitude, salinity, turbidity, pH and soil texture are all abiotic. A rain gauge measures rainfall, a thermometer temperature, an anemometer wind and a hygrometer humidity.

Temperature decides which enzymes work and therefore which species survive. A desert at 45 degrees excludes most fish, while a highland at 10 degrees excludes most cacti. The factor is therefore a filter, not a food.
Wind moves seeds and water, so it redistributes organisms as well as conditions. A coastal plant that needs salt spray can therefore be carried inland by a storm, which is how its range shifts.
Altitude also matters because it lowers temperature with height. A highland that is cool can therefore carry a different flora from a lowland with the same rainfall.
A Secchi disc is lowered until it disappears. The depth at which it vanishes is the measure of turbidity, so the reading is inverse: shallower means more cloudy.
A hygrometer measures humidity, not rainfall. That distinction is why a hygrometer and a rain gauge cannot be interchanged in a question.
bullets: Rain gauge, thermometer, anemometer and hygrometer measure abiotic factors
Temperature filters species by enzyme limits
Wind redistributes seeds and water

content.heading: Go deeper: Water and soil factors
paragraphs: Salinity decides which fish can live in water. A freshwater fish cannot survive in the sea because its cells would lose water to the saltier water. A tilapia therefore lives in fresh water, not in the sea.
Turbidity measures how cloudy water is, and a Secchi disc measures it by how deep it remains visible. Clear water lets light reach submerged plants, while turbid water starves them of light.

Soil pH decides which nutrients are available. An acid soil fixes phosphorus, so a plant that needs it cannot grow there however much is present in total. Texture decides the water that the soil can hold.
A Secchi disc that disappears quickly means turbid water. That turbidity can be caused by silt after rain, so a river may become too cloudy for its plants after a storm.
A soil probe that measures moisture, texture and nutrients was once taught. Modern Ecology measures each factor with its own instrument, so a single probe is not a real device.
A soil probe that measures moisture, texture and nutrients was once taught. Modern Ecology measures each factor with its own instrument.
bullets: Salinity filters fish by water loss
Turbidity by Secchi disc controls light for plants
Soil pH fixes nutrients; texture holds water

content.heading: Go deeper: Biotic factors and human activities
paragraphs: Biotic factors are living conditions: predation, parasitism, competition and disease. A predator can remove a herbivore and allow plants to recover, which is why removing a predator can change a whole habitat.

Human activities are a separate class because they are deliberate. Dams create wetlands, irrigation creates water where there was none and deforestation removes the habitat itself. Each activity redistributes organisms by changing their conditions.

A distribution question must therefore name the kind of factor. Rain gauge and thermometer are abiotic, samplings of predators are biotic and dams are human. That naming is the first step of any answer.
A predator that is removed can allow its prey to multiply. That multiplication can then strip the plants, which is why removing a predator can change a whole habitat.
Irrigated rice at a dam creates shallow wetlands. Those wetlands attract fish and water birds that would not otherwise live there, so the dam redistributes them.
bullets: Predation, parasitism, competition and disease are biotic
Dams, irrigation and deforestation are human activities
Name the kind of factor first in any answer

content.question: Lake Chad is shrinking. Predict two abiotic and two biotic changes that will affect fish and water birds.
hints: Think rainfall and salinity
Think food and predation
Think human fishing and farming

lessons.title: Species Interactions
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to classify species interactions and predict their effects on populations.

content.heading: Species Interactions
paragraphs: At a Lagos market, a woman sells mistletoe growing on mango trees while her goat chews Loranthus leaves, and nearby a tapeworm treatment is advertised for livestock.

content.heading: Symbiosis: Mutualism, Commensalism and Parasitism
paragraphs: Symbiosis is a close living association between two species. In mutualism both partners benefit, as in lichen where fungus and algae live together. In commensalism one benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

Parasitism is when one organism, the parasite, benefits at the host's expense. A tapeworm inside a human intestine absorbs digested food, while head lice feed on blood and skin. Loranthus growing on a mango is a plant parasite that draws water and food from its host.

The key test is who gains and who loses. If both gain, it is mutualism; if only one gains and the other is unaffected, it is commensalism. If one gains and the other loses, it is parasitism, often with little or no benefit to the host.
bullets: Lichen: fungus and algae both gain
Barnacle on whale: barnacle gains, whale unaffected
Tapeworm in humans: worm gains, human loses
content.takeaway: Mutualism helps both, commensalism helps one only, and parasitism harms the host.

check.question: Loranthus grows on a mango tree and draws water and food from it. This is
check.why: Loranthus gains water and food while the mango loses, so the interaction is parasitism.

content.heading: Predation, Competition, Cooperation and Amensalism
paragraphs: Predation is when one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey. A leopard preying on grasscutters and a hawk catching chicks are examples. Predators check prey numbers and keep habitats in balance.

Competition is struggle for food, space or mates. Intra-specific competition is between members of the same species, while inter-specific competition is between different species. Both can reduce growth or push the weaker competitor out of the area.

Saprophytism is feeding on dead and decaying matter, as fungi and bacteria do. Cooperation is working together for a shared benefit, as when ants carry food to the nest and defend the colony together. Amensalism is when one is harmed and the other is unaffected, as Penicillium kills bacteria but gains nothing.
bullets: Saprophytes: fungi digest dead leaves and wood
Penicillium and bacteria: bacteria harmed, fungus unaffected
Hawks and mice: predator gains, prey loses
content.takeaway: Predation and competition reduce numbers, saprophytism recycles matter, and amensalism harms one side only.

check.question: Penicillium kills bacteria in a dish but gains no food from them. This is
check.why: The bacteria are harmed while Penicillium is unaffected, which is amensalism.

content.heading: Classifying Unseen Examples in Exams
paragraphs: Read the scenario and ask who benefits and who is harmed. First check for feeding on dead matter, which points to saprophytism. Then check for killing and eating, which is predation, and for two species both losing from shared resources, which is competition.
Use the same test for symbiotic pairs. Lichen shows both partners gaining, so it is mutualism. A barnacle on a whale gains transport and food while the whale is unaffected, so it is commensalism.

Watch for amensalism and cooperation, which are often confused with other types. Amensalism harms one species while the other gains nothing, as with Penicillium and bacteria. Cooperation means individuals work together for a shared benefit, as when wolves hunt in a pack.
bullets: Both gain: mutualism
One gains, other unaffected: commensalism
One gains, other loses: parasitism or predation
content.takeaway: Ask who benefits, who is harmed, and whether feeding is on dead matter to classify correctly.

check.question: A barnacle on a whale, which gains transport, is
check.why: The barnacle gains while the whale is unaffected, which is commensalism.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If both organisms gain, choose mutualism; if one gains and the other is unaffected, choose commensalism. Parasitism always harms the host, so look for damage in the scenario carefully.

content.problem: Near a Lagos lagoon, a student sees lichen on a rock, a barnacle on a whale, and an orchid on a mango tree. Classify each pair.

steps.operation: Identify who benefits in each pair
steps.reason: Lichen both gain, barnacle gains only, orchid gains only
steps.result: Lichen mutualism, others commensalism
steps.predictPrompt: What extra clue would show parasitism?

steps.operation: Check if any organism is harmed
steps.reason: No harm to rock, whale or tree
steps.result: Commensalism fits both single-benefit pairs
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test for harm?

steps.reason: Both partners gain only in lichen
steps.result: Lichen mutualism, barnacle and orchid commensalism
steps.predictPrompt: Why is orchid not parasitism?

content.heading: Go deeper: Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism
paragraphs: Mutualism benefits both partners. A flower and its pollinator both gain, a fungus and an alga in a lichen both gain and mycorrhizae benefit plant and fungus together. The test is whether both gain.

Commensalism benefits one partner and leaves the other unchanged. An orchid on a tree gains support without harming the tree. The test is therefore gain for one and neither gain nor loss for the other.
Parasitism benefits one partner at the expense of the other. Loranthus on a mango tree gains water and food while the mango loses. The test is gain for one and loss for the other.
A mycorrhiza is mutualism underground. The fungus supplies water and minerals, and the plant supplies sugars, so both partners grow better together than apart.
An ant that protects a plant in return for nectar is mutualism. The plant gains protection and the ant gains food, so both partners benefit.
Lichen is mutualism between a fungus and an alga. The fungus supplies shelter and the alga supplies food, so the pair can live where neither could alone.
bullets: Mutualism: both gain
Commensalism: one gains, the other unchanged
Parasitism: one gains, the other loses

content.heading: Go deeper: Predation, competition and amensalism
paragraphs: Predation benefits the predator and harms the prey. A hawk and a mouse are predation, because one gains food and the other is eaten. Competition harms both, because both lose resources they could have used.

Intra-specific competition is between members of the same species, whose needs are identical. Inter-specific competition is between different species that share a resource. Millet and groundnut sown together are inter-specific.
Amensalism harms one partner and leaves the other unchanged. Penicillium kills bacteria in a dish but gains no food from them. That one-sided harm with no gain is the mark of amensalism.
Competition can be intra-specific between goats of the same species or inter-specific between goats and sheep. The test is whether the competitors are the same species.
A walnut tree releases juglone that stops other plants from growing under it. That chemicals holds the ground for the walnut, which is amensalism by chemistry.
A barnacle on a whale is commensalism. The barnacle gains transport and the whale is not harmed by the small weight.
bullets: Predation: one gains, one is eaten
Intra-specific: same species; inter-specific: different species
Amensalism: one harmed, the other unchanged

content.heading: Go deeper: How to classify an unseen example
paragraphs: Read the example for who gains and who loses. If both gain, name mutualism; if one gains and the other is unchanged, name commensalism; if one gains and the other loses, name parasitism.

If one is eaten, name predation; if both lose resources they share, name competition; if one is harmed and the other is unaffected, name amensalism. Saprophytism is separate because the food is dead matter, not a living partner.
The host rule helps. A parasite feeds on a living host, a saprophyte feeds on dead matter and a predator kills its prey. Naming the food source therefore classifies the interaction.
A hermit crab that uses a shell after the snail has died is commensalism. The crab gains a house and the snail gains nothing, because the snail is already dead.
The orchid rule is a useful check. If the support plant is unchanged, the interaction is commensalism, however large the orchid may be.
A moth that pollinates a flower while drinking its nectar is mutualism. The moth gains food and the flower gains pollination, so both benefit.
bullets: Both gain: mutualism; one gains: commensalism or parasitism
Eaten: predation; both lose resources: competition
Living host: parasite; dead matter: saprophyte

content.question: A hawk catches a mouse, a fungus grows on dead wood, and ants carry food together. Name each interaction and give one reason.
hints: Dead wood means saprophytism
Think who benefits from tick removal
No harm means commensalism or cooperation

lessons.title: Food Chains, Webs and Trophic Levels
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain energy flow, food chains, food webs and trophic levels in Nigerian ecosystems.

content.heading: Food Chains, Webs and Trophic Levels
paragraphs: At a fish market in Calabar, smoked tilapia, grasscutter meat and garri are sold together, but in nature each of these foods comes from a different level of a food chain.

content.heading: Producers, Consumers and Decomposers
paragraphs: Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are producers because they make food by photosynthesis. They form the first trophic level and support all other life. Herbivores such as grasscutters and tilapia eat producers and form the second trophic level.

Carnivores eat other animals and occupy higher levels. Primary carnivores eat herbivores, while secondary carnivores eat primary carnivores. Omnivores eat both plants and animals, as humans and crows do, so they can feed at more than one level.

Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and waste. They release nutrients back into soil and water for producers to use. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not be recycled for new growth.
bullets: Trophic level 1: producers make food
Trophic level 2: herbivores eat producers
Top carnivores: apex predators have few enemies
content.takeaway: Producers feed herbivores, herbivores feed carnivores, and decomposers recycle nutrients to producers.

check.question: In a food chain, the first trophic level is
check.why: Producers such as green plants make food by photosynthesis and form the first trophic level.

content.heading: Food Chains in Aquatic and Land Habitats
paragraphs: A food chain shows the flow of energy from one organism to the next. In water, algae are eaten by tilapia, and tilapia are eaten by the heron. Each arrow points from food to consumer, showing the direction of energy flow.

On land, grass is eaten by the grasscutter, which is eaten by the leopard. A longer chain might start with leaves, go to a caterpillar, then to a small bird, and finally to a hawk. Chains are rarely long because energy is lost at each step.

Most organisms feed on more than one type of food, so chains link together into food webs. A web shows alternative feeding routes and helps communities survive when one food source fails. Exams often test whether you can draw arrows from food to eater.
bullets: Algae to tilapia to heron: aquatic chain
Grass to grasscutter to leopard: land chain
Arrow direction: from food to consumer
content.takeaway: Food chains are straight lines of energy flow, while food webs link many chains together.

check.question: In a food chain diagram, arrows point
check.why: Arrows show energy flow from food to consumer, so they point from food to eater.

content.heading: Energy Loss, Pyramids and Decomposers
paragraphs: At each trophic level, most energy is lost as heat, movement and waste. Only about 5 to 20 per cent passes, often around ten per cent, a pattern called the ten percent law. This is why there are many producers but few top carnivores.

Pyramids show this balance. A pyramid of numbers has many producers and fewer consumers at each higher level. A pyramid of biomass shows total mass, which is usually large for producers and small for large carnivores, though aquatic pyramids can look different.

Decomposers close the cycle by breaking down dead producers and consumers. Their enzymes release minerals that roots and algae absorb again. Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked in dead matter and producers would soon run out of food.
bullets: Ten percent law: little energy reaches top levels
Pyramid of numbers: many producers, few predators
Pyramid of biomass: total mass falls with level
content.takeaway: Energy falls to about ten percent per level, so pyramids narrow and decomposers recycle nutrients.

check.question: According to the ten percent law, about how much energy passes to the next level?
check.why: Only about ten percent of energy passes to the next trophic level, so pyramids narrow quickly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Draw arrows from food to eater, never the reverse. Remember the ten percent law explains why chains are short and why pyramids of numbers are broad at the base.

content.problem: A Niger Delta pond has algae, tilapia, and a heron. The pond also has a small snake that eats fish. Build the chain and web.

steps.reason: Algae make food, tilapia eat algae, heron eats tilapia
steps.result: Chain algae to tilapia to heron
steps.predictPrompt: What if snake adds another route?

steps.reason: Snake also eats fish, so fish have two predators
steps.result: Web shows fish eaten by heron and snake
steps.predictPrompt: How does web help ecosystem?

steps.reason: Energy drops at each level
steps.result: Pyramid narrows toward heron and snake
steps.predictPrompt: Why are there fewer herons than tilapia?

content.heading: Go deeper: Producers, consumers and decomposers
paragraphs: Producers make their own food by photosynthesis. They are the first trophic level and supply energy to the whole web. A grass, a tree and an alga are all producers.

Consumers take ready-made food. Herbivores eat producers and are primary consumers, primary carnivores eat herbivores and secondary carnivores eat primary carnivores. Omnivores eat both plants and animals, so they can feed at more than one level.

Decomposers break down dead matter and release nutrients. Fungi and bacteria are the main decomposers, so they return what producers took from the soil. Without them the web would starve for nutrients.
An omnivore such as a crow eats both plants and animals. That flexibility lets it feed at more than one trophic level, which is why it is hard to place in a single chain.
A detritivore such as an earthworm eats dead matter but is not a decomposer. It breaks matter into smaller pieces, while bacteria and fungi complete the decomposition.
An apex predator has no natural enemy in the web. That is why its numbers are limited by food rather than by predation.
bullets: Producers are the first trophic level
Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores are consumers
Decomposers return nutrients to the soil

content.heading: Go deeper: Food chains and food webs
paragraphs: A food chain shows one feeding route from producer to top predator. A grass to grasshopper to frog to hawk chain is a chain because it follows one route. An arrow points from food to eater in every link.
A food web links many chains together. A hawk that eats frogs, snakes and birds sits in three chains at once. That web shows alternative routes, so a community can survive when one food fails.
Drawing the web therefore tests understanding. An arrow that points from eater to food is wrong, however neatly it is drawn. The direction is always food to eater.
A chain that ends in a top predator shows the fate of energy in that route. A web shows how many routes share the same energy, which is why it is more complete.
A carrion feeder such as a vulture is a decomposer in the web. It removes dead matter and returns nutrients, so it links the web to the soil.
bullets: A chain follows one feeding route
A web links many chains with alternative routes
Arrows point from food to eater

content.heading: Go deeper: Energy loss, pyramids and decomposers
paragraphs: Only about 5 to 20 per cent of energy passes to the next trophic level, often around ten per cent. The rest is lost as heat, waste or movement. That is the ten percent law, and it is a range rather than a constant.

Pyramids show that loss. A pyramid of numbers has many producers and fewer consumers above them, while a pyramid of biomass shows total mass falling with level. Both narrow because energy is lost at each step.

Decomposers recycle nutrients but not energy. Energy that is lost as heat cannot be reused, while nutrients released by decay can be taken up again by producers. That is why a web needs both producers and decomposers.
A pyramid of energy is the most reliable because it is measured as flow. A pyramid of biomass can invert in a pond, where a small crop supports a larger standing mass.
The ten percent law is therefore a rule of thumb. A productive pond may pass more than ten percent, while a woody plant may pass less, which is why the range matters.
bullets: Only 5 to 20 per cent passes to the next level
Pyramids narrow because energy is lost
Nutrients recycle; energy does not

content.question: Explain why a food web is more stable than a single food chain in a Nigerian forest.
hints: Think alternative food sources
Think predators and prey
Think what happens when one species declines

lessons.title: Carbon, Water and Nitrogen Cycles
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe the carbon, water and nitrogen cycles and explain human effects on them.

content.heading: Carbon, Water and Nitrogen Cycles
paragraphs: In a rice farm near Kano, children watch rain fill the dam, plants grow green, and cattle return dung to the soil, all showing water, carbon and nitrogen moving in cycles.

content.heading: The Carbon Cycle and Global Warming
paragraphs: Plants take in carbon dioxide and use it in photosynthesis to make glucose. Animals eat plants and release carbon dioxide during respiration. Respiration and decomposition return carbon dioxide to the air, keeping a balance of carbon and oxygen.

Burning wood, coal and petrol, called combustion, also releases carbon dioxide. Deforestation and fossil fuel use raise carbon dioxide faster than plants can absorb it. Extra carbon dioxide traps heat in the air, causing global warming and changing rainfall patterns.

The ocean is a large carbon sink because carbon dioxide dissolves in surface water. Some carbon is used by shell-forming organisms and sinks as carbonate. Some carbon is stored in limestone and fossil fuels for millions of years, while protecting forests and reducing burning helps keep the balance stable.
bullets: Photosynthesis: uses carbon dioxide, releases oxygen
Respiration and combustion: release carbon dioxide
Ocean sink: dissolves carbon dioxide and stores carbonate
content.takeaway: Photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and decomposition cycle carbon, while oceans store some long term.

check.question: Which processes release carbon dioxide into the air?
check.why: Respiration, combustion and decomposition return carbon dioxide to the air, while photosynthesis uses it.

content.heading: The Water Cycle and Climate
paragraphs: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and rivers under the sun. Plants also release water vapour through transpiration from their leaves. Together, evaporation and transpiration lift water into the air as an invisible vapour.

As warm air rises, vapour cools and condenses into clouds. Water falls as precipitation, such as rain, which is common in southern Nigeria. Some rain soaks into soil as groundwater, while the rest runs off the surface into streams and rivers.

The cycle moves water continuously, so the amount on Earth stays almost constant. Deforestation reduces transpiration and runoff patterns, which can make rainfall less regular. The water cycle therefore affects climate, farming and the availability of clean water, and it carries dissolved nitrates, phosphates and other nutrients through soil and rivers, linking it to the nutrient cycles.
bullets: Evaporation and transpiration: lift water to air
Condensation and precipitation: form clouds and rain
Runoff and groundwater: move water to rivers and wells
content.takeaway: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and groundwater move water through the environment.

check.question: Transpiration is the process by which plants
check.why: Transpiration releases water vapour from leaves into the air, part of the water cycle.

content.heading: The Nitrogen Cycle and Legume Crops
paragraphs: Plants need nitrogen to make proteins, but most cannot use nitrogen gas from air. Fixation converts nitrogen gas into usable compounds. Rhizobium bacteria in legume roots, free-living Azotobacter, and lightning all fix nitrogen for crops.

Nitrification turns ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates, which plants absorb easily. Nitrosomonas acts first, then Nitrobacter completes the change. Animal waste and urea break down to ammonium, feeding nitrification and keeping nitrogen available in soil.

Denitrification returns nitrates to nitrogen gas and completes the cycle. Pseudomonas bacteria carry out denitrification in waterlogged, airless soil. Farmers use leguminous crops such as groundnut and cowpea in rotation to restore nitrogen and reduce fertiliser needs.
bullets: Fixation: Rhizobium, Azotobacter and lightning fix nitrogen
Nitrification: Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter make nitrates
Denitrification: Pseudomonas returns nitrogen gas to air
content.takeaway: Fixation, nitrification and denitrification move nitrogen between air, soil and plants for protein making.

check.question: In nitrification, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter convert ammonium to
check.why: Nitrosomonas and then Nitrobacter convert ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates for plant uptake.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For nitrogen questions, remember the order: fixation, then nitrification by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter, then plant uptake, and finally denitrification by Pseudomonas back to nitrogen gas in the air for exam.

content.problem: A Kano farmer grows millet alone every year and yields fall. He adds cowpea in rotation and returns cattle waste. Explain the change using the nitrogen cycle.

steps.reason: Continuous millet removes nitrates without replacement
steps.result: Soil nitrogen falls and yields drop
steps.predictPrompt: What would fixation add?

steps.reason: Legume roots fix nitrogen gas into soil
steps.result: More nitrates form through nitrification
steps.predictPrompt: What role do manure bacteria play?

steps.reason: Waste breaks down to ammonium then nitrates
steps.result: Plants absorb nitrates and grow better
steps.predictPrompt: How does denitrification complete the cycle?

content.heading: Go deeper: The carbon cycle and global warming
paragraphs: Carbon moves as carbon dioxide in the air and as glucose in organisms. Photosynthesis takes it in, respiration and decomposition return it and combustion releases it from fossil fuels. That loop keeps carbon moving between air, life and soil.

Deforestation and fossil fuel use raise carbon dioxide faster than plants can absorb it. Extra carbon dioxide traps heat in the air, causing global warming and changing rainfall. That warming is therefore a carbon cycle problem.

The ocean is a large carbon sink because carbon dioxide dissolves in surface water. Some carbon is used by shell-forming organisms and sinks as carbonate, while some is stored in limestone and fossil fuels for millions of years.
Protecting forests and reducing burning therefore help the carbon balance. Those actions slow the rate at which carbon dioxide rises faster than plants can absorb it.
The carbon stored in fossil fuels was fixed by plants millions of years ago. Burning it therefore releases ancient carbon that the modern cycle did not plan for.
bullets: Photosynthesis in, respiration and combustion out
Extra carbon dioxide traps heat and changes rainfall
Ocean dissolves carbon dioxide and stores carbonate

content.heading: Go deeper: The water cycle and climate
paragraphs: Water evaporates from seas and leaves, condenses into clouds and falls as rain. It then runs into rivers and groundwater or is taken up by plants and transpired. That loop links the land to the sea every year.
Transpiration returns water to the air from leaves, so a forest recycles rain as well as receiving it. A deforested land therefore loses both the interception of rain and its return to the air.
Water also carries dissolved nitrates, phosphates and other nutrients through soil and rivers. The water cycle therefore links to the nutrient cycles as well as to climate.
A reservoir therefore changes the cycle by storing water that would have run to the sea. That storage creates a wetland that can attract fish and birds.
A cloud that forms over a forest may rain on the same forest. That recycling is why deforestation reduces rainfall downwind as well as on the cleared land.
A reservoir therefore changes the cycle by storing water that would have run to the sea. That storage creates a wetland that can attract fish and birds.
bullets: Evaporation, condensation and precipitation move water in a loop
Forests intercept rain and return it by transpiration
Water carries nutrients through soil and rivers

content.heading: Go deeper: The nitrogen cycle and legume crops
paragraphs: Nitrogen moves as nitrogen gas in the air, as ammonia and nitrate in soil and as protein in organisms. Fixation converts nitrogen gas to ammonia, nitrification converts ammonia to nitrate and denitrification returns nitrate to nitrogen gas.

Nitrosomonas nitrifies ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter completes it to nitrate, which plants absorb easily. Pseudomonas denitrifies nitrate back to nitrogen gas in waterlogged, airless soil. Each bacterium has its own step.

Farmers use leguminous crops such as groundnut and cowpea in rotation to restore nitrogen. Their root nodules fix nitrogen, so the crop enriches the soil for the next one and reduces fertiliser needs.
A legume that fixes nitrogen for itself also leaves nitrogen for the next crop. That is why groundnut is a good predecessor for maize in a rotation.
Denitrification needs airless, waterlogged soil. That is why a flooded paddy loses nitrogen as gas, while a dry soil keeps it as nitrate.
The nodules on a legume root contain bacteria that fix nitrogen. Those bacteria gain food from the plant, so the relationship is mutualism underground.
bullets: Fixation, nitrification, uptake, denitrification in order
Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter make nitrate
Legumes fix nitrogen for the next crop

content.question: How would deforestation and burning in northern Nigeria change the carbon and water cycles together?
hints: Think carbon dioxide release
Think transpiration and rainfall
Think soil erosion and runoff

lessons.title: Aquatic Habitats
lessons.objective: Learners will describe aquatic adaptations in Nigerian ponds, rivers and mangroves.

content.heading: Aquatic Habitats
paragraphs: A student in Awka watches tilapia jump near water lilies in a village pond during the rains and wonders where fish and insects hide when the water rises.

content.heading: Ponds and Lakes: Still Water Communities
paragraphs: Ponds and lakes hold stagnant water that warms easily under the Nigerian sun. Sunlight penetrates only a few metres, so most life stays near the surface. Stagnant conditions also lower dissolved oxygen, especially in deep or polluted water.

Tiny phytoplankton drift near the surface and multiply during the rainy season. Water lilies root in muddy beds while their broad leaves shade the water below. Tilapia feed on plankton, plants and small invertebrates in these warm layers.

Frogs, snails, mosquito larvae and dragonfly nymphs complete the food web in ponds. Farmers often dig ponds near Awka and Onitsha to breed tilapia for food. Seasonal flooding connects small ponds to streams, bringing in nutrients and new colonists.
bullets: Phytoplankton form the base of the food chain in ponds and lakes.
Water lilies provide food and shelter but can trap debris in still water.
Tilapia tolerate warm, low-oxygen water better than many other fish.
content.takeaway: Still ponds are layered systems where plankton, plants and tilapia depend on light and oxygen.

check.question: What forms the food base in ponds?
check.why: Plankton photosynthesise food for small animals.

content.heading: Streams and Rivers: Life in Flowing Water
paragraphs: Streams and rivers carry flowing water that is usually well mixed and rich in dissolved oxygen. Riffles, where water splashes over stones, add oxygen rapidly as currents tumble. Rapid flow also prevents stagnant warming and algal scum common in ponds.

In shallow riffles, insect larvae cling to smooth stones to avoid being swept downstream. Fish such as catfish and tilapia hunt insects, leaves and fallen fruits carried by the current. Freshwater crabs shelter under rocks and scavenge dead organisms.

During the rainy season, rivers flood nearby lowlands and deposit fertile mud. Market gardeners in Ibadan use flood plains to grow yams and vegetables. Fishermen cast nets in calm pools where oxygen remains high and food is plentiful.
bullets: Flowing water supplies a steady supply of dissolved oxygen for animals.
Riffles aerate water and support oxygen-loving insect larvae and fish.
Flood plains enrich soil and provide breeding grounds for fish.
content.takeaway: Flowing rivers stay oxygen rich, so riffles favour insects and fish that need fresh water.

check.question: Why do larvae live in riffles?
check.why: Riffles add oxygen needed by larvae.

content.heading: Seashores and Mangrove Swamps
paragraphs: Seashores along the Lagos coast experience daily tides that alternately flood and expose sand and mud. Intertidal zones endure strong waves, changing salinity and drying in the hot sun. Animals here must tolerate salty water and survive without it for hours.

Mangrove swamps in the Niger Delta grow in soft, oxygen-poor mud under brackish water. Red mangroves send arching prop roots to support trees and trap sediments near the water. Black mangroves push cone-like pneumatophores upward to take in air at low tide.

Fiddler crabs, snails and juvenile fish use mangrove roots as shelter and feeding grounds. Salt tolerance helps these animals pump out excess salt and retain fresh water. Oyster beds and mudskippers also prosper in the damp, sheltered swamp margins.
bullets: Tides shape seashore life by sorting animals into wet and dry zones.
Prop roots support mangroves while pneumatophores allow roots to breathe.
Crabs and fish survive salinity changes through specialised salt control.
content.takeaway: Tides and salty mud demand roots that breathe and animals that control salt.

check.question: What do pneumatophores do?
check.why: They rise from mud to absorb air.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, link each habitat to its water movement and oxygen level. Remember: still ponds favour plankton, riffles favour insects, and mangroves favour salt control. Highlight these contrasts for quick revision.

content.problem: A Delta fisherman catches crabs in mangrove roots at low tide. Explain why.

steps.reason: Mud and roots exposed
steps.result: Crabs hide and feed

steps.reason: Fish enter with seawater
steps.result: Fish feed near roots

steps.reason: Salt and oxygen needs differ
steps.result: Fishers follow tide

content.heading: Go deeper: Ponds and lakes as communities
paragraphs: A pond is a small, shallow body of still water. Its community includes algae, zooplankton, fish and insects, all linked by feeding. The pond therefore has producers, consumers and decomposers like any other habitat.

A lake is larger and deeper, with a littoral zone at the edge and a profundal zone below. That depth creates darkness and cold at the bottom, so the community changes with depth. Tilapia tolerate warm, low-oxygen water better than many other fish.
Temperature stratifies a lake in summer. The surface is warm and the depths are cold, so fish move between them to feed and to rest. That movement is a daily migration within one habitat.
The littoral zone holds rooted plants that oxygenate the water. That oxygen is why fish gather near the edge in the morning, when the night's respiration has lowered it elsewhere.
The deep zone of a lake is cold and dark in summer. Fish that need cold water therefore move down by day and up by night, which is a daily migration.
A pond that is stocked with fish must not be overstocked. Too many fish will eat the algae and then starve, which shows that a pond has a carrying capacity.
bullets: A pond has producers, consumers and decomposers
A lake has littoral and profundal zones
Tilapia tolerate warm, low-oxygen water

content.heading: Go deeper: Streams and the current that shapes them
paragraphs: A stream flows, so its community is shaped by current. Algae and mosses hold to stones, while fish and insects hide among them. That holding is an adaptation to a moving habitat.
Oxygen is higher in a fast stream because the water is aerated. That is why a trout lives in a cold stream and not in a warm pond. Current therefore decides the oxygen supply.
A stream also carries nutrients downstream. That carrying links it to the pond it feeds, so the two habitats are not separate communities.
A stream that is polluted loses its oxygen downstream. That is why a sewage outfall kills fish below the outfall but not above it.
A dam across a stream creates a still pond above it. That pond can silt up, so the stream below loses the current that aerated it.
A stream that is dammed for water becomes a pond. That pond can silt up, so the stream below loses the current that aerated it.
bullets: Current holds algae and mosses to stones
Fast water is more oxygenated
Streams feed ponds, so the habitats are linked

content.heading: Go deeper: Seashores, mangroves and the tide
paragraphs: A seashore is exposed and submerged by the tide in turn. Its community must survive drying and flooding, so it is zoned by height. Barnacles, mussels and algae each occupy a level.
A mangrove swamp is a shore of trees that roots in mud. Its roots trap sediment, shelter fish and birds and store carbon. That trapping is why a mangrove protects the coast it grows on.
The tide therefore creates the habitat. Without the rise and fall of the sea, there would be no shore and no mangrove to read in an examination.
A dambo is a seasonally flooded grassland in the savanna. It is a freshwater wetland that shares the flooding of a mangrove but not its salinity.
A crab that lives on a shore must hide at high tide and feed at low tide. That rhythm is set by the tide, which is why shore animals are active in turns.
A shore that is collected for food therefore loses its community. That loss is why a shore that is overharvested has fewer species than a protected one.
bullets: A shore is zoned by the tide
Mangrove roots trap sediment and shelter young fish
The tide creates the shore habitat

content.question: Where do Lagos crabs hide at low tide?
hints: Exposed mud
Mangrove roots
Salt control

lessons.title: Terrestrial and Arboreal Habitats
lessons.objective: Learners will describe land adaptations in Nigerian savanna, canopy and soil.

content.heading: Terrestrial and Arboreal Habitats
paragraphs: On a farm outside Jos, a boy watches grasscutters dart into tall grass as a harmattan wind spreads dry leaves. The animals are using terrestrial and arboreal habitats.

content.heading: Savanna Grassland and Abandoned Farmland
paragraphs: Savanna grasslands around Bida and Ogbomosho receive seasonal rain followed by a long dry season. Deep-rooted grasses, such as elephant grass, survive drought and recover quickly after fire. Farmers often abandon old fields where grasses and shrubs reclaim the soil naturally.

Fire adaptation is essential because dry-season bush fires sweep the savanna each year. Thick underground stems and waxy leaves protect buds from heat and reduce water loss. After burning, fresh green shoots emerge to feed grazers and attract insects.

Grasscutters hide in dense tufts and feed on tender shoots during the rainy months. Birds such as francolins hunt seeds while reptiles bask on warm laterite soils. In abandoned farmland, shrubs and small trees trap soil and restore moisture for new crops.
bullets: Grasses dominate savanna because deep roots store water and resist fire.
Fire removes dead litter and triggers fresh growth for grazers.
Grasscutters and birds depend on grass cover for food and shelter.
content.takeaway: Savanna grasses persist through drought and fire, feeding grasscutters and other animals.

check.question: What helps grasses survive fire?
check.why: Underground buds regrow after fire.

content.heading: Arboreal Life in the Tree Tops
paragraphs: Arboreal animals live in the canopy of trees in forests and savanna woodlands. Monkeys swing through branches near Zaria, grasping limbs with hands and feet. Their long tails aid balance while they forage on fruits, leaves and insects.

Birds such as hornbills and weavers nest high in branches where ground predators cannot reach. Weavers build hanging nests that sway safely in the wind. Canopy density provides shade, food and escape routes throughout the year.

Ants and termites form large colonies in tree forks and under bark. Their activity supports arboreal food webs by recycling dead wood and leaves. Study canopy life to understand food, shelter and safety in the treetops.
bullets: Monkeys use grasping hands and feet, with tails for balance.
Weaver birds build hanging nests high above ground predators.
Ants and termites recycle organic matter within the canopy.
content.takeaway: Canopy life offers food and safety, but needs limbs and nests for life aloft.

check.question: Why build nests high in trees?
check.why: High nests avoid ground predators.

content.heading: Burrow Life Beneath the Soil
paragraphs: Burrowing animals live in tunnels dug into soil, where temperature and moisture change slowly. Earthworms eat decaying leaves and loosen the soil for roots. Burrows also protect animals from harmattan heat, wind and heavy rain.

Termites build mounds with well-planned chambers that trap cool air and store food. Their colonies regulate humidity so fungal gardens can grow inside the nest walls. In Nigeria, termites often fill soil with tunnels from farms to forest edges.

Other soil animals such as millipedes, beetles and burrowing frogs feed on litter. Their burrows let water soak in and prevent soil flooding during storms. Farmers favour these organisms because they improve soil structure and aeration for crops.
bullets: Earthworms aerate soil and enrich it with nutrient-rich casts.
Termite mounds control temperature and humidity for the colony.
Burrows guard animals from drought, heat and sudden rain.
content.takeaway: Underground burrows keep soil animals cool, moist and safe from weather.

check.question: How do burrows help dry-season worms?
check.why: Burrows stay cool and damp.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often pairs habitat with adaptation. For savanna write fire and drought, for canopy write grip and nests, and for burrows write moisture and temperature shelter during their harsh seasons now.

content.problem: A Jos farmer finds fewer grasscutters after fire. Explain effects.

steps.reason: Food and shelter gone
steps.result: Grasscutters decline

steps.reason: Worms hide underground
steps.result: Soil animals survive

steps.reason: Fruits remain in trees
steps.result: Monkeys suffer less

content.heading: Go deeper: Grassland, savanna and abandoned farmland
paragraphs: Grassland is a habitat of grasses with scattered trees. It is maintained by fire, grazing and seasonal rain. A savanna therefore stays open because trees cannot close the canopy without water and protection.
Deep-rooted grasses such as elephant grass survive drought and recover quickly after fire. Farmers often abandon old fields where those grasses and shrubs reclaim the soil naturally.
Abandoned farmland is succession in progress. Grasses come first, then shrubs, then trees, so the field shows the stages of secondary succession in one place.
A fallow field that is left for two years recovers more than one that is left for two months. That recovery is why shifting cultivation needs a long fallow.
A grass that is grazed grows back from the base. That regrowth is why a grazed savanna can look green within weeks of the rains.
A grassland that is burnt too often loses its seed bank. That loss is why a burnt savanna may take years to recover its grasses.
A grassland that is fertilised changes its species. That change shows that nutrients are a factor as well as fire and grazing.
bullets: Grassland is maintained by fire, grazing and seasonal rain
Elephant grass survives drought and recovers after fire
Abandoned farmland shows secondary succession

content.heading: Go deeper: Tree-top life in the canopy and epiphytes
paragraphs: The canopy is the upper layer of trees where light is strongest. Birds, insects and monkeys live there because food and shelter are available. That layer is a habitat in its own right.
Epiphytes grow on trees without taking food from them. An orchid on a branch gains light and support, while the tree is unchanged. That is commensalism in the canopy.
Lianas are climbers that use trees for support. They reach the canopy by growing up a trunk, so they link the forest floor to the tree tops.
A monkey that lives in the canopy rarely comes to the ground. That is why a ground count underestimates its numbers and a canopy count is needed.
An orchid that grows on a branch must catch rain with its roots. That catching is why its aerial roots are covered in a spongy layer.
A canopy that is opened by logging dries the forest below. That drying kills the epiphytes that needed the humid canopy.
bullets: The canopy holds light, food and shelter
Epiphytes gain support without harming the tree
Lianas link floor and canopy

content.heading: Go deeper: Burrows, bushes and the ground layer
paragraphs: A burrow is a shelter underground that avoids heat and predators. A grasscutter and a rat therefore use the same ground for different reasons. The burrow is a habitat built by the animal itself.
A bush is a low, dense thicket that hides small mammals. That hiding is the reason a grasscutter darts into tall grass when a harmattan wind spreads dry leaves.
The ground layer therefore has its own community. Herbs, fungi and insects live there, while canopy animals rarely come down. A forest must therefore be read in layers.
A burrow is also a store for food. A rat that stores grain underground therefore protects it from rain and from birds that would otherwise eat it.
A burrow also moderates temperature. The air underground is cooler by day and warmer by night, so the animal avoids both extremes.
The ground layer that is cleared for farming loses its herbs and fungi. That loss is why a farmland has fewer species than the bush it replaced.
A burrow that is shared by many animals is a colony. That colony changes the soil by bringing nutrients from the surface to below.
bullets: Burrows avoid heat and predators
Bushes hide small mammals
A forest is read in layers, not as one surface

content.question: Where are Ibadan worms after rain?
hints: Damp soil
Feeding habits
Burrow depth

lessons.title: Tropical Rainforest of Nigeria
lessons.objective: Learners will explain rainforest location and layered structure in southern Nigeria.

content.heading: Tropical Rainforest of Nigeria
paragraphs: In Calabar, heavy rain falls almost every afternoon while tall trees drip and leaves glisten in cool shade under thick clouds. The city sits in a tropical rainforest biome.

content.heading: Location and Rainfall in the South
paragraphs: Nigeria's tropical rainforest grows in the south where annual rainfall exceeds 2000 mm. States such as Cross River, Ondo and Rivers receive the heaviest rain each year. Rain falls in most months across southern Nigeria, leaving only a short dry season.

The Niger Delta and southern uplands sit under constant moist air from the Atlantic. High humidity favours rapid leaf growth and thick plant cover throughout the year. Frequent rainfall leaches nutrients from surface soils, leaving poor, acidic conditions for crops.

Laterite soils dominate under rainforest, as iron and aluminium remain after heavy leaching. Farmers terrace steep slopes to protect this fragile soil from erosion. Conservation of laterite areas preserves water quality and wildlife corridors for towns and farms downstream.
bullets: Rainfall over 2000 mm creates warm, wet conditions for rainforest growth.
Southern states and the Niger Delta host the main forest belt.
Laterite soils are acidic and nutrient-poor due to leaching.
content.takeaway: Heavy southern rainfall and laterite soils shape Nigeria's rainforest climate.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches the rainforest to its location and rainfall?
check.why: Cross River lies in the southern rainforest belt with over 2000 mm of rain; Kano, Borno and Sokoto are drier.

content.heading: Forest Layers and Rich Diversity
paragraphs: Emergent trees rise above the canopy, reaching 40 metres in fertile lowland areas across southern Nigeria. Their tough leaves resist strong winds and occasional dry spells during harmattan. Buttress roots spread wide at the base to support these giants safely.

Below emergents lies the closed canopy of tall trees, where leaves form a green roof. Lianas climb through gaps to reach sunlight and flower at treetops. The canopy layers trap moisture and create cool, still conditions underneath.

The understorey holds shrubs, saplings and herbs that tolerate deep shade and moisture. Gorillas, seed-eating birds and crickets shelter among dense undergrowth nearby. Nigeria's rainforest holds rich diversity because layered plants supply food and habitat vertically.
bullets: Emergent trees and buttress roots support the forest ceiling.
Lianas link canopy to understorey and boost plant diversity.
Understorey shade shelters many small animals and young plants.
content.takeaway: Layered rainforest supports diverse life from canopy to forest floor.

check.question: What do buttress roots do?
check.why: They anchor tall trees on land.

content.heading: Swamp Forest, Threats and Conservation
paragraphs: Niger Delta swamp forest grows in waterlogged soils beside creeks and rivers across southern wetlands. Raffia palms and short mangroves dominate where brackish water meets fresh water daily. Crabs, fish and snails thrive in this rich, flooded environment with organised feeding behaviour.

Deforestation for palm oil plantations, logging and farming now threatens the rainforest. Settlers clear forest rapidly for cocoa and rubber estates near Lagos. Plantation farms often replace diverse forest with single crops that need chemicals.

Conservation now protects remnants through national parks and organised community reserves. Sustainable farming restores buffers of fast-growing trees around degraded areas for wildlife. JAMB favours questions on swamp adaptation and on why forest loss harms climate.
bullets: Swamp forest tolerates flooding and brackish water in the Delta.
Plantations and logging drive rapid rainforest loss in the south.
Parks and reserves conserve species and moderate local climate.
content.takeaway: Delta swamp forests need protection from plantations and logging pressure.

check.question: What most threatens rainforest?
check.why: Plantations clear forests for crops.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Remember the north to south rainfall gradient. JAMB links rainforest to over 2000 mm, laterite soils, buttress roots and high diversity in layered trees to answer Nigerian context questions fast.

content.problem: A Cross River group finds roots and lianas. What to record?

steps.reason: Tall trees exceed canopy
steps.result: Note root support

steps.reason: Need light to flower
steps.result: Link climbing diversity

steps.reason: Shrubs grow below canopy
steps.result: Record moisture needs

content.heading: Go deeper: The tropical rainforest and its layers
paragraphs: Nigeria's tropical rainforest grows in the south where annual rainfall exceeds 2000 mm. States such as Cross River, Ondo and Rivers receive the heaviest rain. Rain falls in most months, leaving only a short dry season.
The forest has layers: canopy, understory, shrubs and herbs. Tall trees form a canopy that shades the floor, so the understory is dim and humid. That shading decides which plants can grow below.
Buttress roots support tall trunks on soft soil. They are plank-like fins at the base that spread the weight. A buttress is therefore a support, not a root for absorption.
Lianas also compete for light in the canopy. A tree that is smothered by lianas gets less light, so the lianas are a burden as well as a link.
The canopy is so dense that the floor is dark at noon. That darkness is why the understory plants are shade-tolerant and the herbs are small.
An emergent tree that rises above the canopy is struck by lightning more often. That exposure is the price of reaching the light.
An emergent tree that is struck by lightning is a gap in the canopy. That gap lets light reach the floor, which is how the forest renews itself.
bullets: Rainforest: over 2000 mm, short dry season
Canopy, understory, shrubs and herbs in layers
Buttress roots support tall trunks on soft soil

content.heading: Go deeper: Swamp forest and the Niger Delta
paragraphs: A swamp forest grows in waterlogged soil where trees cannot breathe normally. Mangroves and raffia palms dominate because they have roots that can take in air. The swamp is therefore a forest that lives in water.
The Niger Delta holds the largest mangrove swamp in Africa. It shelters fish that breed among the roots and birds that roost in the canopy. That shelter is why the Delta is rich in species.
A freshwater swamp is different from a mangrove swamp. One is fed by rain and rivers, the other by the sea, so the plants and animals differ.
The raffia palm that dominates a freshwater swamp gives thatch and wine. That usefulness is why the swamp is valued as well as protected.
The mangrove roots also filter the water that reaches the sea. That filtering is why the Delta water is clearer than the creeks that feed it.
A mangrove that is cut for fuelwood exposes its mud to erosion. That erosion silts the creeks and kills the fish that bred among its roots.
bullets: Swamp trees breathe through roots in waterlogged soil
The Niger Delta holds Africa's largest mangrove swamp
Freshwater swamp differs from mangrove swamp

content.heading: Go deeper: Threats and conservation of the rainforest
paragraphs: The rainforest is threatened by logging, farming and settlement. Plantation farming clears the forest for crops, while fuelwood collection removes the understory. Those pressures reduce the area every year.

Conservation protects the forest in national parks and reserves. Cross River and Gashaka-Gumti are rainforest parks, while Old Oyo protects a drier forest. Each park guards a different part of the biome.
Reforestation restores what farming cleared. It is slower than clearing, which is why conservation of existing forest matters more than planting new trees.
A national park protects a whole community, not a single species. That is why Yankari and Cross River matter more than a reserve for one animal.
A protected forest also protects its soil. That soil holds water and carbon, so the park protects the climate as well as the species.
A park that is well guarded keeps its canopy intact. That intact canopy shades the floor and keeps the humidity that the forest needs.
bullets: Logging, farming and settlement threaten the rainforest
Cross River and Gashaka-Gumti are rainforest parks
Restoring forest is slower than clearing it

content.question: Why Delta swamp not savanna?
hints: Heavy rainfall
Waterlogged soils
Laterite leaching

lessons.title: Savanna, Desert and Highland Biomes
lessons.objective: Learners will compare Nigerian savanna, desert oases and highland grasslands.

content.heading: Savanna, Desert and Highland Biomes
paragraphs: Travelling north from Abuja in harmattan season, grasses shrink, dunes appear, then misty plateaus rise where the air feels cool at night. Each zone is a different biome.

content.heading: Guinea Savanna of the Middle Belt
paragraphs: Guinea savanna occupies the middle belt with 1000 to 1500 mm of annual rainfall; southern Guinea is wetter with taller grass, while northern Guinea is drier with shorter grass. Tall grass grows 1 to 3 metres high during the rainy months. Trees such as Isoberlinia and Parkia dot the grassland and drop leaves in the dry season.

The burn regime helps Guinea savanna maintain open grassland against encroaching forest. Yearly fires clear litter, kill pests and recycle nutrients into soil. Farmers burn before the first rains to encourage fresh shoots for livestock.
Shea, locust bean and dawadawa trees offer nuts and food for families. Antelopes, guinea fowl and grasscutters shelter in the tall grass during rains. Fire favours grasses over trees.
bullets: Guinea savanna receives 1000 to 1500 mm and tall grass 1 to 3 metres.
Isoberlinia and Parkia trees adapt to seasonal fire and drought.
Burn regime clears litter and favours grasses over shrubs.
content.takeaway: Guinea savanna blends tall grass, Isoberlinia parkland and yearly fire.

check.question: How tall is Guinea grass?
check.why: Grasses reach 1 to 3 metres in rains.

content.heading: Sudan Savanna and the Sahel Edge
paragraphs: Sudan savanna covers the north with less than 1000 mm of rainfall each year. Short grasses, often under 1 metre, grow in scattered clumps between trees. The dry season lasts six to seven months under hazy harmattan skies.

Shea and baobab trees survive drought with deep roots and thick trunks that store water. Glaucous leaves reduce water loss while seeds remain dormant through dry spells. This zone is a tsetse-free area because dry air limits the fly.

Farmers in Kano and Katsina grow millet, sorghum and groundnuts with short seasonal crops. Nomadic herders move south in the dry season seeking fresh pasture. Sudan savanna shows adaptation to fierce sun and low moisture year after year.
bullets: Sudan savanna has under 1000 mm rain and short, sparse grass.
Shea and baobab store water to survive long dry seasons.
Tsetse-free dry air supports cattle rearing in the north.
content.takeaway: Sudan savanna shows tree adaptations to low rain and intense sun.

check.question: How do shea trees survive drought?
check.why: Trunks store water for drought.

content.heading: Desert Oases and Highland Grasslands
paragraphs: The extreme north-east holds desert with less than 250 mm of annual rainfall. Active dunes shift with wind near Borno, while xerophytes survive with tiny leaves and succulent stems. Date palms cluster around oases where underground water reaches the surface.

Highland biomes rise in cool mists on the Jos Plateau and Obudu Plateau in Cross River. Mambilla Plateau adds another cool grassland where fog lowers temperature. Patches of montane forest survive in sheltered valleys, while these cool islands stand out from hot lowlands.

Jos Plateau grows Irish potatoes and temperate vegetables that need cool nights and mist. Highland grasses support cattle and attract tourists to viewpoints and canyons. Highland mist supplies moisture to crops that fail in surrounding savanna heat.
bullets: Desert xerophytes cut water loss with small leaves and coatings.
Oases allow desert farming where water reaches the surface.
Highland grasslands enjoy mist and temperate climate for crops.
content.takeaway: Desert oases and misty highlands contrast sharply with hot savanna plains.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches a biome with its feature?
check.why: Date palms grow where underground water reaches the surface at desert oases.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn biomes from south to north. Pair Guinea savanna with 1000 to 1500 mm, Sudan with under 1000 mm, desert under 250 mm and highlands with mist for ridge revision.

content.problem: A trader moves Kano sorghum to Jos and sees frost. Explain why.

steps.reason: Kano is hot and dry
steps.result: Jos is cool and misty

steps.reason: Highland air cools
steps.result: Frost harms sorghum

steps.reason: Potatoes suit cool soils
steps.result: Plant temperate crops

content.heading: Go deeper: Guinea and Sudan savanna
paragraphs: Guinea savanna occupies the middle belt with 1000 to 1500 mm of annual rainfall. Tall grass grows 1 to 3 metres high during the rains, and trees such as Isoberlinia and Parkia dot the grassland. Southern Guinea is wetter with taller grass; northern Guinea is drier with shorter grass.

Sudan savanna covers the north with less than 1000 mm of rainfall. Short grasses grow in scattered clumps, and the dry season lasts six to seven months. Trees such as shea survive by storing water in thick trunks.
The burn regime maintains open grassland against encroaching forest. Yearly fires clear litter, kill pests and recycle nutrients, which is why fire favours grasses over trees.
Shea trees that survive the dry season give nuts for families. That usefulness is why shea is protected in farms as well as in the wild.
A baobab that stores water in its trunk survives the dry season. That storage is why it can be leafless yet alive for months.
A lophira that drops its leaves in the dry season saves water. That deciduous habit is why the savanna looks bare in the harmattan and green in the rains.
A guinea savanna that is burnt in the wet season loses its grass. That is why the burn is timed before the rains, not during them.
bullets: Guinea: 1000 to 1500 mm, tall grass 1 to 3 metres
Sudan: under 1000 mm, short sparse grass
Fire favours grasses over trees

content.heading: Go deeper: Desert oases and the Sahel edge
paragraphs: A desert receives under 250 mm of rain each year. Its plants are xerophytes with thick cuticles and deep roots, and its animals are nocturnal or burrow by day. Water is the limiting factor.

An oasis is a place where underground water reaches the surface in a desert. Date palms grow there because their roots can reach water. That water makes the oasis a different habitat from the surrounding desert.
The Sahel is the transition between desert and savanna. It receives more rain than the desert but less than the savanna, so it is a zone of short grasses and scattered trees.
A date palm at an oasis is planted by people. That planting shows that an oasis is a human habitat as well as a natural one.
The Sahel that is overgrazed becomes desert. That transition shows that the boundary between the two biomes is set by use as well as by rain.
A desert shrub that is cut for fuel exposes the soil to wind. That exposure makes the desert larger, which is how the Sahel can become a desert.
bullets: Desert: under 250 mm, xerophytes and nocturnal animals
Oases: underground water reaches the surface
Sahel: transition between desert and savanna

content.heading: Go deeper: Highland grasslands and montane forest
paragraphs: Highland biomes rise in cool mists on the Jos Plateau, Obudu Plateau and Mambilla Plateau. Fog lowers temperature, so those plateaus are cooler than the lowlands around them. Montane forest survives in sheltered valleys there.
The cool climate supports a different flora. Grasslands dominate because the night frost and mist exclude many lowland trees. A highland therefore looks like a savanna that is cold rather than dry.
Desert, savanna and highland are therefore distinguished by water and temperature together. A biome must be read by both factors, not by rainfall alone.
A highland that is too cold for maize can still grow Irish potatoes. That crop therefore follows the highlands rather than the lowlands.
A highland that is forested in valleys and grassed on ridges shows both at once. The ridge is colder and windier, so trees cannot close there.
A highland that is planted with exotic pines changes its soil. That change can dry the streams that the highland feeds below.
bullets: Highlands: Jos, Obudu and Mambilla plateaus in cool mist
Montane forest survives in sheltered valleys
Read biomes by water and temperature together

content.question: How tell Guinea from Sudan savanna?
hints: Rainfall amount
Grass height
Tree species

lessons.title: Population Density and Size
lessons.objective: Measure population density and explain factors that determine the size of a population in an ecosystem.

content.heading: Population Density and Size
paragraphs: At the University of Ibadan botanical garden, Adebayo counts wild yam seedlings along a shady path. He wonders whether they are crowded or sparse, and how ecologists compare such counts fairly across different places.

content.heading: What Population Density Means
paragraphs: Population density is the number of individuals of a species within a given unit area or volume. It shows whether a species is crowded or thinly spread in its habitat.

Counting every individual is often impossible in a large forest or field. Ecologists sample a small representative part with a quadrat, usually a 1 m² frame placed at random points. Where plants are spread widely, they lay a transect line and sample quadrats along it.

Density is the total count divided by the total sampled area. If 40 yam seedlings are found in four 1 m² quadrats, the density is 40 ÷ 4 = 10 seedlings per m². Sampling must be random and repeated so results represent the whole area.
bullets: Density = total number counted ÷ total area sampled
A quadrat is a 1 m² frame; a transect is a line along which quadrats are sampled
Random placement and repetition improve accuracy and fairness
content.takeaway: Density tells how crowded a species is per unit area, estimated by quadrat sampling.

check.question: A student counts 60 seedlings in six 1 m² quadrats. What is the density?
check.why: Density = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 seedlings per square metre.

content.heading: Factors That Affect Population Size
paragraphs: Biotic factors are living or once-living factors that affect a population. Abundant food, low predation and good reproductive ability allow populations to grow quickly. Pests, disease, competition and predation reduce numbers by lowering survival and reproduction.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions such as temperature, light, water, space and pH. Each species has an optimum range, and harsh conditions lower its density in the soil. For example, yam seedlings grow poorly when water is scarce or soil pH is too acidic.

No factor acts alone: a drought can reduce plant food, so herbivores weaken and disease spreads more easily. Populations usually settle near the carrying capacity of their habitat, where competition increases and density falls. Ecologists therefore measure both biotic and abiotic factors when explaining population changes.
bullets: Biotic factors: food, pests, disease, predation, competition and reproductive ability
Abiotic factors: temperature, light, water, space and soil pH
Optimum conditions favour growth; unfavourable conditions reduce density
content.takeaway: Population size depends on living and non-living factors that affect survival and reproduction.

check.question: Which set lists only abiotic factors affecting population size?
check.why: Temperature, light and water are non-living conditions, so they are abiotic.

content.heading: Overcrowding in Human Populations
paragraphs: Overcrowding means too many people living in an area for its resources and services. It is often caused by a high birth rate and a falling death rate. Good healthcare, sanitation and nutrition keep more children alive, so numbers rise.

Overcrowding puts pressure on food, water, space, housing and jobs. It spreads disease quickly, causes unemployment and creates slums with poor sanitation. Schools, hospitals and roads become congested and fierce competition for resources increases within the community.

Control measures include family planning education, girls' education and child healthcare programmes. Investment in housing, jobs, clean water and farming improves living standards. Such measures slow growth without coercion and improve quality of life.
bullets: Causes: high birth rate, falling death rate and better healthcare
Effects: disease, unemployment, slums and pressure on food and space
Control: family planning, education and improved housing and services
content.takeaway: Overcrowding strains resources and services, so planning and education help control it.

check.question: Which is a direct consequence of overcrowding in cities?
options: More space and food per person
check.why: Overcrowding spreads disease and pressures jobs, housing, food and space, leading to slums.

content.title: Exam tip
