content.body: In JAMB questions, density is always number divided by area. Write the unit, such as individuals per square metre, and check whether biotic factors are living while abiotic factors are non-living before choosing an option.

content.problem: At a primary school garden in Enugu, Chiamaka places four 1 m² quadrats along a transect and counts 36 pawpaw seedlings. Calculate the density and explain what the result suggests.

steps.operation: Add the seedlings in all quadrats: 36
steps.reason: Density uses the total count from the sampled area
steps.result: Total count = 36 seedlings

steps.operation: Add the sampled area: 4 × 1 m² = 4 m²
steps.reason: Each quadrat covers 1 m², so four quadrats cover 4 m²
steps.result: Sampled area = 4 m²

steps.operation: Divide total count by total area: 36 ÷ 4
steps.reason: Density is number per unit area
steps.result: Density = 9 seedlings per m²

content.heading: Go deeper: Density, size and the carrying capacity
paragraphs: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area. A grasshopper count in a square metre is a density, while the total in a farm is a population size. Both are used to judge whether a species is increasing.

Carrying capacity is the maximum population that a habitat can support. It is set by food, water, space and predators. A population that exceeds it must fall back, which is why overshoot is followed by a crash.

Sampling measures density where a full count is impossible. Quadrats and transects are placed by rule, not by choice, so the sample represents the whole. A biased sample therefore gives a biased density.
A quadrat that is placed on a grasshopper path overcounts. That is why the rule, not the choice of the student, decides where the quadrat falls.
A population size that is counted by mark and recapture needs time for mixing. That time is why the recapture must be after the marked animals have dispersed.
A population that is sampled by mark and recapture can be counted without killing it. That method needs the marked animals to mix with the unmarked ones.
bullets: Density: per unit area; size: total number
Carrying capacity is set by food, water, space and predators
Quadrats and transects must be placed by rule

content.heading: Go deeper: Biotic and abiotic factors together
paragraphs: A drought is abiotic, but it can reduce plant food and let disease spread among herbivores. That chain shows that biotic and abiotic factors interact. No factor acts alone in an ecosystem.

Predation and parasitism are biotic factors that limit populations. A predator that is removed allows its prey to multiply, which can then strip the plants. That stripping is the next link in the chain.
Measuring only one kind of factor therefore misreads a population change. A fall in fish may be caused by a single factor, but the cause is found by measuring both kinds.
A biotic factor that is removed can release an abiotic one. A herbivore that is removed allows grass to grow, which then holds more soil and changes the water in it.
A disease that spreads in a drought is a biotic factor driven by an abiotic one. That interaction is why a population crash cannot be read from one factor alone.
A disease that spreads in a drought is a biotic factor driven by an abiotic one. That interaction is why a population crash cannot be read from one factor alone.
bullets: Drought can reduce food and let disease spread
Predation and disease limit populations
Measure both biotic and abiotic together

content.heading: Go deeper: Growth forms and the crash
paragraphs: A population grows exponentially when food is plentiful. It then slows as it approaches carrying capacity and settles near it. That S-shaped growth is the logistic curve.
A crash occurs when the population overshoots and food runs out. A locust outbreak that strips a farm and then starves is the classic example. The crash is therefore a sign of overshoot.
A population that is kept below carrying capacity by a predator does not crash as easily as a free one. That control is why a predator is not an enemy but a regulator.
A population that is sampled by mark and recapture can be counted without killing it. That method needs the marked animals to mix with the unmarked ones.
A pest that is kept below carrying capacity by a predator does not crash. That control is why a field with predators needs less insecticide than a field without them.
bullets: Logistic growth slows near carrying capacity in practice now
Overshoot is followed by a crash
A predator regulates by keeping numbers below capacity

content.question: A farmer in Kano counts 50 millet plants in five 1 m² quadrats. Is the density high or low, and which factor would you check first to explain it?
hints: Divide 50 by the total area
Think of food, water and pests
Consider temperature and rainfall too

lessons.title: Competition and Niche
lessons.objective: Explain intra-specific and inter-specific competition and how niche differentiation reduces competition in an ecosystem.

content.heading: Competition and Niche
paragraphs: On a farm near Zaria, sorghum grows taller than the millet sown beside it. The farmer wonders why one crop wins. This lesson explains how competition for resources shapes the growth of plants and animals.

content.heading: Intra-specific Competition
paragraphs: Intra-specific competition occurs between members of the same species. Their needs are almost identical, so they compete strongly for the same resources. This competition is usually intense because individuals want the same food, mates, space, light and water.

In plants, seedlings of one species shade one another and compete for light, water and mineral salts. In animals, males compete for mates and territories, while all individuals compete for food and shelter. The strongest individuals survive and reproduce, passing on their genes.

Intra-specific competition limits population size and density in a habitat. When resources are scarce, growth slows, reproduction falls and some individuals die. It therefore helps to keep a population near what the environment can support in a crowded habitat.
bullets: Same species, same needs: food, mates, space, light and water
Plants compete for light, water and mineral salts
Strongest individuals survive; density is limited
content.takeaway: Intra-specific competition is contest within a species for identical resources needed for survival.

check.question: Two male goats fight for access to females during the mating season. This is an example of
check.why: Both are males of the same species competing for mates, so it is intra-specific.

content.heading: Inter-specific Competition
paragraphs: Inter-specific competition occurs between different species that need the same resource. One species may gain while the other loses, or both may suffer. This competition is less direct than intra-specific competition, but it can still reduce growth and yield.

Millet and groundnut sown together compete for the same water and light. One crop may shade the other or use water faster, so both can lose yield. Farmers therefore space crops well and remove weeds early to reduce this loss.

Where two species compete strongly, the better adapted species often replaces the weaker one. This replacement changes the composition of the community over time. Understanding the contest helps farmers and ecologists predict crop yields in the field.
bullets: Different species competing for the same food, water or light
Millet and groundnut compete when sown together
Millet and groundnut compete when spaced too closely together
content.takeaway: Inter-specific competition is contest between species, and the better adapted may dominate.

check.question: Millet and groundnut grown together compete for water and light. This is an example of
check.why: Millet and groundnut are different species sharing the same water and light, so the competition is inter-specific.

content.heading: Niche Differentiation and Succession
paragraphs: A niche is the role and position of a species in its ecosystem, including how it obtains food and space. When species partition resources, they use them differently, so competition falls. For example, birds may feed at different heights on the same tree, and individuals of one species may also differ in size or timing.

Partitioning also happens through timing and root depth in plants. One species may grow in the rainy season while another grows later, or roots may occupy shallow and deep soil layers. Each species then obtains enough resources to survive and reproduce.

Competition drives succession as pioneers are replaced by better competitors. Early species modify the soil and shade, allowing shrubs and later trees to invade. Over time, the community changes from pioneer to climax species in a stable environment.
bullets: Niche: feeding height, timing of growth and root depth
Sharing resources differently reduces competition between species
Competition drives replacement of pioneers by climax species
content.takeaway: Niche differentiation reduces competition by partitioning resources among species in a habitat.

check.question: Two bird species feed at different heights on the same tree. This shows
check.why: Feeding at different heights partitions food, so each species uses the tree differently.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often asks whether competition is within one species or between species. Look for the phrase same species for intra-specific and different species for inter-specific. Remember that niche partitioning reduces competition between species.

content.problem: In a school farm at Jos, 20 millet seedlings and 20 groundnut seedlings compete for water in the same bed. After one month, millet is taller and groundnut is stunted. Explain the type of competition and the result.

steps.operation: Identify the competing organisms: millet and groundnut
steps.reason: They are different species needing the same water and light
steps.result: Competition is inter-specific

steps.operation: Compare growth: millet taller, groundnut stunted
steps.reason: Millet obtained more water and light than groundnut
steps.result: Millet outcompeted groundnut

steps.reason: The better adapted species will dominate the bed
steps.result: Groundnut density and yield will fall

content.heading: Go deeper: Intra-specific competition
paragraphs: Intra-specific competition occurs between members of the same species. Their needs are almost identical, so they compete strongly for the same food, mates, space, light and water. That competition is usually intense.
In plants, seedlings compete for light and water in the same place. In animals, males compete for mates and territories. The same principle therefore governs both kingdoms.
Intra-specific competition limits population size. When density rises, each individual gets less of what it needs, so growth falls and the population settles near carrying capacity.
A farmer that spaces maize widely is reducing intra-specific competition. That spacing therefore raises the yield of each plant, even though fewer plants are grown.
Seeds that are sown too thickly compete for light and water. That thinning is therefore a farmer's way of managing intra-specific competition.
A farmer that spaces maize widely is reducing intra-specific competition. That spacing therefore raises the yield of each plant, even though fewer plants are grown.
Seeds that are sown too thickly compete for light and water. That thinning is therefore a farmer's way of managing intra-specific competition.
bullets: Intra-specific: same species, identical needs
Plants compete for light and water; animals for mates and territories
It limits population size near carrying capacity

content.heading: Go deeper: Inter-specific competition
paragraphs: Inter-specific competition occurs between different species that share a resource. Millet and groundnut sown together compete for the same water and light. That sharing is what makes the competition inter-specific.

A predator is not a competitor, and a parasite is not a competitor. Competition is sharing a resource, parasitism is feeding on a host and predation is killing prey. Those tests separate the three interactions.
Inter-specific competition can exclude one species. If two species need exactly the same resource in the same place, the one that uses it better will outcompete the other.
A weed is a competitor that shares the crop's water and light. That is why early weeding matters, because the weed is at its smallest when it competes least.
A parasite that is not a competitor can still reduce a population. That is why Striga on sorghum is parasitism, not competition, however similar the loss may look.
A weed is a competitor that shares the crop's water and light. That is why early weeding matters, because the weed is at its smallest when it competes least.
bullets: Inter-specific: different species sharing a resource
Competition is sharing; parasitism is feeding on a host
Exact sharing can exclude one species

content.heading: Go deeper: Niche differentiation and succession
paragraphs: Niche differentiation reduces competition by letting species use the same resource differently. Birds may feed at different heights on the same tree, and individuals of one species may differ in size or timing.

Succession is the change of a community over time. Competition decides which species dominate at each stage, so succession and competition are linked. A bare rock is first colonised by pioneers that compete for the little soil there is.
A climax community is the stable end of succession. It resists small changes because its species are adapted to its conditions. Disturbance therefore resets succession to an earlier stage.
A niche is the role of a species in a community. Differentiation therefore means that two species play different roles on the same resource.
Succession is the arena in which competition acts. The pioneers compete for the rock, the herbs for the soil and the trees for the light.
A niche is the role of a species in a community. Differentiation therefore means that two species play different roles on the same resource.
bullets: Different heights, sizes or timings reduce competition
Succession changes the community over time
A climax resists small changes; disturbance resets it

content.question: Two bird species feed on the same tree but at different heights. Is this competition, niche differentiation, or succession, and why?
hints: Think of how they partition food
Consider feeding height on the tree
Succession requires change over time

lessons.title: Ecological Succession
lessons.objective: Describe the stages of primary and secondary succession and explain the features of a climax community.

content.heading: Ecological Succession
paragraphs: After a landslide near Idanre exposes bare rock, local farmers watch hardy lichens appear first. Over many years, green plants and trees return. This lesson traces how one community replaces another until it becomes stable and mature.

content.heading: Primary Succession on Bare Rock
paragraphs: Primary succession begins on a bare area where no soil exists, such as exposed rock or cooled lava. It starts slowly because organisms must create the conditions for others to live. The first organisms are pioneers that can survive harsh, dry surfaces with little water and no nutrients.

Lichens break down rock and form a thin layer of soil, then mosses grow and add more humus. Herbs and grasses grow thicker, shrubs follow, and finally trees form a forest. Each stage builds soil that improves water holding and nutrient supply.

The sequence is lichens, then mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest, and it may take many years. Soil becomes deeper, darker and richer as roots and dead organisms accumulate. Small animals and fungi arrive as the habitat becomes sheltered and moist.
bullets: Bare rock: lichens first, then mosses and herbs
Shrubs and trees follow as soil builds up
Each stage improves soil for the next stage
content.takeaway: Primary succession moves from bare rock to forest as pioneers build soil gradually.

check.question: What is the correct order in primary succession on bare rock?
check.why: Lichens colonise rock first and build soil, then mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest follow.

content.heading: Secondary Succession on Cleared Farmland
paragraphs: Secondary succession begins where soil already exists, such as cleared farmland or a harvested forest. Seeds, roots and soil organisms remain, so colonisation is faster. Pioneer grasses and small herbs appear within weeks, not years.

Grasses build cover and add humus, then shrubs and young trees grow rapidly. Because soil is already present, water and nutrients are available from the start. This gives secondary succession a higher net primary productivity, or NPP, than primary succession.

Human clearing often resets land to the grass stage, and farming may repeat the cycle. If land is abandoned, succession continues towards shrubs and forest. The speed depends on nearby seed sources, rainfall and soil quality in the area.
bullets: Cleared farmland retains soil, seeds and roots
Grasses and herbs appear first and grow fast
Higher NPP because soil and nutrients remain
content.takeaway: Secondary succession is faster than primary because soil and seed sources remain.

check.question: Why is secondary succession faster than primary succession?
options: Soil, seeds and roots remain after clearing
Bare rock builds soil very quickly
Lichens are absent in secondary succession
check.why: Cleared farmland still has soil and seed sources, so grasses and shrubs establish quickly.

content.heading: Climax Community and Resetting Factors
paragraphs: A climax community is the final, stable stage of succession in an area under the local climate. It is diverse, mature and self-perpetuating because its species can regenerate themselves. Large trees, many animals and a deep leaf litter characterise such a community.

In Nigeria, Omo National Park in Ogun State and Yankari National Park in Bauchi State show climax-like communities. Omo supports tall trees, primates and diverse plants, while Yankari has stable savanna woodland and many wildlife species. These communities resist small changes.

Fire, farming and drought can reset succession by removing plants and soil cover. Fire clears shrubs and returns land to grasses, while farming clears trees for crops. After such disturbance, succession begins again from an early stage.
bullets: Climax: stable, diverse and self-perpetuating community
Examples: Omo and Yankari climax communities
Fire, farming and drought reset succession
content.takeaway: A climax community is stable and diverse, but fire, farming or drought can reset it.

check.question: Which feature best describes a climax community?
check.why: A climax community is mature, diverse and able to maintain itself under local conditions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB, primary succession starts on bare rock while secondary starts where soil remains. List the order lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs then forest, and remember climax communities are stable and diverse until fire, farming or drought resets them.

content.problem: A landslide near Abeokuta exposes bare rock, while a nearby farm is abandoned after harvest. Which area will become forested faster, and why? Give the pioneer organisms for the faster area.

steps.operation: Compare starting conditions: rock has no soil, farm has soil and seeds
steps.reason: Soil supplies water, nutrients and a site for roots
steps.result: Farm will succeed faster

steps.reason: Grasses and small herbs colonise cleared soil quickly
steps.result: Pioneers: grasses and herbs

steps.reason: Lichens must build soil before larger plants grow
steps.result: Pioneers: lichens, then mosses

content.heading: Go deeper: Primary succession
paragraphs: Primary succession starts on bare rock where no soil exists. Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses colonise it, break it down and add humus. That humus builds the soil that later plants need.

Herbs come next because they need soil but tolerate poor conditions. Shrubs follow because they shade the herbs, and trees follow because they outgrow the shrubs. Each stage changes the conditions for the next.
That sequence therefore needs no prior soil. The pioneers make the soil that the later species require, which is why primary succession is slow. It can take decades to reach a forest.
A lichen that grows on rock has no roots. It holds itself by the rock and takes minerals from rain and dust, which is how it starts the soil.
A moss that covers a rock holds water and dust. That cover makes the rock moist, which is how the next group can establish on it.
A moss that covers a rock holds water and dust. That cover makes the rock moist, which is how the next group can establish on it.
bullets: Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil
Pioneers make the soil that later plants need
Herbs, shrubs then trees in that order

content.heading: Go deeper: Secondary succession
paragraphs: Secondary succession starts on soil that already exists. An abandoned farm is the standard example because its soil is rich and its seed bank survives. That soil makes secondary succession faster than primary.
Grasses and shrubs reclaim the field first, then trees. The same stages appear as in primary succession, but the soil stage is skipped. A fallow field therefore recovers in years rather than decades.
A bush fire that clears shrubs near Ogbomoso resets succession to the grass stage. The climax that follows depends on how long the land is left undisturbed.
The seed bank of an abandoned farm is rich because seeds survive underground. That bank is why secondary succession starts with the species that were there before.
A fallow that is burnt starts again from the grass stage. That burn therefore resets secondary succession, which is why shifting cultivation needs a long fallow.
A fallow that is burnt starts again from the grass stage. That burn therefore resets secondary succession, which is why shifting cultivation needs a long fallow.
bullets: Secondary succession starts on existing soil
An abandoned farm is the standard example
It is faster than primary succession

content.heading: Go deeper: Climax and the resetting factors
paragraphs: A climax community is the stable end of succession for a climate. It resists small changes because its species are adapted to its conditions. In Nigeria, Omo National Park and Yankari National Park show climax-like communities.

Fire, farming and storms reset succession to an earlier stage. A fire that clears a forest returns it to grass, and farming that clears a bush returns it to crops. The climax is therefore stable but not permanent.
The climax is not a single form. A rainforest climax in the south and a savanna climax in the north are both stable, because each matches its climate.
A climax that is burnt does not return to the same climax at once. It must pass through the earlier stages again, which is why a burnt forest is not a forest for years.
A climax in a wet south is forest, while a climax in a dry north is savanna. The same process therefore ends in different communities in different climates.
A climax in a wet south is forest, while a climax in a dry north is savanna. The same process therefore ends in different communities in different climates.
bullets: Climax is the stable end for a climate
Omo and Yankari are Nigerian examples
Fire and farming reset succession

content.question: After a bush fire clears shrubs near Ogbomosho, which stage will appear first, and what will the climax be if left undisturbed?
hints: Fire resets succession to grasses
Think of stages after grasses
Climax is stable forest or woodland

lessons.title: Soil Types and Components
lessons.objective: Compare sandy, clayey and loamy soils and explain their components and properties important for plant growth.

content.heading: Soil Types and Components
paragraphs: At a farm in Nsukka, Musa finds sand in one pit, sticky clay in another, and loam in the third. He wonders why some hold water better. This lesson compares soil types and explains components.

content.heading: Sandy, Clayey and Loamy Soils
paragraphs: Soils differ because their particles differ in size. Sandy soil has large particles linked by large pores, so water drains quickly and air enters easily. Clayey soil has tiny particles and many narrow pores, so water drains slowly and the soil holds water for a long time.

Sandy soil warms quickly and is easy to work, but it dries fast and holds few nutrients. Clayey soil is heavy, sticky when wet and hard when dry. Its total pore space is high, but the narrow pores trap water and leave little air, so it is poorly aerated.
Loamy soil has a mixture of sand, silt and clay, so it balances the qualities of both. It has good porosity, holds water well and allows air for roots. For these reasons, loamy soil suits most crops.
bullets: Sandy: large particles, drains fast, poorly holds water
Clayey: tiny particles, holds water, poorly aerated
Loamy: mixed particles, good water and air balance
content.takeaway: Pore size controls drainage, water retention and aeration in sandy, clayey and loamy soils.

check.question: Which soil drains water fastest and is poorest in water retention?
check.why: Sandy soil has large particles and big pores, so water drains away quickly.

content.heading: Soil Structure, Porosity and Capillarity
paragraphs: Soil structure describes how particles are arranged into crumbs or clumps with spaces between them. Good structure creates pores that allow roots, air and water to move freely. Poor structure compacts the soil and reduces pore space in a fertile topsoil.

Porosity is the amount of pore space in the soil, and it affects drainage and aeration. Capillarity is the rise of water through narrow tubes or pores against gravity. In soil, capillarity draws water upward from moist layers to dry roots.

Humus improves structure by binding particles into crumbs and holding water and nutrients. Soils rich in humus are darker, more porous and more fertile. Capillarity and humus together help roots obtain steady water even in dry spells.
bullets: Structure: arrangement of particles into crumbs with pores
Porosity: pore space for air and water movement
Capillarity: water rises in narrow pores to roots
content.takeaway: Good structure, porosity and capillarity give roots steady water, air and nutrients.

check.question: Capillarity in soil means
options: Water flows down by gravity only
Water rises through narrow pores to roots
Air moves out of the soil
check.why: Capillarity is the upward movement of water through narrow tubes or pores, helping roots absorb water.

content.heading: Components of Soil
paragraphs: Soil has inorganic components and organic components. Inorganic components are mineral particles from weathered rock, plus soil water and soil air in the pores. Mineral particles vary from sand to clay and determine soil type.

Organic components include humus, living roots and dead remains of plants and animals. Humus comes from decayed organic matter and darkens the soil. Roots add organic matter as they die and provide channels for air and water.

Soil organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi break down organic matter and release nutrients, while earthworms also burrow and aerate the soil. Soil air supplies oxygen to roots and soil organisms. To measure soil water, weigh a fresh sample, dry it and weigh again; the loss is water, and to estimate soil air, saturate a known volume of dry soil and measure the water absorbed into its pores.
bullets: Inorganic: mineral particles, soil water and soil air
Organic: humus, roots and dead organic matter
Organisms: earthworms, bacteria and fungi release nutrients
content.takeaway: Soil combines minerals, water, air, humus and organisms that support plant growth.

check.question: Which method estimates the air content of a soil sample?
options: Dry a fresh sample and measure the mass loss
Saturate a known volume of dry soil and measure the water absorbed
Heat the soil and weigh the ash
Add humus and measure the pH
check.why: Water fills the pores and displaces air, so the water absorbed estimates the air space in a known volume of soil.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For JAMB, link particle size to behaviour: sandy drains fast, clayey holds water, loamy balances both. Recall capillarity draws water upward in narrow pores, and soil air supplies oxygen to roots and soil organisms for respiration.

content.problem: A farmer in Makurdi has sandy soil that dries quickly. He adds compost and clay in small amounts. Explain why the change improves water retention and aeration for his yams.

steps.operation: Identify the problem: sandy soil has large particles and big pores
steps.reason: Large pores allow water to drain away quickly
steps.result: Soil holds little water

steps.operation: Add compost: humus binds particles into crumbs
steps.reason: Humus improves structure and holds water and nutrients
steps.result: Water retention improves

steps.operation: Add clay: smaller particles fill large pores
steps.reason: Smaller pore spaces reduce drainage and hold water
steps.result: Soil becomes loamier with better balance

content.heading: Go deeper: Sandy, clayey and loamy soils
paragraphs: Sandy soil has large particles and large pores. It drains quickly, warms quickly and is leached of nutrients. It is therefore poor for crops that need steady water and nutrients.

Clay soil has tiny particles and a high total porosity, but its pores are small. It holds water and nutrients but drains slowly and is hard to work when wet. That small pore size is why clay is heavy.
Loam is a mixture of sand, silt and clay. It drains without waterlogging and holds nutrients without becoming heavy. That balance is why loam is the best soil for most crops.
A clay soil that is limed becomes easier to work. The lime changes its structure, so the amendment for acidity is also a change in texture.
A sandy soil that is manured becomes loamier. The manure adds humus and clay-sized particles, so the texture that is measured in the field changes with use.
A clay soil that is limed becomes easier to work. The lime changes its structure, so the amendment for acidity is also a change in texture.
bullets: Sandy: large pores, drains fast, leaches nutrients
Clay: high total porosity, small pores, holds water
Loam: balanced drainage and nutrients

content.heading: Go deeper: Structure, porosity and capillarity
paragraphs: Soil structure is the arrangement of particles into aggregates. Clay has high total porosity because its particles pack to leave many small pores. Sand has lower total porosity because its large particles leave fewer, larger pores.

Porosity is total pore space, while permeability is the ease with which water moves through it. Clay has high porosity but low permeability, while sand has lower porosity but high permeability. That distinction decides drainage.
Capillarity draws water upward against gravity. That rise is highest in clay because its pores are smallest, which is why clay soil can draw water to roots from below.
A soil that is heavily compacted by feet or wheels all year loses its pores. That loss raises its bulk density and lowers its permeability, which is why a compacted soil waterlogs.
Capillarity can lift water to the surface and cause salt to crust there. That crust is why a soil that is irrigated without drainage becomes salty.
bullets: Clay: high total porosity, low permeability
Sand: lower total porosity, high permeability
Capillarity rises highest in clay

content.heading: Go deeper: Components and soil organisms
paragraphs: Soil is about half mineral particles and half pore space. The pores hold water and air, while humus and organisms make up the organic part. A soil without pores would be solid rock, and a soil without organisms would be inert.
Soil organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi break down organic matter and release nutrients. Earthworms also burrow and aerate the soil, while bacteria and fungi decompose remains.

Soil air supplies oxygen to roots and soil organisms. To measure soil water, weigh a fresh sample, dry it and weigh again; to estimate soil air, saturate a known volume of dry soil and measure the water absorbed into its pores.
A soil that is rich in humus is dark and holds water. That darkness is the sign of organic matter, which is why a dark soil is usually fertile.
A soil that is rich in organisms is also rich in nutrients. That richness is why a dark, crumbly soil is the sign of a fertile one.
A soil that is rich in organisms is also rich in nutrients. That richness is why a dark, crumbly soil is the sign of a fertile one.
bullets: Soil is mineral particles plus pores, humus and organisms
Earthworms aerate; bacteria and fungi decompose
Dry and reweigh for water; saturate for air

content.question: Which soil would you choose for cassava, and how would capillarity help its roots in a dry week?
hints: Think of loamy soil balance
Capillarity draws water upward
Roots need air and water

lessons.title: Soil Fertility and Conservation
lessons.objective: Explain soil fertility, how it is lost, and how farmers can renew and conserve it using Nigerian practices.

content.heading: Soil Fertility and Conservation
paragraphs: Adaeze farms yam near Ibadan, but her tubers have shrunk over seasons. Her father keeps planting the same crop on the same plot without rest. She asks why the once-healthy soil no longer feeds plants well.

content.heading: What Soil Fertility Means and How It Is Lost
paragraphs: Soil fertility is the soil's ability to support plant growth by supplying water, air, and nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Fertile soil holds moisture, allows root growth, and provides humus for steady crop development.

Heavy rain leaches nutrients downward beyond roots, while erosion removes fertile top soil from bare farms. Burning, trampling and machinery compact soil, reduce air spaces, and destroy humus that improves structure and moisture.

Planting the same crop repeatedly removes similar nutrients from the same layer. Yam and maize remove large amounts of potassium, while cassava tolerates poorer soil but still exhausts it over repeated harvests. Yields fall without rest, fallow or added organic matter to replace what harvest removed.
bullets: Leaching: rain carries dissolved nutrients below the root zone.
Erosion removes humus-rich top soil on slopes.
Compaction by feet and tractors blocks water and roots.
content.takeaway: Fertility means nutrients, humus and structure; leaching, erosion, compaction and repeated cropping destroy it.

check.question: Which practice most directly depletes the same nutrients from the same soil layer?
check.why: Repeated cropping removes similar nutrients from the same depth without replacement.

content.heading: Renewing Soil Fertility for Better Harvests
paragraphs: Crop rotation plants different crops in sequence on the same land. Legumes like cowpea and groundnut fix nitrogen through root nodules, while deep-rooted plants bring up nutrients. Rotation breaks pests and balances nutrient use across seasons.

Manure, compost and green manure add humus, improve structure, and feed soil organisms. Inorganic fertiliser such as NPK supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium quickly when crops need them. Farmers in the North often combine manure with NPK for lasting improvement.

Where soil is acidic, liming with crushed limestone neutralises acidity and improves nutrient uptake. Balanced liming also benefits legumes and soil microbes, helping rice, maize and vegetable farms produce better harvests.
bullets: Rotation: alternate yam with cowpea to restore nitrogen.
Intercrop maize with groundnut between rows.
Apply compost before planting rainy-season crops.
content.takeaway: Rotation, legumes, manure, compost, NPK and lime restore nutrients and humus for fertile soil.

check.question: Which crop helps fix atmospheric nitrogen in rotation?
check.why: Cowpea is a legume whose root nodules fix nitrogen for soil and next crops.

content.heading: Conserving Soil to Prevent Further Loss
paragraphs: Mulching covers soil with grasses, crop residues, or leaves to reduce raindrop impact, evaporation, and erosion. Cover crops like melon or Mucuna keep soil protected between planting seasons, bind particles, and add organic matter when they die.

On slopes in Jos and eastern hills, contour ridging follows the land's level to trap runoff. Terracing builds step-like platforms that slow water, while strip-cropping alternates crop rows with grass strips to hold soil and cut erosion.

Mixed cropping or poly-cropping grows yam, cassava, plantain and cocoyam together, giving full cover and varied roots. In shifting cultivation, farmers clear, farm briefly, then allow fallow to regrow, restoring fertility before reuse.
bullets: Mulch with dried grasses around tomato beds.
Ridge along contours, never up and down slopes.
Mix cassava, yam and vegetables in one plot.
content.takeaway: Cover soil, slow runoff, and rest land with fallow to conserve fertility.

check.question: Which conservation method slows runoff on a hillside farm?
check.why: Contour ridging follows the level of the slope and traps runoff and eroded soil.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Examiners often ask for two causes of soil loss and two renewal methods. List leaching, erosion, compaction plus rotation, legumes, manures and liming, linking each choice to a Nigerian farm example for full marks.

content.problem: Mrs Bello in Kano plants maize yearly on the same sandy plot, applying little manure. Yields fall and rain washes soil. Propose a restoration plan.

steps.operation: Rotate maize with cowpea, then sorghum on different rows
steps.reason: Cowpea fixes nitrogen and crops use different nutrients
steps.result: Nutrient balance improves and pest cycles break

steps.operation: Add compost and recommended NPK; lime if test shows acidity
steps.reason: Humus restores structure and NPK replaces nutrients
steps.result: Soil holds water and feeds roots better

steps.operation: Mulch residues and ridge along contours
steps.reason: Mulch cuts evaporation and ridges slow runoff
steps.result: Top soil stays and yields stabilise

content.heading: Go deeper: Why soil loses fertility
paragraphs: Soil loses fertility when nutrients are removed faster than they are replaced. Cropping takes nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from the soil, and a crop that is removed carries them away. Continuous cropping without replacement therefore mines the soil.

Erosion removes the topsoil that holds humus and nutrients. That loss is fastest on bare, sloping land during heavy rain. A soil that has lost its topsoil is thinner and poorer even if its subsoil is still rich.

Cassava tolerates low nutrients, while yam depletes more. That difference is why cassava is planted on poorer soil and yam on richer soil. The crop must be matched to the soil, not the other way round.
A soil that is cropped with yam every year loses more than a soil that rests. That is why yam is a pioneer crop that gives a high yield once and then needs a rest.
A soil that is rich in humus holds water and nutrients. That holding is why a dark soil is usually fertile and a pale soil is usually poor.
A soil that is cropped with yam every year loses more than a soil that rests. That is why yam is a pioneer crop that gives a high yield once.
bullets: Nutrients leave in the crop; continuous cropping mines the soil
Erosion removes the nutrient-rich topsoil
Cassava tolerates poor soil; yam depletes more

content.heading: Go deeper: Fallowing, rotation and legumes
paragraphs: Fallowing rests a field so that nutrients and structure can recover. Bush is allowed to grow, its leaves fall and rot and its roots hold the soil. That rest is why shifting cultivation needs a long fallow.

Rotation changes the crop each season. A legume such as groundnut fixes nitrogen and leaves it for the next crop, while a cereal such as maize uses it. The two therefore alternate as supplier and user.
Manure and compost add humus and nutrients directly. That addition replaces what the crop removed, so a manured soil can be cropped continuously where an unmanured one cannot.
A legume that is intercropped with a cereal fixes nitrogen for both. That intercropping is why groundnut and maize are often grown together in the same field.
A rotation that returns a legume to the same field every third year restores nitrogen. That cycle is why groundnut is a good predecessor for maize.
A legume that is intercropped with a cereal fixes nitrogen for both. That intercropping is why groundnut and maize are often grown together in the same field.
A fallow that is burnt starts again from the grass stage. That burn therefore resets the cycle, which is why the fallow must be left long enough.
bullets: Fallowing restores nutrients and structure
Legumes fix nitrogen for the next crop
Manure replaces what the crop removed

content.heading: Go deeper: Conservation practices
paragraphs: Terracing builds steps on a slope so that water is held rather than lost. Contour ploughing follows the level of the land for the same reason. Both therefore slow runoff and keep soil in place.
Mulching covers the soil with plant remains. That cover reduces evaporation, moderates temperature and feeds soil organisms. A mulched soil therefore holds water longer than a bare one.
Agroforestry plants trees among crops. Those trees fix nitrogen, shade the soil and provide timber, so the farm gains fertility without losing its crop.
A contour bank that is broken lets water rush down the slope. That break is why a bank must be maintained, not only built.
A terrace that is not well maintained becomes a gully in heavy rain. That gully then removes the soil that the terrace was built to save.
A terrace that is not maintained becomes a gully. That gully then removes the soil that the terrace was built to save.
bullets: Terracing and contour ploughing slow runoff
Mulching feeds organisms and holds water
Agroforestry fixes nitrogen and shades the soil

content.question: How would you help a farmer who plants only yam on one plot each year restore the soil?
hints: Think of legumes and rotation.
Which organic matter adds humus?
What covers soil to stop erosion?

lessons.title: Diseases, Vectors and Control
lessons.objective: Identify common diseases, their vectors and causes, and how communities control them.

content.heading: Diseases, Vectors and Control
paragraphs: During the dusty harmattan in Kano, Chidi gets fever and stiff neck, diagnosed as meningitis. His cousin in the Niger Delta suffers repeated malaria. How are these Nigerian diseases spread, and how are they controlled?

content.heading: Common Endemic Diseases and Their Causes
paragraphs: Malaria, Nigeria's commonest disease, is caused by Plasmodium parasites carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Bites during the rainy season transmit the parasites, causing fever, chills, and anaemia, especially in children under five.

Meningitis is caused by Neisseria bacteria in the throat, spreading by coughs and close contact in dry, dusty weather. Tuberculosis, or TB, is airborne: Mycobacterium germs spread through coughs and stay in crowded homes, causing persistent cough and weakness.

Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water and food carrying Vibrio and Salmonella bacteria. Open defecation, poor sewage, and dirty hands in markets or IDP camps allow rapid spread, causing watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever.
bullets: Malaria: Anopheles mosquito carries Plasmodium parasites.
Meningitis: Neisseria bacteria spread in dry season.
Cholera: Vibrio spreads via dirty water and food.
content.takeaway: Malaria, meningitis, cholera, typhoid and TB remain endemic through vectors, dust, water and air.

check.question: Which mosquito spreads Plasmodium parasites that cause malaria?
check.why: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes carry Plasmodium parasites into human blood by bites.

content.heading: Water, Insect and Contact-Borne Diseases
paragraphs: Schistosomiasis, or bilharzia, occurs when skin touches freshwater containing cercariae larvae. Freshwater snails release cercariae into water used for swimming, fishing and washing, causing blood in urine and liver damage.

Onchocerciasis, or river blindness, spreads by Simulium blackflies breeding near fast streams, causing severe itching and blindness. Dracunculiasis is caused by Guinea worms spread when people drink water with copepods, leading to painful skin blisters.

Polio virus spreads through contaminated water and food, attacking nerves and causing paralysis in children. Sexually transmitted infections, including gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV, spread through unsafe sex and blood. Repeated infection can worsen illness and cause treatment failure.
bullets: Bilharzia: freshwater snail releases cercariae into water.
River blindness: Simulium blackfly bites near rivers.
Guinea worm: copepod in drinking water spreads disease.
content.takeaway: Snails, blackflies, copepods, contaminated water and unsafe sex transmit these diseases.

check.question: Which infection spreads through unsafe sex and can cause infertility?
check.why: Gonorrhoea and syphilis are sexually transmitted infections; untreated gonorrhoea can cause infertility.

content.heading: Controlling Diseases Across Communities
paragraphs: Bed nets, indoor spraying with insecticide, and larviciding that kills mosquito larvae reduce malaria. Clearing stagnant water, covering water jars, and improving drainage around homes also stop mosquitoes and blackflies breeding.

Boiling, chlorination, and filtering make water safe against cholera, typhoid, and polio. Pit latrines, proper sewage disposal, hand washing, and food hygiene break the faecal-oral chain in villages and camps. Oral rehydration and antibiotics treat cholera and typhoid, while artemisinin-based drugs treat malaria.

Vaccination protects: Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) against polio, BCG against TB, and meningococcal vaccine against meningitis. TB patients complete DOTS therapy. WHO coordinates global policy, UNICEF supplies vaccines and water programmes, and Nigeria's Federal Ministry of Health and Red Cross support outbreaks.
bullets: Use insecticide-treated nets every night.
Boil or chlorinate water from wells.
Vaccinate with OPV and BCG early.
content.takeaway: Nets, clean water, sanitation, vaccines, DOTS and support agencies prevent spread.

check.question: Which pair correctly matches a disease to its treatment or prevention?
check.why: Artemisinin-based drugs treat malaria; BCG protects against TB, OPV against polio, and cholera needs rehydration and antibiotics.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Remember each disease with its pathogen, vector and control. For malaria, match Anopheles and Plasmodium to nets and spraying; for bilharzia, match snails and cercariae to clean water and avoidance of contact.

content.problem: After flooding in Benue, many families drink well water and mosquitoes breed in pools. Diarrhoea and malaria rise. What control actions should health workers take?

steps.operation: Chlorinate wells and distribute treated nets and insecticide spray
steps.reason: Chlorine kills Vibrio and Salmonella; nets and spray block Anopheles bites
steps.result: Waterborne diseases and malaria transmission fall

steps.operation: Build pit latrines away from wells and clear stagnant water
steps.reason: Sanitation stops faecal-oral spread and larviciding removes breeding sites
steps.result: Cholera risk drops and mosquito numbers fall

steps.operation: Vaccinate children with OPV and BCG; support DOTS for TB cases
steps.reason: Vaccines prevent polio and severe TB; DOTS ensures TB cure
steps.result: Outbreaks prevented and treatment completed

content.heading: Go deeper: Endemic diseases and their vectors
paragraphs: An endemic disease is one that is constantly present in a community. Malaria is endemic in much of Nigeria because the Anopheles mosquito that carries Plasmodium is present throughout the year. That presence keeps the disease in place.

The vector is the insect that carries the pathogen. A female Anopheles mosquito carries malaria, a Simulium blackfly carries river blindness and a freshwater snail carries schistosomiasis. Each disease therefore has its own vector.
Control must target the vector as well as the pathogen. Spraying, nets and larval control work because they reduce the vector, not only because they treat the sick.
A mosquito net that is used every night protects against malaria. That nightly protection is why nets are more effective than spraying alone.
A vector that breeds in stagnant water can be controlled by larval measures. That control is why draining a swamp reduces malaria without treating any patient.
A mosquito net that is used every night protects against malaria. That nightly protection is why nets are more effective than spraying alone.
A vector that breeds in stagnant water can be controlled by larval measures. That control is why draining a swamp reduces malaria without treating any patient.
A vector that breeds in stagnant water can be controlled by larval measures. That control is why draining a swamp reduces malaria without treating any patient.
bullets: Endemic: constantly present in a community
Anopheles: malaria; Simulium: river blindness; snail: schistosomiasis
Control targets the vector as well as the pathogen

content.heading: Go deeper: Water, insect and contact-borne diseases
paragraphs: A borehole that is well protected from contamination prevents cholera and dysentery in practice. That protection is why a covered well is safer than an open one.
Onchocerciasis is insect-borne because Simulium breeds near fast rivers. Living near a river therefore risks the disease, which is why control must target the breeding site as well as the patient.
Schistosomiasis is contact-borne because cercariae penetrate skin in water. Wading in infested water therefore infects, which is why boots and safe water matter.
A freshwater snail that carries schistosomiasis lives in a particular water. That habitat therefore decides where the disease can occur.
A borehole that is protected from contamination prevents cholera. That protection is why a covered well is safer than an open one.
A freshwater snail that carries schistosomiasis lives in a particular water. That habitat therefore decides where the disease can occur.
A public health nurse who sees those signs can decide that the case is an emergency.
A covered well is safer than an open one.
bullets: Cholera: water-borne from faeces to water
Onchocerciasis: Simulium near fast rivers
Schistosomiasis: cercariae penetrate skin in water

content.heading: Go deeper: Controlling diseases across communities
paragraphs: Vaccines prevent disease by training the immune system. OPV prevents polio and BCG protects against severe tuberculosis. A vaccination programme therefore protects a community before the pathogen arrives.

Treatment cures the sick and stops spread. Artemisinin-based drugs treat malaria, antibiotics treat cholera and gonorrhoea, and the choice must match the pathogen. A drug that does not match the pathogen cannot control it.
Sanitation removes the conditions in which disease thrives. Clean water, safe food and waste disposal therefore control more than one disease at once, which is why they are community programmes.
A vaccine that is given before travel protects the traveller. That protection is why starting a course before exposure matters more than starting it after.
A drug that is taken incompletely can leave resistant parasites. That resistance is why a full course must be taken for malaria.
A vaccine that is given before travel protects the traveller. That protection is why starting a course before exposure matters more than starting it after.
A drug that is taken incompletely can leave resistant parasites. That resistance is why a full course must be taken for malaria.
bullets: OPV prevents polio; BCG protects against severe tuberculosis
Artemisinin-based drugs treat malaria
Sanitation controls many diseases at once

content.question: If bilharzia is common in a fishing village, what vector and control methods would you suggest?
hints: Think of snail and water contact.
How should drinking water be made safe?
Which nets or sprays also help?

lessons.title: Drug Abuse
lessons.objective: Define drug abuse and addiction, describe their effects, and explain ways to prevent and treat abuse.

content.heading: Drug Abuse
paragraphs: Tunde, a market trader's son in Onitsha, steals money to buy codeine syrup. He was once bright in school but now sleeps in class. How can a single habit harm his body, mind, and future?

content.heading: What Drug Abuse Means and Common Drugs
paragraphs: A drug is any substance that changes body or mind function. Drug misuse is taking it wrongly, while abuse is deliberate heavy use. Addiction means compulsive use despite harm, with tolerance and dependence developing over time.

Tolerance is needing more of the drug for the same effect, while dependence is the body craving it continuously. Withdrawal signs like shaking, sweating, and anxiety appear when use stops. Without help, users cannot easily quit despite harm.

Commonly abused in Nigeria are alcohol, cannabis (weed), codeine cough syrup, and tramadol tablets. Shisha, cocaine, and heroin are also abused, especially where peer pressure, stress, and idle youths encourage use for pleasure or escape.
bullets: Alcohol: cheap local gin harms liver quickly.
Codeine and tramadol affect brain and control.
Cannabis and shisha damage lungs and focus.
content.takeaway: Abuse means heavy, harmful use leading to tolerance, dependence and addiction.

check.question: Needing more tramadol for the same effect shows what?
check.why: Tolerance is the need for a larger dose to achieve the previous effect.

content.heading: Effects of Drug Abuse on Health and Society
paragraphs: Alcohol damages the liver, causes heart failure, and shrinks the brain. Tramadol and cocaine strain the heart, while smoking shisha and cannabis harms lungs. Overdose can cause seizures, coma, and sudden death.

Drug abuse leads to mental illness, depression, aggression, and violence at home. Users fail school, lose friends, suffer accidents while driving or operating machines, and spread infections through unsafe injections and risky sex.

Families waste school fees and trading money on drugs, deepening poverty. Stolen goods, damaged markets, and hospital costs burden communities. Government loses workers through illness, accidents, and early deaths.
bullets: Physical: liver, brain, heart, lungs weaken.
Mental: violence, depression and school failure rise.
Economic: money lost to drugs and treatment.
content.takeaway: Drugs harm body, mind and society while draining family and national wealth.

check.question: Which is a mental or social effect of drug abuse?
check.why: Violence, depression and school failure are common mental and social effects of abuse.

content.heading: Preventing and Treating Drug Abuse
paragraphs: Parents, schools and communities must teach risks early, set rules, and watch peers and friendships. Sports, music, and clubs give youths positive outlets. Counselling can rethink triggers, stress, and pressure before use becomes addiction.

Addicts need medical treatment, rehabilitation centres, spiritual support, and family backing to recover. Law enforcement arrests dealers but must not only punish users. Linking offenders to treatment saves lives and reduces crime.

NAFDAC regulates drugs and checks fake products, while NDLEA fights trafficking and abuse. In Onitsha, Tunde's mother sought counselling and rehabilitation; he supports his family after learning a trade and avoiding old friends.
bullets: Friends and family: talk early, monitor use.
Schools: sports, clubs and drug education.
NDLEA and NAFDAC check supply and sales.
content.takeaway: Education, sports, counselling, treatment and regulation together prevent and cure abuse.

check.question: Which agency fights drug trafficking in Nigeria?
check.why: NDLEA enforces drug laws and fights trafficking, while NAFDAC regulates drug quality.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In essays, separate definitions, effects and prevention clearly. Explain tolerance before listing alcohol, cannabis, codeine, tramadol, shisha, cocaine and heroin, then name NAFDAC and NDLEA for prevention marks.

content.problem: The market trader's son in Onitsha steals to buy codeine and fails school. His mother seeks help. Outline steps to rescue him and protect others.

steps.operation: Counselling at school and clinic to map pressure and cravings
steps.reason: Identifies triggers and builds coping strategies
steps.result: Motivation to stop and relapse plan

steps.operation: Medical treatment and rehabilitation plus family supervision
steps.reason: Treats withdrawal and restores health gradually
steps.result: Tunde withdraws safely and rebuilds routine

steps.operation: Join sports club, learn a trade, avoid drug-using friends
steps.reason: Positive outlets replace drug rewards and peer influence
steps.result: School and business recovery sustained

content.heading: Go deeper: What drug abuse means and how tolerance works
paragraphs: A drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works. Abuse is the use of a drug in a way that harms health or society. Tramadol, codeine and alcohol are drugs in that sense, whether they are prescribed or not.

Tolerance is the need for a larger dose to achieve the same effect. A user who needs more tramadol for the same high has become tolerant, which is why the dose rises over time. That rise is the first sign of dependence.

Dependence is the state in which the body needs the drug to function normally. Withdrawal then produces symptoms when the drug is stopped. Addiction adds a compulsive search for the drug despite harm.
A drug that is taken in increasing doses is a sign of tolerance. That increase is the warning that dependence may follow.
A user who must take more to feel the same high is tolerant. That need is the signal that the body has adapted to the drug.
A drug that is taken in increasing doses is a sign of tolerance. That increase is the warning that dependence may follow.
bullets: Abuse is use that harms health or society
Tolerance: a larger dose for the same effect
Dependence: the body needs the drug; addiction adds compulsion

content.heading: Go deeper: Common drugs and their effects
paragraphs: Stimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine raise heart rate and alertness. Depressants such as alcohol and opioids slow breathing and consciousness.
Hallucinogens such as cannabis distort perception. The class therefore predicts the effect.
Alcohol is the commonest abused drug in Nigeria because it is cheap and socially accepted. It damages the liver, impairs judgment and increases accidents. That acceptance does not make it safe.
Tramadol and codeine are medicines that are abused when they are taken without prescription. Their legal supply does not prevent abuse, which is why prescription control matters.
A depressant that slows breathing can stop it in overdose. That danger is why an overdose of alcohol or opioids is a medical emergency.
A stimulant that raises heart rate can strain the heart. That strain is why a stimulant overdose can cause a heart attack.
A public health nurse who sees those signs can decide that the case is an emergency.
bullets: Stimulants raise alertness; depressants slow breathing
Alcohol damages the liver and impairs judgment
Prescription drugs can be abused without prescription

content.heading: Go deeper: Prevention and the community
paragraphs: Prevention begins with information. A student who knows that tramadol can cause seizures is less likely to take it for the first time. That knowledge is therefore a public health tool.
Treatment needs medical and social care together. A user who is only detoxified but returns to the same peers will relapse, which is why rehabilitation changes the environment as well as the body.
Families and schools therefore matter. Supervision, structured use of time and a route to help are the community defences that make individual resolve possible.
A school that provides structured use of time reduces the idle hours in which drugs are found. That structure is therefore a form of prevention.
A peer that abuses drugs can recruit others. That recruitment is why a community programme must reach peers as well as parents.
A peer that abuses drugs can recruit others. That recruitment is why a community programme must reach peers as well as parents.
A school that provides structured use of time reduces the idle hours in which drugs are found. That structure is therefore a form of prevention.
bullets: Information prevents the first use
Rehabilitation must change the environment as well
Families and schools are the community defences

content.question: What steps would you take if a friend begins abusing tramadol?
hints: Tell a trusted adult early.
Think of counselling and treatment.
Which agencies fight drug abuse?

lessons.title: Pollution, Conservation and National Parks
lessons.objective: Describe pollution types and control, and explain conservation of resources and national parks in Nigeria.

content.heading: Pollution, Conservation and National Parks
paragraphs: Kola farms near Lagos Lagoon and sees empty nets as oil and plastic clog his water. Smoke darkens the mornings. He asks how pollution harms people and how nature can be protected.

content.heading: Types of Pollution and Their Effects
paragraphs: Air pollution comes from smoke, carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2), vehicle exhaust, and generator fumes common in cities. It causes asthma, coughing, and heart problems, while reducing visibility and acidifying rain.

Water pollution comes from sewage, industrial effluent, and oil spills in rivers and lagoons. It kills fish, spreads cholera, and makes water unsafe. Oil films also smother birds and damage mangrove roots.

Land pollution comes from plastics, e-waste, market waste, and dumped chemicals. It blocks drains, breeds mosquitoes, harbours rats, and poisons soils. Children playing near dumps risk infections and heavy-metal exposure.
bullets: Air: smoke, CO, SO2, exhaust, generators.
Water: sewage, effluent, oil spills kill fish.
Land: plastics, e-waste, market waste poison soil.
content.takeaway: Pollution harms health and ecosystems through air, water and land wastes.

check.question: Which gases cause air pollution near generators and vehicles?
check.why: Generators and vehicles release CO and SO2, harming lungs and vegetation.

content.heading: Controlling Pollution in Towns and Industries
paragraphs: Proper sanitation, pit latrines, and sewage treatment stop water contamination. Regulation forces factories to treat effluent before discharge. Clean markets, drains, and water stores prevent cholera and mosquito breeding.

Segregating solid waste into plastics, paper, organics, and e-waste aids composting and recycling. Market sweepings can become compost, while collection crews must clear dumps promptly. Personal hygiene, including hand washing, closes disease routes.

Traps, scrubbers, and filters on chimneys reduce smoke and sulphur gases. Cleaner fuels, vehicle exhaust checks, and tree planting also cut air pollution. Laws and fines, enforced by environmental officers, keep polluters accountable.
bullets: Treat sewage and factory effluent before release.
Segregate waste for composting and recycling.
Use scrubbers, filters and cleaner fuels.
content.takeaway: Treat wastes, segregate solids, trap emissions and enforce hygiene laws.

check.question: Which method recycles market organic waste into useful material?
check.why: Composting turns organic market waste into valuable fertiliser for soils.

content.heading: Conservation, Parks and Protecting Nature
paragraphs: Renewable resources like forests, fisheries, and soils can regrow if managed well. Non-renewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels, including coal and oil, have fixed amounts and cannot easily replace once used.

Conservation protects biodiversity, prevents erosion and desertification, and secures clean water and timber. In the North, shelterbelts, agroforestry, and anti-desertification belts stop wind and shifting sands threatening farms and homes.

The Nigerian Conservation Foundation (NCF), Federal Ministry of Environment, and National Parks Service manage reserves. Internationally, WWF, IUCN, and UNEP support conservation. Parks include Cross River, Gashaka-Gumti, Yankari, Chad Basin, Kainji Lake and Old Oyo.
bullets: Renewable: forests, fisheries, soils regrow.
Non-renewable: minerals, oil, coal exhaust.
Parks: Yankari, Cross River, Old Oyo, Kainji Lake.
content.takeaway: Protect renewables, use non-renewables wisely, and guard parks for future generations.

check.question: Which of these is a national park in Cross River State?
check.why: Cross River National Park lies in Cross River State; Yankari is in Bauchi, Kainji Lake in Niger and Kwara, and Chad Basin in Borno.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn parks with states and products: name Cross River, Gashaka-Gumti, Yankari, Chad Basin, Kainji Lake and Old Oyo. Distinguish renewable forests and fisheries from non-renewable oil and minerals in short definitions.

content.problem: Dust and smoke from a Lagos market dump and factory effluent pollute air and water. Propose pollution control and conservation actions.

steps.operation: Segregate market waste; compost organics and recycle plastics and e-waste
steps.reason: Less dumping, less drain blockage and compost enriches soil
steps.result: Dumps shrink and water contamination falls

steps.operation: Treat factory effluent and fit chimneys with scrubbers and filters
steps.reason: Traps smoke and sulphur gases before release
steps.result: Air and river cleaner

steps.operation: Plant shelterbelts and protect a nearby forest as a reserve
steps.reason: Trees cut wind, bind soil and preserve biodiversity
steps.result: Anti-desertification and habitat protected

content.heading: Go deeper: Pollution and how to control it
paragraphs: Pollution is any harmful substance introduced into the environment. Air pollution from burning, water pollution from sewage and soil pollution from chemicals are the three main forms. Each needs a different control.

Air pollution is controlled by reducing burning and by treating emissions. Water pollution is controlled by treating sewage before it reaches a river. Soil pollution is controlled by safe disposal of chemicals.
Prevention is cheaper than treatment. A factory that treats its waste before discharge pollutes less than one that must be cleaned afterwards, which is why control is set before production.
A river that receives untreated sewage loses its fish. That loss is the visible sign of water pollution, even before a chemical test is done.
A factory that treats its waste before discharge pollutes less. That treatment is why control is set before production, not after.
A river that receives untreated sewage loses its fish. That loss is the visible sign of water pollution, even before a chemical test is done.
A factory that treats its waste before discharge pollutes less. That treatment is why control is set before production, not after.
bullets: Air, water and soil are the three forms of pollution
Treat sewage before it reaches a river
Prevention is cheaper than treatment

content.heading: Go deeper: Conservation and the parks of Nigeria
paragraphs: Conservation protects habitats and species from loss. Cross River and Gashaka-Gumti protect rainforest, Yankari protects savanna and Kainji Lake protects a lake community. Each park guards a different biome.

The Nigerian Conservation Foundation, the Federal Ministry of Environment and the National Parks Service manage those protected areas. Internationally, WWF, IUCN and UNEP support conservation where national resources are short.

Renewable resources such as forests and fisheries can recover if they are protected. Non-renewable resources such as oil and minerals cannot, so their conservation is a question of use rather than recovery.
A park that is guarded keeps its canopy intact. That intact canopy shades the floor and keeps the humidity that the forest needs.
A park that is overrun by farms loses its habitat. That loss is why a guard post matters as much as a law.
A park that is overrun by farms loses its habitat. That loss is why a guard post matters as much as a law.
bullets: Cross River: rainforest; Yankari: savanna; Kainji Lake: lake
NCF, Ministry of Environment and National Parks Service
Renewable can recover; non-renewable cannot

content.heading: Go deeper: Renewable versus non-renewable in practice
paragraphs: A forest is renewable because trees regrow from seeds and stumps. A fishery is renewable because fish breed and the stock recovers. Both therefore need a harvest that leaves enough to regenerate.

Oil and minerals are non-renewable because they formed over millions of years. Once removed, they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime. Their conservation is therefore a question of how fast they are used.
That distinction decides policy. A renewable resource is conserved by limiting the harvest, while a non-renewable one is conserved by using it sparingly and by finding substitutes.
A fishery that is overfished collapses and may not recover. That collapse is why a quota must be set before the stock is low.
A tree that is cut must be replaced by planting. That replacement is what makes a forest renewable, while a mineral has no replacement.
A fishery that is overfished collapses and may not recover. That collapse is why a quota must be set before the stock is low.
bullets: Forests and fisheries recover if harvest is limited
Oil and minerals cannot be replaced in a lifetime
Renewable: limit the harvest; non-renewable: use sparingly

content.question: Which resources would you conserve first in your town, and where would you learn about protected parks?
hints: Separate renewables from non-renewables.
Think of forests, soils and fisheries.
Name one Nigerian park or reserve.

lessons.title: Morphological Variation
lessons.objective: Explain continuous and discontinuous variation, colour variation and fingerprints in populations.

content.heading: Morphological Variation
paragraphs: During morning assembly in Enugu, Chiamaka notices striking differences in skin shade, eye colour and hair texture among classmates. These visible differences prompt the question of how traits are inherited and distributed in a population.

content.heading: Variation and its two patterns
paragraphs: Variation is the presence of differences in characters among individuals of the same species. These differences arise from genetic and environmental influences on developing organisms. In a population, no two individuals are exactly alike in all traits.

Continuous variation shows a smooth range with many intermediates, as seen in human height and weight. When heights are measured and a frequency histogram is plotted, the bars form a bell-shaped curve with most near the average. Very tall and very short pupils occur rarely at the two ends.

Discontinuous variation separates individuals into distinct groups without intermediates. Human blood groups illustrate this pattern because a person has one clear group. Measuring height and weight gives continuous data, whereas blood grouping gives discontinuous data.
bullets: Continuous traits: height, weight and skin shade show gradual gradation.
Discontinuous traits: blood group and fingerprint pattern show separate classes.
Frequency histograms reveal the distribution shape of continuous traits.
content.takeaway: Continuous variation forms a bell curve; discontinuous variation forms distinct groups.

check.question: Which trait is an example of discontinuous variation?
check.why: Blood group falls into distinct types with no intermediates, unlike height and weight which vary continuously.

content.heading: Colour variation and survival
paragraphs: Colour variation means differences in skin, eye and hair colour among humans. Melanin in the skin determines shade, while pigments colour the iris and hair. These differences are inherited and help show that humans of the same species vary visibly.

Animals show similar differences in coat, scales and feathers. Some grasshoppers are green while others are brown, and butterfly wings display many colour patterns. In plants, flower colour and leaf variegation also differ between individuals of one species.

Colour differences often have adaptive value for survival and reproduction. Camouflage hides animals from predators, while bright colours attract pollinators to flowers. Variation therefore allows some individuals to survive better, pass on favourable traits and adapt the population to different habitats.
bullets: Human colour traits: skin shade, eye colour and hair texture differ.
Animal colour traits: coat, scales and feathers aid camouflage and display.
Plant colour examples: flower colour attracts pollinators; leaf patterns aid survival.
content.takeaway: Colour variation helps organisms survive through camouflage, attraction and protection.

check.question: Why is colour variation important for survival in animals?
options: It helps animals camouflage and attract mates
It makes all members look identical
check.why: Colour differences such as camouflage hide animals from predators and bright colours attract pollinators, giving adaptive advantage.

content.heading: Fingerprints and individual identity
paragraphs: Fingerprints are the ridged patterns on the fingertips that develop before birth. The main patterns are arches, loops and whorls, each with finer ridge endings and bifurcations. These patterns form during fetal development and remain stable throughout life.

No two people have identical fingerprints, even though general pattern types are shared. The detailed arrangement of ridges makes every fingerprint unique and permanent. This uniqueness means a print can identify a person reliably after birth.

Fingerprints are used for identity checks, police records and crime detection. A suspect print from a scene can be matched with recorded prints to confirm presence. Identical twins have different fingerprints because development in the womb and environment shape ridge formation.
bullets: Pattern types: arches, loops and whorls are the three main types.
Unique and permanent: each person has a distinct ridge arrangement.
Uses: identity verification, criminal detection and paternity records.
content.takeaway: Fingerprints are unique, permanent and useful for identification and crime detection.

check.question: A fingerprint found at a crime scene can identify a suspect because fingerprints are
check.why: Ridge patterns are unique and stable throughout life, so a match can identify a person.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In examinations, distinguish continuous traits like height, which form a bell curve, from discontinuous traits like blood group, which form separate classes. State an example, describe the pattern and mention that variation comes from genes and environment.

content.problem: A teacher in Lagos measures the heights of 30 pupils in centimetres and wants to decide whether height shows continuous or discontinuous variation and describe the pattern.

steps.operation: Measure and group heights into 5 cm classes, then count pupils per class.
steps.reason: Organising data shows how values are distributed across the population.
steps.result: Counts rise toward the middle classes and fall at both ends.

steps.operation: Plot a frequency histogram with height classes on the x-axis and frequency on the y-axis.
steps.reason: A histogram displays variation shape clearly for comparison.
steps.result: Bars form a bell-shaped curve with a central peak.

steps.operation: Conclude that height is continuous and name the pattern.
steps.reason: A smooth bell curve with intermediates indicates continuous variation.
steps.result: Most pupils cluster near the average height; extremes are rare.

content.heading: Go deeper: Continuous and discontinuous variation
paragraphs: Continuous variation shows a smooth range with many intermediates. Human height is continuous because measurements form a bell-shaped histogram. Very tall and very short pupils occur rarely at the two ends.

Discontinuous variation separates individuals into distinct groups without intermediates. Human blood groups are discontinuous because a person has one clear group. No intermediate blood group exists between A and B.
The two patterns are read from a histogram. A bell curve means continuous, while separated bars with empty gaps mean discontinuous. Height and weight are continuous, blood grouping is discontinuous.
A height that is measured to the centimetre is continuous because the scale is fine. A blood group that is scored as A or B is discontinuous because the scale has no intermediates.
A weight that is recorded to the kilogram is continuous. A blood group that is recorded as A, B, AB or O is discontinuous.
A height that is recorded to the centimetre is continuous. A blood group that is scored as A or B is discontinuous.
bullets: Continuous: smooth range, many intermediates, bell curve
Discontinuous: distinct groups, no intermediates
Height and weight: continuous; blood groups: discontinuous

content.heading: Go deeper: Colour variation and survival
paragraphs: Colour variation can affect survival. A moth that matches the background is less likely to be eaten than one that does not. That difference in survival is natural selection acting on colour.
The same variation is heritable only if its genes are passed on. A moth that survives and breeds passes its colour genes to its offspring. Colour therefore becomes more common in that habitat.
A habitat change can reverse the advantage. When soot darkened trees, dark moths survived better than light ones. Colour is therefore advantageous only in a particular environment.
A moth that is dark in a sooty wood is cryptic, while the same moth in a clean wood is conspicuous. That habitat decides which colour is camouflage.
A moth that is light in a dark wood is conspicuous. That conspicuousness is why its numbers fell when the trees darkened.
A moth that is light in a dark wood is conspicuous. That conspicuousness is why its numbers fell when the trees darkened.
bullets: Colour matching reduces predation
Surviving colour is passed to offspring
Habitat change can reverse the advantage

content.heading: Go deeper: Fingerprints and individual identity
paragraphs: Fingerprints are unique to an individual and stable throughout life. The ridge pattern is formed before birth and does not change with age. That stability is why a fingerprint found at a crime scene can identify a suspect.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints. The pattern is therefore not determined by genes alone, but by genes and the conditions in the womb. That is why it is a true individual mark.
A fingerprint is therefore a record of identity that cannot be changed. A suspect who claims a different name cannot change the ridges on his fingers.
A fingerprint that is found at a scene is compared by its ridges. That comparison is why a fingerprint can identify a person but a blood group can only include him.
