A fingerprint that is damaged by a burn can still be identified. That is why a fingerprint card is taken as soon as possible after an arrest.
A fingerprint that is damaged by a burn can still be identified. That is why a fingerprint card is taken as soon as possible.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints. That difference is why a fingerprint is a true individual mark.
bullets: Fingerprints are unique and stable throughout life
Identical twins have different fingerprints
A fingerprint match can identify a person

content.question: How would you test whether skin shade in your class shows continuous or discontinuous variation?
hints: Measure shade using a simple scale
Plot a frequency histogram
Look for a bell curve or distinct groups

lessons.title: Physiological Variation and Applications
lessons.objective: Explain tongue rolling, PTC tasting, blood groups and their applications in medicine and forensics.

content.heading: Physiological Variation and Applications
paragraphs: At a science fair in Ibadan, Adaeze demonstrates tongue rolling and PTC tasting and records splits in her class. Some pupils succeed while others fail, raising questions about inherited traits and practical uses.

content.heading: Tongue rolling and PTC tasting
paragraphs: Tongue rolling is the ability to curl the sides of the tongue upward into a roll. The ability runs in families and is often treated as a simple inherited trait in school surveys, although it is not a reliable single-gene character. Most people are rollers or non-rollers, but some can learn the movement.

PTC tasting is the ability to detect the bitter chemical phenylthiocarbamide, often supplied as paper. Tasters perceive intense bitterness while non-tasters taste little or nothing. The difference is strongly inherited, mainly through one taste-receptor gene, but the divide is not perfectly sharp.

A class survey can categorise pupils into tasters and non-tasters. The frequencies are recorded in a table to compare numbers and discuss inheritance patterns. Such practical work reinforces how physiological traits vary clearly within a population in Nigeria today.
bullets: Tongue rolling: family tendency, discontinuous and sometimes learned.
PTC tasting: bitterness detection strongly inherited, with tasters and non-tasters.
Class survey: tally tasters and non-tasters for frequency comparison.
content.takeaway: Tongue rolling and PTC tasting separate people into groups, mainly through inheritance.

check.question: What does a PTC tasting survey show?
options: Distinct groups of tasters and non-tasters
check.why: PTC tasting is inherited and discontinuous, so pupils separate into tasters and non-tasters.

content.heading: Blood groups and inheritance
paragraphs: Blood groups are determined by antigens on red blood cells and antibodies in plasma. The ABO system has types A, B, AB and O, each defined by antigen combination. The Rhesus system depends on the presence or absence of Rhesus factor.

Antibodies react against antigens not present in the body, which informs inheritance and compatibility. A person with type A blood has A antigens but anti-B antibodies. This matching of antigens and antibodies explains why groups differ between individuals.

Blood groups differ because genes control antigen production and antibody formation. Inherited genes from parents determine the group passed to offspring. Understanding these differences helps explain variation that is discontinuous and measurable by simple tests.
bullets: ABO groups: A, B, AB and O defined by antigens and antibodies.
Rhesus groups: Rh positive has factor; Rh negative lacks factor.
Inheritance: parental genes determine offspring blood group.
content.takeaway: Antigens and antibodies determine blood groups, which are inherited discontinuously.

check.question: What determines a person's ABO blood group?
check.why: ABO type depends on antigens present and matching antibodies, controlled by inherited genes.

content.heading: Applications in medicine and forensics
paragraphs: Blood transfusion requires matching donor and recipient blood groups to avoid harmful reactions. Transfusing incompatible blood can cause antibodies to attack donor cells. Correct matching therefore saves lives and shows practical use of blood group variation.

Blood groups also assist paternity determination when inheritance rules exclude a proposed father. If a child has a group impossible from the mother and alleged father, that man cannot be the father. DNA profiles now confirm such evidence with higher precision.

Crime detection uses discontinuous traits such as blood groups, fingerprints and DNA. Bloodstain left at a scene can link a suspect to the location. Fingerprints and DNA provide individual profiles that identify offenders more reliably than general features like height alone.
bullets: Transfusion: donor and recipient groups must be compatible.
Paternity: incompatible inheritance excludes proposed father.
Forensics: blood, fingerprints and DNA identify suspects.
content.takeaway: Blood groups aid transfusion, paternity testing and crime detection.

check.question: Why is blood group matching important before transfusion?
options: To avoid antibody attack on donor cells
To change the recipient blood group
check.why: Incompatible antigens and antibodies cause harmful reactions, so donor and recipient must be compatible.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In examinations, link tongue rolling and PTC tasting to genetic inheritance and blood groups to antigens and antibodies. Mention applications such as transfusion, paternity and crime detection to secure full application marks.

content.problem: A hospital in Kano receives blood from an alleged father, mother and child and must test whether the alleged father could be the biological father.

steps.operation: Determine the blood groups of the mother, alleged father and child.
steps.reason: Genes control antigens, so inheritance rules predict possible child groups.
steps.result: Groups are recorded and compared with inheritance possibilities.

steps.operation: Check whether the child's group can arise from those parents.
steps.reason: Discontinuous blood groups follow clear inheritance patterns.
steps.result: The child's group is impossible from that pair of parents.

steps.operation: Conclude that the alleged father is excluded and suggest DNA testing.
steps.reason: Exclusion by blood group is evidence; DNA gives stronger confirmation.
steps.result: The man cannot be the father; DNA profiling confirms the result.

content.heading: Go deeper: Tongue rolling, PTC and earlobes
paragraphs: Tongue rolling was once taught as a single dominant gene. That teaching is now known to be wrong, because many people can learn to roll their tongue and some who should roll it cannot. The trait is therefore not a simple Mendelian pair.

PTC tasting was also taught as a single gene. It is in fact influenced by several genes and by experience, so a parent and child can differ in a way that contradicts a simple ratio. That contradiction is the proof that the simple model fails.
Earlobes were taught the same way, with attached and free as a dominant pair. Pedigrees show that the trait is developmentally variable, so it cannot be used for a simple paternity test.
A family that has a roller and a non-roller can therefore contradict a simple ratio. That contradiction is the evidence that the trait is not a single gene.
A pedigree that shows a roller with a non-roller parent contradicts the simple model. That contradiction is the evidence that the trait is not inherited that way.
A pedigree that shows a roller with a non-roller parent contradicts the simple model. That contradiction is the evidence that the trait is not inherited that way.
bullets: Tongue rolling is not a single dominant gene
PTC tasting is polygenic, not a simple Mendelian pair
Earlobes are developmentally variable

content.heading: Go deeper: Blood groups and transfusion
paragraphs: Blood groups are determined by antigens on red cells and antibodies in plasma. ABO has four groups and Rhesus has two, so eight combinations are possible. A transfusion must match both.

A person with group O has no A or B antigens, so his cells can be given to anyone. A person with group AB has both antigens, so his plasma can be given to anyone. Those two groups are universal donors in opposite directions.
A Rhesus-negative mother who carries a Rhesus-positive fetus can become sensitised. That sensitisation can damage a later pregnancy, which is why the Rhesus factor is tested in antenatal care.
A Rhesus-positive father and a Rhesus-negative mother can have a Rhesus-positive child. That child is the one who sensitises the mother, which is why the first pregnancy is usually safe.
A group O donor can give cells to anyone. That is why group O is called the universal donor in transfusion.
A group O donor can give cells to anyone. That is why group O is called the universal donor in transfusion.
bullets: ABO: four groups; Rhesus: two
Group O cells to anyone; group AB plasma to anyone
Rhesus sensitisation can damage a later pregnancy

content.heading: Go deeper: Forensic and paternity uses
paragraphs: A paternity test compares the blood groups of child, mother and alleged father. A child must carry one group from the mother and one from the father. A man who cannot supply the child's group is excluded.
That exclusion is reliable only for blood groups that are truly inherited. Tongue rolling and earlobes cannot be used because they are not single genes. Blood groups can be used because they are.
Forensic uses are similar. A blood stain at a scene can be grouped, and the group compared with suspects. A mismatch excludes, while a match only includes, because many people share a group.
A blood group that is shared by many people includes many suspects. That is why a forensic match is evidence but not proof, while an exclusion is proof.
A paternity test that excludes a man is conclusive. That is why it is stronger evidence than a match that merely includes him.
bullets: A child carries one group from each parent
Blood groups exclude; tongue rolling and earlobes cannot
A forensic match includes but does not prove

content.question: How could you use blood groups to investigate a claim of paternity?
hints: Find ABO groups of parents
Apply inheritance rules
Check for impossible combinations

lessons.title: Genes, Chromosomes and Heritable Characters
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will explain heritable characters, genes and alleles, and how chromosomes carry genetic information.

content.heading: Genes, Chromosomes and Heritable Characters
paragraphs: Aminu in Kano discovers he has his mother's tall stature and dark eyes, while his elder brother's deep dimples match their father. At a family gathering, such characteristics spark debate about inherited and acquired traits.

content.heading: Heritable and Non-Heritable Characters
paragraphs: A heritable character passes from parents to offspring through genes. Examples include eye colour, blood group and albinism. A non-heritable character develops during life, such as a scar or a hairstyle.

Muscles built by exercise are non-heritable. Even strong training cannot alter the genes inside your gametes. Children of a weightlifter therefore start with ordinary muscles and improve only with their own practice.

Farmers in Zaria select maize for the same inherited resistance. They keep seeds only from plants that repeatedly resist drought. A tree trained to bear sweet fruit will not produce genetically sweeter seedlings.
bullets: Heritable: eye colour, blood group, dimples
Non-heritable: scar, plaited hairstyle, trained muscles
Test: if children share it across generations, it is likely heritable
content.takeaway: Heritable traits follow family patterns; non-heritable traits are acquired during life.

check.question: Which of these is a non-heritable character?
check.why: A scar is acquired during life and cannot be passed through gametes. Blood group, eye colour and dimples are heritable.

content.heading: Genes, Alleles and DNA
paragraphs: Inside almost every cell, DNA forms a double helix like a twisted ladder. The rails are sugar and phosphate, while paired bases form the rungs, with A pairing with T and G with C. A gene is a section of this DNA that codes for one protein.

All forms of one gene are called alleles. For height, the allele T may code for tallness and t for shortness. Two identical alleles make an organism homozygous, while two different alleles make it heterozygous.
A homozygous tall plant can only give T to its children. A heterozygous tall plant gives T or t each time. This simple difference explains why some crosses produce only tall offspring.
bullets: Gene: DNA section coding for a character
Alleles: different forms, e.g. T and t
Homozygous TT; heterozygous Tt
content.takeaway: Genes are DNA sections; alleles are their alternative forms in homozygous or heterozygous states.

check.question: In DNA, adenine pairs with
check.why: Adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine, held by hydrogen bonds.

content.heading: Chromosomes, Meiosis and Fertilisation
paragraphs: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes in their nuclei. Each chromosome has a centromere, the pinched region where sister chromatids are joined and spindle fibres attach. During cell division, sister chromatids or whole chromosomes move to opposite poles.

Gametes contain only 23 chromosomes, half the body number. Meiosis separates homologous chromosomes so that each gamete carries one of each pair. Crossing-over between homologous chromosomes swaps sections and creates new allele combinations.

At fertilisation, the two sets of 23 chromosomes join again to make 46. Because the pairs separate randomly, each gamete carries a new combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Offspring are therefore genetically different from one another.
bullets: 46 chromosomes in body cells; 23 in gametes
Centromere joins chromatids and directs movement
Meiosis separates homologues; crossing-over reshuffles alleles
content.takeaway: Meiosis halves chromosome number; fertilisation restores it with a new random mix.

check.question: How many chromosomes are present in a human gamete?
check.why: Gametes are haploid with half the diploid number. Body cells have 46, so gametes have 23.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Examiners often ask for the difference between homozygous and heterozygous. Remember: homozygous means two identical alleles like TT; heterozygous means two different alleles like Tt; in both cases the visible character may look alike.

content.problem: A student in Lagos crosses a homozygous tall pea plant (TT) with a homozygous short plant (tt). What is seen in the first generation?

steps.operation: Write the gametes of each parent
steps.reason: Each parent gives only one allele to the child
steps.result: TT parent gives T; tt parent gives t

steps.operation: Combine the gametes in all zygotes
steps.reason: Fertilisation joins one maternal and one paternal allele
steps.result: All children have genotype Tt

steps.operation: State the phenotype of the F1 generation
steps.reason: T codes for tallness and dominates t
steps.result: All F1 plants are tall, heterozygous

content.heading: Go deeper: Heritable and non-heritable characters
paragraphs: A heritable character is determined by genes and passed through gametes. Blood group, eye colour and dimples are heritable because they appear in pedigrees. A scar is not heritable because it is acquired during life and cannot be passed through gametes.

Environment can modify a heritable character without changing its genes. Height is heritable, but malnutrition makes a person shorter. That modification is not passed on, which is why it is not inheritance.

The distinction is therefore between the genotype that is inherited and the phenotype that is seen. A scar has no genotype, while a short height has a genotype that is expressed in a poor environment.
A dimple is heritable because it appears in pedigrees. A scar from an accident is not, because it cannot be passed through gametes to a child.
A character that is acquired by training is not heritable. A scar, a tattoo and a trained skill therefore cannot be passed to a child.
A dimple is heritable because it appears in pedigrees. A scar from an accident is not, because it cannot be passed through gametes to a child.
bullets: Heritable: blood group, eye colour, dimples
Non-heritable: scars and acquired marks
Height is heritable but modified by nutrition

content.heading: Go deeper: Genes, alleles and DNA
paragraphs: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. An allele is an alternative form of that gene. A plant with genotype Tt is heterozygous because it carries two different alleles for height.
DNA pairs adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine. That base pairing is how DNA is copied, because each strand can serve as a template for the other. A mutation is a change in that sequence.
A homozygous plant can only give one allele to its children, while a heterozygous plant can give either. That difference explains why some crosses produce only tall offspring and others produce both.
A gene that is changed by mutation becomes a new allele. That new allele can then be selected if it improves survival, which is how variation grows.
A DNA sequence that is changed by a mutation can produce a different protein. That change is therefore the ultimate source of new alleles.
A DNA sequence that is changed by a mutation can produce a different protein. That change is therefore the ultimate source of new alleles.
bullets: Adenine pairs with thymine; guanine with cytosine
Tt is heterozygous; TT and tt are homozygous
Heterozygous parents can give either allele

content.heading: Go deeper: Chromosomes, meiosis and crossing over
paragraphs: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Gametes contain only 23, one from each pair. That halving is meiosis, and it ensures that fertilisation restores the diploid number.

Crossing over between homologous chromosomes swaps sections and creates new allele combinations. Independent assortment also creates new combinations by the random separation of pairs. Those two processes together produce variation in gametes.
A gamete therefore carries a new combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Offspring are therefore genetically different even when they share the same parents.
Meiosis also halves the chromosome number in the formation of gametes. That halving is why a child has 46 and not 92 chromosomes.
A gamete that carries a new combination of chromosomes is a new genotype. That is why siblings are different even when they share the same parents.
A gamete that carries a new combination of chromosomes is a new genotype. That is why siblings are different even when they share the same parents.
bullets: Body cells 46; gametes 23
Meiosis separates homologues; crossing over reshuffles alleles
Fertilisation restores 46 with a new random mix

content.question: Your friend says the child of a tall heterozygous plant always inherits tallness. What gametes could that plant produce?
hints: Look at its genotype.
Write its possible gametes.
Consider if the child is short.

lessons.title: Genetic Crosses and Probability
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will interpret monohybrid and dihybrid Punnett squares and use probability to explain observed ratios.

content.heading: Genetic Crosses and Probability
paragraphs: Adaobi in Apapa starts a science fair project with pea seeds from her market. She remembers her teacher's warning about unexpected results. Her classmates laugh when she predicts tall and short plants from crossed seeds.

content.heading: Monohybrid Cross and the F2 Ratio
paragraphs: A Punnett square in words lists gametes across the top and down the side. For TT x tt, put T and T across the top and t and t down the side. Each box gives a child genotype.

All four boxes contain Tt, so every F1 child is heterozygous tall. This uniform first generation shows that the tall allele dominates. Self-fertilise the F1 plants Tt x Tt to produce the F2 generation.
For Tt x Tt, use T and t across the top and down the side. Boxes are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. Phenotype ratio is three tall to one short.
bullets: F1: all Tt, tall phenotype
F2 genotype: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt
F2 phenotype: 3 tall : 1 short
content.takeaway: A monohybrid cross reveals dominant and recessive phenotypes in the F2 ratio.

check.question: In a Tt x Tt cross, how many of the four boxes are tt?
check.why: Only one box contains tt, the recessive homozygote. The others are TT, Tt and Tt, all phenotypically tall.

content.heading: Dihybrid Cross and the 9:3:3:1 Ratio
paragraphs: A dihybrid cross follows two characters at once, usually on different chromosomes. For shape and colour, let R be round and r wrinkled, Y yellow and y green. The parent RrYy makes four gamete types: RY, Ry, rY, ry.

Draw a 4x4 Punnett square in words with the four gametes across the top and down the side. Sixteen boxes show all possible children. Count the phenotypes: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green.

The phenotypic ratio is nine to three to three to one. Each character follows the monohybrid ratio independently within the square. This pattern fits independent assortment when the two gene pairs are on different chromosomes, though the ratio alone does not prove it.
bullets: 16 boxes for a 4x4 dihybrid square
Phenotypes: 9 round yellow, 3 round green
3 wrinkled yellow, 1 wrinkled green
content.takeaway: Dihybrid crosses combine two monohybrid ratios into the nine-three-three-one pattern.

check.question: How many boxes are in a dihybrid Punnett square for two heterozygous parents?
check.why: Each parent makes four gamete types, giving four times four boxes. The phenotypic ratio is nine-three-three-one.

content.heading: Probability, Chi-Square and Family Size
paragraphs: Probability predicts ratios, but actual results vary with chance. A chi-square test compares observed numbers with expected numbers to judge if the deviation is accidental. A small chi-square value suggests the data fit the expected ratio.

In a real maize experiment, you might count 760 tall and 240 short plants. Expected 750 and 250 fits well, so the 3 to 1 hypothesis is supported. A large discrepancy would question the hypothesis or suggest counting error.

Observed ratios become unreliable in small families because each birth is a separate chance event. Two heterozygous parents can have four tall children without breaking the rule. Only large numbers reveal the real probability.
bullets: Expected = predicted from ratio for total
Chi-square: sum (observed-expected)² / expected
Small families give erratic, misleading ratios
content.takeaway: Probability predicts ratios, but chance and small samples distort observed results.

check.question: Why can a family with four children not prove a 3 to 1 ratio?
check.why: Small samples allow large chance variations. Probability is reliable only in large numbers of offspring.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Remember to state both genotype and phenotype ratios for crosses. For a monohybrid F2, write one TT to two Tt to one tt for genotype and three tall to one short for phenotype.

content.problem: A farmer in Ibadan crosses heterozygous watermelons (RrYy x RrYy). What proportion are round and yellow?

steps.operation: List the four gametes of each parent
steps.reason: Each parent is heterozygous for two characters
steps.result: RY, Ry, rY, ry

steps.operation: Count boxes that are round and yellow
steps.reason: Round and yellow require dominant alleles R and Y
steps.result: Nine of the sixteen boxes

steps.reason: Probability equals favourable outcomes over total
steps.result: 9/16 or 56.25 per cent

content.heading: Go deeper: The monohybrid cross and the F2 ratio
paragraphs: A monohybrid cross follows one character. In a Tt by Tt cross, the Punnett square has four boxes: TT, Tt, Tt and tt. The phenotypic ratio is therefore three tall to one short.

The four boxes are equally likely because each parent makes T and t gametes in equal numbers. Random union of those gametes therefore gives each box the same chance. Probability is the counting of equally likely outcomes.
A chi-square test checks whether an observed ratio fits the expected one. A large deviation means the expected ratio is unlikely, while a small deviation is consistent with it.
A Punnett square that is drawn for a Tt by TT cross has all tall offspring. That result is therefore a test cross even when it is not named as one.
A ratio that is close to three to one is consistent with the expected one. A ratio that is far from it is not, which is how chi-square is read.
A ratio that is close to three to one is consistent with the expected one. A ratio that is far from it is not.
bullets: Tt by Tt: three tall to one short
Each gamete is equally likely
Chi-square tests the fit of observed to expected

content.heading: Go deeper: The dihybrid cross and 9:3:3:1
paragraphs: A dihybrid cross follows two characters at once. For shape and colour, let R be round and Y yellow. The parent RrYy makes four gamete types: RY, Ry, rY and ry.
The phenotypic ratio is nine to three to three to one. Each character follows the monohybrid ratio independently within the square. That independence is the pattern of independent assortment.
That pattern fits independent assortment when the gene pairs are on different chromosomes, though the ratio alone does not prove it. A single ratio cannot prove that the genes are unlinked.
A Punnett square that is drawn for a dihybrid cross has sixteen boxes. That sixteen is therefore the number of equally likely outcomes in a dihybrid cross.
A ratio that is close to nine to three to three to one fits independent assortment. A ratio that is far from it does not.
A ratio that is close to nine to three to three to one fits independent assortment. That fit does not prove the genes are unlinked.
bullets: RrYy makes RY, Ry, rY and ry
Phenotypic ratio nine to three to three to one
The ratio fits but does not prove unlinked genes

content.heading: Go deeper: Probability and the test cross
paragraphs: Probability decides the chance of an outcome before it is seen. A child of two heterozygotes has one chance in four of being tt, which is why families with short parents can have tall children. The chance is independent of previous children.

A test cross mates an unknown genotype with a recessive homozygote. If the unknown is TT, all offspring are tall; if it is Tt, half are tall and half are short. The ratio therefore reveals the genotype.
Probability therefore works backward as well as forward. A ratio of one to one in a test cross proves the parent was heterozygous, which is how the genotype is determined.
A test cross that gives all tall offspring proves the parent was TT. A test cross that gives half tall proves it was Tt, which is how the genotype is determined.
A probability that is one in four does not guarantee one in four children. That is why a family with three sons can still have a daughter next.
bullets: Each conception is independent of previous ones
Test cross: all tall means TT; half tall means Tt
A one-to-one ratio proves heterozygosity

content.question: A cross gives 140 tall and 40 short plants. Expected for 180 plants is 135 and 45. Does the data fit?
hints: Calculate the expected ratio.
Compare observed with expected.
Consider chi-square idea.

lessons.title: Sex Determination and Sex-Linked Traits
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will explain XX and XY sex determination and how X-linked traits pass through families.

content.heading: Sex Determination and Sex-Linked Traits
paragraphs: Chinedu in Jos met his newborn cousin, a girl born to anxious parents who hoped for a boy. The family grandmother explains why each birth brings surprise. Their questions begin a lesson on sex determination.

content.heading: XX and XY Sex Determination
paragraphs: Human females have two X chromosomes, XX. Human males have one X and one Y chromosome, XY. The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene that directs male development.
A female always gives an X to her children in the egg. A male gives either an X or a Y in the sperm. The sperm therefore determines the child sex.
Each conception has a 50 per cent chance of XX or XY. This probability is independent of previous children. Families with three sons can still have a daughter next.
bullets: Female XX: all eggs carry X
Male XY: sperm carry X or Y
Result: 50 per cent XX, 50 per cent XY
content.takeaway: Sex is decided at fertilisation by whether the sperm carries X or Y.

check.question: Which parent determines the child sex?
options: Mother, because she carries the baby
Father, because his sperm carries X or Y
check.why: Mothers always give X, but fathers give X or Y depending on the sperm. The sperm type decides XX or XY.

content.heading: X-Linked Traits in Males and Females
paragraphs: Some traits are carried on the X chromosome. Haemophilia, a bleeding disorder, and red-green colour blindness are X-linked and recessive. A woman must carry two faulty copies to show fully.
Because males have only one X, one faulty copy makes them show the trait. A carrier mother passes the faulty X to half her sons. This explains why more males are colour-blind or haemophilic.

Baldness is different: it is a sex-influenced trait, not an X-linked one. Male-pattern baldness is polygenic and depends on hormones such as testosterone, so it appears far more often in men. A family history raises the chance, but no single dominant gene decides it.
bullets: Colour blindness: X recessive, commoner in males
Haemophilia: X recessive, bleeding disorder
Baldness: sex-influenced, hormone-dependent and commoner in men
content.takeaway: X-linked recessive traits affect more males; baldness is sex-influenced and hormone-dependent.

check.question: Why are X-linked recessive disorders commoner in males?
options: Males have two faulty X copies
Males have only one X chromosome
check.why: A single faulty X in a male shows fully. A female needs two faulty copies, so she is usually only a carrier.

content.heading: Reading Pedigrees
paragraphs: A pedigree is a family tree drawn in words with symbols. Circles are females, squares are males, and filled symbols show the trait. Draw parents at the top and children beneath them.

To trace a dominant trait, look for it appearing in every generation. To trace a recessive trait, look for unaffected parents producing an affected child. Horizontal lines join couples, while vertical lines drop to children.

Skip generations suggest recessive inheritance, as the trait hides in carriers. A filled circle with unfilled brothers supports this pattern. Careful counting of filled and unfilled symbols clarifies the mode of inheritance.
bullets: Circles female, squares male, filled affected
Dominant: appears every generation
Recessive: skips generations, hidden in carriers
content.takeaway: Pedigrees use symbols to reveal whether a trait is dominant or recessive.

check.question: Unaffected parents have an affected child. What does this suggest?
check.why: Both parents hide the recessive allele as carriers. Their child inherits two copies and shows the trait.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Males receive their X only from their mother and Y only from their father. This single fact explains sex determination and why X-linked recessive traits affect mostly sons in pedigrees.

content.problem: A colour-blind woman (XcXc) marries a normal-sighted man (XCY). What are the risks to their sons and daughters?

steps.operation: List the gametes of both parents
steps.reason: Mother gives Xc; father gives XC or Y
steps.result: Sons get XcY; daughters get XCXc

steps.reason: Sons have only one X, which is faulty
steps.result: All sons are colour-blind

steps.reason: Daughters have one normal and one faulty X
steps.result: All daughters are carriers but sighted

content.heading: Go deeper: XX and XY sex determination
paragraphs: Human females have two X chromosomes, XX. Human males have one X and one Y, XY. The Y carries the SRY gene that directs male development, so its presence decides the sex.

Each conception has a 50 per cent chance of XX or XY because the father makes X and Y sperm in equal numbers. That probability is independent of previous children. Families with three sons can still have a daughter next.
Sex is therefore decided by the sperm, not by the egg. Every egg carries an X, so the father's gamete decides whether the child is XX or XY.
A child who is XX is female and a child who is XY is male. That assignment is made at fertilisation by the sperm that arrives first.
A Y chromosome that lacks SRY cannot direct male development. That child therefore develops as female, which shows that SRY is the deciding gene.
A Y chromosome that lacks SRY cannot direct male development. That child therefore develops as female.
bullets: XX female; XY male; SRY directs male development
50 per cent XX, 50 per cent XY each conception
The sperm decides the sex

content.heading: Go deeper: X-linked traits in males and females
paragraphs: Haemophilia and red-green colour blindness are X-linked and recessive. A male has one X, so one faulty copy makes him affected. A female needs two faulty copies to be fully affected.
A carrier female has one faulty copy and can pass it to her sons. Half her sons will be affected and half her daughters will be carriers. That is why haemophilia appears through carrier mothers.
A father gives his X to his daughters and his Y to his sons. That is why a daughter of an affected father is always a carrier, while a son of an affected father is never one.
A carrier who is a woman can have a son who is affected. That son therefore has a 50 per cent chance of haemophilia from each conception.
A daughter of an affected father is always a carrier. That certainty is why an affected father cannot have a daughter who is not a carrier.
A daughter of an affected father is always a carrier. That certainty is why an affected father cannot have a daughter who is not a carrier.
bullets: X-linked recessive: males affected with one copy
Carrier mothers pass it to half their sons
A father gives X to daughters, Y to sons

content.heading: Go deeper: Baldness and sex-influenced inheritance
paragraphs: Male-pattern baldness is not a simple dominant gene. It is polygenic, androgen-dependent and sex-influenced, so it is expressed differently in men and women. A woman can carry the genes without being bald.
That model replaces the older teaching of a dominant gene that anticipates. Baldness does not skip a generation in the way a simple dominant would, and it does not require two genes in women.
Pedigrees therefore show a pattern that follows the father to his sons and a milder pattern in women. That pattern is the evidence for sex influence rather than sex linkage.
A bald man can have a daughter who carries the genes but is not bald. That daughter can then have a bald son, which is why baldness appears to skip women.
A woman who is bald must carry more baldness genes than a man who is bald. That threshold difference is the meaning of sex influence.
A woman who is bald must carry more baldness genes than a man who is bald. That threshold difference is the meaning of sex influence.
bullets: Baldness is polygenic and sex-influenced, not X-linked
Men express it more readily than women
Pedigrees show father-to-son transmission

content.question: In a pedigree, a trait appears only in males and passes from father to son. What inheritance is likely?
hints: Check the father's contribution.
Is it on the X or Y?
Does it skip generations?

lessons.title: Heredity in Practice
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will describe how heredity improves crops, livestock, preventive medicine and biotechnology.

content.heading: Heredity in Practice
paragraphs: Emeka in Zaria visits a cattle market with his father to buy a bull with strong resistance to trypanosomiasis. The seller praises cross-bred animals. Emeka wonders how breeders use heredity for better crops and livestock.

content.heading: Heredity in Crop and Livestock Breeding
paragraphs: Cross-breeding mates individuals from different varieties to produce new breeds. Crossing two maize varieties in Rigachikun can combine drought resistance and high yield. Offspring may show hybrid vigour in the first generation.

In-breeding mates close relatives to secure desired characters. It makes the herd more uniform but can expose harmful recessive genes. Out-breeding brings in fresh genes and is often used to refresh tired lines.

Farmers must balance vigour against uniformity when improving livestock. N'Dama cattle tolerate trypanosomiasis well, so purebred N'Dama can be more resistant than many crosses; crossing is used for other traits but can dilute this tolerance. Maintaining true breeds, however, protects genetic diversity for future breeding.
bullets: Cross-breeding: new varieties, hybrid vigour
In-breeding: uniformity but exposes defects
Out-breeding: fresh genes, restores vigour
content.takeaway: Cross-breeding refreshes stock; in-breeding fixes type but may reveal weaknesses.

check.question: Which is a disadvantage of long-term in-breeding?
check.why: Close mating makes recessive defects homozygous. Cross-breeding with unrelated stock can hide them and restore vigour.

content.heading: Heredity in Marriage and Pregnancy Care
paragraphs: Pregnancy counselling uses blood grouping and genotype tests before marriage. Knowing both partners’ sickle-cell genotype AS or SS helps predict child risks. AS carriers are healthy, while SS children suffer sickle-cell anaemia.
If two AS partners marry, each child has one in four risk of SS. Counsellors explain these odds without forcing choices. Early diagnosis now allows better care and reduces deaths from crises.

Rhesus factor also matters for newborn jaundice. A Rhesus-negative mother carrying a Rhesus-positive baby may form antibodies that attack later pregnancies. Hospitals give anti-D injections to prevent this damage.
bullets: AS x AS: 25 % SS, 50 % AS
Rhesus-negative mother needs anti-D injection
Genotype screening protects child health
content.takeaway: Blood, genotype and Rhesus tests guide families to plan healthy pregnancies.

check.question: A couple are both AS. What is the chance their child is SS?
check.why: AS x AS gives 1 in 4 SS. Each conception is independent, so past children do not change the chance.

content.heading: Genetic Modification and Medical Products
paragraphs: Genetic modification inserts a selected gene into a foreign host. Scientists obtained human insulin by placing the human gene into E coli. Fermenters now produce insulin instead of relying on pigs.

Recombinant DNA also makes interferon against viruses and enzymes for industry. Gene therapy aims to cure faulty genes by adding correct copies to patient cells. Trials must prove safety before hospitals can use these treatments.

Biosafety rules stop engineered organisms escaping. Laboratories use sealed fermenters and track every modified sample. Regulation balances medical benefit with protection of health and environment, but ethical debate asks whether modifying human genes is acceptable, who owns modified organisms, and who can afford the products.
bullets: E. coli produces human insulin widely
Interferon and enzymes made by recombinant DNA
Containment and regulation ensure biosafety
content.takeaway: Gene technology supplies drugs, but strict safety controls protect the public.

check.question: Which products can be made using recombinant DNA?
check.why: Recombinant microbes can make insulin, interferon and enzymes, and the same technology supports vaccines and gene therapy.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Note AS and SS correctly in counselling questions today. AS carriers look healthy, SS shows sickle-cell anaemia. Also recall that Rhesus-negative mothers receive anti-D to protect newborns well.

steps.operation: Draw AS x AS Punnett in words
steps.reason: Each gives A or S to children
steps.result: Boxes AA, AS, AS, SS

steps.reason: Only the homozygous recessive box is affected
steps.result: One of four boxes

steps.reason: One favourable box over four total
steps.result: 25 per cent SS risk

content.heading: Go deeper: Cross-breeding, in-breeding and out-breeding
paragraphs: Cross-breeding mates individuals from different varieties to produce new breeds. Crossing two maize varieties can combine drought resistance and high yield. Offspring may show hybrid vigour in the first generation.

In-breeding mates close relatives to secure desired characters. It makes the herd more uniform but can expose harmful recessive genes. Out-breeding brings in fresh genes and is often used to refresh tired lines.

Farmers must balance vigour against uniformity. N'Dama cattle tolerate trypanosomiasis well, so purebred N'Dama can be more resistant than many crosses; crossing is used for other traits but can dilute that tolerance.
A cross-bred maize that shows hybrid vigour yields more in the first generation. That vigour fades in the second, which is why seed must be bought fresh each year.
An in-bred line that is uniform can still be crossed to restore vigour. That restoration is why in-breeding and out-breeding are used together.
A cross-bred maize that shows hybrid vigour yields more in the first generation. That vigour fades in the second, which is why seed must be bought fresh.
bullets: Cross-breeding: new varieties, hybrid vigour
In-breeding: uniformity but exposes defects
Out-breeding: fresh genes, restores vigour

content.heading: Go deeper: Heredity in marriage and pregnancy care
paragraphs: Sickle-cell disease is caused by a recessive allele that is carried silently by heterozygotes. Two carriers can have an affected child, so counselling before marriage can reveal that risk. That is why genotype testing is offered at premarital clinics.

Rhesus incompatibility is a blood factor that can damage a fetus. A Rhesus-negative mother who carries a Rhesus-positive fetus can become sensitised. Antenatal care therefore tests the Rhesus factor in pregnancy.
Genetic counselling does not forbid marriage. It gives a couple the information to decide, which is why it is offered as advice rather than as a rule.
A carrier of sickle-cell who marries a non-carrier cannot have an affected child. That is why a premarital test can give assurance as well as warning.
A Rhesus-negative mother who is given anti-D after birth will not become sensitised. That injection is why a second pregnancy can be safe.
A carrier of sickle-cell who marries a non-carrier cannot have an affected child. That is why a premarital test can give assurance as well as warning.
bullets: Sickle-cell: recessive; two carriers can have an affected child
Rhesus factor is tested in antenatal care
Counselling gives information to decide

content.heading: Go deeper: Genetic modification and medical products
paragraphs: Genetic modification inserts a gene from one organism into another. Human insulin is made by bacteria that carry the human gene. That insulin is identical to the human hormone and does not provoke allergy.

Recombinant microbes can make insulin, interferon and industrial enzymes. The same technology supports vaccines and gene therapy. A product can therefore be made in a vat rather than harvested from an animal.

Regulation balances medical benefit with protection of health and environment. Ethical debate asks whether modifying human genes is acceptable, who owns modified organisms and who can afford the products.
Human insulin that is made in a vat is identical to the hormone in the body. That identity is why it does not provoke allergy in the way animal insulin did.
A gene that is inserted into a bacterium is copied with it. That copying is why a vat can make a large quantity of the product.
Human insulin that is made in a vat is identical to the hormone in the body. That identity is why it does not provoke allergy in the way animal insulin did.
bullets: Bacteria with the human gene make human insulin
Recombinant microbes make interferon and enzymes
Ethics: human genes, ownership and affordability

content.question: A cattle breeder wants disease resistance. Should she cross-breed or in-breed? Explain.
hints: Recall hybrid vigour.
Consider resistance outcome.
Check risks of defects.

lessons.title: Biotechnology and Its Applications
lessons.objective: At the end of this lesson, learners can define biotechnology and give examples of its agricultural, medical, pharmaceutical and food-industrial applications.

content.heading: Biotechnology and Its Applications
paragraphs: In a small farm near Jos, a young farmer watches her maize wither from stem borers. She wonders if there is a safer way to protect her harvest and feed her family.

content.heading: Biotechnology in Agriculture
paragraphs: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their components to create useful products for human needs. It involves manipulating organisms, often at the genetic level, to improve crops, animals and processes. Modern work uses tools such as genetic engineering and tissue culture.

In agriculture, farmers grow pest-resistant crops that produce their own insecticides. Bt cotton, for example, is engineered to produce a bacterial toxin that kills bollworms. This reduces the need for frequent chemical sprays on large farms and protects yields.

Other improvements include crops resistant to viral and fungal diseases. Herbicide-tolerant varieties allow weeds to be controlled more efficiently without damaging the crop. Biofortification adds vital nutrients, such as vitamin A or iron, directly into staple foods.
bullets: Pest-resistant crops kill specific insects precisely with inbuilt Bt toxins.
Disease-resistant crops reduce losses from viruses and fungi.
Biofortified crops improve everyday nutrition through added vitamins and minerals.
content.takeaway: Biotechnology helps Nigerian farmers control pests, diseases and weeds while improving nutrition.

check.question: Which crop improvement is an example of biotechnology in agriculture?
check.why: Bt cotton uses genetic engineering to produce its own insecticide.

content.heading: Biotechnology in Medicine
paragraphs: Medicine has been transformed by vaccines produced using living cells and genetic techniques. These vaccines train the immune system to recognise dangerous pathogens safely. They protect communities against diseases that cannot be treated easily or swiftly.

Recombinant insulin is made by inserting the human gene for insulin into bacteria or yeast. The microbes multiply rapidly and produce large quantities of pure hormone for many people with diabetes. This replaced animal insulin and reduced allergic reactions.

Gene therapy introduces corrected genes into patients to treat inherited disorders. DNA-based diagnostic tests detect infections and genetic conditions quickly and accurately. Together, these advances offer more precise, personalised and affordable treatment for patients.
bullets: Vaccines can be produced more safely and cheaply using genetically modified organisms.
Recombinant insulin treats diabetes effectively without using animal sources.
Gene therapy and DNA tests improve early diagnosis and targeted treatment.
content.takeaway: Biotechnology in medicine produces safer vaccines, human insulin and targeted genetic treatments.

check.question: Which medicine is made by recombinant DNA technology?
check.why: Recombinant insulin is produced when yeast containing the human insulin gene multiplies.

content.heading: Pharmaceuticals, Food and Safety
paragraphs: The pharmaceutical industry uses biotechnology to produce antibiotics more reliably and cheaply. Microbes can be engineered to grow faster and yield much higher levels of effective medicine. Engineered enzymes also help manufacture many drugs and process various food ingredients.

Food production depends on fermentation by yeast and bacteria. These organisms produce beer, bread, yoghurt and cheese through controlled biological processes. Genetically modified foods may carry much improved flavour, nutrition or much longer storage life.

In Nigeria, biosafety rules aim to protect health and the environment from risks. Scientists must also consider ethical questions about modifying genes in foods and humans. Public awareness and regulation help ensure fully responsible use.
bullets: Antibiotic and enzyme production uses engineered microbes efficiently.
Fermentation improves food quality, flavour and shelf life.
Biosafety checks reduce risks to people and ecosystems.
content.takeaway: Biotechnology supports drug production and food processing, but safety and ethics must guide it.

check.question: Which product is made by engineered microbes in the pharmaceutical industry?
check.why: Engineered microbes produce antibiotics and enzymes reliably; bread, beer and yoghurt rely on fermentation.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In JAMB questions, match each product to its source: Bt cotton means pest resistance, recombinant insulin means medicine, and fermentation means food processing. Always read whether the question asks about benefit, risk, or process.

content.problem: A man in Ibadan needs daily human insulin, but animal insulin causes allergic reactions. How does biotechnology solve his problem?

steps.operation: Select recombinant insulin produced by modified yeast.
steps.reason: Yeast contains the human insulin gene and multiplies rapidly.
steps.result: Large quantities of human-identical insulin are made safely.

steps.operation: Replace animal insulin with this recombinant product.
steps.reason: Human insulin matches the body and reduces allergic reactions.
steps.result: The man receives effective, affordable treatment daily.

steps.operation: Control dose and monitor blood sugar regularly.
steps.reason: Proper management prevents dangerous highs and lows.
steps.result: Stable health and reduced complications are achieved.

content.heading: Go deeper: Biotechnology in agriculture
paragraphs: Agricultural biotechnology includes tissue culture, selection and genetic modification. A tissue-cultured yam is disease-free, a selected maize is drought-tolerant and a modified cotton resists bollworms. Each technique solves a different farm problem.

Tissue culture multiplies a plant from a small piece of tissue on a sterile medium. It can turn one disease-free mother plant into thousands of copies. That multiplication is why it is used for seed yam and banana.
A modified crop must still be tested for safety. Yield, allergenicity and environmental effect are therefore checked before release, which is why a new variety takes years to reach a farm.
A tissue-cultured yam is planted in sterile soil. That sterility is why it can be certified disease-free before it reaches a farm.
A selected maize that is drought-tolerant must be tested in dry years. That testing is why selection takes seasons rather than one harvest.
A tissue-cultured yam is planted in sterile soil. That sterility is why it can be certified disease-free before it reaches a farm.
A selected maize that is drought-tolerant must be tested in dry years. That testing is why selection takes seasons rather than one harvest.
bullets: Tissue culture: disease-free multiplication
Selection: drought and yield improvement
Modification: insect and disease resistance, tested before release

content.heading: Go deeper: Medicine, pharmaceuticals and the food industry
paragraphs: Medical biotechnology makes insulin, vaccines and diagnostics. Engineered microbes produce antibiotics and enzymes reliably at scale. That scale is why a drug that was once scarce is now available in quantity.

Food biotechnology uses fermentation and enzymes. Yeast ferments sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide in bread and beer, while enzymes improve the flavour and texture of food. Those processes are biotechnology without any genetic modification.
A pharmaceutical product must be pure and consistent. Engineered microbes give that consistency because each culture is identical, which is why a vat can make the same drug month after month.
A vaccine that is made in a fermenter must be purified before use. That purification is part of the cost of a pharmaceutical product.
An enzyme that is used in food must be food-grade. That grade is why an industrial enzyme cannot be used directly in bread.
A vaccine that is made in a fermenter must be purified before use. That purification is part of the cost of a pharmaceutical product.
bullets: Engineered microbes make antibiotics and enzymes
Yeast ferments sugar in bread and beer
Identical cultures give a consistent product

content.heading: Go deeper: Safety, ethics and the environment
paragraphs: Safety testing asks whether a new product can harm health or the environment. A gene that is transferred could move to a weed or could produce a new allergen. Those risks must be tested before release.
Ethical debate asks who owns a modified organism and who can afford it. If a seed is patented, a farmer who saves it may be in breach of that patent. That ownership therefore affects food security.
A decision must therefore weigh benefit against risk and against access. A crop that feeds many but is owned by few is not an unmixed good.
A gene that spreads to a weed cannot be recalled. That irreversibility is why a new crop is tested before release rather than after.
A crop that is patented cannot be saved for seed. That restriction is why a farmer who buys it must buy again each year.
A gene that spreads to a weed cannot be recalled. That irreversibility is why a new crop is tested before release rather than after.
bullets: Test for harm to health and environment
Patented seeds raise ownership and access questions
Weigh benefit against risk and access

hints: Think of Bt crops and insect toxins.
Consider yields, sprays and safety.

lessons.title: Lamarck's Theory of Evolution
lessons.objective: Explain Lamarck's ideas on use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characters, and the criticisms of his theory.

content.heading: Lamarck's Theory of Evolution
paragraphs: In Kano, a storyteller describes a giraffe stretching daily for high acacia leaves until its neck grows longer. Lamarck asked whether such effort could reshape the species forever.

content.heading: Lamarck's Core Ideas: Use and Disuse
paragraphs: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed that living organisms change because of use and disuse through regular effort in daily life. He argued that organs used frequently grow stronger, while those not used gradually weaken and shrink over time. This change happens during the lifetime of the individual through effort and habit.

Lamarck described this process as the inheritance of acquired characters in his writings. Characters gained through use or disuse were believed to pass directly to offspring during reproduction. The giraffe stretching for leaves was his most famous illustration of this idea in everyday nature.

A blacksmith who strengthens his arms through daily hammering provided a simple human example for students. Lamarck claimed that his sons would inherit stronger arms without any training. The theory therefore linked individual effort directly to evolutionary change in descendants over time.
bullets: Use strengthens organs and improves their function over time
Disuse causes organs to shrink and eventually disappear
Acquired changes pass to offspring through inheritance
content.takeaway: Lamarck said use and disuse create acquired characters passed to offspring.

check.question: According to Lamarck, why would a blacksmith's sons have stronger arms?
options: They trained with hammers from childhood
They inherited their father's strengthened arms
check.why: Lamarck believed characters acquired through use, such as stronger arms, were inherited directly by offspring.

content.heading: Criticisms of Lamarck's Theory
paragraphs: Critics argued that acquired characters are not inherited by offspring in repeated laboratory tests. Cutting off the tails of mice for many generations never produced tailless mice in later generations. The acquired change affected the body but did not alter the hereditary material passed on.

There was also lack of direct evidence supporting the inheritance of acquired traits in nature. Many acquired features such as muscle bulk or scars do not appear in descendants at all. Lamarck could not explain how the environment communicated specific changes to reproductive cells.

Experiments testing the theory therefore failed to support its central claim in every case. Animals subjected to repeated mutilation still produced normal offspring with complete features and tails. This showed that use, disuse and injury during life do not reshape heredity in the way Lamarck suggested.
bullets: Acquired characters such as extra muscle are not inherited
Tail-cutting experiments produced mice with normal tails
No evidence showed how effort changes reproductive material
content.takeaway: Criticisms show acquired changes during life are not inherited by offspring.

check.question: What did the tail-cutting mouse experiment show?
check.why: Despite many generations of tail cutting, offspring were born with normal tails, proving acquired injury is not inherited.

content.heading: Contributions, Limits and Neo-Lamarckism
paragraphs: Despite its errors, Lamarck's theory made an important historical contribution in the nineteenth century. He was among the first scientists to argue that species change gradually over time. He also highlighted the influence of the environment on living organisms during their lifetime.

Lamarck correctly emphasised adaptation through behaviour and organ use in daily life. His work encouraged other naturalists to study how organisms respond to their surroundings. These ideas helped prepare the ground for later theories based on natural selection.

Neo-Lamarckism is a modern attempt to revive parts of Lamarck's thinking using new genetics. It suggests that some acquired changes might be transmitted through epigenetic effects on gene expression. Most scientists still accept natural selection as the main mechanism, so neo-Lamarckism remains a minority view.
bullets: First to propose species change gradually over long periods
Linked adaptation to environment and organism behaviour
Neo-Lamarckism explores epigenetic transmission of acquired traits
content.takeaway: Lamarck inspired evolution studies, but his inheritance mechanism was incorrect.

check.question: What is Lamarck's lasting contribution to evolution?
options: He argued that species change gradually over time
He proposed inheritance of acquired characters
He discovered mutation as raw material
check.why: Lamarck first promoted gradual species change and environmental influence, even though his inheritance mechanism was later rejected.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In examinations, state Lamarck's two ideas separately before giving the giraffe example. Mention that acquired characters are not inherited, and link the tail-cutting experiment to this criticism clearly for full marks.

content.problem: A farmer in Zaria notices that well-fed goats grow larger than poorly fed goats. A student claims the larger goats will always produce larger offspring. What would Lamarck predict, and what is the correct explanation?

steps.reason: Larger size results from feeding during life
steps.result: Size is an acquired character

steps.reason: Lamarck claimed acquired characters are inherited
steps.result: Offspring would be larger without good feeding

steps.reason: Feeding does not alter hereditary material
