content.heading: Go deeper: Use and disuse in Lamarck's theory
paragraphs: Lamarck argued that organs develop by use and are lost by disuse. A giraffe that stretches its neck to feed therefore develops a longer neck, and a mole that never uses its eyes loses them. Use and disuse are the motors of change.

The second part of his theory is inheritance of acquired characters. A giraffe that stretched its neck passes the longer neck to its calves. That inheritance is what makes the change cumulative over generations.
Neo-Lamarckism keeps the idea that effort matters but replaces inheritance with other mechanisms. It is therefore distinct from Lamarck's own claim, even though it keeps his name.
A giraffe that stretches to feed therefore develops a longer neck in his view. That development is the engine of his theory, and inheritance is what makes it cumulative.
A mole that loses its eyes by disuse therefore has small eyes in Lamarck's view. That loss is the complement of the giraffe's gain.
A mole that loses its eyes by disuse therefore has small eyes in Lamarck's view. That loss is the complement of the giraffe's gain.
A giraffe that stretches its neck to feed therefore develops a longer neck in his view. That development is the engine of his theory.
bullets: Use develops organs; disuse loses them
Acquired characters are inherited by calves
Neo-Lamarckism keeps effort but changes the mechanism

content.heading: Go deeper: Why Lamarck's mechanism fails
paragraphs: An acquired character such as a stretched neck is not written into the gametes. Cutting the tail of a mouse does not produce tailless offspring, which is the classic test of the theory. That test therefore refutes inheritance of acquired characters.

Weismann proposed the germ-plasm theory to explain the failure. He argued that the germ cells are separate from the body cells, so changes in the body cannot reach them. That separation is why use cannot be inherited.
Genetics confirms Weismann. Variation is present in DNA before selection acts, so effort by the individual cannot create the variation that selection needs.
Weismann cut the tails of mice for twenty generations without producing a tailless offspring. That experiment is the classic test of the theory and its refutation.
Genetics shows that variation is present in DNA before selection acts. That presence is why effort by the individual cannot create the variation that selection needs.
Weismann cut the tails of mice for twenty generations without producing a tailless offspring. That experiment is the classic test of the theory and its refutation.
bullets: Cutting a mouse tail does not produce tailless offspring
Germ cells are separate from body cells
Variation is in DNA before selection acts

content.heading: Go deeper: What remains of Lamarck today
paragraphs: One part of Lamarck's insight survives: use changes the body during life. A blacksmith's arms are larger because they are used, and a mole's eyes are smaller because they are not. That change is real, but it is not inherited.
The distinction is therefore between development and inheritance. Development changes the individual, while inheritance changes the population. Lamarck joined them, and Darwin separated them.
Examiners test that separation. A question that asks why a giraffe's calves do not inherit its stretched neck is testing the failure of Lamarck, not its use.
A blacksmith's arms are larger because they are used. That change is real in the individual, but it cannot be passed to his children.
A child of a blacksmith does not inherit his arms. That is the test that separates development from inheritance.
A child of a blacksmith does not inherit his arms. That is the test that separates development from inheritance.
bullets: Use changes the body but is not inherited
Development changes the individual; inheritance changes the population
Lamarck joined them; Darwin separated them

content.question: A plant kept in darkness grows pale leaves. Will its seeds produce pale plants in sunlight? Explain using Lamarck's theory and the correct view.
hints: Think about acquired characters
Recall the tail-cutting experiment
Consider hereditary material in seeds

lessons.title: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection
lessons.objective: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection and distinguish it from Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters.

content.heading: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection
paragraphs: On a farm near Ibadan, more chicks hatch than survive to adulthood. Some grow faster and find food better. Darwin asked why only some survive and reproduce in each generation.

content.heading: Natural selection in a population
paragraphs: Darwin argued that organisms produce more offspring than can survive. This overproduction creates a struggle for existence for limited food, water and space, and not every individual survives to breed.

Within a population, individuals vary in size, colour and speed from birth. Some variations help an organism find food, hide from predators or resist disease, so those individuals are more likely to reach breeding age.
The environment therefore selects the individuals best suited to it, a process Darwin called natural selection. He saw this in Galápagos finches whose beaks matched their available food.
bullets: Overproduction creates competition for limited resources
Variation gives some individuals a survival advantage
Inherited traits that aid survival become more common over time
content.takeaway: Natural selection favours advantageous variation over many generations.

check.question: Why do finches with different beaks illustrate natural selection?
options: Beaks changed through use during life
Birds inherited beaks acquired by stretching
Beaks suited to their food aided survival
Isolated finches planned new beak shapes
check.why: Finches with beaks suited to their food survived and reproduced better, so those beak shapes spread through the population.

content.heading: Selection in action: finches and moths
paragraphs: Darwin drew his evidence from nature, not only from the laboratory. On the Galápagos Islands, finches on different islands had beaks suited to different food supplies, from crushing large seeds to probing for insects.

In Britain, soot from factories darkened the trees during the industrial age. Birds easily spotted the light peppered moths, so the dark form survived and became commoner; when the air was cleaned, the light form recovered.
Both cases show that selection works on variation already present. It does not create the helpful feature from nothing; it preserves the type that happens to survive and breed.
bullets: Galápagos finches: beak shape matches available food
Industrial moths: camouflage changed with the sooty environment
Selection preserves useful variants; it does not create them on demand
content.takeaway: Darwin's evidence shows selection acting on existing variation.

check.question: Which observation best supports natural selection?
options: All finches on every island look identical
Dark moths survived and bred more on soot-darkened trees
Moths changed colour because they tried to match the soot
Every bird disappeared after factories opened
check.why: Dark moths were better camouflaged, so they survived and reproduced more, and their numbers rose in that environment.

content.heading: Darwin versus Lamarck
paragraphs: Lamarck claimed that organisms inherit characters acquired through use and disuse during life. Darwin claimed that variation exists first, and the environment selects the individuals best able to survive and reproduce.
In Lamarck's view, stretching gives giraffes longer necks that their calves inherit. In Darwin's view, giraffes born with slightly longer necks fed better and left more calves.

The key difference is the source of variation: Lamarck favoured effort by the individual, Darwin favoured pre-existing variation selected by the environment. Genetic evidence supports Darwin; acquired characters are not passed to offspring.
bullets: Lamarck: acquired characters are inherited
Darwin: existing variation is selected by the environment
Genetic evidence supports Darwin's mechanism
content.takeaway: Darwin relies on selected variation, not acquired inheritance.

check.question: How does Darwin explain long giraffe necks?
options: Giraffes stretched until their necks grew
Longer necks were inherited after stretching
Long-necked giraffes survived and bred more
Leaves directed genes to lengthen the neck
check.why: Variation in neck length already existed; longer necks gave better access to food and led to more offspring.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For comparisons, learn one sentence per theory before the examples. State variation first for Darwin and use-and-disuse for Lamarck; add genes and mutation only when the question asks for the modern theory, so the two never blur.

content.problem: In an acacia grove near Kano, giraffes vary in neck length. During the dry season, leaves are only high in the trees. Explain, in Darwin's terms, how neck length changes in the population over generations.

steps.reason: Individuals differ in traits such as neck length
steps.result: Some giraffes are longer-necked than others

steps.reason: High leaves are scarce in the dry season
steps.result: Long-necked giraffes reach more food and avoid starvation

steps.reason: Better-fed individuals are more likely to breed
steps.result: Long necks are passed to more offspring

steps.reason: Advantageous alleles increase each generation
steps.result: Longer necks become commoner over many generations

content.heading: Go deeper: Overproduction and the struggle for existence
paragraphs: Darwin argued that organisms produce more offspring than can survive. That overproduction creates a struggle for existence for limited food, water and space. Only some individuals survive to reproduce in each season.

The struggle is not a fight to the death. It is a competition for resources in which the better adapted are more likely to survive. A finch that finds food is not fighting another finch, yet it is struggling.
Overproduction is therefore the starting point. Without it there would be no selection, because every individual would survive and every trait would be passed on equally.
A dandelion that makes ten thousand seeds overproduces because only a few can germinate. That excess is the struggle in a plant.
A locust that lays a hundred eggs overproduces because only a few can survive. That excess is the struggle in an insect.
A dandelion that makes ten thousand seeds overproduces because only a few can germinate. That excess is the struggle in a plant.
bullets: Overproduction creates a struggle for limited resources
Struggle is competition for resources, not only fighting
Without overproduction there would be no selection

content.heading: Go deeper: Variation and survival of the fittest
paragraphs: Within a population, individuals vary in size, colour and speed from birth. Some variations help an organism feed, hide or escape predators. Those advantageous features increase the chance of survival and reproduction.

Survival of the fittest means survival of the best adapted, not the strongest. A moth that matches the background is fit for its habitat, while a larger moth that does not match is less fit. Fitness is therefore a match to the environment.
The environment therefore selects, but it does not create. Variation is present first, and selection preserves the advantageous variants. That order is the core of Darwin's theory.
A dark moth in a sooty wood is fit for that wood. The same moth in a clean wood is less fit, which is why fitness is a match and not a size.
A plant that is resistant to a disease is fit for that disease. The same plant in a disease-free place gains no advantage from its resistance.
A dark moth in a sooty wood is fit for that wood. The same moth in a clean wood is less fit, which is why fitness is a match and not a size.
bullets: Variation is present from birth
Fit means best adapted, not strongest
Selection preserves; it does not create

content.heading: Go deeper: Darwin versus Lamarck in one comparison
paragraphs: Lamarck claimed that organisms inherit characters acquired through use and disuse. Darwin claimed that variation exists first and the environment selects those best able to survive and reproduce. The two theories differ in the source of variation.

A giraffe that stretches its neck does not pass the stretch to its calf in Darwin's view. A giraffe born with a slightly longer neck feeds better and leaves more calves. One emphasises effort, the other emphasises selection.
Modern genetics supports Darwin. Acquired characters are not passed through gametes, while inherited variation is. That difference is why Lamarck's theory is rejected in examinations.
A calf that inherits a longer neck has not inherited the stretch. It has inherited a variation that selection preserved, which is the opposite order.
A mutation that improves survival is preserved by selection. That preservation is the modern addition to Darwin, not Lamarck's effort.
A mutation that improves survival is preserved by selection. That preservation is the modern addition to Darwin, not Lamarck's effort.
bullets: Lamarck: effort creates variation that is inherited
Darwin: variation exists first; environment selects
Genetics supports Darwin

content.question: Antibiotic-killing drugs are introduced in a hospital. Bacteria vary in resistance. Predict which bacteria survive and explain the process in Darwin's terms.
hints: Think about variation first
Recall the struggle for existence
Consider what survivors pass on

lessons.title: The Organic Theory of Evolution
lessons.objective: Explain how the organic theory combines natural selection with genetics and mutation to explain diversity and the origin of new species.

content.heading: The Organic Theory of Evolution
paragraphs: In a Lagos hospital, one antibiotic kills most bacteria but not every one. The few survivors multiply, and selection starts from them. The organic theory explains how such small inherited differences spread through a population.

content.heading: Selection acts on inherited variation
paragraphs: Darwin himself could not fully explain where variation first came from. The organic theory, also called the modern synthesis, fills that gap with genetics. Genes carry the hereditary information that determines traits such as beak shape and wing colour.

Variation within a population is caused both by genes and by environment. Only inherited variation passes to offspring, so only genetic differences can drive long-term evolution; environmental marks such as scars do not.

Selection favours alleles that improve survival or breeding success, such as resistance to disease or drought. Over generations, those alleles become more common and the whole population adapts to its environment.
bullets: Genes carry the information for inherited traits in every cell
Only inherited variation can drive long-term change in populations
Selection spreads favourable alleles through a population over generations
content.takeaway: Selection operates on inherited genetic variation.

check.question: Why is inherited variation essential for evolution?
options: It lets every organism survive equally
Only inherited differences can build up over generations
It removes all need for selection
It guarantees every mutation is useful
check.why: Acquired differences disappear with the individual; only genetic differences persist and accumulate across generations.

content.heading: Mutation supplies the raw material
paragraphs: Mutations are random changes in DNA. Most recognised mutations are neutral or harmful, while only a few improve survival. Mutation is the only source of entirely new alleles and can occur without any warning or cause.

Crossing over during meiosis and random union of gametes reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations. By themselves they do not create new alleles; they only mix the combinations already available in individuals.
Selection does not invent useful traits to order. It preserves the rare variants that mutation and reshuffling have already produced in the population.
bullets: Mutation creates new alleles at random in DNA of individuals
Crossing over and fertilisation reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations
Selection preserves useful variants; it does not create them on demand
content.takeaway: Mutation, not effort, supplies new genetic material.

check.question: Which process creates entirely new alleles?
check.why: Crossing over and fertilisation reshuffle existing alleles; only mutation can produce alleles that did not exist before.

content.heading: From variation to new species
paragraphs: Over many generations, small adaptive differences accumulate. If populations become geographically isolated by rivers, mountains or islands, they face different selection pressures and accumulate different alleles.

If the isolated groups remain separated long enough, they will no longer interbreed successfully even when brought together. At that point they are reproductively isolated, and each is a separate species.
This explains the great variety of organisms adapted to different habitats and regions throughout the world, and it unites Darwin's selection with modern genetics under one theory.
bullets: Small adaptive differences accumulate steadily over many generations
Geographic isolation lets separate populations diverge from each other
Reproductive isolation defines new species as separate reproductive communities
content.takeaway: Species form when isolated populations can no longer interbreed.

check.question: What most directly produces a new species?
options: Geographic isolation and divergence until reproduction fails
Use and disuse of body parts
check.why: Isolation allows different selection pressures to act, and reproductive isolation is the boundary between species.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When the question names the organic theory, put genes and mutation at the start of your answer. Say selection acts on inherited variation, mutation supplies new alleles, and accumulated differences can produce new species; this order covers the marking points.

content.problem: A doctor prescribes the same antibiotic repeatedly in a Kano hospital. Some bacteria carry a resistance gene, while others do not. Explain, step by step, how the resistant strain becomes dominant in the hospital.

steps.reason: Some bacteria carry a resistance gene by mutation
steps.result: A few resistant individuals are present

steps.reason: The antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria
steps.result: Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce

steps.reason: Survivors pass the resistance allele on
steps.result: The resistant allele increases in frequency

steps.reason: Repeated exposure amplifies selection
steps.result: The resistant strain becomes dominant in the hospital

content.heading: Go deeper: Why Darwin needed genetics
paragraphs: Darwin could not explain where variation came from. He knew that traits were inherited, but he did not know how. That gap was filled by the modern synthesis, which joined selection to genetics.
Genes carry hereditary information in DNA. Selection acts on differences caused by those genes in the population. The environment therefore selects, but genes supply the differences on which it acts.
Without that supply, selection would have nothing to act on in the next generation. Genetics therefore completed Darwin rather than replacing him.
A trait that is inherited must be carried by a material that can be copied. That material is DNA, which is why genetics completed Darwin.
A gene that codes for a protein can mutate to a new allele. That new allele is therefore the raw material that selection acts on.
A gene that codes for a protein can mutate to a new allele. That new allele is therefore the raw material that selection acts on.
Genes carry hereditary information in DNA. Selection acts on differences caused by those genes in the population.
bullets: Darwin lacked a mechanism for variation
Genes supply the differences selection needs
The synthesis completed Darwin

content.heading: Go deeper: Mutation, reshuffling and the new allele
paragraphs: Mutation creates new alleles at random. Most are neutral or harmful, and a few improve survival. That randomness is why mutation cannot be directed by need.

Crossing over and random union of gametes reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations. Those processes increase variation without creating new alleles. They therefore amplify the raw material that mutation supplies.
Selection preserves the rare variants that those processes have produced. It does not invent a useful trait to order, which is why evolution cannot be directed by an organism's effort.
A mutation that changes a gene can be harmful, neutral or useful. Only the useful ones are preserved, which is why most mutations disappear.
A new allele that is useful will spread if it is inherited. That spread is selection, while the appearance of the allele was mutation.
A mutation that changes a gene can be harmful, neutral or useful. Only the useful ones are preserved, which is why most mutations disappear.
A new allele that is useful will spread if it is inherited. That spread is selection, while the appearance of the allele was mutation.
bullets: Mutation creates new alleles at random
Crossing over and fertilisation reshuffle existing alleles
Selection preserves; it does not invent

content.heading: Go deeper: Speciation and the meaning of a species
paragraphs: Over many generations, small adaptive differences accumulate. If populations become geographically isolated, they face different selection pressures and accumulate different alleles.

If the isolated groups remain separated long enough, they will no longer interbreed successfully even when brought together. At that point they are reproductively isolated, and each is a separate species.
Speciation is therefore the end of divergence. It needs isolation, time and accumulated differences, which is why it is slow and why fossils show change over long periods.
A species is therefore a reproductive community, not a body type. Two populations that can no longer interbreed are different species however similar they look.
Two populations that cannot interbreed are different species. That test is reproductive, not anatomical, which is why it is decisive.
Two populations that cannot interbreed are different species. That test is reproductive, not anatomical, which is why it is decisive.
A species is therefore a reproductive community, not a body type. Two populations that cannot interbreed are different species however similar they look.
bullets: Isolation lets populations diverge
Reproductive isolation defines new species
Speciation needs isolation, time and accumulated differences

content.question: Some locusts survive insecticide spraying on a farm in Kebbi. Explain in terms of variation, selection and generations why the insecticide becomes less effective.
hints: Think about variation in resistance first
Identify what the spray acts on
Ask who survives and passes on the allele

lessons.title: Fossil Evidence for Evolution
lessons.objective: Describe fossils and the rock record as evidence for evolution, and interpret transitional fossils such as Archaeopteryx and Tiktaalik.

content.heading: Fossil Evidence for Evolution
paragraphs: At the museum in Lagos, a student compares a fish fossil with a modern lizard. Their bones share surprising similarities despite different appearances. The fossil record preserves that chain of change through deep time.

content.heading: Fossils and the rock record
paragraphs: Fossils are remains of ancient organisms preserved in rock over millions of years. Lower rock layers contain older fossils, while higher layers contain younger ones that lived later. The rock record can therefore be read like pages of a history book by geologists.
Rock layers allow relative dating: the order of fossils can be read without knowing their exact age in years. This sequence shows that life existed in the past and changed over time.
bullets: Fossils preserve past life in rock layers over long periods of time
Lower layers are older; higher layers are younger in the sequence
Rock layers allow relative dating of fossils without exact years
content.takeaway: Fossils show that life changed over time.

check.question: Which fossil is most likely the oldest?
options: One found in a lower rock layer
One found in a higher rock layer
One found on an exposed surface
check.why: Lower layers were laid down first, so fossils there are older than those in higher layers.

content.heading: Transitional fossils
paragraphs: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird, but teeth and claws like a reptile. It is regarded as a link between dinosaurs and birds.

Tiktaalik had fish fins with limb-like bones that could support its body in shallow water. It was an early step towards life on land, showing fins preparing to act as limbs for walking in shallow water.
Such transitional fossils are rare but powerful. They combine features of groups that descended from one another over long periods and show change as a series of small steps.
bullets: Archaeopteryx links dinosaurs with birds through mixed features
Tiktaalik links fins with limb-like bones for support
Transitional fossils show gradual change between major groups
content.takeaway: Transitional fossils link one group to another.

check.question: Why is Archaeopteryx important evidence for evolution?
options: It had feathers and reptile teeth
check.why: Archaeopteryx combines bird feathers and wings with reptile teeth and claws, linking dinosaurs to birds.

content.heading: The horse fossil series
paragraphs: The horse fossil series shows changes in size, teeth and feet over time. It is a branching tree, not a single straight line from small to large.
Different rock layers preserve different species along related branches. Later layers contain larger, single-toed horses with high-crowned teeth suited to grazing on grass.
The pattern supports descent with modification from common ancestors over long periods, with new features accumulating gradually rather than appearing all at once in a single leap.
bullets: Horse fossils show changes in size, teeth and feet over time
The record branches widely rather than forming a straight ladder
Later layers contain more derived species with specialised grazing teeth
content.takeaway: The fossil record shows branching descent over deep time.

check.question: How should the horse fossil series be interpreted?
options: A single straight line from small to large
A branching record of related species
A random set of unrelated fossils
Proof that modern horses appeared unchanged
check.why: The horse record shows related branches with different adaptations, not one unbranched lineage from small to large.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn one example per claim: fossil for the rock record, Archaeopteryx for transitional forms, the horse series for branching descent. When asked to date fossils, name the rock-layer order and avoid drawing evolution as a straight line.

content.problem: A student in Jos finds three fossil layers: shellfish lowest, reptile-like bones in the middle, and a mammal skull highest. What does the sequence suggest, and which layer is oldest?

steps.operation: Arrange the layers from oldest to youngest
steps.reason: Lower rock layers were laid down first
steps.result: Oldest is the shellfish layer; youngest is the mammal layer

steps.reason: Shellfish, reptile-like bones and mammals are different stages of vertebrate life
steps.result: The sequence shows aquatic life, then reptile-like forms, then mammals

steps.reason: Later layers reflect accumulated changes
steps.result: The sequence supports gradual change over deep time

steps.reason: Fossils match related groups appearing in order
steps.result: Life became more complex step by step, not in single leaps

content.heading: Go deeper: Fossils and the order of rock layers
paragraphs: Fossils are remains of organisms preserved in rock over millions of years. Lower layers are older than higher layers, so the sequence can be arranged from the past to the present. That order is relative dating.
A transitional fossil combines features of two groups. Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird but teeth and claws like a reptile. It is therefore a link between dinosaurs and birds.
The horse fossil series shows changes in size, teeth and feet over time. It is a branching tree, not a single straight line, so it supports descent with modification from common ancestors.
A fossil that is found in a lower layer is older than one that is found in a higher layer. That order is the relative dating that the rock record provides.
A transitional fossil that combines two groups is evidence of descent. Archaeopteryx therefore supports evolution because it is a link, not because it is old.
A fossil that is found in a lower layer is older than one that is found in a higher layer. That order is the relative dating that the rock record provides.
A transitional fossil that combines two groups is evidence of descent. Archaeopteryx therefore supports evolution because it is a link, not because it is old.
bullets: Lower layers are older; higher layers younger
Archaeopteryx links dinosaurs with birds
Horse series is a branching tree

content.heading: Go deeper: Homologous and analogous structures
paragraphs: Homologous structures share the same bone plan but serve different functions. The pentadactyl limb in humans, bats and whales is homologous because the bones are arranged alike.
Analogous structures perform the same function but have different plans. Bird wings and insect wings both allow flight but developed from separate ancestors. That similarity is convergent evolution.
Embryology adds the same conclusion. Human embryos develop pharyngeal arches like other vertebrates, which reflects a shared developmental program inherited from a common ancestor.
A bat wing and a whale flipper share the same bones. That sharing is the homology, while their different uses are the divergence.
A pentadactyl limb that is modified for flight is still pentadactyl. That persistence is why the limb is evidence even when the function has changed.
A bat wing and a whale flipper share the same bones. That sharing is the homology, while their different uses are the divergence.
A bat wing and a whale flipper share the same bones. That sharing is the homology, while their different uses are the divergence.
bullets: Homologous: same plan, different functions
Analogous: same function, different plans
Pharyngeal arches reflect a shared program

content.heading: Go deeper: Biogeography, vestigial organs and DNA
paragraphs: Biogeography studies where species live and why. Marsupials are diverse in Australia because long isolation let them radiate from common ancestors. That distribution is a map of ancient geography.
Vestigial organs are reduced structures that have lost most of their ancestral function. The human appendix and whale pelvic bones suggest that ancestors had larger, functional versions.
DNA and protein sequences place species on evolutionary trees. Humans share more DNA with chimpanzees than with dogs, so molecular trees confirm the fossil and anatomical ones.
A marsupial that lives in Australia is confined by its history. That confinement is biogeography, not a preference for a climate.
A marsupial that radiates in Australia fills the many niches in practice of placentals elsewhere. That radiation is therefore a record of adaptive evolution after isolation.
A marsupial that radiates in Australia fills the niches of placentals elsewhere. That radiation is therefore a record of adaptive evolution after isolation.
bullets: Australia's marsupials show radiation after isolation
Appendix and pelvic bones point to larger ancestors
DNA confirms fossil and anatomical trees

content.question: A fossil fish with limb-like fins was found in rock older than the first land animals. What does it suggest about the origin of land vertebrates, and what is it an example of?
hints: Think of Tiktaalik and shallow water
Name the feature that links fins to limbs
Describe it as a link between two groups

lessons.title: Comparative Anatomy and Embryology
lessons.objective: Distinguish homologous from analogous structures and explain how embryological similarity supports common ancestry.

content.heading: Comparative Anatomy and Embryology
paragraphs: A frog, a lizard and a human all begin as embryos with a tail. At the museum, their adult skeletons look different but share clear patterns. Comparing those patterns reveals their common ancestry.

content.heading: Homologous structures
paragraphs: Comparative anatomy studies similarities in body structure among different living species. Homologous structures share the same basic plan but serve different functions in daily life.

The pentadactyl limb in humans, bats and whales has the same bone arrangement despite being used for arms, wings and flippers. The common plan is best explained by descent from a common ancestor that had that plan.
The more closely related two species are, the more features they usually share now. Homologous organs therefore help scientists build evolutionary trees.
bullets: Homologous: same basic plan, different functions in organisms
Pentadactyl limb: arm, wing and flipper share the same bones
Common plan supports common ancestry in evolutionary history
content.takeaway: Homologous organs share a plan from common ancestry.

check.question: Human, bat and whale forelimbs are homologous because they
check.why: Homologous structures share the same basic bone pattern from a common ancestor, despite different functions.

content.heading: Analogous structures
paragraphs: Analogous structures perform the same function but have entirely different basic plans. Bird wings and insect wings both allow powered flight, but they developed from separate ancestral structures over time.
Similar needs in similar environments can independently produce similar features, a process called convergent evolution. Analogous similarity therefore points to similar demands, not common ancestry.
Whales and fish are both streamlined for swimming in water, yet their internal structures are very different. Their resemblance is ecological and convergent, not inherited from a common ancestor.
bullets: Analogous: same function, different basic plans in organisms
Bird and insect wings complete flight by different routes
Convergent evolution explains the similarity between unrelated species
content.takeaway: Analogous organs fit the same job, not the same ancestor.

check.question: Which pair is analogous?
check.why: Bird and insect wings both permit flight but evolved from different structures; they are similar because of function, not ancestry.

content.heading: Embryology
paragraphs: Embryos of different vertebrate animals look surprisingly alike very early in development. Human embryos briefly form pharyngeal arches, similar to those of other vertebrates, before many of them become different adult structures in later growth.
All vertebrates pass through a stage with pharyngeal arches, even though they later become different adult structures. This shared stage points to a shared vertebrate ancestor.
The shared stages reflect a common developmental program inherited from a common ancestor. The earlier the stage examined, the more universal the similarity remains among all vertebrates.
bullets: Early vertebrate embryos look remarkably alike in early stages
Pharyngeal arches appear in all vertebrate embryos early in development
Shared developmental stages suggest shared common ancestry among vertebrates
content.takeaway: Similar embryos support common ancestry.

check.question: Why do fish, frogs, birds and humans all develop pharyngeal arches?
options: They all breathe through gills forever
Embryos try out every body plan
Pharyngeal arches serve no function in any vertebrate
check.why: The arches reflect a shared developmental program inherited from the common vertebrate ancestor.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Classify first: same plan but different function is homologous; same function but different plan is analogous. Then remember the pharyngeal-arch rule: if embryos share it, the ancestry is shared. Analogous structures point to convergent evolution, not descent.

content.problem: A student in Enugu compares the forelimb bones of a human, a bat wing and a whale flipper. All have the same bone arrangement but different functions. Classify the structures and state the evolutionary conclusion.

steps.reason: Same arrangement suggests descent from a common ancestor
steps.result: The structures are homologous

steps.reason: Analogous means same function, different plan
steps.result: These limbs share the plan but differ in function

steps.reason: A shared plan is best explained by common descent
steps.result: Humans, bats and whales inherited the pentadactyl plan from an ancestor

steps.reason: Different environments favour different uses
steps.result: The same ancestral plan was modified for arm, wing and flipper

content.heading: Go deeper: Homologous organs and the pentadactyl limb
paragraphs: The pentadactyl limb in humans, bats and whales has the same bone arrangement despite different uses. The humerus, radius, ulna and carpals appear in the same order. That order is the homology.
The same order appears in a mole's digging limb and a horse's running leg. The function has changed, but the plan has not. That persistence is why the limb is evidence for common ancestry.
An analogous structure such as a bird wing and an insect wing lacks that shared order. Its similarity is therefore function, not ancestry.
A mole's digging limb and a horse's running leg share the same bones. That sharing is why they are homologous despite their different uses.
A whale flipper that is modified for swimming is still pentadactyl. That persistence is why it is homologous to a human arm.
A mole's digging limb and a horse's running leg share the same bones. That sharing is why they are homologous despite their different uses.
bullets: Pentadactyl limb: same bones in the same order
Mole and horse share the plan without sharing the function
Bird and insect wings lack that shared order

content.heading: Go deeper: Analogous structures and convergence
paragraphs: Analogous structures evolve independently in different ancestors. A whale and a fish are both streamlined for swimming, yet their internal structures are very different. That resemblance is ecological, not inherited.
Convergent evolution produces that resemblance because the same environment favours the same form. A dolphin and a shark therefore look alike without being closely related.
The test is therefore anatomy, not appearance. A homologous structure shares a plan, while an analogous one shares only a function.
A shark and a dolphin look alike because water favours that shape. That resemblance is convergence, not close relation.
A dolphin and a shark combine the same shape independently. That independent origin is why they are analogous and not homologous.
A whale and a fish are both streamlined for swimming, yet their internal structures are very different. That resemblance is ecological, not inherited.
A dolphin and a shark combine the same shape independently. That independent origin is why they are analogous and not homologous.
bullets: Whale and fish: streamlined without close relation
Convergence favours the same form in the same environment
Anatomy, not appearance, decides homology

content.heading: Go deeper: Embryology and the pharyngeal arches
paragraphs: Embryos of vertebrates look alike early in development. A human embryo forms pharyngeal arches that look like gill supports, even though they never become gills. That stage is inherited from a common ancestor.

The arches later become jaws, ears and throat structures in mammals. The same developmental program therefore produces different adult structures in different species. That reuse is the embryological evidence.

Haeckel's overstated drawings are not evidence. Modern embryology shows similarity without claiming that an embryo repeats its ancestors in detail. The similarity is in the program, not in the adult form.
A human embryo that forms pharyngeal arches does not breathe through them. Those arches become jaws and ears, which is why they are evidence of a shared program.
A human embryo that forms a tail does not keep it. That tail is a remnant of a shared program, not a sign of a recent ancestor.

bullets: Early vertebrate embryos look alike

lessons.title: Biogeography, Vestigial Organs and DNA
lessons.objective: Explain how species distribution, vestigial organs and DNA similarity provide evidence for evolution.

content.heading: Biogeography, Vestigial Organs and DNA
paragraphs: A student in Enugu notices that marsupials are found only in Australia and South America. Distribution, leftover organs and genetic fingerprints all tell the same evolutionary story.

content.heading: Biogeography
paragraphs: Biogeography is the study of where species live and why. Closely related species are usually found in the same or neighbouring regions of continents, reflecting a shared evolutionary history.

Australia's long isolation allowed marsupials to radiate into many forms from a common ancestor, filling habitats that placental mammals fill elsewhere. Marsupials also occur in South America, showing the same ancient lineage was once widespread.
When the southern landmasses separated, these populations faced different climates and new enemies. Their modern distribution is therefore a map of ancient geography today.
bullets: Related species live near each other in neighbouring regions
Australia's marsupials show adaptive radiation into many habitats
South America's marsupials show old southern lineages
content.takeaway: Distribution records where descent and isolation occurred.

check.question: Why are marsupials diverse in Australia?
options: They recently crossed the ocean there
Long isolation allowed them to radiate from common ancestors
They were placed there by humans
They have no other place to live
check.why: Australia's isolation let marsupials diversify into many niches from shared ancestors.

content.heading: Vestigial organs
paragraphs: Vestigial organs are reduced structures that have lost most of their ancestral function. The human appendix still contains lymphoid tissue, so it is much reduced rather than completely useless. Whale pelvic bones are another example.
Such organs indicate that ancestors had larger, functional versions. Because reduction is simpler than sudden creation, lost and shrunken structures are the usual form of vestigial organs.
The coccyx, a reduced tailbone, remains in humans long after tails disappeared from our ancestors. Its tiny size shows it is a left-over remnant, not a working organ.
bullets: Vestigial: reduced, not completely useless in the body
Human appendix and whale pelvic bones are examples
They point to larger ancestral versions in history
content.takeaway: Vestigial organs are leftovers of former functions.

check.question: What do the tiny pelvic bones in whales suggest?
check.why: Pelvic bones are a vestigial remnant of the hind limbs of whale ancestors that walked on land.

content.heading: DNA and proteins
paragraphs: DNA and protein sequences place species on evolutionary trees. Humans share more DNA sequences with chimpanzees than with dogs, and the closest relatives share the most sequence.
Antibiotic-resistant bacteria also show evolution in action, with selection rapidly favouring resistant strains in hospitals and their numbers rising each generation under selection.

Protein sequences give the same pattern, because the more similar two proteins are, the more recent their shared ancestry is likely to be. Molecular trees and fossil trees agree on the major relationships.
bullets: DNA and protein sequence comparisons show relatedness between species
Humans share more DNA with chimpanzees than with dogs or mice
Antibiotic resistance shows rapid evolution in hospitals and clinics
content.takeaway: Molecular evidence maps evolutionary relationships.

check.question: Which evidence best shows that humans are closely related to chimpanzees?
check.why: DNA sequence comparisons show humans and chimpanzees share more of their genome than either does with more distant relatives.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn one example per evidence type: fossils for deep time, homologous structures for common ancestry, marsupials for distribution, pelvic bones for vestigial organs and DNA for relatedness. Never call vestigial organs useless; they are reduced, not nothing.

content.problem: A student in Enugu compares DNA sequences from human, chimpanzee, dog and mouse. Humans share 98% with chimpanzees, 84% with dogs and 78% with mice. Rank the relatedness and explain what the numbers show.

steps.reason: Higher percentage means closer relationship
steps.result: Chimpanzee is closest, dog is next, mouse is furthest

steps.reason: Shared DNA was inherited from common ancestors
steps.result: A nearer ancestor was shared with the chimpanzee

steps.reason: Descent branches at different times
steps.result: Humans and chimpanzees diverged most recently; mice diverged earliest

steps.reason: Sequence comparison measures descent
steps.result: Molecular data supports common ancestry in an evolutionary tree

content.heading: Go deeper: Distribution and the ancient southern continents
paragraphs: Marsupials are diverse in Australia and also occur in South America, but are absent as native animals in most other regions. Australia's long isolation allowed its marsupials to radiate into many forms.
That distribution records the breakup of Gondwana. When the southern landmasses separated, marsupial populations were carried with them. Their modern range is therefore a map of that breakup.
Bats and rodents also reached Australia, so marsupials are not the only mammals there. The radiation of marsupials happened despite those arrivals, which makes it stronger evidence.
A marsupial that lives in South America is the other half of the distribution. That half shows that the lineage was once widespread across the south.
A continent that has separated can carry a lineage with it. That carrying is why the distribution of marsupials maps the breakup of Gondwana.

A continent that has separated can carry a lineage with it. That carrying is why the distribution of marsupials maps the breakup of Gondwana.
bullets: Marsupials: Australia and South America
Distribution maps the breakup of Gondwana

content.heading: Go deeper: Vestigial organs and what they hint at
paragraphs: Vestigial organs are reduced structures that have lost most of their ancestral function. The human appendix still contains lymphoid tissue, so it is much reduced rather than completely useless.
Whale pelvic bones are another example. They are not attached to the spine and do not support the flippers, yet they are the remains of hind limbs. That absence of function is the hint.
The coccyx is a reduced tailbone in humans. Its tiny size shows it is a left-over remnant, not a working organ. Each example therefore points to a larger ancestral version.
A whale that has pelvic bones is descended from a land mammal. That descent is the hint, because the bones have no present function.
A human appendix that is reduced still contains lymphoid tissue. That tissue is why it is not useless, but its size shows the reduction.

bullets: Appendix: reduced lymphoid tissue, not useless
Whale pelvic bones: remains of hind limbs
Coccyx: reduced tailbone in humans

content.heading: Go deeper: DNA, proteins and the tree of life
paragraphs: DNA and protein sequences place species on evolutionary trees. Humans share more DNA sequences with chimpanzees than with dogs, and the closest relatives share the most sequence.
Antibiotic-resistant bacteria also show evolution in action, with selection rapidly favouring resistant strains in hospitals. That resistance arises by mutation and spreads by selection.
Protein sequences give the same pattern. The more similar two proteins are, the more recent their shared ancestry is likely to be. Molecular trees and fossil trees therefore agree.
A protein that is similar in two species was inherited from a common ancestor in the past. That similarity therefore measures how long ago they shared it.
A protein that is shared between two species was inherited from a common ancestor. That inheritance is why similarity measures recency.
A protein that is similar in two species was inherited from a common ancestor. That inheritance is why similarity measures recency.
bullets: Humans share more DNA with chimpanzees than with dogs
Antibiotic resistance shows rapid evolution in hospitals
Protein similarity measures recency of ancestry
